en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Single Chapter of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
The Introduction to the Work:
I pay homage to the Protector, the abode of compassion and infinite knowledge, who has conquered the five Māras.
The pure Dhamma, which is the cause for the destruction of existence,
and the supreme Saṅgha, by whom all evil has been destroyed—
to that Great Elder Kassapa, the leader of the Saṅgha.
On the island of Tambapaṇṇi, he was one who caused the rising of the Dispensation;
dependent upon right practice, always dwelling in the forest,
he was as renowned within the Teaching as the orb of the moon in the sky.
I pay homage to the father of the Saṅgha, who is highly proficient in the Vinaya;
relying upon him, I dwell and have attained growth within the Teaching.
I pay homage to the venerable elder Sumedha, of great wisdom and renowned for his learning.

I bow my head in reverence to the wise Gaṇavācaka, my teacher, who has attained the arising of pure qualities such as unbroken virtue, who is deeply learned, mindful, self-controlled, peaceful, and concentrated.
In whom the teaching is well-established among his resident monks— those who have mastered the traditional scriptures and logic, and who are experts in the methods of grammar;
he who was the wise and illustrious Lord of Siṃhala.
Of lofty wisdom and subtle skill in the arts,
born into the pure lineage of the sun and moon,
he was possessed of great strength and wondrously radiant power.
Having conquered the host of enemies, so difficult to subdue,
by means of valor not shared by others,
he attained consecration and became a follower of the Victor’s Dhamma.
Having gained full confidence in the Triple Gem,
and having thoroughly subdued the adversaries during the long period when the Conqueror’s teaching was divided, he restored it.
He caused the monks of pure virtue to drink the praised essence of harmony, as if it were nectar;
and having constructed vast and delightful monasteries, he provided for them.
There, for a very long time, he satisfied this entire assembly of one thousand monks without exception with the four requisites, keeping them unbroken.
Desiring the growth of the true Dhamma,
he himself instructed the bhikkhus,
enjoining them to the study of the scriptures and to insight meditation.
He caused the growth of the Victor’s dispensation.
Therefore, I am exceedingly favored by him through a kindness that is not shared with others.
Since he was requested by him whose arms are called "exerted" in the midst of the assembly of monks,
therefore [I shall explain] the meaning of these words that are not obvious.
Relying on the power of the ancient masters,
I shall fully demonstrate this excellent commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya so that it may be easily understood.
Commentary on the Introduction to the Work:

At the commencement of the commentary, desiring to pay homage to the Triple Gem, he said, "Whose heart is cooled by compassion," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the possession of their distinguished qualities.
For it is through the possession of distinguished qualities that they become worthy of veneration; and those who are worthy of veneration—

And the homage performed accomplishes the intended purpose. Herein, the teachers elaborate in various ways on the purpose for making the homage to the Triple Gem at the commencement of the commentary;
however, we shall demonstrate here only the purpose intended in this context.
Therefore, the performance of the homage to the Triple Gem at the commencement of the commentary serves as the unimpeded [condition] for the commentary as promised.
It should be understood that this means "for the purpose of completion. For this alone is the purpose intended here by the Teacher.
Thus he will say: "May the merit consisting of my salutation to the Triple Gem, performed with a mind of faith, cause me to have all obstacles well dispelled through its power."

And here, by means of making this homage to the Triple Gem, there is the completion of the commentary as promised without obstacle through worship of the Triple Gem and the proficiency of wisdom; and that proficiency of wisdom comes from the destruction of the stains of lust and the other defilements.

For it has been said: "Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion."
“...the mind becomes straight; at that time, his mind is indeed upright,” and so forth.
Therefore, through the worship of the Triple Gem, proficiency in wisdom (*paññā*) is achieved for one whose defilements have been washed away.

Alternatively, because the worship of the Triple Gem is the cause of concentration (*samādhi*) which has wisdom as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*), there is proficiency in wisdom. For its being the cause of that [concentration] has been stated:
“Furthermore, Mahānāma, a noble disciple with a straightforward mind gains knowledge of the meaning, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma.
In one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil;
one whose body is tranquil feels happiness; and the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.”
The fact that concentration and wisdom serve as the foundation for one another has already been stated: "One who is concentrated understands things as they truly are.
Therefore, by means of wisdom that has thus become keen, having overcome the weariness caused by the magnitude of his undertaking, he will complete this commentary without hindrance.

Alternatively, it should be understood that its completion without hindrance is due to the increase of longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength resulting from worship of the Triple Gem. For indeed, through dedication to the Triple Gem, longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength increase. Thus it has been said:
“For one whose habit is to pay homage, who constantly honors the elders, four things increase: life-span, beauty, happiness, and strength.
Thus, through the increase of life-span, beauty, happiness, and strength, there is indeed the accomplishment of what is to be done.

Alternatively, it is because reverence for the Triple Gem brings about the non-decline of inspired ingenuity (*paṭibhāna*). For reverence toward the Three Jewels indeed leads to non-decline. Thus it has been said:

"Bhikkhus, there are these seven qualities that prevent decline. Which seven? Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, reverence for concentration, readiness to listen, and friendship with the virtuous.
And through the non-decline of inspired ingenuity resulting from that, one fulfills one's promise as it was undertaken.
Alternatively, it is because of the preeminence of merit resulting from worship toward the objects of confidence. For its preeminence as merit has been stated thus:
“When one worships those worthy of worship—whether Buddhas or their disciples—who have transcended proliferation and crossed over sorrow and lamentation.”
"For one who honors such [beings] as these—those who have attained Nibbāna and are fearless from any quarter—it is impossible for anyone to calculate even this much merit.
And the excellence of merit is the means for accomplishing whatever purpose is intended. As it has been said:
“This is a treasure that grants all desires for gods and humans;
whatever they aspire to, all that is obtained by means of this.

And for one who has entered upon the right means, there is indeed the accomplishment of what is to be done. For the worship of the Triple Gem is the unsurpassed field of merit for the attainment of Buddhahood.

The extraordinary power of merit is immeasurable; even amidst the manifold obstacles inherent in worldly existence, it is capable of destroying all defilements that constitute those obstacles and wards off calamities such as fear. Therefore, it is said:
"At the commencement of the commentary, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of completing the commentary undertaken without obstacle."
Thus, wishing to perform the salutation to the Triple Gem for a specific purpose, he first offers salutation to the Blessed One—since the other Gems are rooted in Him—saying:
"Whose heart is cooled by compassion... [etc. ...who is liberated from all states of existence.
In this context, the teaching he intends to comment upon is not primarily characterized by compassion, as is the case with the teaching of the Vinaya, nor...
While the teaching of the Abhidhamma is characterized primarily by wisdom (*paññā*), this [teaching] is characterized primarily by compassion (*karuṇā*) and wisdom;

thus, in order to praise the Perfectly Enlightened One as one who possesses both these qualities as his primary attributes, it is said: "His heart is cooled by compassion, and the darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom.
In this context, *karoti* means *karuṇā*; the meaning is that she scatters away or removes the suffering of others. Alternatively, *kiṇāti*...
*Karunā* (compassion): when there is suffering in others, it "harms" or "afflicts" the compassionate one; this is the meaning.

Alternatively, *karunā* is so called because, when there is suffering in others, it causes a "trembling" or heartache in the virtuous. Or else, *kam* means happiness (*sukha*); it "obstructs" that, hence it is *karunā*.
For this [compassion] has the characteristic of the desire to remove the suffering of others, and through its disregard for one's own happiness, it is the happiness of the compassionate ones.

The meaning is "it obstructs" or "it hinders. "Cool with compassion" (*karuṇāsītala*) means [a heart] that is cooled by compassion; one whose heart is thus cooled by compassion is "one whose heart is cooled by compassion" (*karuṇāsītalahadayo*);

that is "one whose heart is cooled by compassion. In this context, although [the mind] has a nature that desires to bring about the welfare of others and does not wish for their loss of happiness and so forth, [it is free from] ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and aversion (*arati*).

Although it is observed that loving-kindness (*mettā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) also serve as causes for the cooling of the mind by way of their occurrence in a mode that severs the torment within the continuum of sentient beings through direct opposition [to hatred],
nevertheless, compassion (*karuṇā*)— which consists of non-harming and has the essence of being unable to endure the suffering of others—
is specifically the sign of the mind’s coolness, like the mental tranquility (*cittapassaddhi*) of the Blessed One, because it occurs in a mode of removing suffering.

It is said: “His heart is cooled by compassion. It should be understood that, by way of compassion, the cause for the cooling of the heart through loving-kindness (*mettā*) and gladness (*muditā*) is also stated.

Alternatively, it is compassion itself—serving as the basis for a unique distinction of knowledge—that has attained the state of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) due to its pervasion of its entire object, like the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), being preeminent and exhaustive. This [compassion] belongs to the Blessed One.
He said, "one whose heart is cooled by compassion" (*karuṇāsītalahadayam*), meaning that compassion is the cause for the state of extreme coolness in the heart.

Alternatively, although both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) are also causes for the cooling of the heart to a superior degree, compassion alone is stated to be "the cause for the state of coolness in the Blessed One's heart" because it is the specific cause for all the distinguished qualities of a Buddha. Indeed, all the qualities of a Buddha have compassion as their source.
For the Blessed One—who, through the power of his compassion, had extinguished the burning heat of the suffering of *saṃsāra*;

who, out of a desire to remove the suffering of others, remained untiring even for many incalculable eons; who was devoted to the accumulation of all the qualities that constitute a Buddha without exception;

and who had attained mastery over the Dhamma—even when confronted with signs that inflamed the heart by bringing about the conditioned nature of sentient beings— [The remainder of the sentence follows: ...remained as if he were not at all weary, being ever delighted in the gathering of the factors that produce Buddhahood, having achieved sovereignty over the Dhamma, and even in the presence of those things that cause the heart to burn through the influence of the formations of living beings.

"Even in the slightest degree, there was no alteration in the coolness of his mind. And in this interpretation of the meaning, it should be understood that the Blessed One’s compassion is encompassed throughout all three stages.

"Pajānāti" means wisdom (*paññā*); the sense is that one penetrates [the object] through various modes according to its true nature. Wisdom itself, because it abandons the obscurations of the knowable...
In the sense of illuminating the intrinsic nature (*dhammasabhāva*) of phenomena in various ways, it is "light" (*pajjota*); thus, it is the light of wisdom (*paññāpajjota*).

That which is specifically destroyed, uprooted, and struck down by the abandonment of latent tendencies (*savāsanappahāna*) is "struck down" (*vihata*). That which is struck down by the light of wisdom is "struck down by the light of wisdom" (*paññāpajjotavihata*).

Delusion (*moha*) is that by which beings are deluded, or which itself is deluded, or which is merely the state of being deluded; it is ignorance (*avijjā*). That very [ignorance] is so called because it conceals the intrinsic nature of objects.

Because it resembles darkness, it is "darkness" (*tamo*); thus, "darkness of delusion" (*mohatamo*). One for whom the darkness of delusion has been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom is "one who has destroyed the darkness of delusion by the lamp of wisdom" (*paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo*);

[the Buddha is] that one who has destroyed the darkness of delusion by the lamp of wisdom. For although the darkness of ignorance has indeed been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom in all those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), [there is a distinction]:
compared to those resolved through faith (*saddhādhimutta*), those who have attained through vision (*diṭṭhippatto*)...

Since a distinction exists in the abandonment of defilements among the Perfectly Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhas) due to their having abandoned even the latent tendencies (*savāsanā*)—whereas disciples and Paccekabuddhas have not—the Blessed One is praised for his preeminent abandonment of ignorance (*avijjāpahāna*). Thus, in homage, it is said:

"He who has destroyed the darkness of delusion with the lamp of wisdom. Alternatively, it is because he has produced within his own continuum the total disappearance of the darkness of ignorance without depending on the instruction of another.

And in this regard, because he has attained mastery over omniscience and the [ten] powers, and because the Blessed One alone has caused that [teaching] to proceed correctly within the mental continuum of others through the power of his preeminent excellence in teaching the Dhamma, it is the Blessed One specifically who should be praised for the disappearance of the darkness of delusion; thus he said:
"The darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom. And in this interpretation of the meaning, by the phrase "the lamp of wisdom,"...

It should be understood that the wisdom of the Blessed One’s teaching, like his wisdom of realization, is included under the general designation [of "wisdom"], either by way of a collective description or by the method of mentioning one representative member.

Alternatively, because the Blessed One’s knowledge extends to the very limits of the knowable, it possesses the lamp of wisdom known as unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*), which is capable of awakening to the true nature of all knowable phenomena;
[this lamp] [dispels] the darkness of delusion that obscures the true nature of all knowable phenomena.
Because the destruction of the darkness of delusion by the Blessed One is unique and not shared with others, it is said: "The darkness of delusion was dispelled by the lamp of wisdom.

And here, since the destruction of the darkness of delusion has been attained, unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) should be understood as the destruction of the darkness of delusion within one's own continuum through a metaphorical application of the cause to the effect.

For indeed, the abandonment of the obscurations to the knowable (*ñeyyāvaraṇappahāna*) consists precisely in the abandonment of the defilements (*kilesa*) together with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*) through the perfection of the resolution (*abhinīhāra*).
Furthermore, because it serves as the cause for dispelling the darkness of delusion in the mental continuities of others, unobstructed knowledge is called "the dispeller of the darkness of delusion.

Now, what is the reason that only the eradication of ignorance is taken as the basis for praising the Blessed One by way of his perfection in abandonment, rather than his superlative and complete abandonment of all defilements?
It is because by the very mention of that [ignorance's] abandonment, [the rest] is implied due to their being associated with it.

Because it has been stated that this is the eradication of the entire mass of defilements (*saṃkilesagaṇa*). For there is no such defilement that is not abandoned by the total abandonment of ignorance (*avijjā*).

Alternatively, just as true knowledge (*vijjā*) is the primary cause for the arising of all wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), so too ignorance is the primary cause for the production of all unwholesome states and for the continuation of saṃsāra; therefore, by the statement regarding its destruction, the eradication of the entire mass of defilements is implied.
It is said that he has indeed been described thus:

“He whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom. Humans and gods are *narāmarā*; together with humans and gods is *sanarāmara*. That world which is together with humans and gods is the *sanarāmaraloka*;
one who is honored (*garu*) by that *sanarāmaraloka* is the *sanarāmaralokagaru*. By this [phrase], [he is shown to be honored] by gods and humans...
This demonstrates the Blessed One’s assistance to the remaining beings as well, by bringing about specific qualities in them according to their respective capacities.
Nor should one object here on the grounds of a primary or secondary status; for the order of words is one thing, while the order of meaning is another.
In such compound expressions, even that which is primary is presented as if it were secondary, as in the phrase "the assembly together with the king" (*sarājikāya parisāya*).

In this context, although the world is threefold—consisting of beings, formations, and the receptacle world—the meaning should be understood according to the world of beings (*sattaloka*), because it is the state of being "heavy" that is intended here, and that [state] is applicable only to what is capable of being treated with respect.

For it is called "the world" (*loka*) because merit and demerit, as well as their respective results, are experienced (*lokīyanti*) therein. And by the mention of "immortals" (*amara*) here, the gods of rebirth (*upapattideva*) are intended.
Alternatively, the word *loka* has the sense of "collection," in the sense that it is "worlded" (*lokīyati*) or made known as an aggregate. "Together with men" (*saha narehi*) means *sanarā*;
and those who are both *sanarā* and *amarā* (immortals) are *sanarāmarā*. Their world is the *sanarāmaraloka*, which should be construed according to the previous method.
Furthermore, by the term *amara*, the purified deities (*visuddhideva*) are also included, for they too, due to the absence of death—

In the ultimate sense, they are immortal. And the mention of "humans and gods" (*nara-amarā*) is by way of an inclusive designation (*ukkaṭṭha-niddesa*), just as it is said, "the Teacher of gods and humans.

For indeed, through his unsurpassed perfection of application—which is preceded by the avoidance of all that is harmful and intent upon the provision of every benefit and happiness without exception—he is of ultimate service to the world including its gods and humans; and because he possesses distinctions of power and virtue that are immeasurable and incomparable.
And the Blessed One, the supreme among all beings, is the object of the highest reverence for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems.
Therefore it is said: "Venerated by the world of humans and gods.
He whose going (gati) is beautiful (sobhana) is the Sugata. For the Blessed One’s approach to those who are to be trained is exclusively...
It is beautiful because it accomplishes the welfare and happiness of those beings; likewise,

through the physical body being adorned with the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), its bodily movement and cognitive movement— free from defects such as haste, slowness, stumbling, dragging, pressing, frowning, crookedness, or insincerity— are like the gait of a royal swan,
a bull, an elephant, or the king of beasts, and are accompanied by the excellence of qualities such as vast, stainless compassion, mindfulness, and energy, due to his original resolve (*abhinīhāra*).

"Up to great enlightenment, it is indeed beautiful because of its faultlessness. Alternatively, he is the Sugata because, through his self-existent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*), he has rightly gone to and understood the entire world by means of the realization of full comprehension (*pariññābhisamaya*);

likewise, he is the Sugata because, by abandoning the origin of the world through the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*), he has rightly gone beyond and brought about the state of non-arising (*anuppattidhammatā*).

He is the *Sugata* because he has gone rightly (*sammā gata*) and attained (*adhigata*) the cessation of the world (*lokanirodha*), which is *nibbāna*, by means of the clear realization of its actualization (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*).
He is the *Sugata* because he has gone rightly and practiced (*paṭipanna*) the path leading to the cessation of the world by means of the clear realization of its cultivation (*bhāvanābhisamaya*).

This meaning is also expressed in such passages as: "He is the *Sugata* because he does not bring back, does not return to, and does not go back to those defilements which were abandoned by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimārga*). Thus is the sense of this term.
It is to be made manifest. Alternatively, he is the "Well-Gone" (Sugata) because he has gone to or attained a beautiful state—namely, perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) or even Nibbāna itself.

Or, because he speaks the Dhamma that is real, true, beneficial, and appropriate for those to be trained (veneyya) at the right time, he is the "Well-Speaker" (Sugata), having changed the letter *da* to *ta*. Thus, [he is so called] by virtue of his beautiful gait and other such qualities.
The Sugata, that Sugata.
Because one must go by way of rebirth through meritorious and evil kamma, there are "destinies" (*gati*), which are specific types of existence at rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
These, moreover, are fivefold, according to the hells and so forth. By means of the attainment of the Noble Path, [one abandons] all kamma leading to existence through those [destinies].
Because he has turned back from [rebirth] by making himself a being no longer subject to karmic ripening, the Blessed One is well liberated and dissociated even from the five destinations;

thus he said, "liberated from destinations. By this, he shows that the Blessed One is not included within any destination whatsoever, which is why the Blessed One is called the "God beyond gods. For this very reason, he said:
“Those taints by which one would be reborn as a god, or as a gandhabba, or as a bird;
by which one might go to the state of a yakkha, or attain human status—
those taints of mine are exhausted, shattered, and rendered baseless.”

For since the kamma and defilements that lead to various states of existence were completely abandoned by the Supreme Path even at the foot of the Bodhi tree, there is no inclusion of the Blessed One within any state of existence;

thus the Blessed One is utterly and completely liberated from all realms of becoming, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and classes of beings—that is what is meant by "liberated from those states. "Vande" means I pay homage, or the sense is that I praise him.
Alternatively, "liberated from destiny" praises the Blessed One by virtue of his attainment of the Nibbāna-element without residue.
For here, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in two aspects: through the perfection of his own welfare and through his practice for the welfare of others.
Among these, the perfection of his own welfare consists in the attainment of unobstructed knowledge and the absolute abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies.

It should be understood as the attainment of *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*). Furthermore, the practice for the benefit of others (*parahita-paṭipatti*) is to be known by way of teaching the Dhamma that leads out of all suffering to one whose mind is indifferent to gain, honor, and so forth;
by way of a constant inclination toward the welfare of others even toward those who oppose him; and by way of the arrival of the time for the maturation of his knowledge.

Moreover, this practice for the benefit of others is twofold—by way of disposition (*āsaya*) and application (*payoga*)—and threefold, consisting of the accomplishment of one’s own welfare (*attahita-sampatti*).
It has been revealed. How so? By the phrase “one whose heart is cooled by compassion,” the practice for the welfare of others is shown through one’s disposition (*āsaya*).
By the word *sugata* in the sense of “having gone rightly,” the practice for the welfare of others is shown through one’s application (*payoga*).

And by the phrases “whose darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom” and “released from the [round of] rebirths,” along with the word *sugata* in the sense of the full penetration of the Four Noble Truths, the threefold attainment of one’s own welfare is shown.

By the remainder, namely the phrase “whose darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom,” both the attainment of one’s own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others are likewise manifested.
Alternatively, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood through three aspects: by way of cause, by way of fruit, and by way of benefit.

Therein, the cause is great compassion, which is shown by the first word. The fruit is fourfold: the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of abandonment, [the perfection of power, and the perfection of merit].

[The perfection of the Buddha consists of] the perfection of majesty and the perfection of the form-body. Among these, the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of abandonment are indicated by the second term and by the word *sugata* in the sense of penetration of the truths;

the perfection of majesty is indicated by the third term; and the perfection of the form-body is indicated by the word *sugata* in the sense of the beauty of the body and its gait as previously described, because that [beauty] does not exist without the fullness of the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). The assistance is immediate and not external.
It should be understood that the teaching of the Dhamma for liberation by means of the three vehicles is revealed by the term *sugata* in the sense of having spoken rightly (*sammāgadanattha*).

In this context, by the phrase "whose heart is cooled by compassion," he shows the root of perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). [He is one] whose mind is impelled by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
For the Blessed One, having made the resolution for the sake of uplifting beings from the mire of saṃsāra, gradually fulfilled the perfections and attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
thus, compassion is the root of perfect enlightenment. By the phrase "the darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom," he demonstrates perfect enlightenment.
For path-knowledge has unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause, and path-knowledge has [wisdom] as its proximate cause.

Unobstructed knowledge is called "perfect enlightenment" (sammāsambodhi). By means of the term *sugata* in the sense of "one who has gone rightly," he demonstrates the practice for perfect enlightenment;

for the word *sugata* reveals the Middle Way—accompanied by compassion and wisdom, free from the two extremes such as the adherence to dullness and agitation, the accumulation [of karma], devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification, and the dogmatic clinging to eternalism and annihilationism. By the other [terms...]

This demonstrates the purpose, categorized as primary and secondary, for the striving toward perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). Herein, the primary purpose is the crossing over of sentient beings from the great flood of *saṃsāra*;
the other is the secondary purpose. Among these, by means of the primary [purpose], he shows the practice for the benefit of others, and by the other, the attainment of one's own benefit.

By means of both, [he shows] among the four types of persons—those practicing for their own benefit, etc.— *Note: The final sentence fragment appears to be the beginning of a further classification regarding the four types of individuals (puggala).*

This demonstrates the Blessed One’s status as the fourth type of person (*puggala*). By this, he demonstrates his own state of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), his state of being the supreme object of veneration, and his having become a true field (*khetta*) for the act of one's own prostration.
Furthermore, here, by the inclusion of "compassion" (*karuṇā*), the Blessed One’s uncommon qualities that have attained a sublime state among worldly beings are illuminated.

The attainment of all mundane qualities is demonstrated; by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), the attainment of all supramundane qualities is shown, because it illustrates the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*) which has the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).
For the meaning established by the inclusion of both [compassion and wisdom] is elaborated upon in such passages as "the one revered by the world of men and gods" (*sanarāmaralokagaru*).
Furthermore, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), he shows that his approach is free from defilement (*nirupakkilesa*); by the mention of wisdom...

...the departure. Likewise, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), he shows the Blessed One’s activity in accordance with worldly convention, because compassion is within the domain of worldly discourse;

by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), he shows the non-transcending of that convention. For it is through the failure to understand the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena that one transcends convention and clings to [the notions of] a "being" and so forth.
Likewise, by the mention of compassion, [he shows] the dwelling in the attainment of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*).
By the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), there is shown the unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times, the knowledge of the Four Truths, the knowledge of the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*),
and the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*). By the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), because the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is included,

there are included the remaining unique knowledges, the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the unshakable knowledges in the eight assemblies, the ten powers (*bala*), and the fourteen Buddha-knowledges.

He demonstrates the range of knowledge by way of numerous classifications of wisdom (*paññā*), such as the sixteen modes of the exercise of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*), the eighteen qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadhamma*), the forty-four bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*), and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge.
Likewise, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), he shows the perfection of conduct (*caraṇasampatti*);
by the mention of wisdom, the perfection of true knowledge (*vijjāsampatti*). And by the mention of compassion, self-mastery (*attādhipatitā*).

By the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), there is the preeminence of the Dhamma. By the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), there is the state of being a protector of the world; by the mention of wisdom, the state of being one’s own protector.

Likewise, by the mention of compassion, there is the quality of acting for the welfare of others first; by the mention of wisdom, there is gratitude. Likewise, by the mention of compassion, there is the absence of self-torment;
by the mention of wisdom, there is the absence of tormenting oneself. Or else, by the mention of compassion, there is the accomplishment of the qualities that constitute a Buddha.

By the inclusion of wisdom, the attainment of Buddhahood is established. Likewise, by the inclusion of compassion, the saving of others is shown, while by the inclusion of wisdom, one’s own crossing over is shown.
Similarly, by the inclusion of compassion, a mind of benevolence toward all beings is indicated, and by the inclusion of wisdom, a mind detached from all phenomena is demonstrated.
Of all the qualities of a Buddha, compassion is the beginning because it is their primary cause; wisdom is the end because there is nothing further to be done beyond it.

Thus, by showing the beginning and the end, all the qualities of a Buddha are shown. Likewise, by the inclusion of compassion, the aggregate of concentration—which is preceded by the aggregate of virtue—is shown.
For virtue has its source in compassion, since from that [compassion] arises the practice of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth.
And that [virtue] is associated with the three jhānas. By the term "wisdom" (paññā), the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) is indicated.

Furthermore, since virtue (sīla) is the beginning of all the Buddha-qualities, concentration (samādhi) is the middle, and wisdom is the end, all the Buddha-qualities are shown to be beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end by way of this method of presentation. For this alone is the complete [classification] of the Buddha-qualities.

The method for seeing [the truth] is this: the grasping of the guiding principles (*naya*). Otherwise, who indeed would be capable of demonstrating the qualities of the Blessed One in their entirety, word by word?
For this very reason, it was said:
"Even a Buddha, were he to speak the praise of a Buddha..."
"Even if one were to speak of another for an eon,
and that eon were to be exhausted after a very long time,
the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted."

And for that very reason, even the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, while intent upon defining the qualities of the Buddha, having rejected [the question] with "No indeed, Bhante," said: "But, Bhante, the sequence of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya) is known to me.
Having thus praised the Blessed One in brief by means of all his omniscient qualities, he now spoke the words beginning with "The Buddha too" in order to extol the True Dhamma (saddhamma).
Therein, "Buddha" is a designation of the agent; "the state of being a Buddha" (buddhabhāva) is a designation of the object.
"Bhāvetvā" (having developed) and "sacchikatvā" (having realized) are designations for an action in the prior time. "Yaṃ" (which) is a designation for an object in an indefinite sense.
"Upagato" (approached) is a designation for an action in the subsequent time. "Vandeti" (he worships) is a designation for the action itself. "Taṃ" (that) is a specification.
"Dhammaṃ" (the Dhamma) is a designation for the object of the act of worship. "Gatamalaṃ anuttaraṃ" (stainless and unsurpassed) are its qualifiers.
In this regard, first of all, the meaning of the word *buddha* should be understood according to the method of exposition as: "He is a Buddha because he has awakened to the truths;

he is a Buddha because he awakens the world," and so forth. Alternatively, he is called a Buddha because he has completely departed from the sleep of ignorance along with its latent tendencies (*savāsanā*), or because his awakening (*buddhi*) has blossomed—thus he is a Buddha in the sense of being awake and fully blossomed. Or else, [the derivation is as follows:]...

Since there is no knowable phenomenon (ñeyyadhamma) that has not been understood by him, and because there is no specific object of knowledge to be grasped as an object of action (kamma), there is no desire for a verbal expression of an object;
thus, the designation of the agent (kattuniddesa) is obtained solely in the sense of "having understood" (avagata).

Therefore, he is called "Buddha" in the sense of "one who has awakened" (buddhavā), just as one says, "the ordained person does not give. In terms of its meaning (attha), however, [he is so called] because of his self-dependent knowledge (sayambhuñāṇa) which is fully matured by the perfections (pāramitā).

The Buddha is the continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna) which, together with its latent tendencies (vāsanā), has destroyed and utterly demolished all defilements (kilesa), and which is the locus of an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as great compassion (mahākaruṇā) and omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa). As it is said:

"A Buddha is that Blessed One who is self-become (sayambhū) and teacherless (anācariyaka); he has personally awakened to the truths regarding phenomena never heard before, and therein he has attained omniscience and mastery over the powers (bala)."

The word *api* (even/also) is used here in the sense of esteem (*sambhāvana*). By it, he expresses esteem for the qualities and phenomena about to be described, implying: "Even that Blessed One was indeed endowed with such distinguished qualities.
*Buddhabhāvaṃ* means perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). *Bhāvetvā* means having developed and increased [them].
*Sacchikatvā* means having made manifest through direct experience. *Upagato* means arrived at; the meaning is "attained" (*adhigato*). *Etassa buddhabhāvaṃ* refers to his state of Buddhahood.
By this, the connection [is established]. *Gatamalam* means "gone is the stain"; the sense is "free from defilement. *Vande* means "I bow" or "I praise.
*Anuttaram* means "without superior," the sense being "supramundane" (*lokuttara*). *Dhammam*:

it is called *dhamma* because it holds (*dhāreti*) those who practice according to its instruction, preventing them from falling into the states of misery (*apāya*) or into cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). This, then, is the summarized meaning here.
Thus, the Blessed Buddha, endowed with such a multitude of diverse qualities, having developed that Dhamma known as the Noble Path and having realized the fruit of Nibbāna,
attained unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment (anuttara-sammāsambodhi)—
that very state which is the cause of the Buddhahood even of Buddhas, free from all stains of defilement, and unsurpassed because there exists nothing superior to it.

"I pay homage to the True Dhamma of realization (*paṭivedhasaddhamma*). Since the True Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattisaddhamma*) also elucidates that [realization], it should be understood as being included here.

Alternatively, because it is stated in the Commentary: "He reached the ocean of the Abhidhamma method; he mastered the three Piṭakas," the term "realization" (*sacchikiriyā*) and "mastery" (*sammasana*) can also be applied to the Dhamma of the scriptures; thus, that too is included here.

It should be understood that it is indeed so stated. Likewise, because it is said, "having developed and realized which Dhamma," it should be known that here, by the word *dhamma*, the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and the rest during the prior stage are also included along with the perfections (*pāramitā*), which constitute the qualities that make one a Buddha.
For these too are "free from stains" due to being devoid of opposites, and they are "unsurpassed" due to not being shared by others. Thus...
Indeed, for the sake of all beings’ escape from the entire suffering of saṃsāra, he made a great resolution, his disposition being refined by the endurance of great compassion;
and through the diligent, continuous, and exhaustive cultivation and realization of the supreme qualities— such as generosity, self-control, restraint, and so forth—
which are purified by the excellence of wisdom, for four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons.

The Blessed One— who had attained mastery over karma and other factors, possessed of marvelous, inconceivable, and great power, and who had reached the supreme pinnacle of perfection in higher virtue and higher consciousness—
sent forth the Great Vajira-knowledge through twenty-four million four hundred thousand modes regarding the principle of conditionality,
and thereby fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

And here, by the word "having developed," he praises the Dhamma through the perfection of true knowledge (vijjā); by the word "having realized," he praises it through the perfection of liberation (vimutti).
Likewise, by the first [term] he praises the perfection of jhāna, and by the second, the perfection of deliverance (vimokkha).

Or alternatively, by the first he praises the perfection of concentration (samādhi), and by the second, the perfection of meditative attainment (samāpatti). Or else, by the first, he praises it in terms of the nature of the knowledge of destruction (khayañāṇa).
By means of the second, through the state of non-arising knowledge (*anuppāda-ñāṇa*). Or, by the first, through its resemblance to lightning; by the second, through its resemblance to a thunderbolt.

Or, by the former, through the attainment of dispassion (*virāga*); by the latter, through the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*). Likewise, by the first, through the state of leading out (*niyyāna*);

by the second, through the state of escape (*nissaraṇa*). Or, by the first, through the state of being a cause (*hetu*); by the second, through the state of being unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*). By the first...
Or he praises the Dhamma by way of its quality of vision through the first [phrase], and by way of its quality of seclusion through the second.

Or alternatively, he praises the Dhamma by way of its quality of sovereignty through the first, and by way of its quality of immortality through the second. Or else, with the words "having developed that Dhamma," he praises the Dhamma for its well-expounded nature;
and with the word "having realized," he praises it for its visible nature. Likewise...
By the former [phrase], he praises the Dhamma for its being timeless; by the latter, for its being "come-and-see.
Or alternatively, by the former, he praises it for its leading onward; by the latter, for its being personally verifiable.

By the phrase "with taints gone," he shows the purity of the Dhamma through the indication of the absence of defilement; by the word "unsurpassed," he shows the absence of anything else superior to it.
[It shows] the state of being vast and complete. Alternatively, by the first [phrase], he shows the perfection of abandonment regarding the Dhamma; by the second, the perfection of its source.
Or rather, the state of having removed impurities (*gatamala*) should be applied to the Dhamma because it is to be developed (*bhāvetabba*).

For through the quality of development, it becomes the eradicator of defilements (*dosa*). Its state of being unsurpassed (*anuttara*) should be applied by way of its being realizable (*sacchikātabba*). Because it is produced through realization...
Indeed, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) because there is nothing further to be done beyond it and because it is not shared by others.

Likewise, by the term "having developed" (*bhāvetvā*), the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom belonging to those in training (*sekkha*)—together with the preliminary stages of virtue and so forth—are shown.

By the term "having realized" (*sacchikatvā*), the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom belonging to those beyond training (*asekkha*)—in relation to the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*)—are shown.
3. Having thus praised the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) by way of its qualities in brief, he now spoke the words beginning with “of the Sugata” in order to extol the Noble Saṅgha.
Therein, “of the Sugata” is a statement of relationship; it is connected with the phrase “his sons.
“Orasānaṃ” is an epithet for sons. “Mārasenamathanānaṃ” [is used] in the sense of their being legitimate sons.
The exposition of the cause shows that the very abandonment of the defilements by him is acknowledged as the cause for his status as a legitimate son of the Blessed One.

"Of eight" is an exposition defining the numerical limit; and by this, it shows that although they are distinct beings and exist in numbers of many hundreds of thousands, they do not exceed this numerical limit, because they do not transcend the state of being established on the path or established in the fruit.
"Samūha" is a designation for a collection. "Ariyasaṅgha" is a designation for a harmonious assembly distinguished by its virtues.

By this, he shows that even though there is no physical union among the noble persons (ariyapuggala), they possess the nature of the Ariyasaṅgha because they are united through their commonality of view and virtue.

In this context, "urasā" means those who exist in, are born from, or are connected to the breast; for just as the "breast-born sons" (urasaputta) of beings are so called because they are born from oneself—

Just as [sons] are especially entitled to a share of their father’s inheritance, so too these noble persons (ariyapuggala), by virtue of being born into the noble birth at the ear of the Perfectly Enlightened One, are unconditionally entitled to the bliss of liberation and the jewel of the noble Dhamma belonging to the Blessed One;
thus they are "legitimate sons" (orasā) like those born from the breast. Alternatively, through the power of the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, they have reached the plane of the noble ones.

Noble disciples who are entering or have entered [the path] deserve to be called, in the primary sense, "sons of the breast" (urasaputta) of the Blessed One, by virtue of their noble birth produced through his own effort.

For even when the teaching of the Dhamma is being carried out by disciples, it is still called "the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma," because it has its root in him and lacks any distinction in its essential characteristics and so forth.

Even though, at the time of the noble disciples’ attainment of the Noble Path, neither the Devaputtamāra nor the host of Māra necessarily attempts to obstruct them as they did for the Blessed One, nevertheless, because the grounds upon which they were to be obstructed have been destroyed by those disciples, they too are indeed said to be "crushed.
Thus it is said: "of the crushers of Māra’s army. In this sense, however—

It should be understood that although it ought to be said, “of those who crush Māra and Māra’s army,” the form “of those who crush Māra’s army” is used by means of a *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (an elliptical compound retaining only one member of a similar class).

Alternatively, just as with the Māras consisting of the aggregates and the formative volitions (*saṅkhāra*), the host of the power of defilements is called “the army” because it acts as an ally to the Devaputta-Māra in the act of slaying [virtuous] qualities. As it is said: “Sensual pleasures are your first [army]...”

“An army,” and so forth. That army of defilements—which consists of one thousand five hundred divisions, or rather infinite divisions—has been thoroughly crushed, shattered, and scattered by means of the weapons of the noble qualities such as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, and serenity;
thus they are “crushers of Māra’s army. These are the noble disciples.
By this, he shows that they are the sons born after the Blessed One.

They are "Noble Ones" (*ariya*) according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), because they are far removed from defilements, because they do not proceed in what is not the right way, and because they proceed in the right way.

Alternatively, they are Noble Ones because they are to be sought after (*araṇīya*) and approached by the world including the devas, and because for those who have approached them, their purpose is accomplished;
thus, the community of the Noble Ones is the "Ariya-saṅgha. Or, it is the Ariya-saṅgha because it is both noble and a community. That [community]...

The Noble Saṅgha. It should be understood that the phrase "I revere with my head" was spoken right here in order to demonstrate the great assistance provided by this Noble Saṅgha, showing that after the Blessed One, even the attainment of the jewels of the Buddha and the Dhamma is dependent upon the jewel of the Saṅgha.
And herein, by the words "of the legitimate sons of the Sugata," he demonstrates the excellence of the Noble Saṅgha’s origin.
By the phrase “crushers of Māra’s army,” he demonstrates the perfection of abandonment (*pahānasampadā*), because it illustrates the abandonment of all defilements (*saṃkilesa*).

By the phrase “the assembly of the eight,” he demonstrates the perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*), because it illustrates the state of those established on the paths and those established in the fruits (*maggaṭṭha-phalaṭṭha*).

By the phrase “the Noble Saṅgha,” he shows the perfection of origin (*pabhavasampadā*), because it illustrates the preeminence of all Saṅghas. Alternatively, [it refers to] “the legitimate sons of the Sugata...”

The phrase “of the sons” indicates that the Noble Saṅgha possesses a pure basis; “of those who crush Māra’s army” indicates that they have entered upon the practice of right, upright, and proper conduct;
“of the assembly of the eight” indicates that they possess the qualities of being worthy of offerings and so forth; and “the Noble Saṅgha” indicates that it is an unsurpassed field of merit.
Likewise, by the phrase “of the legitimate sons of the Sugata,” the existence of supramundane going for refuge within the Noble Saṅgha is shown.
He illuminates this. For by going for refuge to the supramundane, they have become the legitimate sons of the Blessed One.
By the phrase "crushers of Māra’s army," he shows the practice of right conduct in the prior stage, which is accomplished through the perfection of the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*).
For those who have made the resolve and have practiced rightly conquer Māra or Māra’s retinue. By the phrase "the host of all eight,"...

By means of the designation of persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), it shows the states of those in training (*sekha*) and those beyond training (*asekha*) who have destroyed their adversaries, because the states of the path and its fruits are thus manifested.
By the term "the Noble Saṅgha," it shows the state of being the most worthy of offerings. And going for refuge is the beginning of all the qualities of disciples;

the states of those in training, including the preliminary practice, such as the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth, constitute the middle; and the states of those beyond training, such as the aggregate of virtue and so forth, [constitute the end].
"Conclusion" (*pariyosāna*) means that, being "excellent in the beginning, middle, and end," all the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha are revealed in brief. Thus,
having performed a salutation to the Triple Gem by way of a concise recitation of its entire range of virtues through these three verses,
he now speaks the words beginning with "Thus to me" (*iti me*), dedicating that very homage toward his intended purpose.
In this context, they are called "jewels" (*ratana*) in the sense that they generate delight; these are the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.

For when one adverts to their qualities as they truly are, according to the passage beginning, "Thus indeed is the Blessed One," a no small measure of rapture and joy arises, which serves as the cause for attaining the Deathless. As it is said:
"Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time he does not [experience]..."
“The mind is not obsessed by lust, nor by hatred... nor by delusion; rather, on that occasion, his mind is directed straight toward the Tathāgata.

And when, Mahānāma, a noble disciple has a mind directed straightly, he gains inspiration from the meaning, he gains inspiration from the Dhamma, he gains joy connected with the Dhamma. In one who is joyful, rapture arises,” and so forth.
Alternatively, the meaning of "jewel" (ratana) is the state of being honored and so forth.
For it has been said: "That which is honored, of great value, incomparable, rare to behold, and the enjoyment of extraordinary beings—therefore it is called a 'jewel'."
Furthermore, qualities such as being treated with honor (*cittīkatabhāva*) are found only in the Buddhas and others, and not shared by anyone else.
"Consisting of homage" (*vandanāmaya*) means simply homage (*vandanā*), just as there are things "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*) or "consisting of virtue" (*sīlamaya*).

Here, homage refers to the inclination toward the virtues of the Three Jewels through body, speech, and mind, or it is praise (*thomanā*). It is called "merit" (*puñña*) because it produces the fruit of a state worthy of honor (*pujjabhāva*). [It is merit] for oneself...
Or, it means "it purifies the continuum. *Suvihatantarāyo* means one for whom obstacles have been thoroughly destroyed.

By this, he shows that through his own perfection of faith and the perfection of the Triple Gem as a field of merit, that merit is capable of destroying the calamities and misfortunes that obstruct the exposition of the meaning.
*Hutvā* is a verb indicating a prior action. Regarding that [prior action], [the thought was]: "I shall expound the meaning."
By this, the connection [is established]. "Of that" means of that merit consisting of the homage to the Triple Gem. "By its power" means by its strength.

Having thus shown the purpose for performing the service of the Triple Gem, he now says, beginning with "of that which is adorned with singles, pairs, etc.," for the sake of introducing—by way of extolling its qualities—the teaching of the Dhamma whose meaning he intends to comment upon.
The meaning is: "of that which is distinguished and adorned by the Suttantas taught by increasing the factors (aṅga) one by one.
By this, he shows that the designation "Aṅguttara" for this Āgama is consistent with its actual meaning.

But surely, it is only the Suttas taught by way of the single [factors] and so forth that constitute the Āgama. To what, then, does the state of being adorned by the singles, pairs, and so forth belong?
This is true from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*); however, the "scripture" (*āgama*) is designated based upon the discourses (*sutta*).

For just as the conventional term "discourse" (*sutta*) applies to a collection of both meaning and phrasing, so too the conventional term "scripture" (*āgama*) applies to a collection of discourses. It is called the *Aṅguttara* because it is progressively higher and more superior by means of the numerical factors (*aṅga*) beginning with one.
It is called "scripture" (*āgama*) because in it, by means of it, or from it, one arrives at one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth.

It is called the *āgamavara* (the supreme scripture) because it is the best in the sense of being endowed with qualities such as being auspicious in the beginning, and because it is a boon (*vara*) since it is chosen by the wise as the cause for the fulfillment of their respective aspirations; or, it is the supreme scripture in the sense of being excellent. Alternatively, it is the *āgamavara* because it is a boon among those recognized as scriptures.
It is the *Aṅguttarāgamavara* because it is both the *aṅguttara* (increasing by factors) and the *āgamavara*; [it refers to] that.

"Bulls" (*puṅgava*) refers to oxen; because they resemble them through qualities such as protecting others and enduring fearlessness and danger, the preachers of the Dhamma themselves are "bulls among Dhamma-preachers" (*dhammakathikapuṅgava*);

[the compound refers] to those [preachers]. Because of their variety of teaching methods, adorned with various similes, causes, and so forth, they generate diverse flashes of inspired eloquence (*vicittapaṭibhāna*).
However, in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* and other works, it is stated: "[of that which has been praised by the Buddhas and those awakened after the Buddhas]."

It has been said. For, following upon the Buddhas’ penetration of the Truths, the Noble Ones—the Chief Disciples and others—have penetrated those Truths and are thus "Buddhas who have awakened after the Buddha" (*buddhānubuddha*).
This scripture (*āgama*) has likewise been commented upon by them by way of explaining its meaning and by way of praising its qualities.
Alternatively, it should be construed as "the Buddhas and those who have awakened after the Buddhas. [This was] by the Fully Enlightened One himself.
For the sequence of the commentary on the meaning of the three Piṭakas has already been spoken of—that which is called the "Miscellaneous Teaching" (Pakiṇṇaka-desanā).
Regarding this, the teachers say it was [compiled] by the disciples through means such as the communal recitation (saṅgāyana).

However, here the praise is made specifically for "the generation of diverse eloquence among the preeminent preachers of the Dhamma. Furthermore, this is the natural style of the teacher in his commentaries.
It is the praise at the beginning of various commentaries by extolling the specific qualities of each respective Dhamma subject to be commented upon.
For instance, in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, *Papañcasūdanī*, *Sāratthappakāsinī*, and *Aṭṭhasālinī* and so forth, it occurs respectively as:
“of that which possesses qualities that inspire faith,” “of that which crushes the arguments of opponents,” and “of that which generates the various types of knowledge.”
Praise was offered with such words as: "Of that which has been plunged into by those of profound knowledge, and which is manifoldly variegated by various methods," and so forth.

6. It is called *aṭṭhakathā* because the meaning (*attha*) is explained (*kathīyati*) by it; it is precisely this that is the *aṭṭhakathā*, having changed the letter *ttha* to *ṭṭha*, just as in the expression "the meaning of oppression (*pīḷana*) of suffering.
"From the beginning" means in the beginning, at the first council. By virtue of possessing the six supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiññatā*).

The "Vasīs" are the elders such as Mahākassapa and others, so called because they possess supreme mastery over the mind and because they have attained the fivefold mastery in the jhānas and other meditative states.
"By five hundred" means by those five hundred elders. "Yāti" refers to that commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
"Saṅgītā" means that in passages suitable for elucidating the meaning, it has been compiled by stating, "This is the meaning of this; this is the meaning of that."
[The Dhamma] was recited and subsequently rehearsed by the Elder Yasa and others during the second and third councils.
By this, he demonstrates the purity of the lineage of his own commentary. 7.
One who takes [the lion’s] skin (lāna) or grasps [its characteristics] is a Sihaḷa; [thus] Sīhakumāra. Because they were born of his lineage, the kṣatriyas in the island of Tambapaṇṇi—
Because they were its inhabitants, the island of Tambapaṇṇi should be understood as having the nature of Sīhaḷa (Ceylon).
"Brought" means brought from Jambudīpa. "Then" means afterwards; for at a later time, the Aṭṭhakathā was established in the Sīhaḷa language for the sake of non-confusion.
Therefore, since that original Aṭṭhakathā was not common to all, this elucidation of the meaning must certainly be composed.
[The author] shows this. For that very reason he says: “for the benefit of those dwelling on the island.

Therein, “of those dwelling on the island” means either of those dwelling on Jambudīpa, or alternatively, “for the benefit of those dwelling on the island” means it was established in the Sinhalese language for the sake of those dwelling on the island of Siṃhala;
such is the construction. 8. “Having removed”: having removed the Sinhalese language which is like a covering. “From there”: from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). “I”: [the author].
He identifies himself. They speak the delightful Māgadhī language; for that, being the natural mode of expression, delights the minds of the wise.
Therefore he says: "conforming to the method of the discourses" (*tantinayānucchavika*), meaning it is in accordance with the course of the Pāḷi and follows the shadow of the Pāḷi.
"Free from faults" means it is devoid of unrefined expressions and other foreign languages.
9. “Not violating the *samaya*” means not contradicting the established doctrine (*siddhanta*). By this, he states the absence of faults in meaning.

For it is precisely because they are non-contradictory that even the doctrines of the Elders (*theravāda*) will be elucidated here. Regarding the phrase “of those belonging to the lineage of the Elders” (*theravaṃsadīpānaṃ*):

they are called “Elders” (*thera*) because they are endowed with the stable aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth; the lineage of the Elders (*theravaṃsa*) is the succession of teachers (*ācariyaparamparā*) handed down by them. Those included within that [lineage]...

Because they have perfected the realization of the scriptures (*āgama*) and their attainment (*adhigama*), and because they cause it to blaze forth by means of the lamp of wisdom (*paññā-pajjota*), they are the "Lamps of the Elder Lineage" (*theravaṃsa-dīpa*);
[this refers to] the Elders who dwell at the Mahāvihāra. It is called a "detailed exposition" (*vinicchaya*) because it is extracted in various ways;

it is a discourse that cuts through doubt, proceeding in the manner of cutting out a splinter at the knotted places [of the text]. Those for whom the detailed exposition is very subtle and refined are [the authors of this work].
"Those of very skillful discernment" (*sunipuṇavinicchayā*). Alternatively, it is "discernment" (*vinicchaya*) because it discerns;
that is, knowledge whose object is the meaning as previously stated. Those who possess a very skillful, clever discernment are "those of very skillful discernment.

By this, he shows the authoritative nature of the discernment of the Mahāvihāravāsins—which has been handed down through the succession of elders beginning with Mahākassapa and is therefore unerring, subtle, and refined.
10. Regarding the phrase *sujanassa ca*: the word *ca* has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*).
By this, he shows: "It is not only for the sake of those dwelling in Jambudīpa, but also for the purpose of pleasing virtuous people.

And by that, the meaning "also for the sake of those dwelling on the island of Tambapaṇṇi" is established, because it is easy for them to learn and so forth, and because it is of great benefit to them as well. *Ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ* means "for the sake of long endurance."

"For the sake of long endurance" means for the purpose of remaining for a long time. For this exposition of the meaning serves as the means for the long endurance of the True Dhamma, by way of the correct arrangement of the phrasing and the well-guided interpretation of the meaning. Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One:

"Bhikkhus, these two things lead to the endurance, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the True Dhamma. Which two? Well-arranged phrasing and word-meaning, and well-guided interpretation of the meaning."
11–12. Desiring to compose a commentary on this [text], he said, “Sāvatthī, etc.,” in order to avoid the excessive length of it.
Therefore he said: “I shall not provide an extensive exposition here; I shall not investigate that here. In this context, “of the Long” means of the Dīghanikāya;
“of the Middle” means of the Majjhimanikāya. “Of the two recitations” refers to...

The reading “me atthaṃ vadantenā” (by one speaking the meaning for me) is also found there. In that case as well, the phrase “of the two collections” (saṅgītīnaṃ dvinnanti) should be understood to mean “of the Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāyas.
The word “me” is a genitive used in the sense of the instrumental; its meaning is “by me. “Su” is merely a particle.
The description of cities such as Sāvatthī and so forth, which occurs below in the context of one speaking the meaning of the Dīgha and Majjhima, [is included here].
"Having been done, I shall not further elaborate upon its detailed exposition here"—this is how it should be connected.
And as for those matters which were stated there in detail, the connection is: "I shall not further elaborate upon their detailed exposition here either. 13.
Now, regarding the meaning stated in general terms as "I shall not elaborate upon the detailed exposition here," [the following is] the most excellent...

To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “But of the suttas... was stated. It should be construed as follows: those meanings of the suttas which are not clarified without [the exposition of] the *vatthus*.
14. Desiring to compose a commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), one should also take the *Visuddhimagga* as being a portion of that same work.
Thus, providing instruction to those who would teach it, he shows the doctrines discussed therein by way of enumeration, beginning with “The discourse on virtue (*sīla*)...”.

Therein, "discourse on virtue" (*sīlakathā*) is an extensive explanation of virtue by way of the rules of conduct and prohibitions. "Ascetic practices" (*dhutadhammā*) are the thirteen qualities that shake off the defilements, beginning with the practice of eating only almsfood.
"All meditation subjects" (*kammaṭṭhānāni*) refers to the thirty-eight found in the Canon and the two in the Commentary;
these are, without exception, the bases for the occurrence of the cultivation of spiritual work (*yogakamma*). "Together with the methods for conduct" (*cariyāvidhānasahito*)...

It is accompanied by the classification of the intrinsic natures and so forth of those whose temperament is dominated by passion and the rest. The "jhanas" are the four fine-material-sphere jhanas; the "attainments" (samāpatti) are the four immaterial-sphere attainments.
Alternatively, even the eight jhanas that have merely been attained are called "attainments" when they have reached mastery in the process of entering them.
Or else, the "jhanas" are the fine-material and immaterial-sphere jhanas, while the "attainments" are the fruition attainment and the attainment of cessation.

15. All six superknowledges (*abhiññā*), distinguished as mundane and supramundane, are classified and synthesized by wisdom according to the method found in the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* and other texts—beginning with the singlefold classification and so forth. This determination is the "determination by the synthesis of wisdom" (*paññā-saṅkalanā-nicchaya*). 16.

The "mode of conditionality" (*paccayākāra*) refers to the state of being a root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and so forth for conditioned phenomena (*paccaya-dhamma*) and the phenomena arisen from conditions (*paccayuppanna-dhamma*).

The teaching of this is the "teaching on the mode of conditionality," meaning the discourse on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-kathā*). Furthermore, that [teaching] is for the purpose of the resolution of the compact mass (*ghana-vinibbhoga*).

Because it is extremely difficult [to master], subtle and delicate, free from the confusion of the tenets of other schools, and endowed with the principle of unity (ekattanaya) and so forth, it is investigated therein;

thus he says, "with perfectly pure and skillful methods. Because it is investigated without abandoning the methods as they have come down in the *Paṭisambhidā* and other texts, its path is not a loose or haphazard one.

17. Regarding the phrase *iti pana sabbaṃ*: the word *iti* indicates completion; the word *pana* is a rhetorical ornament (*vacanālaṅkāra*). Thus, the meaning is "all this. Regarding the word *idha* (here): the intention is that I shall not analyze it in this commentary because it would result in redundancy (*punaruttibhāva*).
18. Now, determining the sole reason for that very non-analysis, he says: "*Majjhe Visuddhimaggo*" and so forth.

Therein, by the expression "*standing in the middle*," which demonstrates its central position, [it is shown that] it is specifically the common commentary (*sādhāraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) for the four Āgamas.
This shows that it is the *Visuddhimagga*, and not like the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* and other such works, which are non-common commentaries (*asādhāraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
Furthermore, the phrase "especially" (*visesato*) is stated with the understanding that the *Visuddhimagga* also serves as a commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma, as appropriate.
19. "Itceva" means "iti eva. "Tampi" refers to the *Visuddhimagga*. "Etāya" refers to the *Manorathapūraṇī*. Here...
By the passage beginning with “brought to the island of Siṃhala,” he shows the cause for the exposition of the meaning;
by the passage “for the benefit of those dwelling on the island, for the satisfaction of the virtuous, and for the long endurance of the Dhamma,” he shows the purpose;
and by the passage beginning with “having removed from there the Siṃhalese language,” he shows the manner of the instrument. In the lower Nikāyas...
For even the non-examination of matters already investigated in the *Visuddhimagga* constitutes here a mode of treatment.
The commentary on the introduction to the treatise is finished.
1. Commentary on the Chapter on Matter, etc. (*Rūpādivagga*)
The Commentary on the Introduction:

Since the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of those things possessing divisions occurs precisely by way of showing their classification, he first spoke the words beginning with “In this regard, that which is called the Aṅguttara Āgama,” in order to demonstrate the classification according to the method of the *nipāta* suttas.
Therein, the word “therein” (*tattha*) refers to [the classification] of the Aṅguttara Āgama.
Regarding the statement, "I shall clarify the meaning," the meaning is that the *Aṅguttara Āgama*— which was promised by the words "I shall clarify the meaning for whom"—
is thus divided according to its *nipāta*, *sutta*, and other categories. Alternatively,
regarding the phrase "the meaning based on the *Aṅguttara*," the meaning is that the *Aṅguttara Āgama* mentioned therein is of such a nature by way of its *nipāta*, *sutta*, and so forth.
Now, desiring to provide a commentary on that [text] starting from the beginning, he said: "In its introductory sections...
the introduction is stated first," etc., in order to show that his own commentary proceeds according to the sequence established during the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti).
Therein, because the Dhamma and Vinaya were taught and laid down in various places according to specific requirements, they were scattered; [the following addresses this].
*Saṅgīti* means singing together after having gathered [the teachings].

By this, the words of the compilers (*saṅgītikāra*)—which were established according to the sequence of connection at the beginning, end, and intervals of each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*) and discourse (*sutta*)—are included.
Because the meaning being recited together is great and worthy of honor, it is called the *Mahāsaṅgīti*, the Great Recitation; that is, the First Great Recitation.
The First Great Council; the time of its occurrence is the time of the First Great Council; at that time of the First Great Council.
It is called a "nidāna" (introductory cause) because it sets forth or points out the teaching by making known what was previously unknown, by way of the place, time, and so forth of the teaching.
That which is called by worldly people an "upodghāta" (introduction), this should be understood here as the textual passage beginning with "Thus have I heard."
It is not the cause for the arising of the teaching through one's own inclination (*ajjhāsaya*), as in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, I teach the Dhamma with its basis" (*sanidāna*).
For this very reason it was said: "The 'Thus have I heard' and so forth is the introduction (*nidāna*) spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council.

Having thus referred by extension to what should be said regarding the external introduction (*bāhiranidāna*) with the words "But this [introduction]," etc., he now begins the internal introduction (*abbhantaranidāna*).
The phrase "but as for this" (*yaṃ panetaṃ*) was stated in order to provide a commentary starting from that point. In that regard, since one who provides a commentary must first show the words,

the analysis of the words, and their meanings regarding the phenomena to be commented upon, and thereafter provide a commentary by way of demonstrating the collective meaning (*piṇḍattha*) and so forth,
he therefore said "‘Evaṃ’ is a particle-word," and so on, in order to first present the words.
In this context, "analysis of words" (*padavibhāga*) refers to the distinction between words, not their grammatical compounding.

Alternatively, it should be understood that by means of the *ekasesa* (single-remainder) compound, both "words" (*pada*) and "analysis of words" (*padavibhāga*)—that is, both word-compounds and word-analyses—are expressed by the term "analysis of words.
Among these, a word-compound is, for example, "Jetassa vanaṃ Jetavanam" (The grove of Jeta is Jetavana), and so forth.
It is to be seen in compound words (*samāsa-padesu*).
"From the meaning" (*atthato*) means from the word-meaning (*padatthato*). Showing that word-meaning first, by way of extracting the meanings, he says "First, the word *evaṃ*...
and so forth. Regarding the phrase "certainty and so forth" (*avadhāraṇādi*), here the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the meanings of "this," "question," "measure," and so on.

The inclusion [of the word *evaṃ*] should be understood. For instance, in such passages as “various fields of craft have come to be thus (*evaṃgatāni*),” and so forth, the word *evaṃ* has the same meaning as the word *idaṃ*.
Indeed, the word *gata* is a synonym for *pakāra* (manner); the same applies to the words *vidha* and *ākāra*.
For worldly people say that when the word *gata* is joined with *vidha*, it signifies the sense of *pakāra* (manner). “Thus indeed were you well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed...”
In such passages as, "Adorned with jeweled earrings and ornaments, dressed in white garments, endowed and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure,
they sport about just as you do now together with your teacher," it refers to a question.
In such passages as, "Thus is its rapid revolution, thus is its limit of lifespan," it refers to a measure.

But is it not the case that in the passage, “Thus indeed you were well-bathed, well-anointed, thus was the limit of your life-span,” the word *evaṃ* (thus) signifies a mode [of being], since it expresses both the mode of questioning and the mode of measurement?

No, because there is a distinction [between the two uses]. For when the word *evaṃ* denotes a mere mode—as in “Thus explained,” and so forth—it is intended to have the sense of a mode; however, it does not denote a specific mode. And so...
Having thus established [the context], the illustrative examples beginning with “By a mortal born in this way... become appropriate.

For instance, in the passage “Just as... much,” the phrase refers to a multitude of things similar to a string of garlands, because they possess qualities such as beauty and fragrance, and because they arise from a collection of causes for merit—such as the attainment of wealth, hearing the true Dhamma, proper attention, reliance on noble persons, rebirth as a human being, and so forth—which stand in the place of a heap of flowers.
Because meritorious deeds are to be performed by a mortal being whose very nature it is to die, they are illustrated by the simile of a heap of flowers or a string of garlands.

Since the manner of that simile was stated without restriction by means of the word "thus" (*yathā*), it is appropriate to say that "the word 'evam' has the sense of concluding the manner of the simile.
However, when that manner of the simile is specified, it becomes in substance the simile itself; thus he said: "In the simile..."

"...has arrived. Likewise, regarding the phrase "thus it should be approached in this manner," etc., the manner of instruction concerning the perfection of deportment (ākappa) befitting a recluse—since that mode of instruction is in substance nothing other than an instruction—it is said: "Thus for you... [etc. ...in the instruction.
Similarly, in the passage "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata," the meaning as spoken by the Blessed One [is confirmed].
“Encouragement” (*sampahaṃsana*) refers to the act of gladdening and inspiring those who know correctly by means of various modes of praising the qualities found therein;
it should be construed as “the manner of encouragement therein.
Likewise, one should construe it here as “the manner of censuring,” and that manner of censuring arises from the presence of disparaging terms such as “outcaste” (*vasalī*).

It is understood that [the meaning] is made manifest right here by the word *evaṃ*. And just as it is here, so too should it be seen that the forms of similes (*upamākāra*) and so forth are present due to the proximity of words such as "heap of flowers" (*puppharāsi*), which are spoken by way of similes and the like.

However, in cases such as "Yes, venerable sir" (*evaṃ, bhante*) and "Indeed" (*kho*), [the meaning] is [manifested] by the monks who have been directed toward the careful hearing and attention of the Dhamma, [indicating] their own state of being established therein.
Because it is spoken by way of formal assent (*paṭijānanavasena*), the word *evaṃ* here is stated to have the sense of accepting what has been said;
thus, it means: "So it is, Bhante; well said, Bhante; excellently said, Bhante.
Furthermore, when it is said, "Speak thus," the manner of speaking—"Speak to the ascetic Ānanda exactly as I speak"—is indicated by the word *evaṃ*, which now expresses that mode of speech.
The sense of illustration has been stated. Regarding the phrase "evam no" (so it is for us):
