here too, in order to produce a firm conviction regarding the fact that those aforementioned phenomena bring about harm and suffering, a question is posed by way of seeking consent—"Is it not so?
How do you stand on this?"—and because the reply given is "evam no ettha hoti" (so it is for us in this matter), the firm conviction regarding that specific mode is clarified by the word "evam."
It is understood. However, when the manner in which those phenomena lead to harm and suffering is being determined, it serves the purpose of restriction (avadhāraṇa);
thus he said: "In 'thus it is for us here,' etc., [the term refers to] restriction.

"Skilled in various methods" refers to those consisting of unity, diversity, non-exertion, and the nature of things—namely, what are known as the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa*, *Tipukkhalaka*, *Sīhavikkīḷita*, *Aṅkusa*, and *Sadisālocana* [methods].

Or, "various methods" (*nānānayā*) refers to the various methods according to the distinctions of the basis (*ādhāra*) and so forth. Alternatively, "methods" (*nayā*) refers to the ways of the textual tradition (*pāḷigati*); and these [ways] exist by way of designation (*paññatti*) and so forth, by way of being partaking of defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth, by way of being mundane (*lokiya*) and so forth, by way of being mixed with both (*tadubhayavomissaka*) and so forth, by way of the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth, by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, by way of the groupings (*saṅgaha*) and so forth, by way of the liberation from time (*samayavimutta*) and so forth, by way of the exertions (*padhāna*) and so forth, by way of the roots of the wholesome (*kusalamūla*) and so forth, and by way of the *Tikapaṭṭhāna* and so forth.
"And of various kinds" (*nānappakārā*) means various methods (*nānānayā*); "skillful in those various methods" (*nānānayanipuṇaṃ*) means subtle, gentle, and refined by them.

"Inclination" (*ajjhāsaya*) is the same as "disposition" (*āsaya*); these are manifold through their divisions such as eternalism and so forth, and through their divisions such as having little defilement and so forth. Alternatively, it is that which has "various inclinations" (*anekajjhāsaya*) as its "source" (*samuṭṭhāna*), meaning its cause of arising; thus, it is "arisen from various inclinations. "Endowed with meaning and phrasing" (*atthabyañjanasampannaṃ*).
It is "complete in meaning and phrasing" because there is nothing further to be added. Alternatively,

the meaning should be understood as being endowed with six factors of meaning— namely, revealing, manifesting, explaining, analyzing, clarifying, and describing— and six factors of phrasing— namely, syllables, words, phrases, modes, etymologies, and expositions.
Regarding the phrase "various miracles" (*vividhapāṭihāriya*), they explain the meaning of the word *pāṭihāriya* as follows:

"It is called a miracle (*pāṭihāriya*) because it removes opposing factors and because it eliminates defilements such as lust. However, the Blessed One has no opposing factors such as lust that need to be removed.

Even for ordinary worldlings, when the mind is free from corruptions and endowed with the eight qualities, its opposing factors have been destroyed; [in this state] the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) [arise].
Because it occurs [only] there, it cannot be designated as a "manifestation" (pāṭihāriya) here by way of the conventional usage current in that context.

However, if it is said to be a "manifestation" because it carries away the defilements residing in those to be converted—which are the adversaries of the Blessed One, the Greatly Compassionate One—then this is appropriate.
Alternatively, they are the adversaries of both the Blessed One and his Teaching.
“Titthiyā”: it is a miracle (*pāṭihāriya*) because of their being taken away.

For they have been taken away and removed by means of the higher powers (*iddhi*), the mind-reading (*ādesanā*), and the instruction (*anusāsanī*), both by way of taking away their views and by way of their inability to manifest their own views.
Alternatively, this word *paṭi* conveys the meaning of "after," as in such passages as: "When he had entered [the water], another brahmin arrived. etc.

Therefore, because one must subsequently remove [the defilements] and set [the mind] in motion once the mind has been concentrated, free from defilements, and the task has been accomplished, it is called *paṭihāriya* (wonderful).
Alternatively, when one's own defilements have been removed by means of the fourth jhāna and the paths [of the noble ones], that subsequent removal is *paṭihāriya*.

Furthermore, the supernormal powers (*iddhi*), the telepathic reading (*ādesanā*), and the instruction (*anusāsani*) are for the benefit of beings by one who is free from defilements and has accomplished the task.
They must be performed again; and because they remove the defilements of other beings from one’s own green (harita) defilements, they are called *paṭihāriya*.

A *paṭihāriya* is simply a *pāṭihāriya*; or, that which exists within the collection of wonders consisting of psychic power (*iddhi*), instruction (*ādesanā*), and admonition (*anusāsanī*) is called each individual *pāṭihāriya*.
Alternatively, the fourth jhāna and the Path are *paṭihāriya* because they remove opposing factors.
*Pāṭihāriya* means that which is born therein, or that which has that as its sign, or that which has come from that; thus it is a "miracle.

Since this [term] is found in the teaching of the Blessed One in many forms—due to the divisions such as *iddhi* (supernormal power) and due to the divisions of its objects—he says: "the manifold miracle" (*vividhapāṭihāriya*).
"Not otherwise" means not otherwise than the manner in which it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One; however, it does not mean [not otherwise] than the Blessed One...
[It is explained] by way of the modes of teaching. For the Blessed One’s teaching possesses inconceivable power.
And by taking it thus, the statement, "Who is capable of understanding it in every aspect? is validated;

furthermore, this does not contradict the demonstration of the power of retention, because what is intended is that there is no contradiction with the modes of what has been heard. For here, there is no need to avoid the charge of [the two statements] having different meanings.
This is because they share the same objective; otherwise, one would have to conclude that the Elder was either entirely capable or entirely incapable of receiving the Blessed One’s teaching.
This is because [the term "self"] is applied to one's own continuity—designated as "one's own internal" (*niyakajjhatta*)—in the statement: "That which is not another is the self."
Although the word *me* is seen in only one sense— namely, as a designation for the instrument (*karaṇa*), the recipient (*sampadāna*), and the possessor (*sāmī*)—
it is stated with reference to its existing distinctions that “the word *me* is seen in three senses.
Furthermore, although a prefix (*upasagga*) qualifies an action, because it functions merely as an indicator, even when it is present, the word *suta* itself [remains the primary term].

He said, "Both with a prefix and without a prefix," demonstrating that when the word *suta* (heard) is being extracted for its meaning in the sense of "it speaks of this or that matter" (*taṃ tamatthaṃ vadati*), it is not contradictory to include the form with a prefix. "Of it" (*assa*) refers to the word *suta*.

Since the instrumental (*kamma*) and abstract (*bhāva*) derivations are possible here for the word *suta*, he stated: "either as 'that which is held' (*upadhārita*) or as 'the holding' (*upadhāraṇa*)."
"Or else, it is the meaning. Regarding "when *mayā* has the sense [of the agent]," this means: when the word *me* functions as an instrument by way of its being the agent, then [it is so].
Regarding "when *mamam* has the sense [of the possessor]," this means: when it functions as a possessor by way of its relationship [to the object], then [it is so].
It is stated that there must be the word *evaṃ*, which indicates the act of hearing and is employed for the purpose of definitively establishing the word *suta*.
"—thus [it is] a demonstration of the function of consciousnesses such as ear-consciousness.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of the receiving consciousnesses and so forth belonging to the ear-door, as well as those consciousnesses belonging to the mind-door that are directed toward them.
Since all sentences possess the sense of the particle "only" (eva), the meaning "heard only" (sutameva) is obtained for the term "heard" (suta).
He said: "By way of the negation of the state of not having heard. By this restriction, he shows the necessity (niyāmatā).
And just as that which is heard must be determined as "heard indeed," so too it is "properly heard"; thus he said: "The indication of grasping [the meaning] without deficiency, excess, or error.
Alternatively, a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meanings of other words; thus, "heard" means it is not un-heard.
"This is its meaning" was said as: "by way of the negation of the state of not having heard. By this, he effects the exclusion of [the claim that it was] seen and so forth.
This is what is meant: "This has not been seen by me, nor realized through self-become knowledge (sayambhuñāṇa);
rather, it has been heard, and that too correctly. For this very reason, he said: "It is an indication of a grasp that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor perverted."
Alternatively, when the word *evaṃ* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇatthe*), this is the application of the meaning:

the word *suta* (heard), which depends on [the verb] *karīyati* (is made), has this meaning stated because it negates the state of not hearing. For this very reason, he said: "It is an indication of grasping that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor erroneous.
And here, the word *savana* should be understood as having the sense of the object (*kammattho*), as in "it is heard" (*suyyati*).

Having thus shown the application of the meaning of the three terms in one way by means of the distinction between the cause of hearing and the hearing itself, he now says "In the same way" and so forth, in order to show that [application] by other modes.
Therein, "of that" refers to that cognitive process of the mind-door (*manodvāraviññāṇavīthi*) which occurred in the presence of the Blessed One in the manner of hearing the Dhamma; for it...
Capable of occurring with respect to an object in various ways. And so it has been said: "By way of the ear-door.
"In various ways" means in the diverse manner of grasping the phrasing and meaning of the many types [of sounds] that are about to be mentioned.
By this, he indicates that in this construction, the word *evaṃ* (thus) is taken in the sense of "manner" (*ākāra*). "The manifestation of the state of occurrence" refers to the occurrence...

The phrase "atthibhāvappakāsanaṃ" means the manifestation of existence. Regarding "sutaṃ," it is said to be the manifestation of the phenomenon (*dhamma*); that is, because the object upon which the aforementioned course of consciousness (*viññāṇavīthi*) proceeds in its various modes is a phenomenon, it is so described, not because the word "heard" (*suta*) itself possesses the nature of a phenomenon.

The clarification of the very meaning already stated begins with "This, indeed, herein... and so forth. In that context, the term "viññāṇavīthiyā" is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇatthe*), while "mayā" is used in the sense of an agent (*kattuatthe*).

Thus, the word *evaṃ* (thus) is employed for the purpose of pointing out, as it serves to indicate the manner in which that which is to be demonstrated is to be shown—since there is no other way for that which is to be demonstrated to be indicated.
By means of that word *evaṃ*, he shows that the entire sutta is referred back [to the preceding context].
Because the word *suta* (heard) is a verb, and because the act of hearing is dependent upon a common continuum of consciousness (*viññāṇappabandha*).
And therein it is said, "the designation of a person" (*puggalavohāra*): "The word 'heard' (*suta*) is the manifestation of a person's function.
For the act of hearing is not found in a mere succession of phenomena (*dhammapabandha*) devoid of the designation of a person.
In such expressions as "of whichever mental continuum," the word *evaṃ* is taken in the sense of manner (*ākāra*), and thus [it is] otherwise than in the previous construction.

This was stated in order to demonstrate the eightfold application (*atthayojana*). Therein, "manifestation by way of aspect" (*ākārapaññatti*) is precisely a manifestation by way of dependence (*upādāpaññatti*), so called because it takes as its basis the mode of occurrence of phenomena.

"The heard" (*suta*) is a designation for the object; it is stated thus because the phenomenon that constitutes what is to be heard is the locus of occurrence for the person who is the agent of the act of hearing, by virtue of that act of hearing. [Regarding] that which is distinct from the continuum of consciousness...
Although in the ultimate sense there is no agent whatsoever, it is stated— by way of conventional linguistic usage—

that "the possessor [of the stream] is [known] by means of the mental continuum," having treated that possessor as if distinct from the mental continuum due to a desire for speech involving a distinction imagined by the intellect.
Furthermore, the dhamma to be heard, which is the object of the act of hearing, is here [referred to] in terms of the mental continuum proceeding by way of the act of hearing.
In the ultimate sense, because there is no state of an agent, or because the activity of hearing exists only as the occurrence of consciousness by way of listening,
it is said— taking into account that this [consciousness] is the agent of that activity and its object—

that "it belongs to the agent who possesses it. And because the Elder, whose manner of learning was characterized by right discernment, stated, "the conclusion of grasping," this is said for the purpose of emphasis.
It should be understood that by taking the word *evaṃ*, this application of meaning has been made.
The word *evaṃ* has the nature of manifesting the determination, the indication, or the ascertainment of the form of the variously arranged meanings and phrasing—termed "suttas"—previously heard;
it is for the purpose of determining that form and so forth.

Because the designation of a person (*puggalapaññatti*) consists in the functioning of a continuum of phenomena that serve as its basis, it is said: “‘Thus’ is the description of the function of the person.
However, since even for a proponent of a person there is no act of hearing independent of consciousness, it is specifically the function of consciousness; thus he says:
“‘Hearing’ is the description of the function of consciousness. Because the occurrence of the word “I” refers exclusively to the category of sentient beings...
And because the function of consciousness must be integrated right there [in that person], it is said: "‘Me’ is a designation for a person endowed with both functions.

Since the meanings of the words *evaṃ* (thus) and *suta* (heard) respectively consist in non-existent designations (*avijjamāna-paññatti*) and existent designations (*vijjamāna-paññatti*), he says—showing them by way of their operation as the basis for such designations: "'Evaṃ' is a designation for the function of the person..."
"Suta" is a designation for the function of consciousness. In this context, it should be understood that four applications of meaning—the second and subsequent ones—are demonstrated:
by way of clarifying the distinctions among instrument, action, agent, and object; by way of indicating the person's activity and the sphere of that person's activity;
by way of designating the mode of apprehension, the act of apprehending, and the specific object; and by way of designating the agent, the instrument, the activity, and the agent.
Since one must proceed by way of the conceptual designation (*paññatti*) alone for every meaning that is to be understood through words,
and since all designations are included within the sixfold division of designations— beginning with "existent" (*vijjamāna*) and so forth—

he stated, "‘Thus’ (*evaṃ*) and ‘I’ (*meṃ*) and so on," while determining the specific nature of the designations such as "thus" among them. Therein, regarding the meaning expressed as "thus" and "I":
Because states such as the aspect (ākāra) and so forth lack the nature of being clearly perceived, they possess the status of a designation for what does not exist; thus it is said:
"A designation for what does not exist by way of the true and ultimate sense. In this context, "by way of the true and ultimate sense" means by way of the actual reality and the supreme reality.
This is what is meant: that which is unreal, like a magical illusion, a mirage, and so forth, and which is to be grasped through hearsay and the like—

And that which is not the ultimate meaning—that is, the nature of visible forms, sounds, and so forth, or the nature of being affected, experiencing, and so forth—is called the "actual meaning" (saccikaṭṭha) and the "ultimate meaning" (paramattha);
the meaning of the phrases "thus it was said by me" is not like that. To make this very point clearer, the passage beginning with "What is there in this?
was stated. However, the word "heard" (suta) is said with reference to the sense-sphere of sound (saddāyatana).
—“It is a designation for what exists. For it is precisely for this reason that it is said: “That which is here apprehended by the ear.
However, when it is said “apprehended by way of the ear-door,” everything including the meaning (attha) and the phrasing (byañjana) is included.
Because it can be expressed by depending on this or that [factor], it refers to the aspects, etc., as they are determined in relation to those phenomena that have come within the range of the ear.
The meaning is: "In this way" refers to the act of referring back; it signifies that the designation "this" must be applied by taking as a basis the aggregates included within one's own continuity.

Although the conventional usage of "heard" occurs in relation to the sense-sphere of sound—which is devoid of the intrinsic nature of being seen and so forth—just like the expressions "second" or "third," it proceeds by depending upon what was previously seen, heard, or cognized. Therefore, he said: "in comparison with what was seen and so forth."
"Because it ought to be spoken. For this meaning—that what has not been heard is not "heard"—is what is being clarified.
The Elder replied, "It illuminates non-delusion," meaning that these are indeed the specific modes of the Sutta as realized by himself.
By the phrase "one who is capable of penetrating in various ways," he indicates the manifold nature of the Sutta that is about to be explained.
And it shows that which is difficult to penetrate. "It illuminates the non-forgetting of what has been heard" is said because the mode of hearing is being shown according to its true nature.
"By non-delusion" means by the absence of delusion; or rather, it refers to the establishment of wisdom at a later time based on the wisdom already produced at the time of hearing.
The same should be said regarding the phrase "by non-forgetting. The mode to be penetrated in the case of the phonemes (*byañjana*) is not excessively profound.

In this context, since "the retention of what has been heard exactly as it was" is the task to be performed, the activity of mindfulness (*sati*) is predominant, while wisdom (*paññā*) is subordinate;

thus it is said: "preceded by wisdom," etc., having taken it as "wisdom is the precursor. Here, "precursor-ship" (*pubbaṅgamatā*) means the state of being primary, as in such expressions as "mind is the precursor" (*manopubbaṅgamā*);
or else, by way of precursor-ship, [it refers to] the functions such as adverting (*āvajjana*) in relation to eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) and the rest.

The meaning "wisdom is the precursor to this [insight] because it is subordinate to it" is also appropriate; thus, in the phrase "preceded by mindfulness," the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated, as far as applicable.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with both meaning and phrasing": this means being complete in both meaning and phrasing, by way of making known, manifesting, explaining, analyzing, clarifying, and describing.

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as: "endowed with six word-meanings" by way of the six [factors] consisting of letter, word, phoneme, mode, etymology, and exposition; and "with six phoneme-words.
By the word *evaṃ*, it illuminates appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) through its meanings of indicating a mode, pointing out, and determining those things being spoken of.
The intended meaning is that its object is the true Dhamma (saddhamma) without error.

"It illuminates non-distraction" is said because, in response to questions such as "Wherein is the 'taking hold of the mind' spoken of?", it is considered that the hearing of the Sutta—which is introduced here and will be explained—is not possible without concentration (samādhi). "Of one whose mind is distracted," and so forth, serves to corroborate that very point.
It has been said. "By all perfections" means by the perfection of meaning, phrasing, teacher, application, and so forth.

Just as right attention is [established] by the aspects, indications, and determinations which have the true Dhamma as their object, and non-distraction is [established] by the hearing of the true Dhamma, so too, by right attention—which is the fruit—there is the state of having rightly directed oneself and having previously performed merit.

Success (*siddhi*) is stated because it is inseparable from that. Thus, by means of non-distraction as the fruit, the success of the causes—namely, hearing the true Dhamma and relying upon virtuous persons (*sappurisa*)—should be demonstrated;
for these do not exist in one who has not heard the Dhamma and lacks reliance upon virtuous persons.
Furthermore, by the statement "one whose mind is not distracted," etc., which expresses capability, non-distraction as the cause is shown through reliance upon virtuous persons.
And the accomplishment of hearing the True Dhamma, which is the fruit [of non-distraction], has been shown. However, this following interpretation would be more appropriate here:
"The support of a good person (*sappurisūpanissaya*) and the hearing of the True Dhamma are not exclusively the causes of non-distraction, because they are external factors;
rather, non-distraction—just like the support of a good person—is an exclusive cause for the hearing of the True Dhamma. Even so...
The demonstration that the accomplishment of relying upon a true person (*sappurisūpanissaya*) is not possible without non-distraction (*avikkhepa*) is indeed not unfeasible.
It is not unfeasible because for those with distracted minds, the very absence of attending upon a true person results in the failure to achieve their purpose.

Herein, the first [example] shows the establishment of a cause by means of its fruit, like the presence of rain upstream indicated by the swelling of a river; the second shows the fruit by means of its cause.
The manifestation of success is to be seen as the occurrence of rain through the rising of a cloud that rains unceasingly.

It is said, "Such is the auspicious manner," because the manner of penetrating the entire excellence of the Dispensation—by way of the distinctions and divisions of the meaning and phrasing of the Blessed One’s word—is the cause for the complete fulfillment of the welfare of others without remainder. Since... [the sentence continues: no...
The connection is "it occurs. "The attainment of the latter two wheels" refers to the pair of qualities consisting of right aspiration for oneself and merit performed in the past.

Furthermore, they are called "wheels" (*cakka*) because of their revolving function; or alternatively, because by means of these, sentient beings move through states of fortunate rebirth (*sampatti-bhava*).
With reference to these, it was said: "Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels, endowed with which gods and humans..."
"...the four wheels turn," and so forth. Here, the sequence of "prior" and "subsequent" should be understood according to the order of the teaching.
"By means of the accomplishment of the latter two wheels" means by virtue of the existence of the latter two wheels.

One whose self is rightly directed, who has previously performed merit, and whose aspiration is pure, becomes so because the defilements that are the causes for the non-accomplishment of those [wheels] have been distanced; thus he said: "purity of aspiration."
“It becomes accomplished. For it has been said: “A rightly directed mind will make him better than before,” and, “You have performed merit, Ānanda;
apply yourself to striving, and you will soon be free from the taints. Therefore he said:

“Through purity of disposition, there is the accomplishment of proficiency in attainment. Regarding “purity of application”: [it refers to] that which is preceded by wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra).
This is due to the clarity of one's application to hearing the Dhamma. Thus it is said: "the accomplishment of proficiency in the scriptures.

Alternatively, it is because of the faultlessness of all bodily and vocal application. For one whose bodily and vocal application is completely pure becomes undistracted in mind—due to the absence of remorse—and thus gains confidence in the textual tradition (pariyatti).

By the passage beginning "by way of illuminating the penetration of various aspects," etc., he demonstrates the application of the meaning by means of the four analytical knowledges (*catuppaṭisambhidā*),

because it illustrates the Elder’s lack of confusion regarding the words *evaṃ* and *suta* within both the meaning and the phrasing. Therein, by the phrase "by way of illuminating the penetration of the various divisions of what is heard" (*sotappabhedapaṭivedhadīpakena*),

this word *suta*— due to its proximity to the word *evaṃ*, or by virtue of its dependence on what is yet to be said— is shown in a general sense to refer to the specific categories of the phenomena that are to be heard.

This shows that [the Buddha] causes [them] to touch. The thorough investigation and correct penetration of the scriptural teachings (pariyatti-dhamma) that form the basis for mental views are especially bound up with attention (manasikāra);

thus, by connecting them with the word "thus" (evaṃ), which illustrates wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra) according to the method already stated, it is shown that the scriptural teachings—consisting of hearing, memorizing, and verbal mastery—are especially bound up with the application of the ear (sotāvadhāna).
Connecting this with the word "heard" (*suta*), which illuminates non-distraction, he shows it and generates enthusiasm for hearing the Dhamma as a perfection of the Dispensation.
In that context, "Dhammas" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*). "Examined by the mind" means:
"Here the virtue is taught, here the concentration, here the wisdom; there are so many connections here," and so forth, according to this method, by means of the mind.

"Examined one by one": they have been thoroughly penetrated through a view that has become "delightful contemplation" (*nijjhānakkhanti*), or through a view consisting of "full understanding through knowledge" (*ñātapariññā*);
that is, having well-defined those material and immaterial phenomena mentioned here and there as "this is material form," "material form is only this much," and so forth, they have been penetrated.
"By the entire statement" is said because it was previously joined separately with each of the three phrases.

"The plane of the bad person" refers to ingratitude; it is the state of ignoble speech described thus: "In this case, a certain evil bhikkhu, having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, burns [them] within himself. That very state of ignoble speech is the non-Dhamma (*asaddhamma*).

But is it not the case that the statement regarding the transcendence of the plane of the unworthy and so forth is purposeless, since the Elder Ānanda lacked the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) of thinking "this is my word," and the Elders Mahākassapa and others likewise lacked any suspicion of such a claim? This is not so;
for by one who says, "Thus have I heard," this meaning is also demonstrated. Some, however, [say] of the deities...
"Speech that depends on reflection," they say, "is such a reproach that it finds no occasion.
For at that moment, it is said, a reflection arose in the minds of certain deities: "The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna;
yet this venerable one, skilled in teaching, now teaches the Dhamma—he who was born of the Sakyan clan, the brother of the Tathāgata, the son of his younger paternal uncle."

"Does he teach a Dhamma that he has realized for himself, or is it merely the word of the Blessed One as he has heard it?"—thus, by way of such doubt and by way of entering the plane of a person of no integrity, the "transcending" and so forth are explained. "Not attributing to oneself" means not establishing [the teaching] within oneself with the thought, "This is mine.
"He offers up" means he points it out. Regarding the goals pertaining to this life, the life to come, and the ultimate goal...
It is a "guide" (*netti*) because it leads beings according to what is appropriate; since it is the Dhamma itself that is the guide, it is called the "Guide to the Dhamma" (*dhammanetti*).
Doubt (*kaṅkhā*) is a state of uncertainty firmly established. Indecision (*vimati*) is a mere divergence of opinion without excessive wandering.

It destroys lack of faith because it was spoken by the Blessed One, because it was received directly from him, and because it is free from the fault of errors such as slips of the tongue or harsh speech.
And here, the three interpretations beginning with the fifth are shown by taking the word *evaṃ* in the sense of "manner" (*ākāra*) and so forth, without grasping any specific distinction;
the four following it are elucidated by taking the word *evaṃ* solely in the sense of "manner";
but the final three take the word *evaṃ* respectively in the sense of "manner," "illustration" (*nidassana*), and "restriction" (*avadhāraṇa*).
It should be understood as "joined" (*yojitā*).
The word *eka* is seen in the senses of "other than," "best," "without companion," and "number. For instance, in such passages as, "Some assert thus: 'The self and the world are eternal;
this alone is the truth, all else is vain,'" it is seen in the sense of "other than. [In the passage] "of the mind... [it is used in the sense of "alone"].
In such passages as “the state of being one” (*ekodibhāva*), it means “best”; in such passages as “alone, withdrawn,” it means “without companion”;

and in such passages as “Bhikkhus, there is indeed only one moment and one occasion for living the holy life” (*brahmacariyavāsa*), it means “reckoning. Here too, showing that it means “reckoning,” he says:
“‘One’ is a designation for a limit of number. “The time and the occasion” means both the appropriate time and the completeness of conditions.

*Khaṇa* means opportunity (*okāsa*). For the arising of a Tathāgata and so forth is the opportunity for the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*), because it is the cause for obtaining its requisite conditions.
*Khaṇa* itself is *samaya*. The meaning is that what is called both *khaṇa* and *samaya* is one and the same thing. *Mahāsamaya* means a great assembly (*mahāsamūha*).
*Samayopi kho* means even the cause for fulfilling the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). *Samayappavādake* means those who propound wrong views (*diṭṭhippavādaka*).
For it is there that the followers of other sects (tīrthikas), sitting down, proclaim their respective doctrines.
"The convergence of meaning" (atthābhisamaya) refers to the attainment of welfare. "That which is to be fully understood" (abhisametabbo) is "convergence" (abhisamaya);

thus, "the convergence of meaning" (abhisamayaṭṭho) means that oppression and the rest are spoken of by being brought into a state of unity through their quality of being what must be fully understood. Alternatively, "the convergence of meaning" means the meaning that constitutes the object of convergence, that is, of penetration (paṭivedha).
These very [terms] are thus stated as synonyms. Therein, "affliction" (*pīḷana*) is the harming of one who possesses that [truth], making them unable to expand.
"Torment" (*santāpa*) is the burning and scorching by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*) and so forth.

In this context, "occasion" (*samaya*) means that which brings together (*sameti*) or meets with (*samaveti*) the auxiliary causes; it is a conjunction (*samavāya*). It brings together (*sameti*) or comes together (*samāgacchati*).
In this context, "occasion" (*samaya*) refers to the holy life of the path (*magga-brahmacariya*) and the persons who are its basis; it is an "opportunity" (*khaṇa*).

Alternatively, it is an "occasion" (*samaya*) because a sentient being or a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*) comes together (*sameti*) with co-nascent factors or with [the characteristics of] arising and so forth; thus it is "time" (*kāla*).
For although time does not exist as a substantial entity apart from the mere occurrence of phenomena, it is nonetheless the locus or the instrument for the occurrence of phenomena.
And it is designated by a form established merely through conceptual construction (*kappanāmatta*). "Sama" means equal, or "saha" means together;
the going, proceeding, or persisting of the parts is "samaya," just as in the term "samudāya" (collection). For a collection is precisely the persisting together of the parts.
Furthermore, "samaya" is that from which the fruit comes (*eti*)—that is, arises and proceeds—through the coming together (*samāgama*) of the remaining conditions.

The cause is as in the phrase "the origin" (*samudaya*). It is called *samaya* because it comes together (*sameti*) and is bound (*saṃyojana-bhāvato*), or because it proceeds (*eti*) within its own domain;
or because beings proceed (*ayanti*) and function (*pavattanti*) in connection with it (*saṃyuttā*) according to their respective inclinations (*yathābhinivesaṃ*).
Thus, *samaya* is view (*diṭṭhi*). For by the fetter of views (*diṭṭhi-saṃyojana*), beings are exceedingly bound. *Samiti*, *saṅgati*, and *samodhānaṃ* mean coming together.
"Samaya" means attainment; it is "samaya" because it is the vehicle of the well-composed (*samas*), or because there is a complete departure (*apagama*) through right proceeding (*sammā-yāna*).
It is "pahāna" (abandonment). "Abhisamaya" means that which is to be approached rightly and realized directly by means of knowledge; it is the non-perverted intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.
"Abhisamaya" also means that which goes toward and awakens to rightly by way of direct confrontation; it is the awakening to the non-perverted intrinsic nature of phenomena. Thus...

The application of the word *samaya* to each respective meaning should be understood. Regarding the extraction of the meanings of the word *samaya*, the example of the word *abhisamaya* should be understood according to the method already stated. "Of it" (*assā*) refers to the word *samaya*.

Its meaning here is "time," because other meanings such as "assemblage" (*samavāya*) and so forth are impossible in this context, just as [time is the meaning] for a discourse (*sutta*) with respect to its place, teacher, and audience.
And because time must be indicated as being the causal condition (*nidāna*).
Why, then, is time specified here in an unrestricted manner rather than by defining it through seasons, years, and so forth?
To this he says: "In that regard, although... and so on. Without establishing a restriction by way of seasons, years, and so forth, [he uses] the word *samaya*...
Showing that this quality is also obtained in the statement [of the Blessed One], he said, "Or those who... and so forth. For a general description settles upon a specific instance.

Therein, the occasion for dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*) is the time spent day by day in the attainment of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), specifically during the seven-week period.
They are "well-manifested" (*suppakāsa*) because of the manifestation of light, trembling, and other such phenomena throughout the ten-thousandfold world system.
[These periods] are evident. To show how these very periods, as previously classified, can be subsumed under different categories, he says, "And that which...
and so forth. For indeed, the period of the function of knowledge and the period of practice for one's own welfare constitute the period of full enlightenment;

the period of noble silence and the period of dwelling in happiness in this very life constitute the period of teaching; and the period of the function of compassion, the period of practice for the welfare of others, and the period of discourse on the Dhamma constitute the period of teaching alone.
The connection is: "The exposition is made by means of the instrumental case. "Therein" refers to the Abhidhamma and Vinaya. "In that way" refers to the locative and instrumental cases.

The sense of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) is the sense of "support" (*ādhāra*). "State" (*bhāva*) is indeed action; the definition of one state by another state through action is "the definition of a state by a state" (*bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇaṃ*).
In this regard, just as time—though itself non-existent in the ultimate sense—is [designated] by way of being a support, delimited by phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*).
It is designated [as "born"] because of its occurrence at that very moment and its non-existence prior to or subsequent to it— as in such expressions as "born in the forenoon,

going in the evening," and so forth. Furthermore, although a collection (*samūha*) does not exist apart from its constituent parts and is established merely through conceptual construction (*kappanāmatta*),
it is nevertheless designated as the locus (*ādhāra*) of those parts— as in such expressions as "a branch on a tree" or "grown in a heap of barley."
Showing that it is the same here as well, he says: “The legal issue... of phenomena. The meaning there is this:

at the very time when a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen in a collection of phenomena, at that same time, contact and the other [mental factors] are also present in that collection of phenomena.
This is just as in the expression, “He went while the cows were being milked; he returned when they had been milked,” where [the action of milking serves as the temporal reference].

The action of going is characterized [by the act of arriving]; likewise, here too, when it is said "at whatever time," the meaning "while existing" (satī) is understood as a matter of course, because the state of the word-meaning lacks an absence of existence.

Thus, by the action of existence of the *samaya*, the action of arising of the mind and the action of becoming of contact and the other [mental factors] are characterized. "At whatever time" (*yasmiṃ samaye*).
In whichever ninth moment, in whichever cause such as wise attention (yonisomanasikāra), or in whichever assemblage of conditions (paccayasamavāya) it may be,

when a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness (kāmāvacara-kusala-citta) has arisen, at that very same moment— and in that very same cause and assemblage of conditions— contact (phassa) and the other factors also exist. Thus,
showing that the locative case ending is used for both terms [“moment” and “cause/conditions”] because they are connected with a state that serves as a defining characteristic (lakkhaṇa), he says:
He said: "The moment... is characterized.

The sense of cause (*hetu*) and the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) are possible here, as in such examples as "he dwells by means of food," "he dwells by means of study," "he cuts with an axe," or "he digs with a spade.
For, having heard of the transgression, he convened the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and, having descended [into the matter]...
Having questioned that individual regarding the matter and having rebuked him, the Blessed One— without letting the time when the matter was brought forward pass by,
but rather prescribing the training rules at that very moment while considering the reason for the prescription of the rules,
as in the case of the third *pārājika* and others— dwells [thereby].
From the very beginning of his undertaking until the conclusion of the teaching, [the Buddha] remained in the abiding of compassion, which is defined as the practice for the benefit of others.

"For the purpose of indicating that meaning" means for the purpose of indicating the sense of absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*); thus, the accusative case ending is employed, as in the expression "he studies for a month" (*māsam ajjheti*).
"The ancient ones" refers to the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*). "A mere difference in expression" means by way of the mere phrasing of the words.
This is the distinction. By this, he shows that the analysis of the grammatical cases (*vibhattivyattaya*) has been performed regarding the Suttas and the Vinaya.
Now, in order to show the meaning of the term "Bhagavā," he says: "Bhagavā means 'the venerable one' (*garū*)," and so forth.
The word "Bhagavā" is the best; it is a word expressing excellence. It is said to be "best" because it is accompanied by excellent qualities. Alternatively,
*Vuccati* means "that which is spoken"; this is the meaning. Since the meaning that is to be expressed by the word "Bhagavā" is supreme, it is the sense of "best.

This same principle applies here as well to the phrase "the word *Bhagavā* is the highest. *Gāravayutto* means "endowed with the state of being venerable," due to his connection with qualities that inspire reverence.
Alternatively, he is "endowed with reverence" (*gāravayutto*) because he deserves exceptional honor; the meaning is that he is one who is worthy of reverence (*gāravāraho*).
Some say that while teachers who instruct in crafts and the like are venerable, they are not worthy of reverence;

however, this [teacher] is not such a person, and therefore, having said "venerable," it is further stated that he is "worthy of reverence. The intention is that he is indeed so described, and need not be stated here again, because this commentary is but a portion of the *Visuddhimagga*.

"It makes the body of the Dhamma manifest" is said because there exists a figurative expression for the Dhamma as the Teacher, based on the statement: "Ānanda, the Dhamma and the Vinaya which have been taught and laid down by me—those shall be your teachers after my passing.
His body is like a diamond-mass because his physical frame is indivisible by others; for indeed, in the Blessed One’s material body...

"Is it possible for anyone to create an obstacle? [He says this] because he indicates the excellence of the teaching by pointing out that the entire sutta which is about to be spoken is thus [perfect]. He indicates the excellence of the disciple by saying:

"It was heard by me, a great disciple established by the Blessed One in the foremost place among five categories because of his attainment of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā); and furthermore, what I have heard is not hearsay."
This is because it illuminates the meaning that [the teachings] do not descend through a mere succession.

It indicates the perfection of time by means of the word *samaya*, which is employed in conjunction with the term *Bhagavā*, because it illuminates that the time is adorned by the arising of a Buddha.
For the perfection of time has the arising of a Buddha as its supreme excellence. Therefore, this is said:—
“In this degenerate age, the Kaliyuga, the arising of a Buddha is indeed a great marvel—
like a lotus with fully developed nectar born in the midst of a consuming fire. Here,
by the term “Bhagavā,” he indicates the excellence of the Teacher, because it is a designation for one who possesses supreme qualities and is revered as the highest among beings.
"In the city named thus": how did this city come to have such a name? It is said:

just as the city built at the dwelling place of the seer Kākanda was called Kākandī, that built at the dwelling place of Mākanda was called Mākandī, and that built at the dwelling place of Kusamba was called Kosambī, so too [the city built] at the dwelling place of the seer Savattha...
The city that was built is called Sāvatthī. Thus, first of all, the etymologists say. However, the teachers of the commentaries (Aṭṭhakathācariyā) state:
"Whatever is a requisite for human enjoyment or use, all that exists here"—thus it is Sāvatthī.
Furthermore, when asked in the context of a market, "What goods are there?", the reply "Everything is there" (sabbaṃ atthi) is based upon which [the name] Sāvatthī is derived.
“Every kind of requisite was always provided for in Sāvatthī;
therefore, taking all these things into account, it is called ‘Sāvatthī.
It is the delightful city of the Kosalans, beautiful to behold and enchanting.”
“Never devoid of the ten sounds, supplied with food and drink,
having attained growth and abundance, prosperous, flourishing, and delightful—
Sāvatthī is the supreme city, like the Āḷakamandā of the gods.”
"Without distinction" means not by way of a specific distinction, but by way of the commonality of the state of abiding (*vihāra*);
this is the meaning. "The abiding in postures... [etc. ...in these abidings" refers to these four abidings: the abiding in postures, the divine abiding, the sublime abiding, and the noble abiding.
"Illuminating possession" means the illumination of the state of being possessed. "This" refers to the word "abides. For it is said: "In this case, someone, associated with householders..."
In such passages as, “He dwells with joy and with sorrow,” it refers to dwelling in the postures (*iriyāpatha*).
In such passages as, “Bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and dwells in the first jhāna,” it refers to divine dwelling (*dibbavihāra*).
In such passages as, “He dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,” it refers to sublime dwelling (*brahmavihāra*). He… [text continues]
“Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that very discourse, right there upon that same prior object of concentration,
I settle my mind within myself, I compose it, I unify it, and I concentrate it— that by which I indeed dwell for all time”— in such passages,
this refers to the noble dwelling (ariyavihāra).
In this context, *iriyā* means moving or proceeding; it is bodily effort. Because standing and so forth are the means for the occurrence of that [effort], they are called *iriyāpatha*.
For one who possesses the state of standing might perform some action with the body, or likewise one who possesses any other of the [postures] such as walking and so on.
Alternatively, *iriyā* is that by which the personal existence (*attabhāva*) moves or proceeds, or by which bodily functions proceed; it is the occurrence of that [movement].
"Posture" (*iriyāpatha*) means "a way" (*patha*) because it is a means; it refers specifically to standing and so forth.

In its actual sense, it is simply a continuity of the fourfold material phenomena (*rūpa*) proceeding in the manner of moving, stopping, and so on. It is called "dwelling" (*vihāra*) because it is a dwelling, or because one dwells by means of it.

"Divine" (*dibba*) means existing in the heavens (*divi*); the meaning is that it exists in the divine worlds such as those of the *Brahmapārisajja* gods due to its frequent occurrence there. In that regard:
That which leads to divine power is "divine" (*dibba*); or, it is "divine" because it possesses a great range due to the exertion of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).

It is a "divine abiding" (*dibbavihāra*) because it is both divine and an abiding; these are the four fine-material-sphere attainments (*rūpāvacara-samāpatti*). The formless attainments (*arūpa-samāpatti*) are also included herein.
They are "divine abidings" (*brahmavihāra*) because they are the abidings of Brahmas, or because they are themselves Brahmas and are abidings; these are the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*).
The noble state, or the dwelling of the noble ones, is the "noble dwelling," which refers to the four fruits of recluseship.

For although the Blessed One is capable of maintaining his physical existence for a much longer time even by means of a single posture, it was nevertheless stated [in this way] to show that such is the inherent nature of the body comprised of the four great elements (*upādinnaka*).
Or else, because the Blessed One—wherever [he dwells]— [Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete. The translation above reflects the portion available.]
Dwelling in some place, teaching the Dhamma to those who are to be trained, and spending his time in various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
he carries, brings, and produces manifold welfare and happiness for beings and for himself; therefore,
"he dwells" (*viharati*) is to be understood here as "he carries [it] in various ways" (*vividhaṃ harati*).
Regarding the phrase "of Prince Jeta": here, he is called *Jeta* because he conquers (*jināti*) his own enemies; for the word *jeta* functions as an agent-noun, just like the word *sota* (ear).
Alternatively, he is called *Jeta* because he was born when King Pasenadi of Kosala had conquered his enemies;
for the prince is called *Jeta*, meaning "the Conqueror," by attributing the king’s victory to himself out of a desire for auspiciousness.

Or rather, it was given that very name [Jetavana] because he was victorious (*jita*). For, out of a desire for auspiciousness, the word *jetava* was used in the sense of "one who is victorious" (*jeyya*).
As for the detailed explanation beginning with the words "in the park of Anāthapiṇḍika," that [donor] was named Sudatta by way of the name given to him by his parents;
however, due to his success in all desires, his freedom from stinginess, and his possession of qualities such as compassion, [he was called Anāthapiṇḍika].
And because he constantly gave alms-food (*piṇḍa*) to those who were without a protector (*anātha*), he became known by the name Anāthapiṇḍika.

Living beings take delight (*āramanti*) here, or especially those who have gone forth; thus it is called an *ārāma*. Because of its beauty of flowers, fruits, and so forth, and because it possesses the fivefold qualities of a dwelling site—such as being neither too far nor too near—people come from various places and find delight (*ramanti*), enjoy themselves (*abhiramanti*), and dwell there without weariness. This is the meaning. [By] the aforementioned kind...
Or, it is called an *ārāma* because even when one has gone here and there, one brings oneself back within its interior and finds delight;
for that [grove] was purchased from Prince Jeta by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika with eighteen crores of gold through a formal exchange,
and after he had caused dwellings to be built for eighteen crores of gold, he [further provided] eighteen crores of gold...
This indicates the following meaning: having completed the monastery by relinquishing fifty-four crores of gold, it was dedicated to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha;
therefore, it is called "Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Regarding the phrase *tatra*:
"At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park."
Regarding that which was stated as "the speech": *siyā* means that someone might have such a reflection;
the meaning is that one might occasionally urge [him] in the manner about to be described. Then, regarding *atha tattha viharati*:

if he dwells in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, it cannot be said [that he dwells at Sāvatthī], because Sāvatthī and Jeta’s Grove are distinct locations. Therefore, [it is said] "at one time."
The intention is that it has been so stated. Now, the objector clarifies his own position with the words beginning, "For it is not possible...
The other [the respondent] says, "But this should not be viewed in this way," and so forth, showing that all of this was spoken by you without understanding the unerring meaning.
In that context, "this" refers to [the passage]: "He dwells at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove..."
The words "in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery" refer to this statement. As for what you have raised with the words "If, first of all, the Blessed One...
and so forth, it should not be understood in that sense; rather, the meaning is that it is not intended to show monasteries in both places simultaneously, neither before nor after.
Now, [I shall explain] the intended meaning as I conceive it, which is unerring, and its...

Having stated that [the Blessed One] had already resided [there previously], he said, “Did we not say... in Jeta’s Grove,” in order to show that [the Blessed One] had not yet penetrated [the truth] by means of that [previous residence].
Even so, one should have said simply, “He was dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery,” rather than “in Sāvatthī.
Keeping this objection in mind, it was stated: “For the purpose of indicating the alms-resort village,” and so forth.
In this context, the description of the alms-village (*gocaragāma*) must certainly be performed.

For just as the description of Jetavana and other such places serves many purposes—such as providing assistance to those who have gone forth (*pabbajita*)—so too the description of the alms-village has various purposes, such as providing assistance to householders (*gahaṭṭha*). Demonstrating this, he said, "by means of the word 'Sāvatthī,'" and so forth.
Therein, by the mention of "receiving requisites" (*paccayaggahaṇa*), [the acts of] approaching and attending upon [the Teacher] are implied.

The assistance rendered to householders should be understood as providing them with space, teaching the Dhamma, establishing them in the refuges and the precepts, and bringing about the attainment of higher distinctions according to their specific potential.
The assistance rendered to those who have gone forth should be understood here as selecting suitable dwellings and locations for their study, inquiries, and application to the meditation subject.
This approach proceeds through compassion, not for the sake of gain and so forth, but through wisdom.
"Departure" means not being caused by opposition and so forth; this clarifies the absence of defilements in both approaching and departing.
"Righteous happiness" (*dhammikasukha*) refers to blameless happiness. Deities have a great desire to be of service because of the seclusion from people;
for deities consider a place secluded from common folk to be a suitable place to visit. "The accomplishment of that purpose" refers to the accomplishment of the welfare of the world.

The meaning is "the fulfillment of the Buddha’s duties. By the phrase "and so forth," the word "etcetera" (ādi) indicates, through the mention of Sāvatthī, the sustaining of the form-body (rūpakāya), and through the mention of Jetavana and so on, the sustaining of the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya).
Likewise, by the former [set of examples], there is the performance of actions dependent on others;
by the second, the performance of actions dependent on oneself. Or, by the former, there is the duty of compassion (karuṇā); by the other, the duty of wisdom (paññā). By the former...
This demonstrates his possession of supreme compassion through the first [phrase], and his possession of supreme equanimity through the last.
For the Blessed One feels compassion for all beings with supreme compassion, yet he is not beset by the fault of attachment therein due to his state of supreme equanimity;
and though equanimous, he is not indifferent to bringing about the welfare and happiness of others due to his state of great compassion.
By virtue of his great compassion, he is the Lord of the World; by virtue of his equanimity, he is the Lord of himself.
For thus, when he was a Bodhisattva, his mind being impelled by great compassion, he became intent upon the welfare of the entire world;
from the time of his Great Resolve onwards, he fulfilled the equipment of merit and knowledge for the sake of accomplishing that goal for an immeasurable period.
For a long time he experienced suffering; yet, due to his equanimity, he was unshaken by those sufferings that fell upon him rightly.
Through his great compassion, he turned toward *saṃsāra*; through his equanimity, he felt world-weariness (*nibbidā*) toward it.
Likewise, through his equanimity, he turned toward *nibbāna*; through his great compassion, he attained it. Similarly, through his great compassion, he brought about non-harming toward others.
Through equanimity (*upekkhakatā*), one does not fear others; through great compassion (*mahākāruṇikatā*), while protecting others, one protects oneself;
and through equanimity, while protecting oneself, one protects others. Thus, his status as the fourth type of person among those practicing for their own welfare and so forth is established.
Likewise, through great compassion, there is the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) and the foundation of generosity (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*).
And there is the fulfillment of equanimity, as well as the fulfillment of the foundation of serenity and the foundation of wisdom.

Thus, for one whose intentions and applications are perfectly pure, there is the attainment of success in sovereignty and other worldly fortunes solely for the benefit and welfare of the world through great compassion;
and through equanimity, there is the relinquishing of those same things without regarding them even as a blade of grass. Such is the one whose approach and withdrawal are thoroughly purified.
Through his great compassion, he relinquishes his attainments by way of giving solely for the welfare and benefit of the world;
and through his equanimity, he has no expectation of reward for that fruit. Thus, from the time of its origination onwards, he is endowed with marvelous and wonderful qualities:
through his great compassion, he performs what is exceedingly difficult to do for the sake of the welfare and happiness of others; and through his equanimity, he does not even adorn his own body.
Likewise, in his final existence, through his great compassion, he was moved by the sight of an old man, a sick man, and a corpse;
yet, through his equanimity, he remained indifferent toward magnificent enjoyments comparable to those of the gods and went forth on the Great Renunciation.

Likewise, through his great compassion, the commencement of his insight meditation began precisely through the gateway of compassion, as expressed in the thought, "Alas, this world has fallen into hardship," and so forth; whereas through his equanimity—
The passing of seven days by the one who had become a Buddha solely in the bliss of seclusion;

his making of an opportunity for teaching the Dhamma—though he had become indifferent to preaching because he reflected on the profundity of the Dhamma out of great compassion—by means of the request of Great Brahmā;
and his remaining unchanged even when the conduct of those to be trained, such as the group of five, was unsuitable, due to his equanimity.
Due to his great compassion (*mahākāruṇikatā*), because there is no aversion toward anything, he has no perception of enmity toward anyone;

due to his equanimity (*upekkhakatā*), because there is no attachment toward anything, he has no affection or intimacy toward anyone. Due to his great compassion, there is the inspiring of confidence in others;
due to his equanimity, there is no wavering from that state of inspired confidence. Due to his great compassion, there is an absence of passion for worldly phenomena (*dhamma*).

In this regard, there is an absence of the "teacher’s closed fist" (the withholding of knowledge); due to his equanimity, there is an absence of favoritism toward disciples and thus an absence of concern for their attendance and service.
Because of his great compassion, even when he enters into association with others in order to teach the Dhamma, he finds no delight therein due to his equanimity.
Because of his great compassion, even though he dwells in places near villages and the like, he remains in forest dwellings due to his equanimity.
Such is the dwelling. Therefore it was said: “It illustrates his possession of supreme compassion for the former [beings].

The word *taṃ* (that) refers to the word *tatra* (there). By saying, “It illustrates the time...,” he shows that this is an illustration of those places and times which are mentioned here as qualifiers of the action of dwelling. For the word *taṃ*—

This is an explanatory restatement (*paṭiniddesa*) of what has already been stated; therefore, here it ought to be an explanatory restatement of either the time or the place, and not anything else. This, first of all, is the analysis of the meaning regarding the word *tatra* as an explanatory restatement.
However, because in such instances the word *tatra* clarifies both the place and the time as distinguished by the teaching of the Dhamma, it is therefore said:

“Or he illustrates [the teaching] in a place and time appropriate for speaking. By this, “therein” means in such a place or time where the Blessed One addresses and speaks to the bhikkhus for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. With the words beginning “for it is not,” etc., he supports that very point.
But was it not the case that, standing where he was, the Blessed One refused to teach the Dhamma to Bāhiya, saying, “It is not the right time yet,” and so forth?
"Did he stand right there in the middle of the street and teach him the Dhamma? "This is true;
this is an example of not teaching at a time when it should not be taught. For that very reason he said, 'It is indeed the wrong time for now.
As for what was said there, 'We have entered among the houses,' that too refers to the fact that it was the wrong time for him."
This was said for the purpose of showing a particular method (pariyāya).
For at that time, his physical body (rūpakāya) had become unworkable due to the fatigue of the journey, and his mental body (nāmakāya) was overwhelmed by the force of intense joy.

As he was approaching the subsiding of both these states, the Blessed One rejected [the request] by way of a method, saying, "It is not the right time," in order to avoid further proliferation (papañca). However, the following is an illustration of the non-teaching regarding that which should not be taught.
“Then the Blessed One, having stepped down from the path, sat at the foot of a certain tree;
he sat on a seat prepared in the shade of the monastery”—such passages as these are included here by the word *ādi* (“and so forth”).
In passages such as “Then, monks, that fool, having previously been a hunter here and having performed evil deeds here,” it serves merely to complete the phrasing.
The word *kho* has the sense of emphasis in such passages as, “Indeed, one who lacks respect and deference dwells in suffering”;
it has the sense of the initial time in such passages as, “To what extent, friends, do disciples not train in seclusion when the Teacher dwells in seclusion?”;
and its meaning is also the commencement of a sentence. In those cases, by filling out the meter, it serves merely as an ornament for the speech.
The word "vā" (or) serves as a mere introduction to the sentence in the sense of "from the beginning. However, in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), it shows a limitation;
therefore, by saying "he addressed [them] thus," the restriction regarding the act of addressing is shown.

As for the statement, "‘Bhagavā’ is a designation that illuminates the World-Honored One (*lokagaru*)": why was this said, given that the meaning of the word "Bhagavā" has already been explained previously?

Even though it was already stated, that [term] was used for the purpose of showing the specific agent of the action of dwelling in the place already described, and not for the purpose of the act of addressing;

however, here it is for the purpose of addressing. Therefore, to show the meaning of why the word "Bhagavā" is stated again in the text for that purpose, he said: "‘Bhagavā’ is a designation indicating the world-honored one. By this, because of his status as one honored by the world...

This shows that, aspiring to practice in accordance with that [attainment], he addressed those monks who had approached him in order to teach the Dhamma to them according to their individual inclinations.

"Speech directed toward persons capable of hearing the discourse" refers to the speech of a person suitable for hearing the teaching on the conquest of the mind (cittapariyādāna) which is about to be spoken.
Among the four assemblies, it was the monks alone [who were addressed].

Having shown that the inclusion of the word "bhikkhu" here is for the purpose of demonstrating his preeminent status as a recipient of the Teaching—specifically, that he is a distinguished vessel for such teachings—the author now states "Furthermore...
(*apicā*) and so forth, in order to show the etymological meaning (*saddattha*).

In this context, "a bhikkhu" (*bhikkhu*) means one who is a "beggar" (*bhikkhaka*); the sense is that he is a bhikkhu by virtue of having the nature of begging (*bhikkhana-dhammatā*). He is "one who has entered upon the practice of alms-gathering" (*bhikkhācariyam ajjhupagato*).
A *bhikkhu* is so called because he has entered upon and undertaken the alms-gathering lifestyle (*bhikkhācariya*) and the gleaning lifestyle (*uñchācariya*) followed by the Buddha and others;

that is, because he has undertaken and established himself in them. For whoever, having abandoned a small or large mass of wealth, goes forth from the home life into homelessness, abandons the means of livelihood such as plowing and cattle-herding, and—merely by accepting the [monastic] emblem—enters upon the alms-gathering lifestyle.

A bhikkhu is so called because he has entered upon the life of wandering for alms, either because his livelihood depends on others even while eating solid food in the midst of a monastery, or because he has generated the aspiration for the going-forth by relying on the practice of eating morsels of alms-food;
this is how the meaning should be understood here. By way of such a method: "one who wears tattered and torn robes..."
"A bhikkhu is so called because he breaks (bhindati) evil, unwholesome states;
he is a bhikkhu because of his having broken off evil, unwholesome states"—this is according to the method found in the Vibhaṅga. "Ñāpana" means making known; the sense is "making understood.
"Bhikkhanasīlatā" means the habit of living by begging, not the habit of living by agriculture, trade, and so forth. "Bhikkhanadhammatā" means...
“‘The Noble Ones stand for the sake of alms’: this refers to the natural disposition of begging, not the disposition of one who is habitually a beggar.
‘Being skilled in begging’ means being diligent therein by recollecting the teaching, ‘One should rise up and not be negligent.
Alternatively, while ‘virtue’ (sīla) refers to one’s natural disposition, here it refers to its formal undertaking. ‘Dharma’ means a religious observance. ‘Being skilled’ means—”

"Attentive performance" means acting with reverence. "Practiced by those who are inferior and superior" refers, respectively, to both types of people: first, those who, though established in the state of a bhikkhu, are arrogant and conceited due to pride in their birth and so forth;

and second, those in the state of householders who, because they have not attained a superior status over others, consider the life of alms-seeking to be the height of wretchedness. By the word "bhikkhus," [the Buddha] addresses these inferior people.
By demonstrating the mode of livelihood practiced by those who have reached the height of compassion through poverty and who sustain themselves by wandering for alms among other families,
he effects a restraint against arrogance. By demonstrating the mode of livelihood practiced by the Buddha and others—
who were of superior standing, having gone forth from noble clans of great wealth— for the sake of purifying their means of living, he effects a restraint against dejection.

"Does" (*karoti*) should be supplied [to complete the sense]. Since the word "monks" (*bhikkhave*)—by virtue of being an address, brings about facing toward [the speaker], and by virtue of its context and inherent capacity, generates a desire to listen and enjoins careful listening and attention—it is for this reason that he said, "By means of the words 'monks,' etc.," in order to demonstrate that meaning.
In that context, "careful listening and attention" (*sādhukaṃ savanamanasikāra*)...
[It is so] in regard to thorough hearing and thorough attention. But how are hearing and the rest, when they have occurred, said to have occurred thoroughly?

By means of the application of reverence and respect, thinking: "Surely, through this right practice, the entire excellence of the Dispensation will come into one's hands," and by not treating the talk and so forth with contempt. For it is said: "By five qualities, monks..."
Endowed with these five qualities, one who hears the true Dhamma is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
What are the five? He does not despise the speaker; he does not despise what is said; he does not despise himself;
he listens to the Dhamma with an undistracted mind and a one-pointed mind; and he attends to it with wise attention. It is with these five qualities, monks, that one is so endowed.
“Endowed with five qualities, one who hears the true Dhamma is capable of entering into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.
For this very reason it was said: “For the success of the Dispensation depends upon careful listening and attention.
Although the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma was previously common to all assemblies, [he now speaks] to the bhikkhus with the words “the eldest and the best,” and so forth.

Having thus shown the reason for the address, he now raises the objection—"But for what purpose did the Blessed One [speak]?"—in order to show the purpose of the teaching of the Dhamma after having addressed the bhikkhus.
In that context, "thinking of something else" means being preoccupied with another matter.
"With distracted minds" means with unconcentrated minds. "Reflecting on the Dhamma" refers to [what was said] yesterday and so forth.
However, as they reflect individually in their minds upon the Dhamma they have heard over the course of days,
they are able to discern the teaching from the beginning onwards when the bhikkhus are addressed and the Dhamma is being taught;
it is to show this point by way of contrast that the passage beginning with “without addressing them” was spoken.
Regarding the term *bhikkhave*: here, the elision of the vowel *i* should be understood as occurring by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).

As for the word *iti* in the phrase *bhikkhavo iti*, this particle *iti* has many distinct meanings, such as cause, completion, and so forth; it functions as a marker for the meaning of a word, its opposite, a qualification, a restriction, an illustration, and others.
Thus, for example, in passages such as "It is deformed (*ruppati*), monks, therefore it is called 'form' (*rūpa*)," it is seen in the sense of a cause.
In such passages as, “Therefore, monks, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things.
I have compassion for you; how may my disciples be heirs to the Dhamma and not heirs to material things? it marks the conclusion of a discourse.

In such passages as, “Thus, or in this manner, he abstains from dancing, singing, music, and the viewing of spectacles,” it indicates the sense of ‘beginning. In the passage, “Māgaṇḍiya... [it indicates a name].

In such passages as, "For that brahmin, it is a designation, a convention, a description, a common usage, a name, a naming, a denomination, a linguistic expression, a phrasing, a verbalization," there is a reversal of the meaning of the terms.
"Thus, monks, the fool is full of fear, while the wise man is free from fear;
the fool is beset by calamity, while the wise man is free from calamity; the fool is beset by misfortune... [and so forth].
In such passages as “a wise man,” it means *pakāra* (manner). In such passages as, “When asked, ‘Is there aging and death conditioned by this? one who is questioned, Ānanda, should say, ‘There is.
If he should ask, ‘Conditioned by what is there aging and death? he should say, ‘Aging and death are conditioned by birth,’” it means *avadhāraṇa* (determination).
In such passages as, “‘It is,’ Kaccāna, is one extreme; ‘it is not’ is [the other].”

In such passages as "This, Kaccāna, is the second extreme," the particle *iti* is used in the sense of illustration (*nidassana*). Here too, it should be understood as being used in the sense of illustration alone.
For the word *bhikkhave* is a form of address; this particle *iti* indicates that [the Buddha] addressed them as "Bhikkhus.
Following this method, the meaning of the particle *iti* should be understood accordingly in cases such as "Bhadante" and so forth. Previously...
Because it was stated, “The Blessed One addressed [them],” the genitive case here in “from the Blessed One” (*bhagavato*) depends upon the act of addressing itself as its correlative;

with this intention, it is said, “they responded to the address of the Blessed One. Furthermore, this term “of the Blessed One” (*bhagavato*) is a dative of purpose by virtue of its connection to the act of responding.
As in the phrase, “He promises to Devadatta. The connection is: “the source from which this was spoken.

For the sake of easy comprehension of this sutta—just as for the purpose of easy descent into a lotus pond whose waters are radiant with lotuses and water-lilies, stainless, and sweet in taste—one constructs a jeweled staircase beautified by the elegance of its arrangement of pure stone slabs, with ground areas white with sand-dust resembling a scattered bed of pearls.

Like a flight of stairs for the easy ascent of that preeminent palace—which, like a sacred bathing place (*tittha*), was surrounded by a railing of variegated walls well-proportioned, and whose lofty height seemed to stretch out as if desiring to touch the path of the stars;
which was radiant with the mass of light from clusters of gems entwined with golden creepers upon smooth, soft ivory planks;
and which resounded with the mingled sounds of golden bracelets and anklets clashing, intermingled with the sweet tones of speech, laughter, and the playful movements of the household folk—

Just as a great gate with well-established, wide doorposts, brilliantly illuminated by the radiance of gold, silver, gems, pearls, coral, and other jewels, serves for the easy entry into a magnificent mansion adorned with sublime majesty and wealth;
so too does this sutta— endowed with both meaning and phrasing and indicative of the profound nature of the Buddhas’ knowledge of teaching— serve for the easy immersion [of the mind].

Here it is asked: "For what purpose, however, is the introductory statement (nidāna) included when the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya is being performed? Should not the compilation be made only of the words spoken by the Blessed One?
It is replied: for the sake of ensuring the stability, non-confusion, and credibility of the teaching.
For a teaching established by being bound together with the indications of time, place, teacher, occasion, and assembly remains stable for a long duration.
It is free from the quality of forgetfulness and is worthy of trust. It is like a legal decision established by means of place, time, agent, cause, and characteristic.

For this very reason, when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked questions regarding place and so forth—beginning with, "Friend Ānanda, where was the *Cittapariyādāna-sutta* spoken?"—the Dharma-keeper (Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika) provided the answer to those questions by saying, "Thus have I heard," and so on.
The introduction (*nidāna*) of this sutta has been spoken. Furthermore, the statement of the introduction is for the purpose of manifesting the perfection of the Teacher.
For the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the status of being a Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) is established by the absence of prior conduct, scripture, and reasoning.
Indeed, there is no need for a Fully Enlightened One to have prior conduct and so forth, because his range of knowledge is unimpeded in all respects.

And because [the Buddhas] are of one measure regarding all knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*). Likewise, the establishment of their state as having destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) follows from the absence of the teacher’s closed fist, the stinginess regarding the Dhamma, and lack of affection for disciples.
For these do not occur at all in one whose taints are destroyed; thus, there is the activity of benefiting others in one who is perfectly pure.
Thus, by means of those [qualities] which indicate the absolute absence of ignorance and craving—which are the defilements of the teacher and the corrupters of the perfection of view and conduct—...
The Blessed One’s possession of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*) and his practice for the benefit of himself and others are revealed by the introductory statement (*nidānavacana*).

For, through the pure qualities of a Perfectly Enlightened One that manifest the perfection of knowledge and abandonment, the first two grounds of self-confidence are established; and from that, because the absence of delusion regarding obstructive and liberating phenomena is established, the latter two grounds of self-confidence are established.
Thus, the Blessed One’s endowment with the four grounds of self-confidence and his practice for his own welfare and the welfare of others are made known.

This is so because, in various places, he illuminates the teaching of the Dhamma through spontaneous presence-of-mind (*ṭhānuppattika-paṭibhāna*) in accordance with the inclinations of the assembled audience;

here, however, it should be understood that he illuminates the teaching of the Dhamma through spontaneous presence-of-mind in accordance with the inclinations of those persons who value form (*rūpa*).
Therefore it was said: "The introductory statement (*nidānavacana*) is for the purpose of manifesting the excellence of the Teacher."
Likewise, there is the introductory statement (nidāna) for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the Dispensation.
For the Blessed One, whose every action is encompassed by wisdom and compassion, there is no practice that is fruitless or performed for his own benefit.
