Therefore, all the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Perfectly Enlightened One, who acts solely for the welfare of others, proceed exactly as they do.

That which is being spoken of is called the *sāsana* (teaching) in the sense of instructing beings appropriately according to the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal; it is not a mere poetic composition.

This very conduct of the Teacher is manifested in various places through introductory narratives (*nidāna*) along with the appropriate details of time, place, teacher, and assembly. "In this case, however, for those persons who are fond of form," and so forth.
Everything is exactly as before. Therefore it was said: "The introductory statement (nidāna-vacana) is for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the Dispensation.
Furthermore, the introductory statement is for the purpose of showing that the Dispensation possesses authority by means of a statement that demonstrates the Teacher’s status as an authority;
and that demonstration of the Teacher’s status as an authority is expressed as "the Blessed One" (bhagavā) according to the method explained below.

And it should be understood that this meaning is elucidated by this very term. For in the word "Bhagavā," this matter is explained in every respect through the statement that demonstrates the Tathāgata’s abandonment of all stains of defilement and misconduct—such as lust, hatred, and delusion—as well as through the demonstration of his possession of extraordinary and perfectly pure qualities such as knowledge and compassion, and thereby through the demonstration of his state as the supreme among all beings. This is the purpose of the introductory statement here.
This is the demonstration of the very beginning.

"Of what has been laid down" means of what has been taught. For "laying down" (*nikkhepa*) is so called because the teaching is the laying down of the meaning to be taught—such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth—within the mental continuums of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
Since it becomes clear only when spoken after having investigated the laying down of the Sutta, [it is explained thus].

Having shown the classification of the origin of the Blessed One’s teaching in general, it was stated [in the commentary] because, once the origin of the teaching has been shown by way of the thought, "In this case,

this teaching has such an origin," the exposition becomes easy to understand through the correct thorough comprehension of the Sutta's *nidāna* (introduction). In that regard, although the Suttantas are divided into many hundreds and thousands of types,
they are [classified] according to the method of the *Paṭṭhāna* (Foundations), such as those dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), and so forth.

They do not exceed these sixteen types; thus, because of the fourfold manner of the Sutta’s presentation—such as through one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*) and so forth—it is said: "For there are four ways of presenting a Sutta.

And here, just as for one's own inclination, a distinction through combination with the origin of the subject (*aṭṭhuppatti*) and the inquiries of others' inclinations (*parajjhāsaya-pucchā*) is possible: "One's own inclination and another's inclination..."

And because there exist connections based on intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*) and connections based on questions (*pucchānusandhi*), such as: "one’s own intention" and "dependent on a question," and "arising from a circumstance" (*aṭṭhuppattika*) and "another’s intention," and "arising from a circumstance" and "dependent on a question"—
thus, although a distinction through combination with one’s own intention is possible even for that which arises from a circumstance,
[it is distinguished] by means of one’s own intention and the others standing before it, in relation to what arises from a circumstance.
Since there is no association [in this case], a complete method of detailed exposition is not possible here;

therefore, it is said, "the four ways of laying down the Suttas. Alternatively, because the remaining ways of laying them down are included within these, only four are shown by way of the primary laying down.
This classification of association should be understood here according to how it has been demonstrated.
Herein, this is the word-meaning: it is deposited (*nikkhipīyati*), thus it is a "deposition" (*nikkhepa*); the discourse itself is the deposition, hence "discourse-deposition" (*suttanikkhepa*).
Alternatively, the act of depositing is "deposition"; the deposition of a discourse is "discourse-deposition," meaning the teaching of a discourse.
One's own inclination is "personal inclination" (*attajjhāsaya*); that which has this as its cause is "motivated by personal inclination. Personal inclination...
"Etassa" (of this) refers to one's own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*). The same method applies to the inclination of others (*parajjhāsaya*).
"Pucchāvaso" means the influence of a question; that which possesses this is "pucchāvasiko. "Atthuppatti" is the arising of the meaning that serves as the basis for the teaching of the Sutta;
"aṭṭhuppatti" is simply "atthuppatti," having changed the letter *ttha* to *ṭṭha*. That which possesses this is "aṭṭhuppattiko."
Alternatively, *suttanikkhepa* means that by means of this the discourse (*sutta*) is laid down; it refers precisely to one’s own inclination and so forth.
In this interpretation of the meaning, "one’s own inclination" (*attajjhāsaya*) is the inclination of oneself; "another’s inclination" (*parajjhāsaya*) is the inclination of others.

That which is asked is an "inquiry" (*pucchā*), meaning a matter to be inquired about. The speech of those who receive the Dhamma, which proceeds by way of such an inquiry, is "occasioned by inquiry" (*pucchāvasika*).
That very term is stated in the masculine gender in dependence on the word *nikkhepa* (deposition), as in the expression “dependent on a question” (*pucchāvasika*).
Likewise, the meaning here should be understood as follows: the occasion for the arising of the teaching itself is the "occasion-arising" (*aṭṭhuppatti*).

Furthermore, in this context, because it is independent of external causes such as the ripening of the faculties of others, the state of being a separate deposition of a sutta belongs to one's own internal inclination (*attajjhāsaya*).
This is because it was delivered solely through his own inclination for the purpose of establishing the framework of the Dhamma.

However, there is no restriction on the category of "arising from a specific occasion" (*aṭṭhuppatti*) regarding those discourses delivered when others' inclinations and questions—which serve as the cause for the delivery of the teaching—arose;
or rather, in the case of those arising from questions based on a specific occasion, they occur in accordance with the inclinations of others.
How is it that there is no restriction regarding the inclinations of others (*parajjhāsaya*) among those discourses already set in motion? This need not be questioned.

For, since the occurrence of the causes for teaching a discourse—when it is entirely free from [requests such as] a formal resolution (*abhinīhāra*) or a detailed inquiry (*paripucchā*)—is taken as the state of being "originated by a specific occasion" (*aṭṭhuppatti*), there is a separate mention of those [discourses] dependent on the inquiries arising from the inclinations of others.
Thus, in the case of the *Brahmajāla*, *Dhammadāyāda*, and other suttas, the motives for the teaching were praise or blame, the acquisition of material goods (*āmisa*), and so forth.
This is called “the origin of the discourse. That which is taught by taking as its basis the inclination of others, without their having asked a question, is “based on another’s inclination”;
that which is taught by means of a question is “question-based”—this meaning is well known.

“He spoke solely according to his own inclination” means he spoke for the purpose of establishing the continuity of the Dhamma. The factors conducive to the ripening of liberation are the faculties of faith and so forth.
*Adhijāsayaṃ* means inclination (*adhimutti*). *Khanti* means the acceptance of contemplation regarding views (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*).

*Manaṃ* means the consciousness of conceptualization (*paññatticitta*). *Abhinīhāraṃ* means aspiration (*paṇidhāna*). *Bujjhanabhāvaṃ* means the nature of awakening (*bujjhanasabhāva*), or the mode of penetration. *Rūpagarukānaṃ*:
among the five objects of sense, those who esteem the object of form are "those who esteem form" (*rūpagarukā*); they are inclined toward form by their mind.
“Inclined toward form, leaning toward form, intent upon seeing forms, their hearts dragged away by form—for those who hold form in high esteem.
The sense of negation is the sense of prohibition. But of what is it the sense of prohibition? For a sentence has action as its primary focus;
therefore, the sense of prohibition here is the prohibition of the action of “regarding,” as in “I do not regard. Thus he said: “But of this...”
“...of the foot,” and so forth. That which is not another is the self; referring to the continuum of a sentient being established merely by way of worldly convention, the Teacher says “I.
He does not refer to the object of the conceit of “I” as imagined by outsiders, because that conceit of “I” was utterly eradicated at the very root of the Bodhi tree.
For the Buddhas’ engagement in teaching regarding mundane matters proceeds precisely without overstepping worldly conventions.
The reason for the address "Bhikkhave" has already been stated above. Regarding the word "añña" (other):

because its meaning is established through a correlative reference, he says it means "other than the female form that is about to be described. "Ekaṃ pi rūpaṃ" (even a single form) refers to a single sense-sphere of color.
"Samanupassanā" (contemplation) is knowledge; it is so called because it sees (*passati*) each thing (*anu anu*) correctly (*sammā*) and as it truly is (*yāthāvato*). By way of defilement...
“Samanupassanā” means seeing each [aspect] individually; it is a view (*diṭṭhi*). In the phrase “not as permanent,” the word “iti” has the sense of “beginning with”;

the meaning is “beginning with this. By that, it includes such expressions as “he sees as suffering,” and so forth. “Even while looking” means even while looking, by means of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), at all forms without exception—such as those belonging to the celestial palaces of gods and humans, the wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*), jewels, gold, and so on.
Although the word “yaṃ” is a general term, [it is specified here] as “even a single form.”

Because form has been attained, the object of form is desired; thus it is said, "whatever form. Likewise, since the word "person" (purisa) refers to the mind and the individual who are to be consumed, it is specified as "one for whom form is heavy.
What is intended by "seizing" (gahaṇa) and "casting down" (khepana) is "consumption" (pariyādāna), which is the prevention of arising; hence he says, "wholesome consciousness of the four planes."
For that material form prevents even the arising of such limited wholesome consciousness; how much more so, then, that of sublime or supramundane consciousness?
Thus, it is capable of preventing the arising of supramundane wholesome consciousness as well.
Since there is no need to mention its prevention of the arising of mundane wholesome consciousness, it is said: "having exhausted wholesome consciousness of the four planes."
For in a person who is habitually addicted to the gratification of the strands of sensual pleasure, the arising of wholesome states through the practice of giving and so forth is not possible.
"Having grasped and exhausted" means: having taken hold—as if seizing it by the fist—of unwholesome consciousness that is occurring while relishing itself, by way of obstructing its continuation;
and having exhausted it, as it were, by the cessation of its non-arising, he stands [firm].

Since a place for its exhaustion can be found without interruption within such a vast world-system, he said, "it stands," just as one says, "mountains stand" or "rivers flow. Therefore he said, "here both [meanings] are appropriate," and so forth.
Regarding the form *yathayidaṃ*, he stated, "just as this," explaining that the vowel *ā* has been shortened due to euphonic combination (*sandhi*) and the letter *y* has been inserted.
"Form of a woman" refers to the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) pertaining to and connected with a female body.

Regarding ultimate reality (*paramattha*), first the definitions of words according to common usage and technical grammar (*saddasattha*) should be clarified, and afterwards those that are not common.
To clarify these by way of the Canon (*pāḷi*), he said: "It is called 'form' because it is deformed... [etc. ...it should be understood. In this context, "it is deformed" means:

It undergoes change (*vikāra*) due to opposing conditions such as cold, or rather, it "attains" [change]—this is the meaning. Furthermore, the arising of change is a more manifest production of something dissimilar when there is a convergence of opposing conditions.
If one asks, "From what does this distinction arise? it is from the statement beginning with "By cold," and so forth.
And having established it thus, the designation "all-form" (*anavasesa-rūpa*) regarding feeling and the rest is the general characteristic (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*), common to all form-phenomena.
Regarding "rūppanaṃ" (being affected): now, explaining the word *rūpa* by way of extracting its meaning (*atthuddhāranaya*), he says, "But this... and so forth.
It occurs in the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) because of such statements as "whether gross or subtle. Regarding "rūpūpapattiyaṃ" (in the arising of form):

here, "form-existence" (*rūpabhava*) is called "form" (*rūpa*) through the elision of the latter member of the compound; thus, the meaning here is "in the arising of form-existence. Regarding "kasiṇanimitta" (the sign of the kasiṇa): it refers to what is designated as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.
Regarding the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*): it is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is affected (*ruppati*), meaning it produces its own specific nature for its fruit;

thus he said, "having form... here, in the condition. It is called "form" because it is formed (*rūpiyati*) and defined (*nirūpiyati*) by way of being an aggregate of parts such as hands and feet; thus he said, "space... here, in the body."

It is called *rūpa* because it "forms" (*rūpayati*), that is, by undergoing a transformation of color, it manifests the state of what is in the heart; thus it refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*).
Because one attains a sense of beauty based on the excellence of shape—consisting of the various forms such as height and circumference—it is said to be "the measure of beauty.

Therefore he says: "In this case, regarding shape. In phrases such as "a beautiful form" (*piyarūpa*), the word *rūpa* has the meaning of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [other examples are included].

This is the summary of the form-jhānas and so forth. Regarding the phrase “one possessing form sees forms”: here, the “form” refers to the form-jhāna obtained by means of the preliminary perception directed toward internal things such as hair;

because he possesses that, he is called “possessing form” (*rūpī*). In the case of a woman’s fourfold origination, only the form included within the female body is taken, as well as the form of the garments, ornaments, and so forth associated with it.
However, in order to show that [the mind] completely engulfs the male mind, the passage beginning with “Moreover” (apicā) was stated.
By the mention of “fragrance and color,” the application of ointment is implied.

Granted, even if the color of the ornaments of a certain woman—though not actually attached to her body—is perceived as such, it might remain engulging the mind of a man whose heart is bound to her; yet that is not an absolute certainty.
Showing its absolute certainty, he said, "bound to the body. It "serves" means it serves for the total consumption of the mind.
This was stated for the purpose of strengthening the very meaning previously explained, just as one says, "a double binding is a firm binding.
Alternatively, it should be understood that this was stated by way of a conclusion. It was stated by way of a simile: "that which..."
"Thus it remains, having taken possession of a man's mind"—this entire preceding statement was spoken by way of a simile;
however, in order to show the meaning that serves as the basis for the simile, it was said: "Just as this... [and so on] ...the form of a woman.
The power of taking possession (*pariyādānānubhāva*) is the capacity for total appropriation; it was stated by way of demonstrating that power.
Furthermore, this statement beginning with “the form of a woman” serves as the illustrative basis (*vatthu*) for establishing and demonstrating the power of thorough comprehension (*pariyādāna*).

The king was named Nāga; however, because he had long fangs, he was called “Mahādāṭhika-nāgarāja. By way of non-restraint (*asaṃvara-niyāmena*) means by means of the process of non-restraint occurring at the eye-door.
Having grasped the sign (*nimittaṃ gahetvā*) means having grasped the beautiful sign (*subha-nimitta*), which is the form that serves as the cause for the arising of lust.
"Having taken [them], he went to see the charnel ground," meaning he went to see the cemetery (*sivathika*).

For it is there that the contemplation of the dangers (*ādīnavānupassanā*) succeeds. Out of greed for the cloth, and not believing that such a death could happen to them, he spoke derisively to those young novices, saying, "Your faces are the color of smoke."

Because of his profound clarity regarding the Three Jewels, and for the purpose of distinguishing him from Kākavaṇṇatissa and others, that Great King Tissa is spoken of by qualifying him with the word "faithful" (saddha).
The phrase "it remains, having taken possession of the mind of the youth" is stated by way of context.
"Having completed the duty of pointing out [the danger]" refers to the teacher [thinking]: "In this village, seeing unsuitable forms might lead to harm for him."
Having been prevented from entering the village, he stood there after having finished his duties regarding the designated spot. Therefore it was said:

“Without accepting the words of those who desired his welfare. “Recognizing the garment she had worn” means recognizing the garment she had worn on the day he saw her, which he had obtained on the day of her death when he went to the charnel ground to view her corpse. “Even in this way” means even by way of bringing about her death.
This, then, is the elucidation of the meanings not already explained in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) regarding this section.

Now, we shall provide a commentary on the meaning of the text according to the method of the *Netti*. As for that commentary on the meaning: [The text continues: ...because... [the commentary on the meaning... (Note: The provided source text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.)

When the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*), purpose (*payojana*), and the vessel (*bhājana*)—as well as the summarized meanings (*piṇḍattha*)—have been determined, [the exposition] becomes easy to perform and easy to understand.
Therefore, we shall first determine the origin and other factors of the discourse’s teaching. Therein, "origin" refers to the source of the teaching;
it is twofold: common (*sādhāraṇa*) and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). Of these, even the common [origin] is divided into internal and external.
It is twofold. Therein, the common [cause] arising from within is called the Great Compassion of the Lord of the World.
For it was by being impelled by that [Compassion] that the Blessed One’s mind arose for the teaching of the Dhamma to those to be trained;
with reference to this, it is said: “Out of compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye,” and so forth. Herein—

And even at this stage, the inclusion of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) should be understood as occurring for the purpose of ferrying sentient beings across the great flood of *saṃsāra* by means of the gift of the hand of the teaching of the True Dharma, because it arises for that end.

And just as with great compassion, so too omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) and the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabalañāṇa*), etc., should be described as having their internal origination within the teaching.
For all knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*) are the modes to be taught by them.

Knowing the inclinations, latent tendencies, and so forth of sentient beings as they truly are, the Blessed One, through his skill regarding what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhāna*), set forth a diverse method of teaching in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained.
As for the external, common origin, it was the exhortation of Sahampati Brahmā, who was accompanied by a retinue of ten thousand great Brahmās.
Indeed, following that exhortation, [the Buddha’s resolve] arose from reflecting upon the profundity of the Dhamma.
Having calmed his lack of concern, the Master of Dhamma became inspired to teach the Dhamma.

Furthermore, the uncommon [qualities] are twofold, distinguished as internal and external. Therein, the "internal" should be understood as both that Great Compassion and that Knowledge of Teaching by which this Sutta was set in motion. The "external," however, [is for those] who value form...
The inclination of individuals [is the cause]. This very point has already been stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

The purpose (*payojana*) is also twofold: common and uncommon. Among these, the common [purpose] is due to the savor of liberation found in the Blessed One’s teaching until final Nirvana through non-clinging.
For this reason, it was said: "This is the goal of discourse, this is the goal of deliberation," and so forth.
But the unique [purpose] for those individuals who esteem material form is the abandonment of desire and lust for form; both of these are indeed external.

However, if one were to consider that even the purpose residing within the mental continuum of those to be trained—which is termed the "accomplishment of the power of the teaching"—is indeed the purpose of the Greatly Compassionate Blessed One as well, because it constitutes the fulfillment of his intention through the achievement of the intended goal, then by this...
In a certain sense, it may also be internal to them.
Furthermore, the origin of this teaching is the failure of those individuals who are preoccupied with form to understand, as it truly is, the danger inherent in form;
its purpose is the understanding of that very danger. For by means of this teaching, [they come to know] the Blessed One...
It is called the "purpose" (*payojana*) because it is considered the teaching that is intent upon accomplishing that [result].
For whatever fruit is to be accomplished by the teaching is called the "purpose," since the teacher applies himself to the teaching because that fruit is desired.
Likewise, here there is the demonstration of the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) in the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*) by way of form for those individuals and other disciples (*veneyya*).

The purpose is as follows: the turning back of the wheel of saṃsāra, the setting in motion of the true Dhamma-wheel, the refutation of wrong views such as eternalism and so forth, the prioritizing of right view, the uprooting of the roots of unwholesomeness, the planting of the roots of wholesomeness, the closing of the doors to the states of misery, the opening of the doors on the path to heaven, the pacification of the obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna), the eradication of the underlying tendencies (anusaya), and the thought: "Being liberated myself, I shall liberate others."

The purposes to be understood here include, for example, the non-deception of previous promises, the non-deception of the aspirations of those who hold opposing views, the crushing of the doctrines of the non-Buddhist sects (tīrthikas), and the establishment of the Buddha’s Dhamma.
Just as those individuals were devoted to form (rūpa), so too others are devoted to self-identity (sakkāya) and cling to it; [the teaching serves] regarding conditioned phenomena...
Those seekers of liberation from existence who do not know the practice of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
who are intent on attending to the hearing of what is not the True Dharma and on common service, and who are averse to hearing, retaining, practicing, and penetrating the True Dharma—
such disciples are the vessels for this teaching.
And herein, by the inclusion of "form" through the term "lump" (*piṇḍa*), there is the grasping of the form element, the form base, and the form aggregate;
by way of form, there is the means for severing the three rounds of existence; the discrimination of the taints, the floods, and so forth; the removal of delight; the overcoming of attachments;
the relinquishing of the root of dispute; the application to the three trainings; the illumination of the three abandonments; and the undertaking of serenity and insight.
The "accomplishment through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-sacchikiriyā-siddhi*), and so forth, should be understood in this manner.

Hereafter, however, the sixteen modes of conveyance (*hāra*) must be shown. In that context, "form" (*rūpa*) refers to all material and immaterial phenomena—excluding craving—that are co-nascent with it, serve as its support, and are bound up with it;
these constitute the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*). Those [phenomena] which originate from it and have it as their object [are the truth of origination].
And craving is the truth of the origin. The non-occurrence of both of these is the truth of cessation. The practice that leads to the realization of cessation is the truth of the path.
In this context, gratification is found in the origin, danger in suffering, and escape in the path and cessation.
The fruit is the exhaustion of unwholesome and wholesome states of mind that have form as their object. For that which is taught by the teaching...
The purpose to be accomplished is the fruit; this is the meaning of what was said. It is for that purpose that this discourse was taught by the Blessed One.

Just as that wholesome consciousness is not exhausted, so too is the guarding of the sense doors, supported by the power of reflective development (*paṭisaṅkhānabhāvanā*), the means. This is shown by way of pointing out that, through the exhaustion of a person’s wholesome consciousness, their form is not shared with other forms.
"Therefore, those who desire welfare should carefully guard the mind. "This is the Blessed One’s instruction here"—this is the *desanāhāra* (the mode of teaching).
For the *desanāhāra* is characterized by the demonstration and analysis of gratification (*assāda*) and so forth. Indeed, this has been stated in the *Nettippakaraṇa*:
"Gratification, danger, and the escape, as well as the fruit and the means;"
"And the command of the Blessed One is the 'mode of conveying' for meditators.
Here, "conveying" (*desanā*) refers to that by which the meaning of the Sutta is conveyed and expounded;

or, it is called "conveying" because it accompanies the act of conveying. But surely other modes of conveying (*hāra*) also accompany the conveying, since they are the expounding of the meaning of the Sutta which is reckoned as "conveying"?

Does it blow? This is true; however, this mode of interpretation (hāra) deserves to be called "concomitant with the teaching" because it is for the most part understood through the literal expression itself, whereas other modes are not so.
For there is no teaching of a Discourse (sutta) that is devoid of the demonstration of gratification (assāda), danger (ādīnava), and escape (nissaraṇa), and so forth.
But is the statement of all those [factors] such as gratification and the rest the Mode of Interpretation of the Teaching, or rather...

"Of some"? It refers to those without exception. For in a discourse where the gratification (*assāda*), the danger (*ādīnava*), and the escape (*nissaraṇa*) have been presented in their own form, there is nothing further to be said.

However, in cases where they are presented only partially and not in their own form, the method of interpretation (*hāra*) should be applied by determining what has not been stated through the meaning (*atthavasena*).
It is called “I” because of its state as the universal eye, and because it is seen as such in its true nature.

It is called “O monks” for the purpose of addressing them by virtue of their possession of qualities such as the habit of begging (*bhikkhana-sīla*). It is called “another” for the purpose of showing that there is no self (*attā*) and to demonstrate the absence of anything other than that.
And it is said “even a single form” for the purpose of demonstrating the non-apprehension of a single [substantial] entity and for the purpose of negating a manifold existence.
It was stated [as such] because of the absence and non-perception of such form; it was stated as "I do not perceive" because of its being referred back and because of its indefiniteness.

It was stated as "this" (*yaṃ*) because of referring to the mode that is about to be described and because of the negation of other modes. It was stated as "just so" (*evaṃ*) because of referring to the mode currently being spoken of and because of the exclusion of other modes.
It was stated as "of a man" (*purisassa*) because of the basis of a dissimilar faculty and because of the absence of that [form] in a similar basis.
It has been stated [thus]. Because it serves as the basis for grasping the sign (*nimitta*) and because it is so conceptually constructed, it is said that "it persists, having seized the mind.
The word "as" (*yathā*) is used both to refer back to the manner in which it was stated by "thus" (*evaṃ*) and for the purpose of illustration.
The word "this" (*idaṃ*) is used because it is within the personal experience of the speaker and to bring it within the direct experience of the monks.
Because it is included within the continuity of a woman and because its state is bound up with that [continuity], it is called "female form" (*itthirūpa*);

thus, there is the Mode of Conveying Investigation (*vicayahāra*) by way of investigating each word. It is called "investigation" (*vicaya*) because by means of it, or in it, the words, questions, and so forth, are investigated;

or else, it is "investigation" because they are investigated by it. By way of determining the distinctions among the words, questions, answers, preceding and following [contexts], and the gratification (*assāda*) and other factors:
For the Mode of Conveying Investigation (vicaya-hāra) has the characteristic of investigating.

And this has been said: "That which is asked and that which is answered, The restatement of the Thread, and the investigation of the Thread— This is designated as the Mode of Conveying Investigation."
In beginningless saṃsāra, because of the mutual delight of women and men in each other’s forms, it is appropriate to say, “The form of a woman remains seizing the mind of a man.

This is the Mode of Conveying the Reasonable (*yuttihāra*). For the Mode of Conveying the Reasonable is characterized by the illumination of the distinction between what is reasonable and unreasonable regarding both the phrasing and the meaning.
And this has also been said:

“The ground and the range of all the modes (hāra), as well as the investigation of the appropriate and the inappropriate—this is designated as the mode of ‘reasoning’ (yutti). Regarding “reasoning” (yutti):

it is logical proof (*upapatti-sādhanayutti*); however, in this context, it refers to the investigation of reasoning (*yuttivicāraṇā-yutti*), where the middle term is elided, just as “the existence of form” (*rūpabhava*) is called simply “form” (*rūpa*). Alternatively, it is called “reasoning” because it accompanies reasoning (*yuttisahacaraṇato*).
The form of a woman, when looked upon without wise attention, is the proximate cause for lack of restraint in the sense faculties;
it is the proximate cause for the non-cultivation of wholesome states; and it is the proximate cause for the increase of the entire side of defilement.
Conversely, however, the form of a woman, when looked upon with wise attention, is the proximate cause for the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness.
That is the proximate cause for the fulfillment of the development of the factors of enlightenment; it is the proximate cause for the fulfillment of true knowledge and liberation.
The exhaustion of wholesome consciousness is the proximate cause for the adherence to delusion; that [adherence] is the proximate cause for volitional formations;
and volitional formations are the proximate cause for consciousness—thus the entire wheel of existence revolves. But by way of contrast, as for wholesome consciousness...

"The non-exhaustion of those various wholesome states for the sake of their arising and fulfillment is the proximate cause"—this, first of all, is the method without distinction. But in detail, the non-exhaustion of virtue is the proximate cause of non-remorse;
non-remorse is that of gladness, and so on, leading up to final Nibbāna through non-clinging. This is the proximate cause.

The Stringing Together (Hāra). The Mode of Conveying Footings (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra) is characterized by the discernment of those states that serve as the footing for the states taught in the Suttas, and also of those states that serve as the footing for them. For it is possible [to identify both]. And this has been said:
"The Victor teaches the Dhamma, and whatever is the footing for that Dhamma..."
"Thus, up to all phenomena (sabba-dhammā), this is the Mode of Conveying the Footing (padaṭṭhāna-hāra).

"Footing" means the proximate cause. Here, however, the investigation into the footing and so forth should be understood according to the method already stated in the Mode of Conveying the Logical Connection (yutti-hāra).
Furthermore, by the mention of the "single form" (ekarūpa), there is the inclusion of all six external sense-bases (bāhira-āyatana) by virtue of their status as external bases.

Because they have a single characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇattā*). By the mention of "mind" (*citta*), there is the inclusion of all six internal bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*), because they share the single characteristic of being internal bases.
In this way, their having a single characteristic may also be stated by way of the aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth.
This is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇo hāro*). By means of this, or in this [mode], things that have a single characteristic—even if not explicitly mentioned—are characterized.

"By way of a single statement" refers to the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-hāra*). Even when phenomena not explicitly mentioned in the Sutta arrive, that analytical exposition which treats them as if they had been stated is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics. And this has also been said:
"When one phenomenon has been stated, whatever other phenomena possess the same characteristic..."
"All these have been stated; that method is called the 'Characteristic' (lakkhaṇa).
In this introductory context, it is stated that for those individuals who are attached to form, the failure to see the danger in form has been expressed. [The question is:
"How indeed, having heard this teaching, will they come to see the danger in all five aggregates by way of seeing the danger in form?"
The Blessed One’s intention here is this: "May they, having abandoned desire and lust in every way, be liberated from the entire suffering of saṃsāra, and may they establish others therein.

The etymological analysis (*nirutta*) of the words follows the method explained in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) and its sub-commentary (*līnatthavaṇṇanā*) for the introductory phrases beginning with "Thus" (*evaṃ*) and the scriptural phrases beginning with "I am not" (*nāhaṃ*).
We have not elaborated [further] because it is easy to understand.
There are five kinds of *sandhi* (connection/junction) by way of: word (*pada*), meaning of a word (*padattha*), teaching (*desanā*), presentation (*nikkhepa*), and sutta.
Among these, the connection between one word and another word is *padasandhi*; the connection between the meaning of one word and the meaning of another word is *padatthasandhi*.

That which is called the "connection between action and agent. The connection of a sutta with multiple thematic continuities (anusandhi) through those respective continuities, and the connection between what precedes and what follows in a sutta with a single continuity, is the "connection of the teaching" (desanā-sandhi).

This is analyzed in three ways in the commentary as: "connection by way of inquiry" (pucchānusandhi), "connection by way of intention" (ajjhāsayānusandhi), and "connection according to the sequence" (yathānusandhi). And here, "intention" (ajjhāsaya) refers to...

It should be understood as twofold: one's own inclination and another's inclination. The connection regarding the presentation of the teaching should be understood by way of the four modes of presenting a discourse (*suttanikkhepa*).
Here, the connection between the discourses should be understood specifically by way of the first mode of presentation.
As for the inquiry, "Why, however, is this very *Cittapariyādāna-sutta* presented here as the first?", such an investigation does not fail to apply anywhere.
Furthermore, these beings, wandering through beginningless saṃsāra as men and women, are delighted by the forms comprised of the five strands of sensual pleasure.
In this regard, a woman is attached, infatuated, clinging, stuck, and bound to the form of a man; and that attachment of hers toward it is difficult to disentangle.
Likewise, a man is [attached] to the form of a woman; and in that case, visual contact is even more weighty.
And it is the root of all others. For this very reason, when asked, "How indeed should one behave toward women?", the Blessed One said, "By not seeing them at all.
Therefore, for the purpose of removing desire and lust for forms among the five strands of sensual pleasure, the Blessed One taught this very discourse first.
It is called "practice" because it is the beginning and the starting point of the practice for the attainment of Nibbāna.
Furthermore, the correlation of one teaching with another teaching is also a "connection of teaching" (*desanā-sandhi*).
That should be understood here as follows: "Bhikkhus, I do not [see]... it remains," this is the first teaching.
"Bhikkhus, whatever forms cognizable by the eye are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust—if a bhikkhu... [the rest follows].
This accords with the teaching: "One delights in it, welcomes it, and remains attached to it;
for one who delights in it, welcomes it, and remains attached to it, various evil unwholesome states arise. Likewise:
"One conceives regarding form, one conceives in forms, one conceives from form, one conceives 'form is mine. Form, bhikkhus..."

"This teaching accords with such instructions as: 'One who does not directly know, does not fully understand, does not cause the fading away of passion for, and does not abandon [this], is incapable of the destruction of suffering'—thus it is the Fourfold Array (catubyūha).
It is called *byūha* because things are arrayed (*viyūhīyanti*) therein, either by way of classification or by way of being grouped together;

it is the "array of four" because it is the array of the four [methods] beginning with etymology (*nibbacana*), hence it is the "Fourfold Array. Alternatively, it is the "Fourfold Array" because there is an array of four [factors] therein."
The Fourfold Array (Catubyūha) method of analysis is characterized by the fourfold division of derivation, intention, and so forth. For it has been said:
“Etymology, intention, the phrasing, the meaning, the source of the teaching, and the connection between what precedes and what follows—this is the Fourfold Array method.”
“Bhikkhus, I do not see another... [as I do] the form of a woman”—by this, improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is illustrated.
That by which the mind is overwhelmed therein is proper attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*). In that context, for one who attends improperly, craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) increase.
By the mention of craving, the nine states rooted in craving are included; by the mention of ignorance, [the nine states rooted in ignorance are included].
The entire wheel of existence (bhavacakra) revolves with ignorance as its root; by means of grasping through wise attention (yonisomanasikāra), those phenomena rooted in wise attention revolve;
and there is the fourfold wheel of prosperity. This is the Mode of Conveying the Turning Back (āvaṭṭa-hāra).

It is called "turning back" (āvaṭṭa) because by means of it, or in it, similar and dissimilar phenomena are turned back, or because it is the turning back of them. [It refers to] the phenomena grasped in the teaching...
The Mode of Conveying the Conversion (Āvaṭṭa-hāra) has the characteristic of turning [the mind] toward things by way of those that are similar and those that are dissimilar. For it is said:
“When, in the case of a single footing, one seeks out the remaining footings;
When it turns toward the opposite side, that is the Mode called Conversion.”
Form is fourfold: produced by kamma, produced by consciousness, produced by temperature, and produced by nutriment;
likewise, it is desirable, desirable-neutral, undesirable, and undesirable-neutral. Here, however, the desirable is intended.
Consciousness should be understood here as wholesome consciousness. That is of the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere.
"Supramundane" is fourfold; it is manifold according to the distinctions of the mental factors associated with feeling and so forth—this is the Mode of Analysis (vibhatti-hāra).
It is called "analysis" (vibhatti) because by means of it, or in it, the common and uncommon grounds for defiled and purified phenomena are analyzed;
or, it is analysis because it is the ground for their classification. [It applies to] both defiled phenomena and purified phenomena.

The Mode of Conveying Analysis (vibhatti-hāra) is characterized by analyzing [the teaching] according to what is common and what is uncommon, according to the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), and according to the plane (bhūmi). And this has been said:
“This Mode of Conveying analyzes the Dhamma, the proximate cause, and the plane;
it should be understood as ‘Analysis’ with respect to what is common and what is uncommon.”
"The form of a woman takes possession of a man’s mind for one who attends to it inappropriately;
it does not take possession of one who attends to it appropriately because his faculties are well-restrained and he is established in virtue"—this is the "turning-back" method (*parivatto hāro*).

By means of this, the factors stated in the discourse are turned back by way of their opposites; or else, they are the "turning-back" of those [factors] within this discourse. Thus it is called "turning-back."
The Reversal Mode (parivatta-hāra) is characterized by the turning back [of things] from the opposite of those phenomena that have been demonstrated. For it has been said:
“When wholesome and unwholesome phenomena have been demonstrated—whether as cultivated or abandoned—they turn back toward their opposites; this is the mode named Reversal.”
“Monks, ‘ascetics who have gone forth’ is a synonym. ‘Another, someone else, something different’ is a synonym.
‘Form, color, cognizable by the eye’ is a synonym. ‘I regard,’ ‘I look upon,’ ‘I know’ is a synonym.
‘Thus,’ ‘in this way,’ ‘of this kind’ is a synonym. ‘Of a man,’ ‘of a person’—”
“Pariyāyavacanaṃ” (synonymous expression). “Cittaṃ,” “viññāṇaṃ,” and “mano” are synonymous expressions. “Pariyādāya,” “gahetvā,” and “khepetvā” are synonymous expressions.
“Tiṭṭhati,” “dharati,” and “ṭhāti” are synonymous expressions. “Yathā,” “yena pakārena,” and “yenākārena” are synonymous expressions.
“Itthī,” “nārī,” and “mātugāmo” are synonymous expressions—this is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Vevacana-hāra). “Vividhaṃ” (various).

*Vivacanaṃ* means that which expresses the meaning of a single thing; *vevacanaṃ* is simply a synonym for *vivacanaṃ*. Alternatively, it is called *vivacanaṃ* because various meanings are expressed by it; *vevacanaṃ* is simply a synonym for *vivacanaṃ*. For the method of synonyms (*vevacanahāra*) is characterized by the application of many synonymous terms to a single meaning. Indeed, this has been stated: [The text continues with the cited verse: "By means of synonyms, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma in various ways; For those who delight in synonyms, the meaning is easily understood. This is the method of synonyms. It should be applied according to the context. For example: "The Tathāgata is the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Worthy One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Trainer of men to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. Here, although the meaning is one, there are many synonyms. Furthermore, in the case of the Four Noble Truths, the synonyms are as follows: suffering is the truth of the origin, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of the cause, and the noble truth of the condition; the origin is the truth of suffering, the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the fruit, and the noble truth of the manifestation; cessation is the noble truth of the path, the noble truth of the way, the noble truth of the practice, and the noble truth of the escape; the path is the noble truth of cessation, the noble truth of cessation, the noble truth of peace, and the noble truth of the goal. In this way, the method of synonyms should be applied according to the context. This concludes the section on the method of synonyms. Now follows the method of analysis (*vibhattihāra*). The method of analysis is characterized by the breaking down of a single meaning into its constituent parts. For example: "In this world, O monks, whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation. Here, the single meaning of "all" is analyzed into its constituent parts. Furthermore, in the case of the Four Noble Truths, the analysis is as follows: suffering is analyzed into its internal and external aspects; the origin is analyzed into its internal and external aspects; cessation is analyzed into its internal and external aspects; the path is analyzed into its internal and external aspects. In this way, the method of analysis should be applied according to the context. This concludes the section on the method of analysis. Now follows the method of sequence (*ānupubbīhāra*). The method of sequence is characterized by the arrangement of things in their proper order. For example: "First, O monks, one should develop loving-kindness; next, compassion; next, sympathetic joy; next, equanimity. Here, the sequence of the four immeasurables is established in their proper order. Furthermore, in the case of the Four Noble Truths, the sequence is as follows: first, suffering is to be fully known; next, the origin is to be abandoned; next, cessation is to be realized; next, the path is to be developed. In this way, the method of sequence should be applied according to the context. This concludes the section on the method of sequence. Now follows the method of reversal (*paṭilomahāra*). The method of reversal is characterized by the presentation of things in reverse order. For example: "First, O monks, one should develop equanimity; next, sympathetic joy; next, compassion; next, loving-kindness. Here, the sequence of the four immeasurables is presented in reverse order. Furthermore, in the case of the Four Noble Truths, the reversal is as follows: first, the path is to be developed; next, cessation is to be realized; next, the origin is to be abandoned; next, suffering is to be fully known. In this way, the method of reversal should be applied according to the context. This concludes the section on the method of reversal. Now follows the method of combination (*sankhepavipphārahāra*). The method of combination is characterized by the contraction and expansion of meanings. For example: "All phenomena are non-self. Here, the single meaning of "non-self" is expanded to include all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena. Furthermore, in the case of the Four Noble Truths, the combination is as follows: suffering is combined with the origin; the origin is combined with suffering; cessation is combined with the path; the path is combined with cessation. In this way, the method of combination should be applied according to the context. This concludes the section on the method of combination. Now follows the method of distinction (*vibhattihāra*). The method of distinction is characterized by the differentiation of meanings based on specific characteristics. For example: "Suffering is of three kinds: the suffering of pain, the suffering of change, and the suffering of formations. Here, the single meaning of "suffering" is differentiated into its specific characteristics. Furthermore, in the case of the Four Noble Truths, the distinction is as follows: suffering is distinguished by its characteristic of oppression; the origin is distinguished by its characteristic of accumulation; cessation is distinguished by its characteristic of peace; the path is distinguished by its characteristic of leading out. In this way, the method of distinction should be applied according to the context. This concludes the section on the method of distinction. Now follows the method of demonstration (*nidassanahāra*). The method of demonstration is characterized by the pointing out of meanings through examples. For example: "Just as, O monks, a man might throw a handful of dust into the great ocean, so too, O monks, the suffering experienced by beings in the realms of existence is like a drop of water compared to the mass of suffering. Here, the meaning of the vastness of suffering is demonstrated by the example of the ocean. Furthermore, in the case of the Four Noble Truths, the demonstration is as follows: suffering is demonstrated by the example of a disease; the origin is demonstrated by the example of a tumor; cessation is demonstrated by the example of health; the path is demonstrated by the example of medicine. In this way, the method of demonstration should be applied according to the context. This concludes the section on the method of demonstration. Now follows the method of cause (*hetuhāra*). The method of cause is characterized by the explanation of the reasons for a given state. For example: "Because of ignorance, O monks, volitional formations arise; because of volitional formations, consciousness arises. Here, the cause of the arising of volitional formations is explained as ignorance. Furthermore, in the case of the Four Noble Truths, the cause is as follows: the cause of suffering is the origin; the cause of the origin is past craving; the cause of cessation is the path; the cause of the path is right view. In this way, the method of cause should be applied according to the context. This concludes the section on the method of cause. Now follows the method of function (*kiccaniddesahāra*). The method of function is characterized by the description of the activities performed by various factors. For example: "The eye, O monks, performs the function of seeing; the ear performs the function of hearing; the nose performs the function of smelling; the tongue performs the function of tasting; the body performs the function of touching; the mind performs the function of cognizing. Here, the specific functions of the six sense bases are described. Furthermore, in the case of the Four Noble Truths, the function is as follows: the function of suffering is to be fully known; the function of the origin is to be abandoned; the function of cessation is to be realized; the function of the path is to be developed. In this way, the method of function should be applied according to the context. This concludes the section on the method of function. Now follows the method of comparison (*ūhanahāra*). The method of comparison is characterized by the drawing of analogies between similar things. For example: "As a lamp, O monks, shines in a room, so too, O monks, does the mind of a bhikkhu shine when it is developed in concentration. Here, the mind is compared to a lamp. Furthermore, in the case of the Four Noble Truths, the comparison is as follows: suffering is compared to a burden; the origin is compared to the taking up of the burden; cessation is compared to the laying down of the burden; the path is compared to the carrier of the burden. In this way, the method of comparison should be applied according to the context. This concludes the section on the method of comparison. Now follows the method of inquiry (*paripucchāhāra*). The method of inquiry is characterized by the posing of questions to clarify the meaning. For example: "What, O monks, is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering... Here, the meaning of suffering is clarified by posing questions. Furthermore, in the case of the Four Noble Truths, the inquiry is as follows: "What is suffering? What is the origin? What is cessation? What is the path? In this way, the method of inquiry should be applied according to the context. This concludes the section on the method of inquiry. Now follows the method of summary (*saṅgahahāra*). The method of summary is characterized by the grouping of related meanings together. For example: "All phenomena are included within the five aggregates. Here, all phenomena are grouped
“There are indeed many synonyms for a single state taught in the Sutta;
he who knows them, O knower of the Suttas, possesses what is called the Mode of Conveying Synonyms.
Form is designated in manifold ways, such as black, brown, and so forth. A person is designated in manifold ways, such as a kshatriya and so forth.
The mind (*citta*) is designated in many ways by way of being limited (*paritta*), exalted (*mahaggata*), and so forth. Regarding the term "having exhausted" (*pariyādāya*):
here, "exhaustion" (*pariyādāna*) is designated in many ways by way of the evil states (*pāpadhamma*) that exhaust it, such as transgression (*vītikkama*) and obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).

This is the Mode of Designation (*paññatti-hāra*). It is called "designation" (*paññatti*) because things are made known (*ñāpīyanti*) by means of various modes (*pakāra*) or through their distinctions; or, "designation" is that wherein the meaning resides.

The Mode of Conveying Descriptions (paññatti-hāra) has the characteristic of revealing the various ways in which each single state (dhamma) is to be described by means of numerous descriptions. For this has been said:
“The Blessed One teaches a single state by means of diverse descriptions;
that mode should be known as ‘description,’ for that is the Mode of Conveying Description.”

When opposing conditions come together, there occurs a change in color through the arising of a dissimilar production; the manifestation of the state present in the heart of one possessing that [body] is the "place of form" (*rūpaṭṭhāna*).
This is an entry by way of impermanence. Furthermore, because what is impermanent is suffering, it is an entry by way of suffering;
and because what is suffering is non-self, it is an entry by way of emptiness. Mind (*citta*) is the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*); that which exhausts it is—
Craving and the evil states associated with it are the "element of phenomena" (*dhammadhātu*); this is the entry by way of the elements (*dhātu*).
In the same way, the entry by way of the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, should also be stated; this is the Mode of Conveying the Entry (*otaraṇahāra*).

It is called "entry" (*otaraṇa*) because by means of it the teachings found in the Suttas—such as dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and the rest—are entered into or introduced. [This refers to] the meaning of the Sutta by way of dependent origination and so forth.
For the Mode of Conveying the Entry has the characteristic of entry. Indeed, this has been said:
"Dependent arising, the faculties, the aggregates, the elements, and the bases—he who enters by means of these, that is the Mode of Conveying called the Entry."

"Monks, I do not... [as before]... perceive," this is the *ārambha* (the undertaking). "Thus it remains, having taken possession of a person's mind"—this is the purity of the words (*padasuddhi*), but not the purity of the undertaking (*ārambhasuddhi*).
"Just as this... and so forth is both the purity of the words and the purity of the undertaking. This is the "purifying method" (*sodhano hāro*).
By means of this, or in this Sutta, the words, word-meanings, questions, and undertakings are purified and brought into harmony (*samādhīyanti*).
The Purification (Sodhana). For the Mode of Conveying Purification has the characteristic of purifying the questions concerning the meaning of the words in a sutta. Indeed, this has been said:
“When a question has been answered, beginning from the verse in which it was asked, the investigation into what is pure and what is impure—that is the Mode of Conveyance named Purification.”
"Another" (*añña*) is a general determination because no specific distinction is mentioned. "Even a single form" (*ekarūpam-pi*) is a specific statement made without qualifying that [general term].
"Just as this" (*yathayidam*) is a general determination because it is an unrestricted expression. "A female form" (*itthirūpa*) is a specific statement made without qualifying that [general term].
This is the Mode of Determination (*adhiṭṭhāna-hāra*). By means of it, things are determined (*adhiṭṭhīyanti*) and brought into continuity (*anuppavattīyanti*).
By this, the mode of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is defined as the determination of phenomena that constitute both the general and the specific, without conceptual differentiation (*vikappa*).

For the mode of resolution is a method of conveying meaning characterized by the discernment of the general and the specific through the very absence of conceptual differentiation regarding the phenomena contained in the discourses. And this has also been said:
“Those phenomena which are shown through their unity, and those which are shown through their diversity;”
"It should be resolved by that; this is the Mode of Conveying Determination.
For material form, the causes are karma, ignorance, and so forth, as well as karma, consciousness, and so forth. For the act of contemplation, the causes are adverting and so forth.
For wholesome consciousness, the causes are wise attention and so forth. Regarding the term "having exhausted": here, the causes for exhaustion are unwise attention and so forth.
This is the Mode of Conveying Requisites (*parikkhāra-hāra*). It is called a "requisite" (*parikkhāra*) because it surrounds, constructs, and bears fruit; that is, it refers to causes and conditions.
It is called a "requisite" because it explains requisites, or because its subject matter consists of requisites, or because it accompanies requisites.
Its characteristic is the commentary that extracts and defines the causes and conditions designated as "requisites" among the phenomena presented in the Discourses.
For this is the requisite mode of conveyance. Indeed, it has been said:
"Those states which, as conditions, produce another state in succession—drawing out the cause—this is the requisite mode of conveyance."
Regarding the phrase "it persists by taking hold of the mind of a person":

here, it should be understood that craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) are specifically what take hold, because it is through them that such persistence occurs. Among these two, form (*rūpa*) is the basis for craving, and the formless (*arūpa*) is the basis for ignorance.
Specifically, calm (*samatha*) is the antidote to craving, and insight (*vipassanā*) is the antidote to ignorance. The liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) belongs to calm.
The wisdom of fruition-insight is liberation through wisdom (*paññāvimutti*). For it is said, distinguishing them as "fading away from lust" and "fading away from ignorance.

This is the Mode of Conveying Coordination (*samāropana-hāra*). By means of this, or in this regard, phenomena are coordinated by way of their proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*) and so forth; thus it is "coordination.
It has the characteristic of investigating the coordination of the proximate causes, synonyms, development, abandoning, and [the nature of] the phenomena as they appear in the Sutta.
For this is the Mode of Conveying Coordination. For it has been said:
"Those phenomena which have a certain root, and those which are declared by the Sage to be identical in meaning—these should be coordinated;
this is the Mode of Conveying Coordination."
And to this extent:
“Exposition, investigation, reasoning, proximate cause, and characteristic;
the fourfold array, the turning back, analysis, and reversal.”
“Synonym, designation, entry, purification, foundation, equipment, and coordination—these are the sixteen [modes of conveying].

Thus it should be understood that the sixteen modes of conveying (haras) have been shown as they were stated. By means of these, or in these, the subjects such as the discourses (sutta), verses (geyya), and so forth, are conveyed (harīyanti).
"Strings" (*hāra*) refers to ignorance, doubt, and perversion. They are called "strings" either because they themselves carry [these faults], or because they are merely the act of carrying;

thus they are "strings" by way of a metaphorical designation for their fruit. Alternatively, they are called "strings" because they are carried—that is, they are expressed—by those who describe the Dhamma and those who receive the Dhamma, through the process of giving and receiving the Dhamma.
Or else, they are "strings" because they are like strings. For just as a collection of many jewel necklaces is designated as a "string," so too... [their own]...
Just as the pleasure of delight arising from contact with the various gems that constitute its parts allays the bodily heat of those who enjoy it—
heat produced by the burning fever of the summer season— even so these particular commentaries,
which are a collection of various gems of ultimate meaning (paramattha-ratana), produce the bliss of Nibbāna through the attainment of the gems of ultimate meaning that constitute their own parts.
They pacify the distress in the hearts of those who receive the Dhamma, which is caused by the defilements such as sensual lust.
Alternatively, they are called *hārā* because they take away (*hārayanti*) ignorance and so forth, effecting their removal, or because they explain them.

Or else, they are *hārā* because they captivate and delight the minds of those who hear them, according to the method of etymology, just as it is said: "The Blessed One is one who has vomited out existence" (*bhavesu vantagamano bhagavā*).
From here on, however, the fivefold methods beginning with the "turning of the ray" (nandiyāvaṭṭa) should be understood. In this context, craving and ignorance are the truth of the origin;
the material phenomena that serve as their basis and so forth are the truth of suffering; their non-occurrence is the truth of cessation;

and the way leading to the realization of cessation is the truth of the path. And here, by the inclusion of craving, [all defilements] are included by way of deceit, fraud, conceit, arrogance, vanity, negligence, evil desire, bad friendship, lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, and so on.

The unwholesome side is to be understood. By the inclusion of ignorance (*avijjā*), the unwholesome side is to be understood by way of distorted attention, anger, resentment, denigration, disparagement, envy, avarice, contentiousness, harshness of speech, the view of existence (*bhavaditthi*), the view of non-existence (*vibhavaditthi*), and so forth. The wholesome side is to be understood as the opposite of what has been stated. How?
By way of absence of guile, absence of deceit, and so forth; by way of non-distorted attention, and so forth.

Likewise, the side of purification (*vodānapakkha*) should be understood by way of the factors belonging to serenity (*samatha*), such as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), and the factors belonging to insight (*vipassanā*), such as the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).
This is the ground for the "Conversion of Relishing" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa*) method.

For it is that which, by way of applying the Four Noble Truths, links the meaning of the Sutta concerning the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*)—consisting of craving and ignorance—with the side of purification consisting of serenity and insight.
This specific method of exposition characterized by leading [the mind] is called the "method of the turning of the ploughshare" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya*). For it has been said:
"He who leads craving and ignorance by means of serenity and insight, Having joined them with the Truths—this method is the 'turning of the ploughshare'."
It is called the "Nandiyāvaṭṭa" because its turning is like that of a *nandiyāvaṭṭa* (a "joy-turner" or "hook").

For just as a *nandiyāvaṭṭa* turns outward by means of the main part situated inside, so too does this method; such is the meaning. Alternatively, it is called the *nandiyāvaṭṭa* because it is the turning (*āvaṭṭa*) of *nandi*—that is, craving or delight—within it.

Among the states belonging to the categories of craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) taken up according to the method explained below: craving is greed (*lobha*), and ignorance is delusion (*moha*).
When there is greed associated with ignorance, resentment (*āghāta*) arises like pus when blood is present; this resentment is hatred (*dosa*).
Thus, by the inclusion of these three unwholesome roots, and by the inclusion of the wholesome mind through their opposites, the three wholesome roots are also established.

They are indeed already included. Here too, the application of the Truths should be understood as follows: greed is either all the wholesome roots associated with the taints (*āsava*), or the Truth of Origination;
and the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*) produced by them, which serve as their basis and domain, are the Truth of Suffering, and so forth.

Furthermore, the fruit here should be determined by way of the three liberations, [and] by way of the threefold corruption of the stains of misconduct—namely, unwholesome perception, thought, and so on—arising from the three unwholesome roots.

The side of the unwholesome is to be led forth; likewise, the side of purification is to be led forth by means of the three roots of the wholesome, the threefold good conduct, the perception of the wholesome, thought-conception, the true Dhamma, concentration, the doors of liberation, and so on—this is the ground of the Tipukkhalā method.

For it has the characteristic of leading, by way of the application of the Four Noble Truths, the meaning of the Sutta regarding the side of defilement through the roots of the unwholesome and the side of purification through the roots of the wholesome.
This specific method of exposition is called the Tipukkhalanaya (the Three-Point Method). It is "tipukkhalo" because it is beautiful (*pukkhalo*) by means of three points (*tīhi*):
the side of defilement consisting of greed and so forth, and the side of purification consisting of non-greed and so forth. For this has been said:
"Whoever, with regard to unwholesome states together with their roots..."
"Not so" regarding wholesome things and wholesome roots;
that which is real, true,
and not false— this they call the Tipukkhala method.

Among the phenomena included under craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) according to the method already stated, one should understand that, specifically by way of craving and views, there are the perversions of perceiving the "beautiful" (*subha*) in the ugly, and the "pleasant" (*sukha*) in the painful;

and by way of ignorance and views, there are the perversions of perceiving the "permanent" (*nicca*) in the impermanent, and the "self" (*attā*) in the non-self. By taking wholesome consciousness as their antidote, [the wholesome states are established].
When the faculties of mindfulness, energy, concentration, and wisdom are perfected, the four foundations of mindfulness are likewise perfected.
In this regard, four types of persons are to be demonstrated by means of the four faculties. How so? For those who are temperamentally dominated by craving are of two kinds:

those with dull faculties and those with keen faculties; likewise for those temperamentally dominated by views. Among them, the first [type] grasps at the perverted notion that the unattractive is "attractive."
By the power of wisdom, correctly observing the true nature of the body, and by the power of meditation, uprooting that perversion,

he enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*). The second type, who grasps what is not pleasure as "pleasure," dispels the opposing factor by means of the power of energy— which consists of the restraint of energy— as described in the passage beginning, "He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire."
Having dispelled that perversion by the power of meditation (*bhāvanā-bala*), he enters the certainty of rightness (*sammatta-niyāma*).

The third person, who grasps at the perversion of "permanent" in regard to the impermanent, with a mind concentrated through the power of serenity (*samatha-bala*), perceives the momentary nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*);

having eradicated that perversion by the power of meditation, he enters the certainty of rightness. The fourth person, due to being deceived by the density [of perception] regarding the continuity, the collection, the function, and the object...

One who falsely adheres to a self within what is merely a collection of phenomena such as contact—though it is non-self—destroys that false adherence by means of mental attention to the emptiness of the fourfold tetralemma, and thus realizes the fruit of recluseship.

Furthermore, the truth of the origin is comprised of the four perversions, such as the perception of beauty; and the five aggregates of clinging, which serve as their basis and object, constitute the truth of suffering, and so forth.
The application of the truths should be understood. As for the fruit here, it consists of the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).

Furthermore, in this context, the unwholesome side should be understood by way of the four perversions (*vipallāsa*), as well as the four taints (*āsava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), ties (*gantha*), states of being (*agati*), craving (*taṇhā*), clinging (*upādāna*), arrows (*salla*), stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), and non-penetration (*apariññā*).

Likewise, [the wholesome side] should be understood by way of the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the fourfold abiding in jhāna, the factors conducive to happiness, the immeasurables (*appamaññā*), the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), and so forth.
"The side of purification is to be led forth"—this is the ground for the method called the "Lion’s Play" (*sīhavikkīḷita*).

For that specific mode of exposition characterized by the leading forth of the entire side of defilement through perversions such as the perception of beauty, and the side of purification through the faculties of faith and so forth, by way of application to the Four Truths, is what is known as the "Lion’s Play. Indeed, it has been said:
“He who, by means of the perversions,
the defilements, the faculties, and the true Dhamma,
does not [misconceive]— the knower of methods should lead him according to this method.”
"It is called the 'Lion’s Play' (Sīhavikkīḷita).
Because he possesses distinctions such as fearlessness, speed, and prowess, the Blessed One is a lion;

his "play" (vikkīḷita) refers to his teaching, which is an abiding consisting of vocal action. Since it elucidates the antidotes to the perversions, that which contains the lion’s play herein is the "Lion’s Play" (Sīhavikkīḷita).
This is the method (*naya*). Alternatively, because it illustrates the application of specific powers and resembles the lion’s sport (*sīhavikkīḷita*), it is called the "lion’s sport" method.
Here, the "specific power" refers either to the powers of faith and so forth, or to the ten powers (*dasabala*) themselves.

Furthermore, with the establishment of these three methods of meaning (*atthanaya*), the two methods of conventional expression (*vohāranaya*) are necessarily established as well. For, by means of the directional aspect of these three methods of meaning, the examination of phenomena such as the wholesome is "directional examination" (*disālocana*). Thus it has been said:
“Indeed, whatever wholesome and unwholesome [states] have been explained here and there in the analytical discourses (veyyākaraṇa),
one surveys them with the mind.”
"Indeed, that is called the 'surveying of the directions.
Because it brings together those phenomena thus surveyed by joining them with the three methods of meaning, it is like a hook; hence it is called a "hook. For this has been said:
"Having surveyed with the surveying of the directions, that which one raises up and brings together..."
“All wholesome and unwholesome states—this method is called the ‘goad.

Therefore, the “surveying of directions” (disālocana) is the surveying by means of the mind of the meanings, methods, directions, and phenomena; and the “goad” (aṅkuśa) is the bringing together of those. Thus, all five methods are appropriately applied.
And up to this point—
“The first is the ‘Turning of Delight’ (Nandiyāvaṭṭa), and the second is the ‘Three-Fold’ (Tipukkhalo);
the third is called the ‘Lion’s Play’ (Sīhavikkīḷita), and the fourth is the ‘Pattern of the Method’ (Nayalañjaka).
They say the ‘Determination of Directions’ (Disālocana) is the supreme method.”
"The fifth is called the Hook; all five methods have been traversed.

Thus, it should be understood that the five methods mentioned here are also demonstrated in this [work]. It is called a "method" (*naya*) because it leads one to understand defilement and purification by way of their distinction.
It is called a "pointer" (*lañjaka*) because it points out and reveals the meaning of the Sutta. Being both a method and a pointer, it is a "method-pointer" (*nayalañjaka*).

And this discourse should be understood as belonging to the "partaking of defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) within the sixteenfold *suttanta-paṭṭhāna*, and as belonging to the "penetration" (*nibbedha*) and "beyond-training" (*asekkha*) sections by way of contrast.
However, within the twenty-eightfold *suttanta-paṭṭhāna*, it should be known as: mundane and supramundane; based on seven factors;
consisting of knowledge and the knowable; vision and development; our own doctrine; that which is to be answered; wholesome and unwholesome; and that which is permitted and prohibited.
Therein, the sixteenfold *suttanta* is called the *paṭṭhāna*: the discourse dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), the discourse dealing with purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*),
the discourse dealing with penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), the discourse dealing with the state of one beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*),

the discourse dealing with both defilement and purification, the discourse dealing with both defilement and penetration, and the discourse dealing with both defilement and the state of one beyond training.

a discourse on the side of purification, a discourse on the side of habitual cultivation and on the side of penetration, a discourse on the side of habitual cultivation and on the side of the one beyond training,
a discourse on the side of penetration and on the side of the one beyond training, a discourse on the side of defilement, on the side of habitual cultivation, and on the side of penetration,
and a discourse on the side of defilement, on the side of habitual cultivation, and on the side of the one beyond training.
The discourse dealing with defilement, the discourse dealing with penetration, and the discourse dealing with the state beyond training;
the discourse dealing with habituation, the discourse dealing with penetration, and the discourse dealing with the state beyond training;

the discourse dealing with defilement, the discourse dealing with habituation, the discourse dealing with penetration, and the discourse dealing with the state beyond training; and that which deals with neither defilement nor habituation.

The sixteen foundations of the Dispensation (*sāsana-paṭṭhāna*) are stated as follows: "a discourse that pertains neither to penetration (*nibbedha-bhāgiya*) nor to the state of one beyond training (*asekha-bhāgiya*).

In this context, it is called *saṃkileso* because one is defiled by means of it; thus, that which occurs in the portion pertaining to defilement (*saṃkilesa-bhāga*), in the section concerning defilement, is "pertaining to defilement" (*saṃkilesa-bhāgiya*).
Habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) is the cultivation of merit; that which occurs in the portion pertaining to perfuming is "pertaining to perfuming" (*vāsanā-bhāgiya*). [This refers to] perfuming...

Or, it is "conducive to purification" (*vāsanābhāgiya*) because it causes one to partake in purification. "Penetration" (*nibbedha*) is the piercing through and the crushing of the mass of greed and so forth;
that which occurs in the portion of penetration, or that which causes one to partake in penetration, is "conducive to penetration" (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).

"Dharmas whose training is completed" are those of the "one beyond training" (*asekha*); that which occurs in the portion of the one beyond training, or that which causes one to partake in the state of the one beyond training, is "conducive to the one beyond training" (*asekkhabhāgiya*). Among these:
Where the defilement consisting of craving and so forth is analyzed, this is the section on defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*).

Where the bases for meritorious action such as giving are analyzed, this is the section on purification by habituation (*vāsanābhāgiya*). Where the aggregates of virtue and so forth pertaining to those in training (*sekkha*) are analyzed, this is the section on penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).

However, where the aggregates of virtue and so forth pertaining to those beyond training (*asekkha*) are analyzed, this is the section on the beyond-training (*asekkhabhāgiya*). The others [are] their...

These have been stated by way of the method of combination (*vomis-sakanaya*). They should be understood as "pertaining to all" (*sabbabhāgiya*) by way of the discourse on the restraint of all taints (*āsava*) and so forth;
