for therein are analyzed the phenomena of defilement, the phenomena of mundane good conduct, the phenomena of those in training (*sekkha*), and the phenomena of those beyond training (*asekkha*).
Furthermore, that which pertains to all should be understood as the figurative expressions regarding water and so forth, such as: "One who sees does not see."
Furthermore, the twenty-eightfold *suttanta-paṭṭhāna* consists of: the mundane, the supramundane, the mundane-and-supramundane;
that which is based on beings, that which is based on phenomena, that which is based on both beings and phenomena; knowledge, the object of knowledge, knowledge-and-the-object-of-knowledge;
vision, cultivation, vision-and-cultivation; and one’s own teaching, the teaching of others.
One’s own statement and another’s statement; that which is to be answered, that which is not to be answered, and that which is both to be answered and not to be answered;
action, result, and both action and result; the wholesome, the unwholesome, and both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
what is permitted, what is prohibited, and what is both permitted and prohibited; and praise—these are the twenty-eight foundations of the Teaching as they have been handed down.
In this context, "mundane" (*lokiya*) means that which is connected to the world (*loka*), or that which is known in the world.
Furthermore, a discourse in which a mundane matter is stated is a mundane discourse; likewise for the supramundane (*lokuttara*).

However, a discourse in which what is mundane is stated in one part and what is supramundane is stated in another part is both mundane and supramundane. This is by way of the sevenfold intention and the sevenfold description.
That which is taught by way of beings is a teaching based on beings (sattādhiṭṭhāna). That which is taught by way of phenomena is a teaching based on phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna).
That which is taught by way of both is a teaching based on both beings and phenomena. The meaning in all instances should be understood according to this method.
Furthermore, a discourse that proceeds by way of extolling the virtues of the Buddha and others is called a hymn (thava).
“The Eightfold Path is the best of paths, the Four Truths are the best of truths;
dispassion is the best of states, and the One with Vision is the best of bipeds.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Nettippakaraṇa* method.
2. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "those who value sound and so forth," one includes those who value fragrance, taste, and touch.

"By way of disposition" (*āsaya-vasena*) means by way of underlying inclination (*ajjhāsaya-vasena*). Sound produced by temperature (*utu-samuṭṭhāna*) that has entered the continuum of a woman is also found;

however, since that is not intended here, it is stated as "mind-produced" (*citta-samuṭṭhāna*). "Spoken sound" (*kathita-sadda*) refers to the sound of conversation and the like. "Sung sound" (*gīta-sadda*) refers to the sound of singing with melody.
The sound of a woman’s laughter is included here because that too is to be relished by a man. Therefore he said:
“Furthermore, he hears the sound of a woman laughing, speaking, or singing through a wall or through a fence;
he relishes that,” and so forth. “Of the upper and lower garments” means of the lower garment made of coarse, stiff cloth.
“Of an ornament” means of an ornament such as an anklet and so forth. “It should be understood as the sound of a female” is said because it is dependent upon a female.
Therefore he says, “all of it,” and so forth. “In a place not far away” means in a place not distant from the dwelling place of that herd of elephants.
“Endowed with a body” means possessing a well-proportioned body, a firm, sturdy, and large body. “A great elephant” means one of great majesty.
An elephant. "Making him the eldest" means making him the leader of the herd.
Because his tusks—referred to as *aḷa*—are like horns due to their sharpness, he is called *siṅgī* (horned).
Because he resembles wild animals such as lions and elephants due to his golden color and great strength, he is like a deer (*miga*), thus he is called *miga*. In various places, there is a task...
The eye itself is the "guide" (*netta*) by virtue of its being a guide; because it is long in the sense of being prominent, he is one whose eyes have long guides—thus, "one with long-eyed guides.
"Bone-skin" (*aṭṭhittaco*) means that his skin is nothing but bone. "Overpowered by that" means overpowered, overwhelmed, and rendered motionless by that deer.
"I weep piteously" means, having fallen into a state of compassion, I weep and cry out. [This is] from the fear of an enemy.
Liberation, it is said, comes to one who has a companion, not to one who is alone; thus he said, "Do not indeed abandon me.
In that context, "Do not indeed abandon me" means: do not abandon me, who have met with such calamity, you who are as dear to me as my own life and my beloved husband.
He delights and finds pleasure on the peak of a mountain, or wanders there, or wanders while uttering the cry of a heron.
"Earth" (*pathavī*); because he endures by striking against it, he is an "elephant" (*kuñjara*). "In his sixtieth year": at the time of sixty years from birth, elephants decline in strength;
it is with reference to this that he spoke thus. "Of the earth bounded by the four oceans":
of the earth that stands reaching as far as the ocean in the four directions. "Suppiya" means very dear. Of them...

"You are the best of aquatic creatures"—meaning that among all the crabs born in the water, whether in the ocean or in the Ganges, Yamunā, or Nammadā rivers, you alone are the most excellent and most praiseworthy due to the perfection of your color and your great size;
therefore, because you are the best of all, I beg you to release the husband of this weeping woman. I entreat you, who are the most excellent of all.
“Release my husband. *Athā* means immediately after loosening the grip. *Etassa* refers to the crusher of enemies.
*Nissāya pabbatagahanaṃ* means having passed beyond three mountain ranges and taking recourse in a mountain thicket on the fourth mountain range.
*Evaṃ vadati* means he speaks while reciting this Buddha-mantra beginning with, “This one with eyes is rising.”
In this context, "rises" means that it emerges from the eastern world-system.

"The One with Eyes": having dispelled the darkness for all inhabitants of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), he has given them eyes by means of the instrument that causes the acquisition of sight; he is "the One with Eyes" because of those eyes.
"The Sole King": among those who create light throughout the entire world-system, he is the "Sole King" in the sense of being preeminent and in the sense of being a ruler.
*Harissavaṇṇo* means having a color like gold; the meaning is "golden-hued. *Pathaviṃ pabhāseti* means he illuminates the earth;
thus, he is *pathavippabhāso*. *Taṃ taṃ namassāmi* means: therefore, I pay homage to and revere you who are such as this.
*Tayājja guttā viharemha divasaṃ* means: being protected by you today, may we dwell happily for this day through the four modes of deportment.

Thus, having paid homage to the Sun with this verse, the Bodhisatta, in the second verse beginning with "Those brahmins," pays homage to the Buddhas who have attained final Nibbāna in the past and to the qualities of a Buddha.

Therein, "those brahmins" refers to those pure brahmins who have cast out evil. "Vedagū" means one who has gone to the further shore of the Vedas, or one who has reached the beyond by means of the Vedas.
Or, he is a *vedagū*. Here, however, he is called a *vedagū* because he has made all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) known and manifest. For this very reason it says:

"all phenomena" (*sabbadhamme*). Having made all phenomena—the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—known and manifest to his own knowledge by way of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), and having crushed the summit of the three Māras, he attained perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
"Attained" means they have transcended *saṃsāra*. "They pay homage to me" means:
may they accept this homage from me. "And may they protect me": may those Blessed Ones, thus honored by me, protect and guard me.
"Homage to the Buddhas... for the sake of liberation": this homage of mine is [offered] to the Buddhas of the past who have attained *parinibbāna*.

"May this homage of mine be for them; may it be for their enlightenment, which consists of knowledge regarding those very four fruits; likewise, may it be for those who are liberated by the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship;

and may this homage of mine also be for that fivefold liberation of theirs, which consists of liberation by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), eradication (*samuccheda*), tranquillization (*paṭippassaddhi*), and final escape (*nissaraṇa*). This is the meaning. He—
Having performed this protection, "the peacock wanders seeking," these two lines were spoken by the Teacher after he had attained full enlightenment.

Their meaning is as follows: "Monks, having performed this protection, this safeguard, that peacock wanders through his own feeding grounds for the sake of various kinds of food, such as flowers and fruits."

Having thus spent the day, sitting on the mountain peak in the evening and gazing at the sun as it was setting, he recollected the qualities of the Buddha and, in order to provide protection and a shield for his dwelling place, spoke the Brahma-mantra once more, beginning with “Apetaya.
Therefore he said: “Having taken his range during the day,” and so forth. Therein, *apeti* means he departs; he goes to its setting.
"Having made this protection (*paritta*), that peacock established his dwelling"—this too was said by him after he had attained full enlightenment (*abhisambuddha*). Its meaning is:
"O monks, having made this protection, this safeguard, that peacock resolved to dwell in his own place of residence.
"Even before the performance of the protective rite" means even prior to the carrying out of the protective ritual. "By the female peacock" means...
[This refers to] a peahen resembling a hen. 3.
In the third [case], since there is no distinction between the odor-base (gandhāyatana) and the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) in terms of their originating conditions, he says:
"originating from four [causes]. This refers to the scent of a woman’s body and the scent of ointments and such applied to the body.

And since there is the possibility of grasping [the term "smell"] without distinction because of its general connection [to all odors], he says "this [smell]" and so forth, in order to specify the smell intended here.
In that context, "of a woman" means of an ordinary woman.
"Foul-smelling" means it is foul-smelling by virtue of being the bodily odor of an ordinary woman. It is said to be "intended here" because it is desirable and thus to be relished.
But how is it that the body odor of a woman is foul-smelling? To this he says: "Some," and so forth.
In this context, she who has an odor like a horse's is "horse-odored" (*assagandhinī*). She who has an odor like a ram's is "ram-odored" (*meṇḍakagandhinī*).
She who has an odor like sweat is "sweat-odored" (*sedagandhinī*). She who has an odor like blood...

"It has blood" means it smells of blood. "One is indeed impassioned" means that in this beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), because the heart is dragged along by the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of defilements such as ignorance, and because the mind is attached to the gratification of touch, the blind fool is impassioned even for a woman with a body such as this, which is foul-smelling.
Having thus shown the foul-smelling nature of the scent of an ordinary woman’s body, [the text continues:]
Now, in order to show that this [fragrance] is absent in certain distinguished women, he says: “But for a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti), etc.
If this is so, why is the body-fragrance of such a woman not intended here? He replies:
“This does not belong to all,” and so forth. [The fragrance] of the body of a female animal and of certain human females is exceedingly...
Because he sees that it is to be relished, he further permits that very thing without distinction, saying, "Let there be the scent of a woman," and so forth.
It is stated as "to be known simply as the scent of a woman" because it is bound up with that [the body]. 4. Regarding the fourth and subsequent [questions]:
"What is the use of that?"—if the taste cognizable by the tongue is what is intended here, what is the use of that [separate] constituent taste and so on?
The purpose [of this] has already been stated. "Anointing the flesh of the lips" (*oṭṭhamaṃsasammakkhana*) refers to saliva and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the taste of betel, mouth-perfumes, and the like—which smear the flesh of the lips—is included. All that is "female lust" (*itthirasa*), because it must be grasped by a woman. 5.
Regarding "the touch of a woman" (*itthiphoṭṭhabba*), the same method applies here as well. However, if in this context the objects of form and so forth belonging to a woman are meant...
Since these [defilements] remain seizing the mind of a person without distinction, why were they taught by the Blessed One by taking them individually?
To this he says: "Thus the Teacher," and so forth. He supports that very point with the words beginning "For just as...
"He leads away" means he leads away into distraction; or rather, this is the reading: "he leads. And "he leads" means he causes attachment. The others do not do so.
By the statement "sounds and so forth [are not so], whereas visible forms and so forth are objects," it is shown that among beings there is an unmixed predominance for visible forms and the rest;
however, to show that this should not be viewed in such a way because of the manifold nature of the inclinations (*ajjhāsaya*) of beings, it was said:
"And for some... and so forth. "By way of the fivefold predominance" means by way of the predominance of the five kinds of objects.
For some person, there is a state of being "weighty" (*garukatā*) toward all five of the aforementioned objects;

for another, it is toward only a few among them, or even toward just one. All of these should be understood as being "fivefold weighty," just as in the expression "the seven sets of swords and the eight liberations.
This is not because of the *Pañcagaruka-jātaka*, since that does not intend to refer to someone who is weighty toward only a single object.
For since that Jātaka was included among the five persons who were heavy with attachment to a single object, it is called the "Pañcagaruka-jātaka.
If this is so, one might ask what the purpose of including it here is; thus he says, "for the sake of providing testimony.
It should be cited and explained to show that these people met with ruin and disaster due to their excessive attachment to forms and other sense objects.
6–8. *Tesam* means "of those suttas. He did not wish to take them after mocking [the others] because he was slightly disfigured in his physical form.
*Anatikkamanto* means "without exceeding," that is, while reconciling [the two]. *Dve hatthaṃ pattānī* means "two lotuses reached his hand.
*Pahaṭṭhākāraṃ dassetvā* means "showing an appearance of joy," thinking, "While each woman received only one, I have received two."
Having displayed an appearance of contentment, she wept, recollecting the fragrance of her former husband’s mouth;

for from his mouth a scent like that of a blue lotus (*uppalagandha*) wafted forth. "Having removed" means having taken away from that place; or the reading is "having caused to be removed," which has the same meaning. "Speaking 'Well done! Well done!
means speaking "well done, well done" by way of expressing appreciation for the discourse on the Dhamma. Like a blue lotus...
"Like water": just as the lotus and the scent of the lotus are produced from the mouth [of the Buddha].

It is said that "only the round of existence (vaṭṭa) is spoken of" because it was stated according to the literal sense. Even though it was stated thus, nevertheless, one should not remain at the literal meaning but should explain by drawing out the turning away from existence (vivaṭṭa), because the Blessed One’s teaching has liberation as its essence.
The commentary on the Rūpādivagga is finished.
Thus ends the Elucidation of the Unexpounded Meanings for the Commentary on the First Vagga of the Manorathapūraṇī, the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
2. Commentary on the Chapter on the Abandoning of the Hindrances (Nīvaraṇappahānavagga) 11.

Regarding the phrase "of the second": this refers to the second chapter. In the expression "even a single phenomenon" (*ekadhammam-pi*), it is shown by the phrase "even a single intrinsic nature" (*ekasabhāvam-pi*) that the word *dhamma* here has the sense of "intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva*), as in such expressions as "wholesome phenomena" (*kusalā dhammā*). And to the extent that it has the sense of "intrinsic nature,"...

Since the meaning of "insubstantiality" (nissatta) is thus established by that very fact, it is said: "Dhamma should be understood in the sense of insubstantiality. The term "sign of the beautiful" (subhanimitta) is stated as a synonym for *dhamma*.
For in its actual meaning, it may be either sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) itself;

for that [desire], by way of its mode of grasping, is "the beautiful," and because it serves as the sign for another sensual desire that occurs in that same mode, it is called the "sign of the beautiful."
And it is so called. Its object is the sign of beauty (*subhanimitta*). For any object such as visible form (*rūpa*), etc., when apprehended in an agreeable aspect, is called the "sign of beauty.
And here, the "sign" (*nimitta*) is simply the object itself; for he will say later:
"The 'sign of beauty' is an object that is a basis for lust. Or, the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction, because it possesses multiple meanings.
Of the particles (*nipātānaṃ*). "For further increase" (*bhiyyobhāvāya*) means for repeated becoming. "For abundance" (*vepullāya*) means for a state of vastness; the meaning is "for growth.

"Unborn" (*ajāto*) is one who has been born out [of the world]. The remaining words are synonyms for that very same term. "In sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu*) refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

"Sensual desire" (*kāmacchando*) is desire characterized as sensual pleasure; it is not the desire for action (*kattukamyatā-chando*), nor is it desire for the Dhamma (*dhammacchando*). By way of sensual pleasure...

Through the state of being impassioned (*rajjana*), sensual pleasure itself is lust; thus it is "lust for sensual pleasures" (*kāmarāga*). Through the state of desiring (*kāmana*) and through the state of delighting (*nandana*), sensual pleasure itself is delight;

thus it is "delight in sensual pleasures" (*kāmanandi*). Through the state of desiring and through the state of craving (*taṇhāyana*), there is "craving for sensual pleasures" (*kāmataṇhā*). By the word "etcetera," the inclusion of these terms—"affection for sensual pleasures" (*kāmasneha*), "fever of sensual pleasures" (*kāmapariḷāha*), "infatuation with sensual pleasures" (*kāmamucchā*), and "clinging to sensual pleasures" (*kāmajjhosāna*)—is to be understood. Therein, according to the method already stated:

Having understood the meaning of sensual desire (*kāma*), it should be known that sensual attachment (*kāmasneha*) is so called in the sense of sticking; sensual fever (*kāmapariḷāha*) in the sense of burning;
sensual infatuation (*kāmamucchā*) in the sense of being stupefied; and sensual clinging (*kāmajjhosāna*) in the sense of swallowing and finishing off.
Sensual lust (*kāmacchanda*) itself is the hindrance of sensual lust (*kāmacchandanīvaraṇa*) in the sense of being an obstruction to the arising of the wholesome; that is sensual lust.
"By way of non-occurrence" means by way of the state of not occurring.

"By way of an object not previously experienced" means by way of an object that has not been experienced within that particular existence (*attabhāva*), even after having designated it through its basis as "this is such-and-such.
However, there is no object whatsoever—whether distinguished as form, sound, and so forth—that has not been experienced even within a single existence, let alone throughout beginningless saṃsāra.
Regarding what was stated—“and by way of non-occurrence,” etc.—that was said too briefly; therefore, he spoke the words beginning with “therein” in order to show it in detail.
Therein, by the mention of “existence” (bhava), sublime existence (mahaggata-bhava) is included, for that is devoid of the occurrence of coarse defilements.

The eighty-two minor observances (khuddaka-vatta) are those to be practiced during the period of probation (pārivāsika-kāla) and at times such as when a formal act of censure (tajjanīya-kamma) has been performed.
For those [other duties] are not to be practiced in all circumstances; therefore, they are not included within the Mahāvattas (Great Duties).
Thus it is said, "There are fourteen Mahāvattas.

Likewise, there are the duties for guests, residents, those going on a journey, the expression of appreciation (*anumodanā*), the meal-offering (*bhattagga*), alms-round (*piṇḍacārika*), forest-dwellers (*āraññaka*), lodgings (*senāsana*), the sauna (*jantāghara*), the restroom (*vaccakuṭi*), the preceptor (*upajjhāya*), the co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*), the teacher (*ācariya*), and the resident pupil (*antevāsika*).

These are called the fourteen major duties (*mahāvatta*). As for the others, beginning with the words, "I shall prescribe the duty for monks who are on probation (*pārivāsika*)," there are sixty-six duties to be practiced by those who are in their normal state (*pakatatta*), stated as:
"One should not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*); one should not walk the meditation path (*caṅkama*) while [the other] is walking on the ground.
Following that, [it says]: "Monks, one who is on probation..."

"A bhikkhu who is a *pārivāsika* (one undergoing probation) must not dwell under one roof in a residence with a bhikkhu who is senior to him, nor with a bhikkhu who is subject to *mūlāya-paṭikassanā* (sending back to the beginning), nor with one who is subject to *mānatta* (penance), nor with one who is practicing *mānatta*, nor with one who is subject to *abbhāna* (rehabilitation).

These and similar rules do not count as separate offenses for each individual among the various persons— such as those senior in probation (*pārivāsikavuḍḍhatara*) and so forth— because they are not distinct from the rules that apply to a regular (*pakatatta*) bhikkhu.

By way of those duties that must be performed, they are condensed and counted as five each; thus there are seventy-one duties. Regarding the duties for one who has undergone an act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), it is stated by way of the establishment of the duties:
"One must not accept the salutation, rising from one's seat... [and so on] ...or back-massage from a regular (*pakatatta*) monk. This refers to the salutation and the other such acts.
There is one [rule] concerning indulgence, and ten others such as “A regular bhikkhu must not be accused of a failure in virtue,” making eighty-two in total.
However, among these very rules, some are duties for those who have undergone a *tajjanīya-kamma* (censure) and so forth, while others are duties for those on probation (*pārivāsika*) and so forth;
thus, by including what has not yet been included, they should be understood as twenty-two duties. This refers to the “fourteen great duties.”
Even though it has already been mentioned, the separate inclusion of these two—“the duties for newcomers and those departing”—is made because they occur frequently;
due to being constantly occupied with the performance of these duties, defilement finds no opportunity.

“Improper attention” (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) refers to unskillful mental engagement that proceeds by perceiving what is impermanent and so forth as “permanent,” and so on. “Laxity of mindfulness” (*sativossagga*)...

The meaning is "an answer by means of mindfulness" or "devoid of mindfulness. The particle *pi* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly stated, with reference to what will be said later [in the phrase] "even in this way.

"By way of connection" means by way of the connection of the question and so forth. "By way of the sequence of what precedes and what follows" means by way of observing the sequence of the preceding and following text.
"Of one who learns" means of one who learns from the mouth of the teacher. "Of one who recites" means [of one who recites] the text learned from the mouth of the teacher.
Of one who recites; of one who causes others to recite means of one who causes others to learn the text and its meaning by way of teaching them.
Of one who teaches means of one who teaches the Dhamma to others by way of exposition.
Of one who explains means of one who explains the meaning as it truly is to those who ask about points of doubt in their respective [minds]. Defilement finds no opportunity.

Because his mind is occupied solely with the work of stringing together [garlands] day and night. The particle *pi* in the phrase *evampi* serves the purpose of inclusion; it applies in the same way to the remaining cases as well.
The expression “he is a bearer of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*)” clarifies the very meaning already stated: “having undertaken and practicing the thirteen qualities of the ascetic practices.
The term *bāhullāya* means for the sake of abundance, that is, for the abundance of requisites such as robes and so forth, so that these requisites may arise in great quantity.

"Likewise" means for one who has turned back or who has proceeded. "Of one whose jhāna has declined" means of one whose jhāna has been lost due to some cause such as the sight of unwholesome forms, which acts as an obstacle to jhāna.
"Of one who has abandoned jhāna" means of one who has relinquished jhāna by way of not entering it.
"In talk and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," he includes socializing with crowds, sleep, and unwholesome actions. Or, "in the seven contemplations."
Herein, the seven contemplations are: contemplation of impermanence, contemplation of suffering, contemplation of non-self, contemplation of disenchantment,
contemplation of dispassion, contemplation of cessation, contemplation of relinquishment, contemplation of destruction,

contemplation of vanishing, contemplation of change, contemplation of the signless, contemplation of the desireless, contemplation of emptiness, and insight into phenomena through higher wisdom (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*).
Among these eighteen great insights— namely, knowledge and vision according to reality, contemplation of danger, contemplation of reflection, and contemplation of turning away—
the seven beginning with the contemplation of impermanence and ending with the contemplation of relinquishment are mentioned first.
Whatever needs to be said regarding this should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*.

"By way of non-habituation" means that in a previous existence, there was an absence of the habituation to sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth for one whose defilements had been suppressed by *jhāna*.
"Never experienced before" means never previously experienced in that particular existence. "Born" is a synonym for this term, as in "fully born" and so on.
But surely, because all phenomena are momentary, at the very moment sensual desire has arisen—
Since cessation necessarily occurs, and since once that has ceased another [state] arises again, how can there be its repeated occurrence or its state as a mass?
To this he said: "In that regard, sensual desire that has arisen once," and so forth.
"This is impossible" means this is without cause—that is, there is no reason why sensual desire that has arisen would not cease, nor [why it would arise again] once it has ceased.
The meaning is that there is no such cause for it to arise again.

"Conducive to lust" means that which generates lust. Here, "unwise attention" (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) refers to the distorted mental attention that perceives the impermanent and so forth as permanent and so forth;
thus he says, "in the impermanent, 'permanent,'" and so on. "Unwise attention" means unskillful mental attention regarding the manifestation of wholesome states.

The meaning is that it is a mental application (*manasikāra*) that has not become a cause. "Improper mental application" (*uppatha-manasikāra*) means a mental application that has not become a path for the arising of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*).
"In opposition to the truths" means by way of being contrary to the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truths.

By the phrase beginning with "advertence" (*āvajjanā*), there is the occurrence of unwholesome impulsion (*akusala-javana*) at the mind-door, which arose prior to that [advertence] and serves as a condition for it; this is designated by the term "fruit" (*phala*).

It is spoken of in that way because, by its power, it serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the arising of unwholesome states. *Āvajjanā*: It is called "adverting" (*āvajjanā*) because it adverts toward the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*).

*Anvāvajjanā*: It is called "re-adverting" (*anvāvajjanā*) because it adverts again and again. *Ābhogo*: It is called "mental application" (*ābhogo*) because it bends toward (*ābhujati*) an object other than that of the life-continuum.

*Samannāhāro*: It is called "attention" (*samannāhāro*) because it brings [the mind] together with the object. That very same [attention], arising while following after itself with respect to the object...

It is called *manasikāra* because one attends to (*manasi karoti*) and places [the object] in the mind. This is called "unwise attention" (*ayonisomanasikāra*); this unwise attention, characterized by an improper method and a wrong path of mental engagement, is what is so termed.
12. "Like a corruption of food": just as a corruption occurs through the putrefaction of food, so it is with the mind.
“Corruption” (*byāpajjana*) means bringing about a state of transformation in the mind. For this very reason it is said:
“the state of abandoning one’s natural condition. Because the mind is corrupted by it and abandons its former natural condition—just as spoiled rice and so forth—it is called ill will (*byāpāda*).
And because it serves as the sign for successive instances of aversion as they arise, it is the “sign of aversion” (*paṭighanimitta*); furthermore, it is the cause of aversion.
He said, "The object is the sign of resistance," because "this is a designation for both resistance and the object of resistance.
"In the Commentary" means in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. 13.
In the third [synonym], *thīnatā* is *thīna*; it is the state of being thickened due to the lack of expansion in the mind, like a lump of ghee, a state of being bound together.
The meaning [of *middha*] is as follows: it is called *middha* because it "stupifies" (*medhati*); the meaning is that it harms by way of making one unfit for action.

This is stated because in the Abhidhamma, *thina* (sloth) is defined as "that which at that time is the unfitness of the mind," and so forth, while *middha* is defined as "that which at that time is the unfitness of the body," and so forth.
Thus it is said: "Sloth is the unfitness of the mind; [it pertains to] three aggregates..."

“Unwieldiness and drowsiness. Although there is a mutual dissociation [between them], just as in the case of mental lightness and so forth, there may be a specific distinction between the mind and mental factors according to their respective order;
however, that which constitutes the specific condition for their lack of fitness and so on should be understood as their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
The phrase “of monkey-drowsiness” clarifies the meaning already stated: “the state of nodding off.”
That which causes the eyelids to become heavy is *pacalāyika*; the state of being *pacalāyika* is *pacalāyikabhāva*, which is to say, the condition of drowsiness (*pacalāyikatta*).
"Of both" refers to sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*). The connection with the phrase "the detailed exposition should be understood" is to be recognized here.
"Unwieldiness of the mind" is the state of illness of the mind; for one who is ill is indeed called "unwell."
It is said [in the Vinaya]: "Venerable sir, I am not unwell. For "kalya" means that which accords with time, namely health;
one who is intent upon that is "kalyaka," and one who is not so is "akalyaka. "Unwieldiness" (akammaññatā) is simply the mode of unwieldiness consisting of mental illness.
"Sluggishness" (olīyanā) is the mode of sluggishness; for the mind, when propped up by the postures (iriyāpatha), [becomes sluggish].
Unable to sustain itself, it clings and hangs down like a bat on a tree or like a pot of molasses stuck to a wooden post;
with reference to that state of his, it is called "clinging" (*olīyanā*). The second term is augmented by a prefix.

"Of the body" (*kāyassa*) refers to the mental body (*nāmakāya*), which consists of the three aggregates beginning with feeling. "Incapacity" (*akalyatā*) means unwieldiness (*akammaññatā*). [The rest] is as explained below.
It is exactly as previously stated. It is called *onāha* because it covers over like a cloud covering the sky. "Covers over" means it conceals or envelops;
thus, covering on all sides is *pariyonāha*. The meaning of *arati* and the others should be understood according to the method explained in the *Vibhaṅga*;
therefore, he says "For it is said," etc., in order to show the textual passage (pāḷi) stated therein.
In that context, "in remote places" means in distant or secluded locations. "Higher wholesome states" refers to the phenomena of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"Discontent" (*arati*) is the opposite of delight. "State of discontent" (*aratitā*) is the mode of being discontented. "Non-delight" (*anabhirati*) is the state of not finding delight.

"Mode of non-delight" (*anabhiramanā*) is the manner of not finding delight. "Weariness" (*ukkaṇṭhitā*) is the mode of being weary. "Agitation" (*paritassitā*) is the state of agitation resulting precisely from that weariness.
It means that for one who is dissatisfied, there is a yearning here and there. Or, "agitation" (*paritassita*) means trembling.

"Languor" (*tandi*) means natural laziness; the meaning is innate indolence. For thus, the lack of physical expansiveness when performing wholesome deeds is called "languor" (*tandi*), which is a state of sluggishness (*līnatā*);
it is not a bodily ailment caused by disease, the elements, or other such factors. "Tandiyanā" refers to the manner of being languid.
*Tandimanatā* is the state of the mind being overcome by sloth (*tandi*). *Ālasyaṃ* is the nature of one who is indolent; *ālasyāyanā* is the mode of proceeding toward indolence.
*Ālasyāyitattaṃ* is the state of having proceeded toward indolence. Thus, by all these terms, physical indolence is described by way of the defilements.

For it is through the influence of the defilements such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth—which are the causes of lethargy and drowsiness—that there is indolence of the mental body (*nāmakāya*); that very [indolence] is...
"Of the form-body as well" should be understood. *Jambhanā* means quivering. *Vijambhanā* is quivering again and again.
*Ānamanā* is bending forward. *Vinamanā* is bending backward. *Sannamanā* is bending all around.
*Paṇamanā* is like when a weaver, having risen from his loom, grasps something and straightens up his body.
Such is the "upright posture" of the body. "Afflicted by disease" means being afflicted by an arisen illness.

Thus, by all these terms, what is described is precisely the state of being bound to the body by way of the defilements such as lust, which are the causes of sloth and torpor. "One who has eaten" means one who has finished eating.
"Drowsiness after a meal" is the languor caused by food; for through heavy food, one becomes as if fallen into a swoon.
"Battled by food" (*bhattakilamatha*) means the state of being exhausted by food. "Feverishness from food" (*bhattapariḷāha*) means distress caused by food;
for at that time, one's faculties are impaired by the arising of fever, and the body decays. "Bodily sluggishness" (*kāyaduṭṭhulla*) means the body’s lack of functional efficiency due to food.
"Ill-health" (*akalyatā*), and so forth, follow the same method as explained below. "Lethargic" (*līna*) refers to a lack of expansion [of the mind].

*Paṭikuṭitaṃ*: contracted. The other two [terms] are descriptions of its mode of manifestation (*ākārabhāvaniddesa*). *Thinam*: it stands in a dense state due to its lack of expansion, like a lump of ghee.

*Thiyana*: a description of its mode of manifestation. *Thiyibhāvo* (the state of being thickened) and *thiyitattaṃ* (the quality of being thickened) mean being bound precisely by way of non-expansion.
By all these terms, however, the defilements such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth, which are the causes of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), are indicated.

It should be understood that the state of illness of the mind is described by way of these factors. "The four preceding states" refers to these four states: discontent (*arati*), sloth (*tandi*), yawning (*vijambhitā*), and drowsiness after eating (*bhattasammada*).
When dullness and torpor (*thinamiddha*) have arisen, since discontent and the others may also occur at that time, it is said:
"But [they exist] as a proximate cause (*upanissaya-koṭiyā*). This refers to them as a proximate cause.
The meaning is "it becomes a condition.

14. In the fourth [case], the state of being agitated is *uddhacca* (restlessness). That phenomenon by virtue of which the mind becomes agitated, or the phenomena associated with it—that phenomenon is *uddhacca*.
*Kukata* means that which is done badly; it is misconduct (*duccarita*).
And good conduct (*sucarita*). For even that which has not been done is indeed "badly done" (*kukata*);
for people speak thus: "That which was not done by me is badly done. Thus, misconduct and good conduct—whether performed or unperformed—are "badly done.

However, the mind that arises here with remorse (*vippaṭisāra*) directed toward that is what should be understood as "badly done" (*kukata*). Its state is worry (*kukkucca*). It is a state of agitation of the mind.
Only the mode of non-tranquility of the mind has been stated [as its characteristic]. For restlessness has non-tranquility as its characteristic.
Regret is a distorted resorting [to the mind] by way of grieving over misconduct and good conduct distinguished by what was done and what was left undone as they occurred.
Since remorse also possesses the state of mental distraction by way of grieving over what was done and what was left undone, it too has the mode of non-tranquility; thus he said: "of the mind..."
“Non-tranquility is the name for restlessness and remorse alone. And it is precisely this non-tranquility of mind that has been specified as restlessness and remorse themselves.
Since that [non-tranquility] does not arise simultaneously with itself, he said: “But this is a condition by way of decisive support (upanissaya).
And its status as a decisive-support condition is to be understood by virtue of having arisen previously.

15. In the fifth [definition], *vicikicchā* means that one has departed from (*vigatā*) healing (*cikicchā*). Alternatively, it is *vicikicchā* because one is distressed (*kiccati*) while investigating the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
16. In the sixth, "one does not obtain a cause (*hetu*) or a condition (*paccaya*). Here, by the mention of "cause," he refers to the productive reason (*janaka-kāraṇa*);

by the mention of "condition," he refers to the sustaining reason (*anupālanaka-kāraṇa*). Alternatively, "cause" (*hetu*) is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), and "condition" (*paccaya*) is the cooperative cause (*sahakāraṇa*).

It has been said. "That" refers to the defilement (*kilesa*). "Having turned away from it, he attains Arahantship" means that by directing the mind toward turning away (*vivaṭṭa*), he increases insight (*vipassanā*) and attains the fruit of Arahantship. "Where they wander for alms" is *bhikkhācāra*;
this is a designation for the village of resort (*gocaragāma*). "In that wandering for alms. "Having come to decline" means [having come] in accordance with the supporting of a wife.
"Having come to us. "Accumulating" means piling up. "Baked on coals" means cooked over glowing charcoal embers.
"What indeed?"—this was said by the monks in order to censure him. "A being who is a living peta":
this is stated by way of a supposition, meaning that while still alive, he will become a being who has attained the state of a *peta* in that very same physical form. "Pot" refers to a water-jar.

"Extremely cruel" (*ativiya dāruṇaṃ*) means exceedingly cruel. "What kind of result will there be? (*vipāko kīdiso bhavissati*) means: what kind of result, to be experienced in the future, will there be for the deed committed by you?
"Having destroyed" (*visaṅkharitvā*) means having ruined it by means of cutting, breaking, and so forth. "The island-dwelling animals and birds" refers to those who were sitting upon him.

Because they were "illuminated" (dīpana), the birds and deer acquired that name; having led them into the forest, the hunter would kill and capture whichever birds and deer arrived at the sound of their voices.

"The Elder" refers to the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa. "Having fashioned by means of supernormal power" (iddhiyā abhisaṅkharitvā) means having fashioned the supernormal power through such means as resolution (adhiṭṭhāna);
here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative. "A spark of fire" (aggipapaṭikaṃ).
*Accikaraṇaṃ* means "emitting sparks. *Passantasseva* is a genitive used in the sense of disregard (i.e., "even as he was looking on").
*Tassa therassa* refers to that Elder Milakkhatissa. *Tassā* refers to that spark of fire. *Paṭibalassa* means one who is capable in matters such as learning and recitation.
*Dukkhūpanisā* means that which has suffering as its proximate cause; it is that which is bound to suffering, having suffering as its cause.
"Have faith" is what is meant. Because the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) has been explained by way of the duties (vatta), it is said, "standing at the head of the duties.
"A heap of straw" means a pile of straw.
"Exert yourselves" means apply energy toward serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and so forth. "Depart" means depart from indolence (kosajja).
"Either for the removal of sensual desires, go forth"—by both of these, it is *vīriya* (energy) that is spoken of.
For *vīriya* is called "exertion" (*ārambha*) by way of its undertaking, and it is called "striving" (*nikkama*) by way of its departure from indolence.

"Exert yourselves in the Buddha’s teaching" means: apply yourselves with diligence to the threefold teaching of the Blessed Buddha, which consists of the study (*pariyatti*), the practice (*paṭipatti*), and the realization (*paṭivedha*).
Exert yourselves! Thus applying yourselves, shake off and shatter the army of Death. In this context, "the army of Death" refers to:
"Sensual pleasures are your first army; the second is said to be discontent.
The third is hunger and thirst for you; the fourth is called craving."
“Sloth and torpor are your fifth, the fearful are called your sixth;
doubt is your seventh, and hypocrisy and obstinacy are your eighth.
Gain, fame, and honor—”
And that fame which is wrongly acquired,
when one exalts oneself and disparages others.
“This is your army, Namuci, the attacking force of Kaṇha;
no coward conquers it, but having conquered it, one finds happiness.
Thus has come the army of Death, consisting of the divisions of sensual desire and the rest. And herein, because from the very beginning sentient beings have been householders...
The defilements of sensual pleasure deceive one regarding the objects of sensual pleasure;

having overcome those, for those who have gone forth into the homeless life and dwell in remote lodgings or in various other superior wholesome states, a lack of delight arises. For this has been said:
"Friend, it is difficult for one who has gone forth to find delight. Consequently, because their livelihood depends on others, they...
Hunger and thirst afflict them; being afflicted by these, the craving for seeking exhausts their minds.

Then, as their minds are exhausted, sloth and torpor descend upon them. Consequently, for those who fail to attain distinction while dwelling in remote lodgings in forest and jungle retreats that are difficult to endure, fear characterized by terror arises. For them—
For those who dwell with apprehension and suspicion, yet for a long time relish the flavor of seclusion, doubt arises regarding their practice, thinking, "Could this not be the path?

Having dispelled that, as they dwell on, pride, disparagement, and rigidity arise due to the attainment of even a slight distinction. Having dispelled those as well, as they dwell on, something even greater than that—
Based on special attainments, gain, honor, and fame arise. Becoming infatuated with gain and the rest, they proclaim counterfeit teachings;
having attained false renown, they remain therein, exalting themselves by birth and other such factors and disparaging others.
Therefore, it should be understood that sensual desires and the like constitute the first army and so forth. "A reed-hut" means a house thatched with grass woven from reeds.

"Will dwell" (*vihassati*) means he will dwell by means of learning, recitation, mental attention (*manasikāra*), and so forth. "The cycle of birth-and-death" (*jātisaṃsāra*) refers to the round of saṃsāra consisting of repeated births.
"He will make an end of suffering" (*dukkhassantaṃ karissati*) means he will realize Nibbāna, which is designated as the end of suffering.
"From a heap of straw" (*palālapuñjāhaṃ*): the word division is *palālapuñjaṃ ahaṃ*. "The third place" (*tatiyaṃ ṭhānaṃ*).
He speaks with reference to the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).

Regarding the phrase "the time of a three-year bhikkhu" (tivassabhikkhukāla): one who has had three years since full ordination (upasampadā) is "three-year-old" (tivassa); such a person is both "three-year-old" and a "bhikkhu," thus a "three-year bhikkhu" (tivassabhikkhu).
The time characterized by him, or by his [status], is the "time of a three-year bhikkhu" (tivassabhikkhukāla); [it refers to] at that time.
"When he has become a three-year resident bhikkhu" means when he has reached that status. "He performs work" means he performs the work of meditation (*bhāvanākamma*).
"The work of study" refers to the work of learning and so forth pertaining to the scriptures.

"Having honored the alms-food" means having paid honor—that is, performed worship—by bringing about the destruction of defilements through the alms-food given during the three months of the rains retreat. While honoring the alms-food...
For indeed, O monk, desiring that the alms-food given by those who gave it to him should bear great fruit,
he purifies his own continuum by bringing about the destruction of the defilements and thus attains Arahantship.
In the phrase "Mahābhūti," the word *mahanta* is a term for "worshipful," and *bhūti* refers to the Elder Tissa-Bhūti by means of a portion of his name.
He addresses [him]. For there is indeed a conventional usage even by means of a single part, as in "Devadatta" for "Datta. Or, "Mahābhūti" is a term of endearment;
he is called "Mahābhūti" because he possesses great *bhūti*—that is, greatness, splendor, or the excellence of merit, knowledge, and so forth.

"At the foot of a dense-sepaṇṇi grove" means at the base of a *sepaṇṇi* tree that is covered with branches, foliage, and the like, providing thick shade. This is the meditation subject of the foul (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Making it the basis" means making the access concentration or the absorption concentration obtained through the cultivation of the meditation subjects such as the foulness of the head-hairs,

etc., the basis. Here, "kammaṭṭhāna" (meditation subject) refers to the preliminary work of access jhāna and so forth directed toward the object of foulness, because it serves as the cause for the further development of the meditative work to be practiced above that.
It is called a "great assembly" because it numbered two thousand or more.

"Having gone from his own dwelling place to the presence of the Elder" means that he went through the air from his own dwelling place, descended near the monastery, and approached the Elder who was seated in his daytime resting place.
"Why have you come? means for what purpose have you come? Throughout all parts of the day and night...
"Unable to find an opportunity": it is said that although the Elder told him, "Friend, you will have no opportunity," he replied, "Venerable sir, I will ask when I am standing at the thought-hall.

When told, "Others will be asking there," he said, "Venerable sir, on the alms-round path. When told, "Others are asking there too," he mentioned the place where he wears his inner robe (*dupaṭṭa*) and the place where he puts on his upper robe (*saṅghāṭi*).
"At the place where the bowl is brought back; after wandering through the village, at the time when rice-gruel is being drunk in the refectory, 'Venerable Sir.
There too, the elders dispel their own doubts, saying, 'Friend. At the time of departing from within the village, 'I will ask, Venerable Sir.
There too, others ask, 'Friend. On the way, 'Venerable Sir. In the dining hall, at the conclusion of the meal."
"Venerable sir, at the time of washing the feet in the daytime rest-house, venerable sir. From that point on, until dawn, others ask him, "Friend.
When he takes a tooth-stick and goes for the purpose of rinsing his mouth, [others ask], "Venerable sir. At that time too, others will ask.
When he returns after having rinsed his mouth, [others ask], "Venerable sir. There too, others will ask.
“When he had entered his lodging and was seated, [he said], ‘Venerable sir. There too, others asked him, ‘Friend.
Thus, though he requested it throughout all parts of the day and night, he did not obtain an opportunity; it was with reference to this that it was said:
‘When there is no such opportunity, how will you obtain an opportunity for death? ‘Venerable sir, have you not washed your face?’”

Having entered the dwelling and warmed three or four meditation cushions (pallaṅka), he says this with the intention that there must be an attainment of a suitable place for those performing the work of wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra).
"In the color of a jewel" means in the color of a sapphire (indanīla-maṇi).
"Only while striving" means only while making an effort. "The invitation of purification" refers to that which proceeds thus: "I am pure."
The invitation for purity (*visuddhipavāraṇā*). This invitation belongs only to those who are Arahants. "A black spot" refers to a large black mark; "a mole" refers to a small one.
By both terms, he clarifies only the state of complete purity of their virtue (*sīla*).

"Those engaged in the work of striving" means those appointed to the task of striving. "One who has attained the path" means one who has found the means, that is, one who has first obtained the instruction.
It has been said. "Fallen" means discarded. "Just like gourds in the autumn" means like gourds scattered here and there, struck by wind and sun during the autumn season.
"Ash-colored" means having the color of pigeons. Having seen such bones as these, what pleasure can there be?
What kind of delight indeed could you have upon seeing such bones; is it not even a trivial thing?

The meaning is that it is simply not proper to take pleasure [in that]. "One who has never spoken a second word" means one who has never spoken a counter-word—a response to what was said by someone senior to oneself.
"By way of its constituent part" (*tadaṅgena*):
the abandoning of something by way of its own constituent part is "abandoning by way of its constituent part" (*tadaṅgappahāna*). For instance, when a lamp is lit during the night...

Just as darkness is dispelled by light, so too, by means of each respective factor of knowledge that constitutes a limb of insight (vipassanā), there occurs the abandoning of each corresponding defilement through its specific opposite;
this is called "abandoning by substitution of opposites" (tadaṅga-pahāna).
Just as sensual desire and the other defilements no longer remain by obsessing over the mind, so too is the prevention of their obsession and the bringing about of their non-arising.

Suppression is the abandonment by suppression. For just as moss is suppressed by a jar thrown into water covered with moss, so too the suppression of obstructive states such as the hindrances by means of various mundane concentrations is called "abandonment by suppression.
It is "complete cutting off" (samuccheda) because by this means the defilements are completely cut off; they are abandoned.
By this, "defilements" refers to abandoning; that abandoning known as eradication (*samuccheda*) is abandoning without remainder, which is "abandoning by eradication.

For when defilements such as the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned by means of the noble path-knowledge (*ariyamagga-ñāṇa*) in such a way that they do not recur—just like a tree struck by the wheel of a thunderbolt—that is what is called "abandoning by eradication. It subsides (*paṭippassambhati*).

"Tranquillization" (*paṭippassaddhi*) is so called because by means of it the distress of the defilements (*kilesa-daratha*) is stilled; it is the fruit, and that very fruit is "abandonment," hence "tranquillization-abandonment.
"Escape" (*nissaraṇa*) is so called because by means of it all defilements or all conditioned things escape and depart;
it is Nibbāna, and that very thing is "abandonment," hence "escape-abandonment. "Being tranquillized" (*paṭippassambhayamāna*) refers to the tranquillizing, which is the subsiding of the defilements.

"Performing. Regarding "by the mundane and supramundane": this is stated because the abandonment by way of substitution of the opposite (*tadaṅga*) and suppression (*vikkhambhana*) are mundane, while the others are supramundane.
It is called a "sign" (*nimitta*) because the fruit is "marked" (*nimīyati*) by it, as if being cast into the place of its arising; this is a term for a cause.
It is a designation (*adhivacana*). The sign of the foul, or the foul itself as the sign, is the "sign of the foul" (*asubhanimitta*).
For even the jhāna based on the foul is designated as "the foul" by way of a metaphorical expression for the support applied to what is supported, just as one says, "The beds are making a noise.
Therefore it is said: "The first jhāna, which has arisen with an object among the ten foul subjects. [This is stated] by way of "impermanence in the impermanent," and so forth.
By the phrase "stated according to the method," he shows the fourfold wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
It should be understood that the inclusion of both the fourfold unwise attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*) and wise attention here, as well as below, is intended to demonstrate them exhaustively.
Among those, however, what is intended here is the attention directed toward the foul as "foul," because it is conducive to that [insight].
Or rather, the inclusion of the others should also be understood.

The apprehension of the aspect of repulsiveness among the eleven kinds of foulness, or the practice in such a way that the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*) arises therein, is the apprehension of the foulness sign (*asubhanimitta*).
It is the application to the development of foulness (*asubhabhāvanā*) which brings about access concentration (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*).

It is said that by devoting oneself to the development of the foul (asubha-bhāvanā), sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is abandoned because, when one knows the proper measure in eating, sloth and torpor (thinamiddha) cannot gain an entry point due to their being overcome. Furthermore, there is the perception of repulsiveness regarding food dependent on such eating;
the seeing of the foul nature of its transformation, of its support, and of its state as undigested food in the stomach; and the seeing of how the body subsists upon nutriment.
He who develops this is specifically called "one who knows the measure in food," and for him sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is indeed abandoned.
Although it was stated [above] that the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*) is tenfold by way of its manifest forms, when bodily mindfulness (*kāyagatāsati*) is included,
the sign of foulness should be understood as elevenfold.
“Without having eaten, he drinks water” means that he should drink water after having consumed four or five mouthfuls (ālopa), for the purpose of making room for the drink.
Therefore it was said: “when there is space for four or five mouthfuls.
However, the commentator on the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammaṭīkākāra), having conjectured a different reading here—namely, “having eaten four or five mouthfuls, let him drink water”—explains it otherwise.

The meaning [of the term] has been explained, but it does not accord with the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). The Elder Tissa, a practitioner of the meditation on the foul (*asubha-kammika*), was one who saw teeth and bones.
17. Seventh: It is called *mitta* because it "moistens" (*mijjati*) by way of radiating welfare; it is a person seeking the welfare [of others].

That which exists toward such a friend, or that which belongs to a friend, is *mettā*; it is the state of desiring welfare. In this context, when "loving-kindness" (*mettā*) is mentioned, it refers to both absorption (*appanā*) and access (*upacāra*).
Because it is appropriate to speak of it as being common to both, he says: “By this much, even the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga) is included.

The word *api* includes absorption (*appanā*). Since there is no true liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) in loving-kindness that has not reached absorption, it is stated that “only absorption is intended” by the term *cetovimutti*.
The arousing and setting in motion of the bringing about of welfare for beings through loving-kindness is the apprehension of the sign of loving-kindness (*mettā-nimitta*).
The initial attention directed toward loving-kindness is itself the sign of loving-kindness, because it serves as the cause for the subsequent arising [of that state].
Those who have karma as their own are "owners of their karma" (*kammassaka*); beings are so called, and the state of being such is "the ownership of one's own karma" (*kammassakatā*).
Being heirs to one’s own kamma. Here, "reflective discernment" (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) refers to the investigation that reflects upon the dangers and benefits of ill will exactly as they are.
Here, "having good friends" (*kalyāṇamittatā*) refers to being possessed of a virtuous friend who dwells in loving-kindness. Regarding the "specified," "unspecified," and "directional" pervasions:

specification occurs by way of oneself, those very dear, neutral persons, and enemies; non-specification occurs when the boundaries have been broken down; and [the directional pervasion] occurs by way of pervading one direction and so forth.

The pervasion of the directions by loving-kindness should be understood according to the method of apprehension. There is the directed pervasion of the directions by means of a monastery, a road, a village, and so forth;
and there is the undirected pervasion of the directions by means of the eastern direction and so on, without reference to a monastery or the like.

It is with reference to this twofold apprehension that it is said: "the directed and undirected pervasion of the directions. And this apprehension extends as far as the access concentration (upacāra).

It should be seen. Cultivation is the repeated practice of what has been grasped. In that regard, it is fivefold by way of "all beings," "living creatures," "beings," "persons," and "those included within individual existence.

When directed toward each of these in four ways—thinking, "May they be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness"—it becomes twentyfold as the "unspecified pervasion" (anodhisopharaṇā).

Loving-kindness (*mettā*). It is sevenfold or twenty-eightfold when it proceeds by way of the basis of beings—namely, all women, men, noble ones, non-noble ones, deities, humans, and those in the states of loss—or tenfold when it proceeds by way of the basis of directions across the ten directions;
or, within each direction, it is divided into four hundred and eighty types according to the distinctions of beings, women, and enemies, and so forth.
And the specific pervasions are to be understood. "One developing loving-kindness" means one developing the jhāna of loving-kindness.
"Are you angry with him? and so forth, is a demonstration of the method of reflection. "Like a gift not accepted" means like a present that has not been received.
"In reflecting" means in investigation. "In the Vattaniya forest" refers to those such as the Elder Attagutta.

18. In the eighth [chapter], because it has the nature of establishing the practice of wholesome states and the nature of withering away their opposites, it is called "the energy of initial undertaking" (*paṭhamārambhavīriya*), meaning the energy that proceeds from the very beginning as the element of undertaking (*ārambhadhātu*).
Since there is neither the dispelling of laziness nor the gaining of firmness through mere initial undertaking alone, it is therefore said: "Because it has emerged from laziness, from that..."

"Stronger. However, because [the practice] becomes exceedingly firm—bringing about ever-increasing distinction through repeated cultivation as it arises again and again—it is therefore said: "Stronger even than that, by virtue of ascending to higher and higher stages.
"For the purpose of expulsion" means for the purpose of removal, just as [it is for the removal] of a great crossbar by those who lift it up.
Great effort must be exerted; thus it is said here: “Exertion of the mind for the removal of the crossbar.
Only through great prowess can one cut the bond made by another; thus it is said here:
“Prowess of the mind for the cutting of the bond.”
One whose energy (*vīriya*) is undertaken, accomplished, and fulfilled is "one of aroused energy" (*āraddhavīriyo*).

One whose energy has been brought to fruition, or one whose energy is undertaken and established, is "one of aroused energy. He said, "Of one of aroused energy," meaning "of one whose energy is perfected as well as exerted.
"Free from the four faults" (*catudosapagataṃ*): [text continues]
It is free from the four faults, beginning with excessive laxity (*atilīnatā*). He clarifies this very state of being free from the four faults with the words, "And not too lax," and so forth.
For a mind of development that is excessively lax would belong to the side of indolence (*kosajja*), while one that is excessively strained belongs to the side of agitation (*uddhacca*).
Excessive laxity is the occurrence of contraction without having entered the path of development; internal contraction after having entered it is [excessive] inwardness.
Contraction is excessive exertion, which is over-aroused energy. Distraction externally is the pursuit of thoughts that have scattered outward.
This energy is bodily when it brings about physical application such as walking meditation; otherwise, it is mental.
"Five periods of the day and night" refers to the five divisions consisting of morning, evening, the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch.
"Both of these" refers to physical and mental energy (*vīriya*). The stories of the Elder Milakkhatissa and the Elder Mahāsīva have already been shown above.
However, the story of the Elder Pītimallaka should be understood as follows: it is said that in his time as a householder, he was a wrestler.
While wandering through the three kingdoms with a banner in hand, he arrived at the island of Tambapaṇṇi;
having seen the king and received his favor, one day as he was passing through the door of the palanquin-hall, he recited the *Natumhākavagga*: "Form, monks, is not yours;
abandon it. When it is abandoned by you, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time."
Having heard this, he thought: “It seems that neither form nor feeling is the self.
Taking that very [teaching] as his goad, he departed, went to the Mahāvihāra, requested the going-forth, and was ordained.
Having mastered the two Matikas, he took thirty monks and went to the courtyard of Avaravāliya, where he practiced the duties of a recluse. As his feet began to fail him...
He was walking back and forth on his knees. During the night, a deer-hunter, thinking him to be a deer, struck him;

the spear passed right through him. Having had that spear removed and having filled the openings of the wound with a roll of grass, he had himself seated upon a stone slab, cleared a space, and by developing insight, attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having answered the monks who had arrived at the sound of his coughing, he uttered this inspired utterance:
“This was spoken by the Best of Buddhas, the Foremost Teacher of all the world:
‘This form is not yours; you should abandon it, O monks.’”
“Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena, subject to arising and passing away;
having arisen, they cease—their subsiding is bliss.
This is how the story of the Elder Tissa, son of a householder, is to be understood. It is said that in Sāvatthī there was one named Tissa...
The son of a householder, having renounced forty crores of gold and gone forth, was dwelling in a forest remote from villages.
His younger brother’s wife sent five hundred bandits, saying, "Go, take his life!
They went and sat surrounding the elder. The elder asked, "Why have you come, lay followers?"
“We shall deprive him of life. “Lay followers, take a guarantee from me and give me my life for this one night.

“Who will be your guarantor in this matter, ascetic? The Elder took a large rock, broke his thigh bones, and said, “Lay followers, a guarantor is sufficient. They departed and went to the head of the walkway.
Having made a fire, they lay down. As the Elder suppressed his painful sensations and reflected upon his virtue, rapture and gladness arose in him supported by that pure morality.

Then, gradually increasing his insight and practicing the duties of a recluse throughout the three watches of the night, he attained Arahantship at the rising of the dawn and uttered this inspired utterance:
“Having split both my feet, I shall make you understand:
‘I am repelled and ashamed; I am one whose death is accompanied by lust.
Having thought thus, I perceived things as they truly are.”
“At the break of dawn, he attained Arahantship.
Regarding “the grasping of the sign in over-eating”: this refers to the grasping of the sign for sloth and torpor in the context of over-eating;

it is the grasping of what is and is not a cause for sloth and torpor, thinking, “When one has eaten this much, that food becomes a cause for sloth and torpor; when one has eaten this much, it does not.”

The meaning is "it occurs. This has been stated by way of contrast; therefore, it should be understood that what is shown in substance is moderation in eating itself—namely, that when one has eaten this much, that food does not become a cause for sloth and torpor. Hence he said: "Four or five [mouthfuls]...
that does not occur. "The daylight of the sun" means that even for one who brings to mind at night the daylight of the sun as a sign perceived during the day.

The meaning here should be understood in this way. Because the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) are dependent upon energy, it is said: "even by talk that is appropriate and based on the ascetic practices.

In the ninth [section], the phrase "of one whose mind has been stilled by either jhāna or insight" means of one whose mind has been stilled through the departure of those defilements that prevent the stilling of the mind by either jhāna or insight.
"Remorse" (kukkucca) also occurs by way of grieving over what has been done and what has not been done.
It is stated that [restlessness] has the same characteristic as agitation (*uddhacca*) because it brings about a lack of tranquility in the mind while it is occurring;

thus, the cause for abandoning both is spoken of by treating them as non-distinct. For one who is well-versed and investigates the discourses and so forth according to their texts and meanings, and who dwells frequently therein, there arises the attainment of the "knowledge of meaning" (*atthaveda*) and so on, and thus no distraction occurs.
Just as through practice according to the method, there occurs the performance of duties appropriate to that stage.
Since there is neither distraction nor regret over what has been done or left undone, it is said: “Restlessness and remorse are abandoned even by great learning.

It should be understood that to the same extent that restlessness and remorse are abandoned through great learning, they are also abandoned through being inquisitive and knowing the discipline (*vinaya*) as it was formulated.
And service to the elders brings about the character of an elder, because it leads to the tranquility of the mind.

It is said, "one who effects the abandoning of restlessness and remorse"; however, it should be understood that those who dispel remorse without regard for seniority are called "virtuous friends" (kalyāṇamitta) who are experts in the Vinaya.

Furthermore, since distraction for renunciants is for the most part caused by remorse, qualities such as being one who asks many questions were specified through the very method of the Vinaya, beginning with the phrase "of one who is frequently inquiring about what is allowable and what is unallowable."

20. In the tenth [chapter], it is said: “By great learning... [etc. ...doubt is abandoned,” because for those who have heard much, there is no opportunity for doubt due to the arising of the realization of the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).
Granted that all eightfold doubt is abandoned through great learning and thorough inquiry; nevertheless, the remaining doubts are rooted in doubt regarding the Triple Gem.
He said: “Even for one who is abundant in thorough inquiry concerning the Three Jewels.
Because of the realization of the qualities of the Triple Gem, doubt (*vicikicchā*)—expressed in such phrases as “he doubts the Teacher”—is impossible.

Regarding the phrase “one who has mastery in the Vinaya,” he said this because such a person effects the abandonment of the doubt described as “he doubts the training”; for one who possesses abundance in resolve (*adhimokkha*), which is termed “conviction-based faith” (*okappaniyasaddhā*).

It is for one who is frequently intent upon resolving through the resolve known as faith—that which does not fail to enter into an object worthy of faith. And it should be understood that this "intentness" (adhimuccana) is simply the act of generating resolve (adhimokkha).
Alternatively, resolve (adhimutti) or resolution (adhimokkha) is the state of being inclined or leaning toward that [object] by means of faith.
Because both the condition for the hindrances and the destruction of that condition have been clarified, it is said: "The cycle of existence and its reversal have been explained."
The commentary on the Chapter on the Abandoning of the Hindrances is finished.
3. Commentary on the Chapter on Unwieldiness. 21.
In the first [sutta] of the third [chapter], "undeveloped" means not developed by way of the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). Thus.
Because it has not been developed. For that is called "unincreased" due to the absence of nourishment caused by the overcoming of its opposites.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "It becomes unwieldy. 22.
In the second [sutta], the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated. "In the first" refers to the first sutta of the third chapter.
"By way of the round" means by way of the round of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*). "The round of the three planes" refers to the round of result pertaining to the three planes of existence.
"Kamma for the acquisition of the round" should be understood as the kamma that serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the acquisition of the round of result;

it should also be understood that the round of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*), which acts as its companion, is included by the mention of "kamma" alone. "Kamma for the acquisition of the non-round" refers to the attainment of the non-round (*vivaṭṭa*).

Kamma that has become a decisive support (*upanissaya*). As for the kamma that produces the final existence (*carimabhava*), is it kamma for the attainment of the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*)? It is not; because it serves as a basis for the round (*vaṭṭa*).
However, it can be understood that, like the rebirth-linking of the final existence, it is a decisive support for the turning away.
For there is never the attainment of distinction (*visesādhigama*) without a rebirth-linking endowed with three roots (*tihetuka*).
It is possible. Regarding "in these suttas": in these first two suttas, the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its reversal (*vivaṭṭa*) are explained respectively.

23. In the third [sutta], regarding the term "undeveloped" (*abhāvita*): here, "development" (*bhāvanā*) refers to the development of concentration (*samādhi*). That wherein such development might be expected is intended as the "undeveloped" state, namely the great wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth; thus he says, "the prosperity of gods and humans," and so on.

24. In the fourth [case], since "mind" (*citta*) is intended specifically as the mind arisen by way of turning away (*vivaṭṭa*), the construction should be understood thus: "it conduces to great benefit because it does not produce the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and so forth.

25–26. In the fifth and sixth [cases], "arisen" (*uppanna*) refers to that which has not yet passed through the three moments of arising and so on—that is, it is undeveloped, devoid of cultivation, and not yet manifest—because it does not accomplish the function of what is considered "arisen" by the wise, just as one says of a man "he is sonless" [when he has not yet fathered a son]. It...
For just as one who, being capable, fails to perform the duty of a son toward his father is called "sonless" in the world, so it is with this case.
Therefore he said, "Why," and so forth. Regarding "in those states": this refers to the supramundane jhānas that serve as the basis, and so on.
However, the Elder, demonstrating that the mind has been developed only to its ultimate perfection, said, "the path-consciousness itself."

27–28. “Repeatedly not done” means it was not performed again and again by way of frequent cultivation through meditation (*bhāvanā-bahulīkāra*). “These two as well” refers to these two types of consciousness mentioned in these two suttas.

29–30. “In the ninth [sutta], ‘it brings’ (*adhivahati*) means it leads. ‘With difficulty’ (*dukkhena*) means with hardship. ‘Because of its being difficult to urge’ (*duppesanatā*) means because it must be urged with difficulty.
He said that the bliss of insight (*vipassanā-sukha*) which has reached its culmination is indeed more peaceful and more sublime than the bliss of ordinary jhāna.
“From the bliss of jhāna comes the bliss of insight. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For a bhikkhu who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is peaceful, there is a superhuman delight as he correctly discerns the Dhamma.”
“From whatever [angle] one contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one gains rapture and gladness; that is the deathless for one who understands.
For that mind is like a released thunderbolt of Indra, because it is unfailing.
The commentary on the section on the "Intractable" is finished.
4. Commentary on the section on the "Untamed," verses 31–36.
Regarding the first verse of the fourth section: "Untamed" means not tamed without the cultivation of the mind. Therefore, it is said: "devoid of restraint through mindfulness."

In the fourth [sutta], the meaning should be understood as the reverse of what was stated in the third. In the fifth and sixth, it is exactly like the first; thus, they are similar to the third and fourth.
Regarding the seventh and eighth:

"But here the similes" means that just as in the first and subsequent [suttas] untamed elephants, horses, and so forth were taken as the basis for the similes, so too here in the seventh and eighth they should be understood "by way of an unsecured house door and so on," as it is said.

39–40. Regarding the phrase "in the ninth and tenth [sections] by means of all four terms": the construction is that the ninth and tenth suttas are stated by connecting them with the four terms beginning with *adanta*.
The commentary on the *Adantavagga* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Paṇihitacchavagga*.
41. In the first [section] of the fifth [chapter], "upamā" means a simile (*opamma*); it is that very same meaning.
It is a particle used when that meaning of a simile is to be made known. *Seyyathāpi* means "just as" (*yathā*).
And here, the Blessed One sometimes presents a simile by surrounding it with the subject matter, as in the *Vatthasutta*, or in suttas such as the *Pāricchattakopama* and the *Aggikkhandhopama*.
And [the phrase] "as if": in some places it shows the meaning by surrounding it with a simile, as in the *Loṇambilasutta* and in such suttas as the *Suvaṇṇakāra-satta-sūriya-upama*.

However, in this *Sālisūka-upama*, they write in the manuscripts that [the Buddha] spoke the passage beginning with "Just as, monks" (*seyyathāpi, bhikkhave*) in order to show the meaning by surrounding it with a simile;
this is according to the commentary on the *Vatthasutta* in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*.
It does not correspond. For this is what is stated there:
"Bhikkhus, it is just as if there were a cloth"—this is merely a statement of a simile.
And when the Blessed One employs a simile, in some cases he first shows the simile and afterwards shows the meaning; in other cases, he first shows the meaning.
Regarding the simile: in some places it shows the meaning by surrounding it with the simile, while in others it shows the simile by means of the meaning.

For instance, in the *Devadūta-sutta*, he first presents the entire simile—“Just as if, monks, there were two houses with doors, and a man with sight standing in the middle could see them”—and only afterwards [presents] the meaning.

He spoke showing [the meaning].
