However, by way of the method beginning with, "He goes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains, as if through space," he first showed the entire meaning of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) and subsequently spoke while showing the simile.
By way of the method beginning with, "Just as, O Brahmin, a man seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood... he [showed] the entirety [of the simile].
Presenting the meaning by surrounding it with a simile, he spoke the *Cūḷasāropama-sutta*.
By way of the passage beginning, “But here, monks, some clansmen master the Dhamma—the discourses...
just as if, monks, a man were seeking an *alagadda* [snake],” he showed that the entire *Alagadda-sutta*, the *Mahāsāropama-sutta*, and other such suttas, are similes by way of their meaning.

Having surrounded [the meaning] by showing it, he said: "This [method], having first shown the simile here and afterwards showing the meaning, is called 'showing the meaning by surrounding it with the simile' when one speaks of the simile again after first stating the simile in the *Cūḷasāropama* and other such suttas, and then stating the meaning to be illustrated (*upameyya*) immediately thereafter. In the *Alagaddūpama-sutta* and others, however—
However, having first stated the meaning and immediately thereafter stating the simile, he speaks the meaning once more;
thus it is said that he shows the simile by surrounding it with the meaning. For this very reason, it is stated here in the *Līnatthappakāsinī*:

"Having first stated the meaning which is the object of the simile (*upameyyattha*), and then immediately thereafter stating the meaning once more while speaking the simile, he surrounds the meaning with the simile."

"...he shows," it was said. "By surrounding the simile with the meaning"—here too, the method is the same. However, in this context, in some instances he shows the simile by surrounding it with the meaning, as it was stated:
"As in the *Vatthasutta*, and as in suttas such as the *Pāricchattakopama* and the *Aggikkhandhopama*. Regarding that, first, in the *Vatthasutta*: "Just as, monks, a cloth that is soiled..."
Suppose there were a cloth stained with dirt; whatever dye a dyer applied to it—whether blue, yellow, red, or madder—the color would remain poorly rendered and impure. Why is that?
Because of the impurity of the cloth, monks. Even so, monks, when the mind...
Having first shown the simile by saying, “When it is defiled, a miserable destination is to be expected,” etc., the meaning of the simile is stated afterwards; however,
it is not the case that the meaning is stated first, followed immediately by the simile, and then the meaning is stated again—
by which [method] one might show the simile as being surrounded by some meaning here or there, as one might say in the *Vatthasutta*.

Likewise, in the *Pāricchattaka-upama* it is said: "Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas becomes yellowish-brown, at that time the Tāvatiṃsa devas are glad, thinking:
‘The Pāricchattaka koviḷāra is now yellowish-brown; it will not be long before it becomes leafless... [and so on]..."
"In the same way, monks, at whatever time a noble disciple intends to go forth from the home life into homelessness, at that time, monks, the noble disciple is like a withered leaf," and so on;
having first shown the first simile, the meaning was subsequently stated. In the Simile of the Mass of Fire: "Behold, monks, that..."
"A great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing. "Yes, venerable sir.

"What do you think, monks? Which would be better: that one should embrace that great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing, and sit down near it or lie down upon it, or [that one should embrace] a Kṣatriya maiden?"
Or having embraced a young brahmin girl or a young householder’s daughter with soft and tender hands and feet, one might sit down near her or lie down near her.

Thus, by first showing the simile and subsequently stating the meaning, and not by first stating the meaning and then immediately showing the simile and again stating the meaning, it is said: “In some places...”
One should not say: "He shows the simile by surrounding it with the meaning, as in the Vatthasutta, and as in the Pāricchattakopama, Aggikkhandhopama, and other such suttas.
However, some here explain it thus: "Having first stated the meaning and subsequently showing the simile, [he does so] by means of the meaning..."

"It is said that one 'shows by surrounding the simile' when one shows the meaning after first stating the simile; whereas one 'shows by surrounding the simile with the meaning' when one shows the meaning after first stating the simile.

To indicate the places where both of these occur, he says, 'As in the Vatthasutta,' and so forth. That too [occurs] "in some cases, showing the simile surrounded by the meaning, as in the Vatthasutta."
It should be stated, “as in the *Pāricchattaka-upama-sutta*, the *Agni-khandhopama-sutta*, and so forth.

And when it is stated thus, one need not separately say, “in some cases he shows the meaning by surrounding it with a simile, as in the *Loṇambila-sutta*,” because [the latter] is already included by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “as in the *Agni-khandhopama-sutta* and so forth. For even in the *Loṇambila-sutta*:
“Bhikkhus, suppose a wise, competent, and skilled cook were to present a king or a royal minister with various kinds of curries:
those that are sour, bitter, pungent, sweet, acrid, and non-acrid; salty, and non-salty.
“Monks, that wise, competent, and skilled cook grasps the signs regarding his own meal:
‘Today this curry for my meal pleases me; he brings more of this; he takes much of this;
he speaks in praise of this. Today this sour-topped curry pleases me; of the sour-topped—’”
Or he brings [the food] forward; or he takes much of that which is sour; or he praises the color of that which is sour...
[and so on] ...or he praises the color of that which is unsalted. That wise, competent, and skilled cook, monks, gains clothing, gains wages, and gains extra offerings. For what reason?

For just as that wise, clever, and skilled cook learns [the tastes] for the sake of his own meal, even so, monks, here a certain wise, clever, and skilled monk dwells contemplating the body in the body...

pe... he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... pe... he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind... pe... he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful.
Possessing mindfulness, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, as he dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena, his mind becomes concentrated,
his defilements are abandoned, and he grasps that sign.
"Monks, such a wise, competent, and skillful monk is indeed one who attains [realization] in this very life."
“He becomes one who gains pleasant dwellings and possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension. Why is that?
Because, monks, that wise, competent, and skillful bhikkhu has grasped the sign of his own mind.
Thus, having first shown the simile, the meaning was subsequently stated. [This is found] in such discourses as the *Suvaṇṇakāra-sūriya-upamā*.

And as for the phrase "and like," this is included merely by way of illustration, because it was not shown by means of a simile at the outset in such discourses as the *Suvaṇṇakāra-sutta*. For in those, first of all, in the *Suvaṇṇakāra-upama-sutta*:
"Monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind should from time to time attend to three signs:..."
From time to time, the sign of concentration should be brought to mind; from time to time, the sign of exertion should be brought to mind;
from time to time, the sign of equanimity should be brought to mind.
Monks, if a monk devoted to higher consciousness were to bring to mind only the sign of concentration exclusively, it is possible that his mind would lead to indolence.
“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of exertion,
it is possible that his mind would lead to restlessness. If, bhikkhus,
a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend exclusively to the sign of equanimity, it is possible that his mind would not become rightly concentrated.”
For the destruction of the taints. But when, monks, a bhikkhu devoted to higher consciousness from time to time attends to the sign of concentration...

[as before] ...the sign of exertion... [as before] ...the sign of equanimity, then his mind becomes pliant, wieldy, bright, and not brittle; it is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
“Just as, monks, a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice might prepare a furnace; having prepared the furnace, he might heat the mouth of the furnace;
having heated the mouth of the furnace, he might take gold with tongs and cast it into the mouth of the furnace;
having cast it into the mouth of the furnace, he might blow upon it from time to time, and from time to time—”
He sprinkles it with water and from time to time looks on with equanimity.
Monks, if the goldsmith or his apprentice were to blow upon that gold all at once, there is the possibility that the gold would burn up.
Monks, if the goldsmith or his apprentice were to sprinkle that gold with water all at once...

He would sprinkle it; that gold would cool down. But, monks, if the goldsmith or the goldsmith’s apprentice were to look on with total indifference at that gold, it is possible that the gold would not reach full maturity.
However, monks, when the goldsmith or the goldsmith’s apprentice [attends to] that gold...
From time to time it is heated, from time to time it is sprinkled with water, and from time to time it is left to cool;
that gold becomes soft, workable, radiant, and not brittle, and it properly adapts itself to its work.
Whatever kind of ornament one desires—whether a flat band or a coil—it can be fashioned into that.
“Whether it be by means of a neck-ornament or a golden garland, one experiences its benefit.
In the same way, monks, for a monk devoted to the higher mind... he becomes rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.
And whatever state that is to be realized through direct knowledge, toward the realization of which he inclines his mind, [he realizes it].”

"In each and every case, one attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is a suitable occasion"—having thus shown the first meaning and immediately thereafter stated a simile, the meaning was stated once more in this way; having again shown the first meaning and immediately thereafter stated a simile, the meaning was stated yet again.
And in the Simile of the Seven Suns:
“Monks, conditioned phenomena are impermanent; monks, conditioned phenomena are unstable; monks, conditioned phenomena are unreliable.
To this extent, monks, it is enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them.
Monks, Sineru, the king of mountains, is eighty-four thousand yojanas in height.”
It is eighty-four thousand yojanas in width; it is plunged eighty-four thousand yojanas into the great ocean, and it rises eighty-four thousand yojanas above the great ocean.
There comes a time, monks, when after the passing of a long period—after many years, many hundreds of years—
“For many thousands of years, for many hundreds of thousands of years, the rain does not fall.
When it does not rain, monks, whatever plants, seeds, and vegetation there may be—herbs, grasses, and forest trees—they wither, they dry up, and they cease to exist.
Thus, monks, are conditioned phenomena impermanent; thus, monks, are conditioned phenomena unstable,” and so forth.
Having first shown the meaning and immediately thereafter stated the simile, the meaning is stated once more. Or else:
"Bhikkhus, for the rising of the sun, this is the precursor, this is the forerunner, namely the dawn.
Even so, bhikkhus, for the arising of the Noble Eightfold Path in a bhikkhu, this is the precursor..."
"This is the prior sign, namely, having virtuous friends"— this which has come down in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* might here be intended as the *Sūriyopama Sutta*.

However, even that does not accord with the statement "in some cases it shows the meaning by surrounding it with a simile," because after stating the first simile, it shows the meaning immediately thereafter, and then again...
Because no simile was stated [there]. For in that case, the simile was shown right from the beginning:
"But in this Simile of the Rice-Grain, showing the meaning by surrounding it with a simile, he said, 'Just as if, monks,' and so forth.
This statement is also not included, because there is no difference between the Vattha Sutta and this one; for in both cases, having first shown the simile—

The meaning was stated last; therefore, the reading here ought to be as follows: "In this regard, the Blessed One sometimes first shows the simile and afterwards shows the meaning, as in the *Vatthasutta* and in suttas such as the *Pāricchattaka-upama* and the *Aggikkhandha-upama*;
and sometimes he shows the simile by surrounding it with the meaning, as in suttas such as the *Suvaṇṇakāra-satta-sūriya-upama*."
"But in this simile of the rice husk, having first shown the simile, [the Buddha] spoke the words beginning with 'Just as, monks,' while subsequently showing the meaning.
Otherwise, it would contradict the *Madhyamāgama-aṭṭhakathā*. Furthermore, even here, what precedes and what follows do not agree.
Or rather, the reading should be accepted here exactly according to the method stated in the *Madhyamāgama-aṭṭhakathā*.
The awn that arises at the tip of the grain of rice, resembling a thorn, is the *sālisūka*; likewise for the *yavasūka* (the awn of barley).
Because the awn is thin and possessed of a fragile nature, its piercing is not very great; thus he said: "It will pierce," meaning it will cut the skin.
Just as a rice-awn or the like, when wrongly positioned, does not pierce the hand or other parts even when stepped upon, [so too is this case].

Because it exists in a state unfit [for that purpose], this shows the meaning: "the mind leading to accumulation does not break through ignorance because it has arisen in a state unfit to do so," by means of the passage beginning with "by being wrongly established.

"In eight places" refers to the eight locations: the four truths, beginning with suffering (as stated in the phrase "ignorance regarding suffering"), and the four [extremes] such as the prior limit (*pubbanta*).
In these instances: "Dense and thick" means extremely dense due to long-term cultivation.

Because it has a vast domain, possesses great adversaries, has a large retinue, and involves much suffering, ignorance is "great"; thus, it is "great ignorance" (*mahā-avijjā*). For the word *mahā* also signifies "abundance," as in "the great multitude" (*mahājana*) and so forth.
[The phrase] "by way of having emerged from the possession of craving" refers to that state.
He speaks of the very absence of craving.

Regarding the second line, when it is said that what is stepped upon is "trampled," he says, "It is called 'stepped upon' just as if it were trampled by the hand," because this is a conventional usage (ruḷhi).
He explains: "'The noble idiom' refers to those who dwell in the Noble Land."
This is conventional usage. To show the purpose for taking only a small amount instead of a great one, the passage beginning with “But why? is commenced.

By this it should not be thought that “the wholesome state which is a prerequisite for the turning away from existence (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) is called ‘small’ because it was produced through careful attention”;
rather, having gradually obtained its conditions and increasing, it is like a small river that, upon encountering a great flood, plunges into the ocean.

It is explained that, in due course, it leads the person to the great ocean of Nibbāna itself. "Paccekabodhi" (solitary enlightenment) and "Buddhabhūmi" (the stage of Buddhahood) are used here in the accusative case as direct objects.
"The cycle of existence and its cessation have been explained" refers to what was stated in their respective order.
43. In the third [verse], "a mind defiled by hatred" refers to the associated mental states within the continuum in which they arise.
His mind is corrupted by a fault that, through its defilement, is like putrid urine mixed with poison.

"By his own mind" means by his own mind accompanied by either the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) or the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). "Having delimited" means having delimited it by means of knowledge.
It goes in a desirable manner, thus it is *ayo*, which is happiness. That from which all *ayo* (happiness) has departed entirely is [the word] *apāya*. From this...
Alternatively, "bad destination" (*duggati*) means a state of going or a place of occurrence for bodily and mental suffering;

"falling away" (*vinipāta*) means that beings are cast down there by various means and through diverse transformations; and "hell" (*niraya*) means that even the slightest *ayo*—which is happiness—is not found there.
This is how the meaning should be understood here.
44. “Clear through serene confidence” (saddhāpasādena pasannaṃ) means clear by means of the clarity known as faith, not by the lack of clarity of the sense faculties.
“The destination of happiness” (sukhassa gatiṃ) is the place where happiness occurs. Or, it is called a “good destination” (sugati) because only happiness goes there, not suffering.
It is called “heaven” (sagga) because it is together with the highest things, such as agreeable forms and so forth; that world.
45. It is called a *rahada* because it is a lake (*rahado*) where the fever of distress (*pariḷāha*) is stilled. A lake full of water is an "aquatic lake" (*udakarahada*).
It is called an "aquatic fire" (*udakadaha*) because it burns—that is, sustains—water. "Turbid" (*āvila*) means agitated due to an abundance of mud;

hence he said, "not clear. "Agitated" (*luḷita*) means stirred up by the wind; hence he said, "not settled. Due to the agitation caused by the impact of the wind, there is a state of being crowded with waves, ripples, and impurities.
For it is not settled all around, nor is it unsettled. Because it has become turbid due to the impact of the wind and the scarcity of water, reaching the state of mud, he says:
"become muddy. "Shells" refers to mother-of-pearl shells and the like. "Snails" refers to specific types of conch-spires.
"Whether moving or standing still"—this should be understood as a statement regarding whatever is available. For that indeed is what is meant by the expression "whatever is available."
In order to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “ettha” (herein) was commenced.
“By being enveloped” means by being concealed. This is a demonstration of the state of turbidity through its cause.
That which exists in the present life, in this very selfhood, is “pertaining to the present life” (*diṭṭhadhammika*); and since that may be both mundane and supramundane, he said:
“Mixed with the mundane and the supramundane. Because one must go to and pass away [into] it, it is the "hereafter" (samparāya), that is, the world beyond. Therefore he said:

“For that which has its benefit in the other world is ‘benefit for others’ (parattha). Thus, since both types [of benefit] are included as being comprised within one’s own personal continuity (sakasantati), he said “Moreover,” and so forth, in order to show them by including the other as well.
“This” refers to what is designated as the wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha).
The Dhamma is tenfold. "At the end of an intermediate aeon" (*satthantarakappāvasāne*) is said with reference to its proximity;

however, it should be understood as referring to the end of any intermediate aeon whatsoever. "Suitable for the Noble Ones" (*ariyānaṃ yuttaṃ*) means suitable for the state of being Noble Ones (*ariyabhāva*);
for that very reason, it is capable of producing the state of being Noble Ones. Knowledge itself [is so called] in the sense of making the knowable directly manifest (*paccakkhakaraṇa*).
He said, "It is indeed knowledge," and so forth, referring to "seeing. But what is that? He said, "The divine eye," and so forth. 46.
In the sixth [case], *accha* means thin. It is with reference to this very state of being thin that it is called "not thick" (*abahalā*).
Since that which is clear (*pasanna*) is thin and not thick, therefore it is said, "it is also appropriate to call it 'clear' (*pasanna*). *Vippasanna* means especially clear.
He is serene. Furthermore, he is called "rightly serene," which is why it says, "well serene.
"Untroubled" means unstained; hence it says, "completely pure," and so forth. "Sankha" refers to small moss, which is called "sesame-seed moss.
"Sevāla" refers to *kaṇṇika* moss. "Paṇaka" refers to water-impurity. The state of turbidity in the mind has the hindrances as its cause.
He said: “‘Untroubled’ means being free from the five hindrances.
Regarding the seventh [section], “kinds of trees”: here, the word *jāta* is used merely for metrical expansion, as in the expression “born from a sheath” (*kosajāta*).
He said: “This is a designation for trees themselves. For some tree is preeminent in color, such as that—
[This refers to] red sandalwood and so forth. Some [are distinguished] by scent, such as Gośīrṣa sandalwood; some by taste, such as Khadira wood;
and some by hardness, such as Campaka flowers. That which is developed by way of insight (vipassanā) for the sake of bringing about the paths and fruits is also included.

Because of the statement, "In each respective case, one attains the capacity to be a witness," it is specifically the fourth jhāna consciousness that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā).
"Friend," says the Elder Phussamitta.
Regarding the eighth [section], he says that the turning of the mind consists in its arising and ceasing: "Thus, having arisen so quickly, it ceases quickly.
In the sense of exceeding measure means in the sense of transcending measure; that is, by way of surpassing all measure.
This is the meaning. Therefore he said: “It is not easy at all. Eye-consciousness is also intended here;
this is stated because all consciousness shares the same momentary duration. To illustrate, according to the Theravāda, the extreme rapidity with which consciousness turns over, he said:
“But in this matter,” and so forth. By “mental formations” (*cittasaṅkhārā*), he refers to consciousness together with its associated mental factors.
"O Great King, 'of a hundred cartloads of rice' is what is written in the manuscripts; however, the reading should be 'a hundred cartloads of rice,' O Great King.
For this very reading is seen in some places even in the *Milindapañha*.
Or, it should be understood that "vāhasatānaṃ" is used as a genitive of apposition (*paccatte sāmivacanaṃ*) by way of grammatical variation (*byattayena*). "Aḍḍhacūḷaṃ" means... [text fragment ends]
"Less by a quarter" means half. Of what is it half? It is understood to be half of a *vāha* by virtue of the context.
Some say "thirteen and a half"; others say "three and a half. They state emphatically that it is more than one hundred and fifty *vāhas*, but this should be investigated.
A *tumba* consists of four *nāḷikas*. Regarding the absence of a question: "But is it possible, Bhante, to give a simile... [The text continues: ...without a question being asked.
Because there was no question put forward in the form "Is it possible to do so?", the simile was not employed.
"At the conclusion of the teaching of the Dhamma" means at the end of the discourse on the Dhamma that had been commenced for the assembled assembly. 49.
In the ninth [verse], "radiant" (*pabhassara*) means pure in the sense of being naturally purified. Therefore he said: "bright" (*paṇḍara*).

"Completely pure. [The questioner asks: "What indeed is this so-called 'color' of the mind? [The respondent] replies: "Luminosity and the like are specific qualities obtainable within the color-element (vaṇṇadhātu).

Having rejected [the notion of color] on account of the mind's formless nature, saying "there is none," the other [respondent] says "of blue and so forth," etc., showing that this is a figurative statement intended to illustrate the state of purity of such a mind.
For it is said: "When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, and bright... Therefore he says:
"This too is luminous because it is pure through the absence of defilements. But is the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta) free from defilements?
Yes, it is free from defilements by its very nature; however, it may become defiled by way of adventitious defilements. Thus he says:

“*Taṃ ca kho*,” and so forth. Therein, having previously said “this” (*idaṃ*) because it was directly evident to himself and to those bhikkhus, he now says “that” (*taṃ*) by way of referring back to it.
The word *ca* (and) is used for the purpose of introducing a meaning; the word *kho* is for the ornamentation of speech, or for emphasis.
This is because the meaning about to be explained is certain and because there is no co-existence with the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*).
He said, "by those not co-nascent," etc., because the defilements are adventitious.
He said, "by the defilements, such as lust," because lust and the rest approach the mental continuum and defile it, afflict it, and torment it.
In the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) mind being defiled by defilements, because of its state of non-contact; for it is comprised within a single continuity.
However, since "being defiled" is a synonym for this, he said: "It is called 'defiled'.
Now, in order to clarify that meaning by means of a simile, he said: "Just as," and so forth.
By this, he shows the distinction that in the world, even conduct occurring in a different mental continuum is seen to be censurable, let alone conduct occurring within a single continuum.
Therefore he said: "At the moment of impulsion... it is called defiled.

In the tenth [case], the mind that is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is what is meant by "mind"; thus, it is the life-continuum mind itself that was spoken of in the passage, "This mind, bhikkhus, is luminous.
To the extent that the life-continuum mind becomes defiled upon the convergence of such conditions...
It is said that, by virtue of that, when there is a convergence of conditions contrary to it, it is called "freed from defilements. Therefore he said:
"It is called 'completely freed from defilements'. The rest here should be understood according to the method explained in the ninth sutta.
The commentary on the section on the "well-directed clear eye" is finished.
6. Commentary on the Chapter on the Snap of the Fingers (Accharāsaṅghātavagga) 51.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the sixth [chapter]: in the phrase “the uninstructed person” (*assutavā*), the particle *vā* indicates mere existence, as in such passages as “a man possessed of wisdom is good.
In passages such as “he is virtuous and of lovely character,” it indicates a state distinguished by praise.
In such passages as, "He is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away," the meaning refers to a state of existence distinguished by excellence.
Therefore, one who possesses what is praised or heard with excellence is "learned" (*sutavā*).
This term "learned" refers both to the hearing of the *pariyatti* Dhamma—which is capable of destroying defilements—and to the practice toward suchness (*tathattāya*) after having heard it.

It has been proclaimed. One who has heard what is worth hearing, by way of accomplishing what ought to be done, is "one who has heard" (*sutavā*); by contrast, one who has not heard it is "one who has not heard" (*assutavā*).

For this negative particle *a-* is seen in such instances as "states without cause" (*ahetukā dhammā*) and "a residence without a resident monk" (*abhikkhuko āvāso*), where it denotes the exclusion of association with that [positive term].

“Dhammas that are not conditions” (*appaccayā dhammā*): this is for the purpose of excluding their connection [to being a condition]. For that which is conditionally arisen (*paccayuppanna*) is connected to a condition;
thus, by virtue of not being conditionally arisen, the state of not being connected to that [condition] is illuminated here. “Dhammas that are non-demonstrable” (*anidassanā dhammā*):

this is for the purpose of excluding their own-nature (*sabhāva*). For here, "demonstrable" (*nidassana*) means visibility. Alternatively, it is "demonstrable" because it is seen—that is, eye-consciousness. This [term] serves to exclude its being graspable by that [consciousness].
Likewise, "states without taints" (*anāsava-dhammā*); "states without resistance" (*appaṭigha-dhammā*) and "states without an object" (*anārammaṇa-dhammā*) are used to exclude those functions.
"Immaterial states" (*arūpin-dhammā*) and "non-mental factors" (*acetasiaka-dhammā*) are used to exclude that specific nature.

For here, what is being demonstrated is their difference from those. "Non-human being" (*amanussa*) is used to exclude merely that state; it means there is no mere humanity, but something else similar to it.

For here, similarity (*sādissatā*) is indicated. In the phrase, "One who is not a recluse, yet claims to be a recluse; one who does not lead the holy life, yet claims to lead the holy life," there is the exclusion of those qualities by which he would be esteemed.
For here, censure (*garahā*) is understood. In the phrase, "Is your honor free from illness?
Is the maiden slender-waisted? there is the exclusion of its non-occurrence. In the phrase, "Dhammas that have not arisen," there is the exclusion of a similar state.

For past phenomena possess conformity to what has arisen because they have previously arisen; and because phenomena subject to arising have established a portion of their conditions, they possess the state of having begun to arise.
Furthermore, since that which is independent of time exists, there is conformity to what has arisen, let alone for present phenomena; thus, their dissimilarity [to the past] is understood here.
“Phenomena of one beyond training” (asekkhā dhammā) refers to the cessation of the final limit of that [training]. For it is the culmination of that which is intended here.

“Proclaimed” means that which illuminates many such meanings. Here, however, it should be understood as the exclusion of those specific natures—as in the cases of “formless phenomena” (*arūpino dhammā*) or “non-mental factors” (*acetasikā dhammā*).
The meaning is “elsewhere. By this, he shows its lack of knowledge derived from hearing and so forth.
Therefore it was said: “One should be known as ‘unlearned’ due to the absence of scripture and realization.”

Now, explaining its meaning, he says “yo hi” and so forth. In this context, even through skill in the aggregates, elements, and so on, there exists much learning (*bāhusacca*) which serves as the cause for knowing those things defiled by the secondary defilements (*upakkilesa*). As it is said:
“To what extent, venerable sir, is one ‘much-learned’? To the extent, monk, that one is skilled in the aggregates... skilled in the elements... and so on.
“He is skilled in the sense bases... pe ... he is skilled in dependent origination. To this extent, bhikkhu, one is ‘learned. Therefore, it was said:
“And for whom [there is mastery] regarding the aggregates, elements, sense bases, the modes of conditionality, the foundations of mindfulness, and so forth.

In that context, *uggaha* (learning) is the act of committing [the text] to memory by means of speech. *Paripucchā* (inquiry) is the thorough questioning of the meaning. Together with those who are skilled, it consists of the posing of questions and the providing of answers.

*Vinicchaya* (decision) is the act of making a decision. *Āgama* (tradition/scripture) is the understanding of the meaning and the Dhamma by means of knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*), following upon having attended upon a teacher.
*Adhigama* (realization) is the actualization of the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna.

They are called "productions" because they arise from the non-affliction of many various types of views such as personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), or because they are produced by those [non-afflictions].
Ordinary persons (*puthujjana*). Alternatively, the word *jana* expresses simply "not being struck down" (*avighāta*). Regarding the phrase "those who look toward the faces of various teachers":
here, "ordinary persons" (*puthujjana*) means those for whom there are many (*puthu*) people recognized as teachers. Regarding the phrase "not emerged from all destinies" (*sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhita*):

here, "destinies" (*jana*) are so called because beings are to be produced (*janetabba*) or are born (*jāyanti*) therein; since they have many such destinies, they are "ordinary persons. Beyond this, they are born.
"By these" refers to the people; "formations" (*abhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth are meant. Because these [formations] exist manifoldly (*puthu*) in them, they are called "worldlings" (*puthujjana*).
Alternatively, the word *jana* should be understood as having the meaning of "formations" and so forth. The "floods" (*ogha*) are the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*) and the others.

The "torments" (*santāpa*) are the fire of passion (*rāga-aggi*) and so forth. Or else, all those defilements (*kilesa*) are the "fevers" (*pariḷāha*). Regarding the phrase "delighting manifoldly in the five strands of sensual pleasure," here a person (*jana*) is one who is born [into such states]; thus, passion (*rāga*) is greed (*gedha*).

Those who belong to this class and so forth are "worldlings" (*puthujjana*). Alternatively, the word *jana* should be understood in the sense of lust and so on, as in "people born among various [objects] and stained [by them].
"Stained" means they are colored by desire-lust, which—like dye on cloth—causes a transformation of the mind; they are thoroughly stained.
They are *giddhā*—greedy—by way of longing and intense craving. They are *gadhitā*—bound—as if tied with a knot, being difficult to release and thus attached to that object.
They are *mucchitā*—infatuated—having fallen into delusion, rendered as if unconscious by the power of the defilements and having no other purpose.
They are *ajjhopannā*—possessed—having swallowed and finalized it as if making it their own, exclusive property.

*Ṭhitā*: "Attached" means clinging like [a fly] to a crooked thorn; "submerged" means being sunk so that one cannot lift oneself out, like a person mired in a great quagmire up to the tip of the nose. *Laggitā*:
"Entangled" means being caught by the power of the five faculties, like a monkey smeared with monkey-glue. *Palibuddhā*: "Obstructed" means bound, or afflicted.
*Āvutā* means obstructed. *Nivutā* means hindered. *Ovutā* means covered over or enveloped. *Pihitā* means closed off. *Paṭicchannā* means concealed.
*Paṭikujjitā* means turned face downwards. By the term "unlearned" (*assutavā*), the state of being blinded by ignorance is expressed;
thus he says, "the blind worldling is spoken of. This is the stability of the mind (*cittatthiti*).

"There is no grasping of the mind" means that the cultivation of the mind (*cittabhāvanā*) and the stabilization of the mind (*cittaṭṭhiti*) is that practice by which one knows the defilements of the mind and its liberation from them according to their true nature.
Having made firm establishment on a single object through thorough concentration the basis, it proceeds together with the associated states and the objects of support.
There is no development of insight characterized by the discernment of the mind, by means of which one might know the aforementioned matter according to its true nature. 52.
The meaning of the second phrase, "one who has heard," has already been explained in the immediately preceding sutta.

Regarding the term "noble disciple" (*ariyasāvaka*), a fourfold classification is possible; to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "there is a noble one" is commenced. They have awakened to the truths individually.
[They are] Paccekabuddhas. Is it not the case that all Noble Ones (ariya) likewise penetrate the Truths individually, because the Dhamma is to be personally realized?

This was not said with reference to such a penetration. Rather, it refers to how disciples penetrate the Truths by means of dependence on others, since the path of vision does not arise for them without the voice of another; and as [it is with] the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas.
Others awaken to the truths by way of dependence on another, but these are not so;

rather, having become independent of others, they penetrate the truths by virtue of not being led by another. Therefore it is said: "They are Paccekabuddhas because they have awakened to the truths individually.
Regarding the statement, "There is one who is a disciple but not a noble one," here even a person of faith—one who has deep conviction in the Three Jewels through ordinary, worldly faith—is included.
It is indeed taken up. However, the phrase "a layperson who has not yet attained the fruit" should be regarded as a mere illustration.
For the person described above, from the moment of going for refuge onwards, may rightly be called "one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.
This meaning is to be illustrated by the Dakkhiṇāvisuddhi Sutta. As for the term "learned" (*sutavā*), its meaning is as stated here.
The name [of this practice] is the cultivation of one's own welfare and the welfare of others; it is by means of this that one is "endowed with learning. With reference to this, it was said:
"And he is endowed with what has been heard, even if he speaks but little that is beneficial," and so forth.
He should be understood as a "noble disciple" because he is constantly engaged in the duty of hearing the Dhamma from the Noble One, the Blessed One. By means of the secondary defilements...

"Complete liberation" means being undefiled; the knowledge of its true nature occurs only through a more powerful development of the mind, and not otherwise—thus it is said, "powerful insight is spoken of.

(53) Regarding the "occasion for the discourse on the simile of the mass of fire" in the third [section], it refers to the occasion for the teaching in the Discourse on the Simile of the Mass of Fire.
For the Blessed One taught this discourse by taking as a sign the wrong practice of certain bhikkhus, which was caused by that very teaching.
It remains unseparated at all times because of his well-established mindfulness and clear comprehension.
This is because the physical body of the Buddhas is unstained by external or internal impurities, resembling a well-polished natural gem.

Therefore it was said: "For the sake of favoring his attendants and for the sake of bodily comfort. "Having spent [the time]" means having spent it through the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
Spending time in a secluded seat by way of delimiting the time is both due to being inclined toward seclusion and for the purpose of others following his example.
"Having dressed" means having dressed by way of changing from the robe worn in the monastery.
Sometimes he entered villages alone, sometimes surrounded by the community of monks;

sometimes in his ordinary manner, and sometimes while performing miracles—entering in such various ways according to the persons who were to be trained. "Having brought" means having brought from flowering trees and the like in the Himalayas and other regions.
"Levelness of the ground" refers to the attainment of evenness at the time of the Teacher’s placing his foot down, due to its being lowered and raised.
And the receiving of the lotus that has blossomed through pleasant contact is the natural outflow (*nissanda-phala*) of having well-planted feet,
not a feat of supernormal power (*iddhi-nimmāna*). This is merely an illustration,
since at that time other things— such as the removal of pebbles, gravel, thorns, and mud, and the attainment of purity— are also obtained.
The phrase "as soon as it was placed within the Indakhīla" is stated because the Teacher’s miracles were performed solely for the purpose of training those who were to be converted.
The phrase "with his right foot" is used because Buddhas always proceed by circling to the right.
Although it says "six-colored rays," the addition of "as if yellowed with liquid gold" is due to the predominance of the golden luster on the bodies of Buddhas.
It has been said. They produce sounds in a sweet manner because they perceive the essential value of what is seen.
As for the sounding of drums and the like, that is simply their natural property (*dhammatā*).
"They honor" means they revere and worship with devoted minds, thinking: "Today we have obtained something very difficult to find; we who serve the Blessed One with such exquisite food."
"Having observed their mental continuums" means having observed the mental continuums of those individuals who were thus attending, as they occurred in the past and in the present.
"They are established in arahantship" is the connection [of the sentence]. "Therein" means in the monastery.
"In the perfumed pavilion" means in the pavilion that had been anointed with a mixture of four kinds of fragrant scents.

“Rare is the attainment of the opportune moment” means that even when one has acquired human birth, qualities such as dwelling in a suitable locality, the integrity of the sense faculties, and the acquisition of faith are difficult to find.
“They go to the realms of the Four Great Kings... up to... the realm of Vasavatti”—this is said with reference to the empty celestial mansions (*vimāna*) therein.
After the meal, the Blessed One entered his fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭi*) and [divided the day] into three parts.
Having done this during the first watch, if he so desires, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture.
If he so desires, he enters the fruition-attainment (phalasamāpatti) practiced by the Buddhas.

Then, having emerged from that at the appointed time, during the second watch—the final watch—he surveys the world, as in the third section, for the ripening of the wisdom of those to be trained (veneyya).
In order to see this, he said, "If he so desires," and so forth.
"Appropriate to the time" (kālayutta) means what is timely (pattakalla), that is, suitable for that particular occasion, such as "at this moment, this should be said to him.

"Appropriate to the occasion" (samayayutta) is a synonym for the same; or it means appropriate to the specific context (aṭṭhuppatti). Alternatively, "appropriate to the occasion" means connected with the noble doctrine (ariyasamaya).
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dhamma precisely according to the place and time;

and in teaching, they teach while illuminating the principle of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), which is esteemed by the Noble Ones. Alternatively, "conjoined with the occasion" means accompanied by reasons and examples.
For the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma with its specific application at the proper time; having discerned the right time, he dismisses the assembly, and not until...
He teaches the Dhamma in the midst of darkness;
the intention is that he causes [the disciples] to grasp the weather, but does not wash away their impurities. For no dust or dirt adheres to the Blessed One’s body.

"From here and there" means from their respective daytime resting places and so forth. "Finding opportunity" refers to the times before the meal, after the meal, and during the first watch of the night.
Not having found an opportunity [earlier], she now finds an opportunity during the middle watch; or, finding an opportunity because one was granted by the Blessed One.
Since the adoption of the lion’s posture is not invariably possible during the first of the three periods following the meal, he said:
“of the body oppressed by sitting from the time after breakfast onwards. For that very reason, in that context...
“If he so desires”: this indicates that the adoption of the lion’s posture was not fixed at all times. “Fatigue” means weariness.
It should be understood that he adopts the lion’s posture for the purpose of releasing the body from fatigue. “He surveys the world with the Buddha-eye”:
this is stated because it was the Blessed One’s habitual practice during the last watch of the night; yet sometimes it was also done at other times.
The Blessed One establishes that matter by means of the remaining powers and knowledges, as well as the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
"In this very task" refers to the task of the last watch of the night. Because a great fever arises in the physical body (*karajakāya*) due to the intensifying power of remorse, he said:
"When the mental body (*nāmakāya*) is inflamed, the physical body is inflamed. "Stored away" means...
This was said with reference to accumulated blood. "Warm blood gushed from his mouth" means that the blood, having become warm, gushed from his mouth.
"The place" refers to the profession of being a monk. "That evil increasing" means that because he did not abandon the profession of a monk, his evil increased accordingly.
Even for those who have committed an offense involving the ultimate penalty (*antimavatthu*), if [the evil] proceeds by means of a stratagem...

Showing that right attention (yonisomanasikāra) is indeed beneficial, he said, "Those who have become spiritually stirred" (jātasaṃvegā), and so forth. "Aho sallekhitaṃ" means "O, how well-refined!"—it refers to that which has proceeded with extreme refinement.

"Kāsāvapajjoto" (the radiance of the saffron robes) refers to the fact that because of the great number of bhikkhus wandering here and there, they shine with the brilliance of their saffron-colored garments.
"Isivātaparivāto" (surrounded by the fragrance of the seers) refers to the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and the other aggregates.

Because he was seeking Nibbāna, it was perfumed on all sides and everywhere by the fragrance of the virtues of the seers and bhikkhus, and by the fragrance of his own body which had been scented by their virtues.
A sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*) arose without his having to direct his attention, because that matter had not been understood by him previously. "Sense of spiritual urgency" means...
And in such a matter, there arises, by way of the nature of things (dhammatā), the knowledge of self-reproach (sahottappa-ñāṇa).
"The basis for consolation" means the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that is the cause for the mind's consolation. "The prior stage of all duties" means the stage preceding everything.

For, by means of [the thought] "May all beings be free from enmity," etc., there is the establishing, the presence, and the pervading with welfare of the mind. The other [term] is used because it is somewhat greater than this.
This is called the "Cūḷaccharāsaṅghātasutta" (The Short Discourse on the Snap of a Finger).

A "snap of a finger" refers to the moment of snapping the fingers, the time it takes for an eye to blink, which is the duration required to utter a single syllable. Thus he said: "Merely making a sound by clapping two fingers.
"A mind pervading with welfare for all beings" means [a mind] correctly [directed] toward all beings whatsoever.
It is the mind proceeding by way of the desire for welfare. "While adverting, he cultivates" means while adverting by way of the desire for welfare.
Even while inclining [the mind] through adverting, he is said to cultivate it by means of knowledge-dissociated [consciousness]. "Knowing" means even while merely giving rise to such knowledge.
"Seeing" means even while insight-observing as if directly before one's eyes by means of the eye of knowledge. "Reflecting" means that object...
“Even while looking at each object” and “resolving with faith,” etc., are stated by way of the five faculties (*indriya*).
“To be directly known,” etc., are stated by way of the Four Noble Truths. All of this, in detail, is simply the demonstration of repetition (*āsevana*) in a general sense;
therefore, in order to show the specific meaning of repetition intended here, the passage beginning with “But here” was stated.

“Possessing unimpaired jhāna” (arittajjhāno) means not devoid of jhāna. “Possessing non-empty jhāna” (atucchajjhāno) means not empty of jhāna. Or rather, “non-abandonment” (apariccatta) is a synonym; thus he says, “possessing unrenounced jhāna.
To show the meaning of the word “dwells” (viharati) according to the method given in its analysis (vibhaṅga), he says, “‘Dwells’ means moves about,” and so forth.
Here, however, is the etymological meaning (saddattha): regarding the word “viharati,” the prefix *vi-* [is used].
It signifies the sense of interruption. "Carries" (*harati*) means "leads" or "maintains";

the meaning is that he carries on by interrupting [one posture]. Thus it is said: "he dwells" (*viharati*), because having interrupted one bodily posture with another, he carries and maintains his personal existence (*attabhāva*) without it falling away;
therefore, he is called "one who dwells. "He moves" (*iriyati*) refers to actions such as standing, sitting, and so forth.
It proceeds while performing [its function]. "Proceeds" means it proceeds by being endowed with the postures (*iriyāpatha*) and so forth.
"Protects" means it protects by guarding against the impairment of one posture through the other postures. "Sustains" and "maintains" are synonyms for that same term.
For, by interrupting the impairment of one posture with another posture, it sustains and maintains the personal existence (*attabhāva*) so that it does not collapse.
It is said: "He walks" (*carati*) means that he proceeds while being endowed with one of the postures, such as standing or sitting.
"By this term" refers to the term "he dwells" (*viharati*).
Regarding "dwelling in the postures" (*iriyāpathavihāra*): here, *iriyā* is the act of moving or proceeding; it is bodily exertion, bodily activity. Of that...
The term *iriyāpatha* (posture) means the way of movement (*iriyā*) because it is the means for its occurrence; it refers to standing, sitting, and so forth.

Indeed, it is not possible to perform any bodily action without the states of standing, sitting, and the rest. For one who possesses the state of standing might perform some action with the body, or one who possesses any one of the others, such as walking.
Alternatively, *vihāra* means "dwelling" (*viharaṇa*), or that by which one dwells; thus, it is simply posture.

“Abiding” (*vihāra*) refers to abiding in the postures (*iriyāpatha*); and in its actual sense, this is merely a continuous stream of the fourfold materiality (*rūpa*) occurring in the modes of standing, sitting, and so forth.

To show that the distinction between exhortation (*ovāda*) and instruction (*anusāsani*) is merely one of specific instances—such as being given once or many times—and not a difference in their ultimate reality (*paramattha*), he says: “But in the ultimate sense... and so on. In that context, regarding such expressions as *ese*, *eke*, and *ekaṭṭhe*:
The meaning should be understood through such phrases as "this one is alone" and so forth.
A *raṭṭhapiṇḍa* (country alms) is an alms-meal obtained from a country or from a country. Therefore he said: "Having abandoned the circle of kinsmen," and so on.

In that context, they are called *ñātī* (kinsmen) because they are recognized as "these are ours"; they are so called in the sense of revolving around [the self] by way of grandfather, father, sons, and so forth.
“Retinue” means a circle of relatives; thus, it is a “retinue of relatives. “Enjoyment by theft” means the enjoyment of one who is unworthy.
For in the Blessed One’s teaching, requisites are permitted for the virtuous, not for the immoral.
Even for donors, their relinquishment is intended only for the virtuous, not for the immoral, because the latter expect a great fruit for their own deeds.

Thus, because it has not been authorized by the Teacher and has not been relinquished by the donors, the consumption by one who is immoral—even while sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha—is "consumption by theft" (*theyyaparibhoga*).
"Consumption as a debt" (*iṇaparibhoga*) means consumption on account of a debt;
the meaning is that it is like consuming after having taken up a debt, due to the absence of purification of the offering for the recipient.
In the sense of being something to be given, it is a "gift" (*dāya*); those who take that [gift] are "heirs" (*dāyādā*), which is a designation for sons. Their state is "inheritance" (*dāyajja*);
enjoyment by way of inheritance is "enjoyment of inheritance" (*dāyajjaparibhoga*). What is meant is: enjoyment by virtue of being a son.
For the monks who are trainees (*sekkha*) are the Blessed One’s own legitimate sons; being heirs to what belongs to their father, they—
They make use of requisites. But do they make use of the Blessed One’s requisites, or rather those of householders?
Even though given by householders, they belong to the Blessed One because he has authorized them;

for there is no use whatsoever of what has not been authorized, while use is possible only for what has been authorized. In this regard, the *Dhammadāyāda-sutta* (The Discourse on the Heirs of the Dhamma) is the supporting proof.

Only those free from lust (vītarāga), having transcended the servitude of craving, enjoy [the requisites] as masters; thus it is said: "The enjoyment of one whose taints are destroyed is called 'enjoyment by a master'.
For those not free from lust, because they are subject to the power of craving, there is no state of mastery in the enjoyment of conditions.
Due to the absence of that [craving], those free from lust possess mastery therein, since enjoyment according to their own preference is possible for them.

For they consume requisites by regarding the repulsive as non-repulsive, the non-repulsive as repulsive, and by avoiding both of these through a mode of equanimity; thus they fulfill the wishes of the donors.
Furthermore, this consumption by one who is virtuous after due reflection is a consumption free from debt, because it is the opposite of a consumption that is like a debt.
It is called [debt-free enjoyment]. For just as a debtor cannot go wherever he pleases, so one who is bound by the consumption of debt cannot escape from the world;
therefore, because it is the opposite of that, the reflective enjoyment of one possessed of virtue is called "debt-free enjoyment.
Thus, in the primary sense, this is distinct and separate from the four types of enjoyment.
It should be understood as "use. This is not mentioned separately here, as it is included within "use by inheritance" (*dāyajjaparibhoga*).
For even one who is virtuous is called a "trainee" (*sekha*) precisely because he is endowed with this training.
Among these types of use, use as an owner (*sāmiparibhoga*) and use by inheritance are permissible for both Noble Ones (*ariya*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), whereas use by debt (*iṇaparibhoga*)...
It is not permissible. There is no discussion whatsoever regarding enjoyment through theft.

But how, in this context, can there be enjoyment as an owner (*sāmiparibhoga*) and enjoyment as an heir (*dāyajjaparibhoga*) for worldlings (*puthujjana*)? It is by way of figurative usage (*upacāra*).
For when even a worldling, established in the practice of effacement (*sallekha*), abandons greed for requisites and enjoys them with a mind unstained by them, that is "enjoyment as an owner."
For one who is virtuous, however, enjoyment after reflection is like the enjoyment of an inheritance, because it does not fail the wishes of the donors.
There is no need to speak further regarding the enjoyment by a noble worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*), since he is included among those in training (*sekkha*).
The *Sekkhāsutta* is the proof for this point.
"For this bhikkhu": for a bhikkhu who cultivates a mind of loving-kindness even for the duration of a finger-snap.

"The enjoyment of the country's alms is not in vain" means that because this renunciant, a recluse, a bhikkhu, expels from his own continuum the stain of hatred and those evil states associated with it by means of that cultivation of loving-kindness for those giving material gifts, the consumption of the alms is fruitful.

Because it brings about the subsiding [of defilements], because it correctly perceives the danger in *saṃsāra*, and because it does not deceive one’s own aspiration, the consumption of the country’s alms-food is not in vain.
“Of great benefit” (*mahatthiya*) means having a great purpose and a great utility. “Of great fruit” (*mahapphala*) means having abundant fruit.
“Of great advantage” (*mahānisaṃsa*) means having the fruit of a great outflow. “Of great radiance” (*mahājutika*) means having great majesty. “Of great expansion” (*mahāvipphāra*)...
"Of great extent. Herein, the first reason is that by practicing loving-kindness, that bhikkhu becomes worthy of consuming the alms-food of the kingdom as its master and so forth;
the second is that it makes the gift given by others possess great fruit.
Now, if even the mere practice of loving-kindness is of such great power, what need is there to speak of its frequent cultivation?
The meaning is: "In this case, there is simply nothing further to be said. 54.
Regarding the fourth [section], the fact that the word *bhāvanā* (development) carries the sense of "producing" (*uppādana*) and "increasing" (*vaḍḍhana*) has already been stated previously. 55.
Regarding the fifth, "in these two" refers to the fourth and fifth [sections]. It should be understood "in the same manner as stated in the third."

Having said this, in order to show how it should be understood, he stated: "For he who cultivates," and so forth. By that, he expresses the lack of any difference in meaning between cultivation (*āsevana*), development (*bhāvanā*), and attention (*manasikāra*).
If this is so, one might ask: "How then is the teaching of the Suttanta? To this he replied: "But the Perfectly Enlightened One," and so forth.

By the phrase "by which element of phenomena" (*yāya dhammadhātuyā*), he refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). For by that [knowledge], he discerns the differentiation of the modes of phenomena.

Having understood this, the Blessed One analyzes even a single teaching accordingly and demonstrates it. "By way of three divisions" refers to the portions of cultivation through repetition (*āsevana-bhāvanā*), mental attention (*manasikāra-bhāga*), and so forth.
For loving-kindness (*mettā*) is "repetition" (*āsevanā*) when it has been brought about by way of extending loving-kindness toward every object;
its "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) is the increasing of that [loving-kindness]; and "mental attention" (*manasikāra*) is the fixing of the mind upon it without letting go.
56. In the sixth [case], the statement is indefinite because it was not stated by specifying them as "these are named...";

the statement is definite because they were stated in their own form as "unwholesome" (*akusala*). They are "exhausted without remainder" because there is no portion of the unwholesome left ungrasped, however small.
They "partake of the unwholesome," thus they are *akusalabhāgiya*. They "exist on the side of the unwholesome," thus they are *akusalapakkhika*.
Therefore he said, "Only unwholesome," and so forth. "Goes first" means it occurs earlier;

the sense is that it proceeds as the primary or foremost. For among the four immaterial aggregates that arise together by way of simultaneous origination and so on, there is no such thing as this one arising first; however, as in the case of the supramundane paths, [it is distinguished].
Because the existence of the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) and, among mundane phenomena, the faculty of mind (manindriya), precedes [all others] to an exceptional degree, it is said:

"All these are preceded by the mind. For likewise, even in the Abhidhamma, when teaching that "at whatever time a wholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere has arisen," the teaching proceeds by making consciousness the precursor and the foremost. This is also the case in the Suttas.
It is said: “Mind precedes all phenomena; mind is the lord, the master of the six doors. Therefore he said, “For these,” and so forth.

And as for the statement that “mind is their arouser”: it is said because, insofar as the mind functions as the senior among the associated states, it causes them to follow after itself and thus brings them into being in that manner. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*...

However, with reference specifically to the mind’s status as the senior [factor], even its simultaneous arising is treated as if it were its first arising, according to the analogy of a king’s procession;
this is the meaning shown here. By the word "anvadeva" (immediately following), it should be understood that the absence of a first arising for the mind in terms of a discrete moment is indicated.
For this very reason, he says: "The meaning is 'from one and the same [moment]'."
57. In the seventh [section], even wholesome states belonging to the four planes are mentioned; thus it is said by way of an exhaustive inclusion with the words, “whatever wholesome states there are.
58. In the eighth, the term *idam* is a designation used with a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*), or it is a particle (*nipātapada*) like in expressions such as *yadidam*.
Therefore he says: “The meaning is ‘this negligence. The mode of being negligent is the state of negligence (*pamādāpatti*). It is the relaxation of the mind.
In these aforementioned instances, the non-restraint of the mind by means of mindfulness is the absence of mindfulness (*sativiraha*).
"Non-application" (*vossaggānuppadāna*) means the successive application of relinquishment; that is, repeated letting go.

"Lack of earnestness in performance" (*asakkaccakiriyatā*) refers to a person’s lack of earnestness in the practice of these wholesome states such as giving, or a lack of earnestness regarding the object to be given. This is the state of being constant.

"Constantly" (*sātaccam*): action performed constantly is "constant action" (*sātaccakiriyā*); that very state is "constancy of action" (*sātaccakiriyatā*). "Not constancy of action" (*asātaccakiriyatā*) is the absence of constancy of action.
"Unfinished action" (*anuṭṭhitakiriyatā*) means the state of action being uncompleted; it is not merely the non-performance of action at intervals.
"Sluggish conduct" (*olīnavuttitā*) refers to sluggishness of conduct due to the absence of expansion, which is characterized by uninterrupted performance.
"Relinquishing zeal" (*nikkhittachandatā*) means the state of having abandoned the desire for vigor (*vīriya-chanda*) toward wholesome activity.

"Relinquishing the burden" (*nikkhittadhuratā*) is the laying down of the burden of vigor; the meaning is a shrinking back of the mind. "Lack of resolve" (*anadhiṭṭhāna*) is the state of not being established in the performance of what is wholesome.

"Lack of application" (*ananuyoga*) is the failure to apply oneself. "Non-habituation" (*anāsevanā*) and so forth refer to the absence of cultivation (*āsevana*) and other such practices regarding wholesome states. "Heedlessness" (*pamāda*) is...

“Sarūpaniddeso” (the description of the essential nature) refers to the definition of the characteristic. “Pamajjanā” (negligence) is the description of the mode. “Pamajjitattaṃ” (the state of being negligent) is the description of the entity.

By the word “parihāyanti” (they decline), he shows the blameworthiness of negligence. This, however, is by way of those in the world (*lokiya*), not those who have transcended the world (*lokuttara*); thus he said: “When... pe... this,” and so forth.
59. It is called *appamāda* (heedfulness) because by means of it one does not neglect. It is the opposite of negligence (*pamāda*), consisting in the non-separation from mindfulness (*sati*).

In terms of its meaning, this is the name for mindfulness that is constantly established. Negligence, however, should be understood as an unwholesome state of mind that stands in opposition to mindfulness or to mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*).
Therefore he said: "By way of being the opposite of negligence..."
"It should be understood in detail. 60.
In the tenth [verse], "one who sinks into what is contemptible" is *kusīta*; by changing the letter *da* to *ta*, the state of that is *kosajja*, meaning idleness (*ālasiya*).
The commentary on the Chapter on the Snap of the Fingers is finished.
7. Commentary on the Chapter on the Arousing of Energy, etc.

61. Regarding the first [sutta] of the seventh [chapter]: "The work of the heroes" (*vīrānaṃ kammaṃ*). *Vīriya* is so called because it is to be stirred up or set in motion according to the proper method.
That very same energy, in the sense of being a primary exertion for wholesome action, is the "arousing of energy" (*vīriyārambha*). It is the state of having energy aroused.
The term *vīriyatā* (the state of energy) should be applied individually to both "exerted energy" (*paggahita-vīriyatā*) and "perfected energy" (*paripuṇṇa-vīriyatā*). 62.
In the second [case], one who has great desire is *mahiccha*; the state of being such is *mahicchatā*.
Great greed is *mahālobha*, because it covets vast objects and many things. By the phrase "this or that," etc., [it refers to] those who have gone forth.
"Great desire" (*mahicchatā*) is what has been stated. The passage beginning with "by means of the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañcahi kāmaguṇehi*) is spoken with reference to householders.
"Desire" (*icchā*) is a designation for its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "Possessed of desire" (*icchāgata*) means one in whom desire is active. "Great desire" (*mahicchatā*) means great longing.
As for its actual meaning, it is said to be lust (*rāga*), as in the passage: "lust, infatuation," and so forth.

63. Regarding the third [phrase], *appicchassa*: here the word *appa* has the sense of "absence," as in such expressions as “he is free from illness, free from affliction” (*appābādho hoti appātaṅko*).

Thus he says, “of one who is without desire” (*anicchassa*). For in the world, the term “free from illness” (*appābādho*) is used with reference to the absence of well-known ailments, such as eye diseases, stomach diseases, and so forth.
Now, in order to make this very meaning even more clear, he says: “here...”
The words beginning with “no” have been stated. The phrasing (*byañjana*) appears as if incomplete because the term “little sound” (*appasadda*) is seen even in the case of the limited;
however, the meaning (*attha*) is complete, since what is intended is the total absence of desire for conditions. Therefore he said, “No,” and so forth.
To illustrate by another way this point—that one is called “of few desires” precisely through the absence of desire—he said, “Furthermore,” and so forth.

It has been said. "Desiring much" (*atricchatā*) means desire for this or that. "Evil desire" (*pāpicchatā*) is a base, worldly, and inferior desire arising from the conceit of possessing qualities one does not actually have.

That by which one conceives oneself to possess qualities that exist [only] within oneself for the sake of procuring requisites, and which knows no moderation in accepting those requisites—this is "great desire" (*mahicchatā*). "Conceit of possessing qualities one does not have" refers to oneself...
The proclamation to others of qualities that do not exist as if they did exist.

"Esteeming of existing qualities" means the manifestation within oneself of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and the ascetic practices (*dhuta-dhamma*), while remaining established in right conduct. There is also a lack of moderation in accepting [offerings] even from such a person;
that too has indeed been included in the Abhidhamma—this is the connection. "Difficult to satisfy" (*dussantappo*) means difficult to appease.
"Extremely coarse" (*atilūkhabhāva*) refers to the extreme coarseness of his bowl and robes. Seeing this, people thought, "This is an inauspicious day;
the noble one’s bowl and robes are so rough and dull that he should be made the leader," and they said, "Venerable sir, please stay outside for a short while.
"He emerged" (*ummujji*) means [he emerged] from the earth while the people were still unaware.
Having submerged himself, he emerged just as he was taking hold [of the bowl].

If the Elder had wished, "Let them know my state of having destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*)," people would not have told him, "Stay outside"; for one who has destroyed the taints, such a thought simply does not arise.
Having thus shown the fourfold division of desire by way of the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*) with a focus on fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*), once again, by way of the person...
Showing the fourfold division of desire, he said: "Furthermore, there is another fourfold [type of] one who has few desires," and so forth.

One who has few desires regarding requisites (*paccaya-appiccha*) is one devoid of longing for requisites. One who has few desires regarding the ascetic qualities (*dhutaṅga-appiccha*) is one devoid of longing for the esteem of possessing the ascetic virtues.

One who has few desires regarding learning (*pariyatti-appiccha*) is one devoid of longing for the esteem of being well-versed in the scriptures. One who has few desires regarding realization (*adhigama-appiccha*) is one devoid of longing for the esteem of being a "noble one" (*ariya*).
"Under the power of the donor" means under the influence of the donor's intention, whether he wishes to give little or much;

"under the power of the object to be given" means due to the scarcity of the object to be given; "one's own strength" means one's own capacity—the taking of only as much as one can sustain oneself with.
As for the passage beginning with "If indeed," etc., it refers to what was stated in brief.
This is the exposition of the meaning. "By the measure alone" means by the measure of mere subsistence.
"Not even a single monk knew [of it]" means that because he had conducted himself perfectly according to the duties of a cemetery-dweller (*sosānika*), not even one monk recognized him.
"Uninterrupted" means without break. "May a second know me" means that even a second person, who was his companion, might come to know him.
One could not [do so]; likewise, I have dwelt continuously in the charnel ground for sixty years; therefore, oh, I am the supreme charnel-ground dweller (*sosānikuttama*).
"Having been a benefactor" means having been a benefactor by way of the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) through such means as formal learning (*uggaha*) and inquiry (*paripucchā*).

"Having stirred the countryside with a discourse on the Dhamma" refers to those who had gathered together and others as well, by way of causing hair to stand on end, giving shouts of "Well done!", and the tossing of garments.
"How indeed shall we hear a little of the Dhamma from the presence of the Noble One?"—thus, by means of a great clamor, he agitated the multitude.
If the Elder had wished to make known his state of being learned (*bahussuta*), he would have preached the Dhamma even earlier, while still agitating the countryside.
"Gata" (gone) means: "This is he by whom the Dhamma discourse was given during the night," thus by way of recognition.
Before dawn had even broken, he departed out of his desire for mastery of the scriptures (*pariyatti-appicchatā*).
He was like three clansmen: just as the three clansmen Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimila dwelt together in harmony in the Pācīnavaṃsa forest grove;
for among these too, the Blessed One said to the Elder Anuruddha: "Anuruddha, do you have..."
“When asked, ‘For those who dwell thus—heedful, ardent, and resolute—has any superhuman state, a distinction in noble knowledge and vision, or a comfortable dwelling been attained?

we replied: ‘In this case, venerable sir, as much as we desire, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, we enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.’”

When the successive attainments of the meditative dwellings (*anupubbavihārasamāpatti*) had been announced by [Anuruddha] with the words, "Let us enter and dwell in jhāna," the other elders did not wish to do so.
For when the Blessed One had departed, they said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Did we indeed announce to the Venerable Anuruddha, 'We [shall enter] these and those meditative attainments'?"
“Are we recipients [of this], since the venerable Anuruddha has declared the destruction of the taints even in the presence of the Blessed One?
Was not Ghaṭīkāra also displeased when King Kikī was informed by the Blessed One of his own noble state?
Therefore he said, “like the potter Ghaṭīkāra. But in this context: “Bhikkhus, just as this...”

When "fewness of wishes" (*appicchatā*) is mentioned, it refers to the meaning designated as fewness of wishes. "By strong non-greed" (*balava-alobhena*) means by non-greed that functions with greater intensity.

In the fourth [verse], "non-contentment" (*asantuṭṭhi*) is that for which there is no contentment; its state is non-contentment (*asantuṭṭhitā*). Showing its specific nature, he says: "In a person who is discontented... [down to] greed. "One who serves," etc., are synonyms for one another. In the fifth [verse], *tuṭṭhi* is the act of being content (*tussana*).
One who is content with what is his own (*sakena*) or with what is peaceful (*santena*) is "content" (*santuṭṭhi*).

The state of that [contentment] is *santuṭṭhitā*. To show that contentment by whose existence a bhikkhu is called "contented," he said: "endowed with contentment with whatever requisites are available.
The meaning is: being possessed of satisfaction with any suitable requisite, such as robes and so forth, wherever they may be found. Alternatively, "the other" (*itara*) is said to be...
The inferior is other than the excellent, and likewise the excellent is other than the inferior; for their "otherness" is established through mutual dependence.

Thus, whatever state—whether inferior or excellent—by which one is content with requisites such as robes, that state, as it occurs, is non-greed known as "contentment with whatever requisites are obtained. This belongs to one who possesses it, according to what is obtained, in accordance with his own gains.
Contentment is contentment with whatever is obtained. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. Alternatively, "gain" (*lābha*) means that which is gained;

"whatever gain" is "according to gain" (*yathālābha*); contentment with that is "contentment with whatever is obtained" (*yathālābhasantosa*). "Strength" (*bala*) refers to bodily strength. "Suitability" (*sāruppa*) refers to being appropriate for a monk.

Since the absence of longing for anything other than what has been obtained can also be a mode of proceeding characterized by fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*), [the text] specifically excludes that possibility.
Showing the true nature of contentment (*santoṣa*), he said, "Even if one obtains [a robe], one does not take it.
Having exchanged that [robe], for those who are naturally weak and so forth, a heavy robe brings about discomfort and physical exhaustion;

therefore, he said that using a light robe after exchanging it for such purposes—rather than out of excessive desire and the like—is not contrary to contentment: "even while subsisting with what is light..."
“He remains contented. Having obtained robes of great value or many robes, he discards them and takes up others;
because this is done according to the method of what is appropriate, it does not contradict contentment. Thus he said: “Even while wearing them...
he remains contented. In the same way, regarding the description of what is appropriate for the remaining requisites as well, the word “api” (even/also) is included.

The underlying intention (*adhippāya*) should be understood. "Harītakī treated with urine" means either that which has been infused with cow’s urine or a *harītakī* fruit discarded due to its rotten state.

"Praised by the Buddha and others" means it was commended by the Buddha and his disciples in such passages as, "The going forth is dependent upon medicine consisting of putrid urine," in order to enjoin monks to fewness of wishes and contentment.
One becomes supremely contented—that is, possessed of the highest excellence.

Because of being endowed with contentment. Since contentment that is appropriate to the occasion is the foremost, it is "foremost" because the bhikkhu proceeds there by way of being satisfied based precisely on what is appropriate. There is nothing further to be said regarding the sixth and seventh [factors]. 68–69. Regarding the eighth and ninth:

one who does not possess clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) is "unclearly comprehending" (*asampajāna*); the state of such a person is "lack of clear comprehension. Clear comprehension should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated.
70. In the tenth [verse], "evil friends" refers to those like Devadatta. Indeed, they are called "evil" (pāpa) because of their base conduct or because of their bringing about suffering.

"Of those proceeding in that manner" means: whatever mode there is—such as the approval, inclination, resolve, leaning toward, and devotion to an evil friend—it is by way of that mode that they proceed. This refers specifically to the four aggregates.
The name “bad friendship” (pāpamittatā) refers to the four formless aggregates (arūpakkhandha).

Because individuals endowed with unwholesome states such as lack of faith (assaddhiya) and so forth are particularly evil due to their lack of merit and liberation, one whose friends and companions are such persons is a “bad friend”;
the state of being that is “bad friendship. Therefore, he said: “Those persons who are without faith,” and so forth.
The commentary on the *Vīriyārambhādivagga* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Kalyāṇamittādivagga*. 71.

In the first [sutta] of the eighth [chapter], "the Buddhas" or "Sāriputta and others" are the good friends (*kalyāṇamitta*). "By way of the opposite of what was stated" means by way of the opposite of the term "association with evil friends" (*pāpamittatā*) as it was stated [in the previous section].

72–73. "Yoga" in the second [case] means the state of being possessed of; "payoga" means application or practice; "ayoga" means the state of not being possessed of; "appayoga" means non-application or non-practice; "anuyogena" means by reason of application. 74.
"Of a being who awakens" (bujjhanakasattassa) in the fourth [case] means of the person who penetrates the four noble truths.
"Becoming factors" (aṅgabhūtā) means becoming the causes for that very penetration. And herein, one awakens to the four noble truths.
