The noble disciple, who has obtained the name "Awakening" (bodhi) because he awakens from the sleep of ignorance, is the sentient being who awakens; [the phrase refers to] "of that awakening sentient being.
"Of Awakening" (bodhiyā) means of that Awakening consisting of the collection of factors (dhamma-sāmaggī). They are called "Awakenings" (bodhiyo) in the sense of awakening;
thus it is said that these very Awakenings are the factors for the full realization of the Truths. "They awaken, therefore they are factors of awakening" (bojjhaṅgā).
They are called *bojjhaṅgas* because they awaken in accordance with their causes—such as insight (*vipassanā*)—and with the truths that are to be awakened to;
they are called *bojjhaṅgas* because they awaken by facing toward [reality] through direct perception;
and they are called *bojjhaṅgas* because they awaken correctly and without error. Thus, [the term is explained] by means of these illuminations of specific meanings.
It is said, "They awaken through the obstacles," and so forth. The word *bodhi* (awakening) includes, by way of the commonality of awakening, all that is associated with its specific qualities.
By the phrase "they conduce to awakening," it shows that this harmony of factors (*dhammasāmaggi*) is the exclusive cause for awakening.
Furthermore, this term has been analyzed in this way; thus, by the manner already stated, this term "factors of awakening" (*bojjhaṅgā*)— [...is explained.]
This has already been explained in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* in the *Niddesa*. 75.
Regarding the fifth [section], "the stage of the true nature of things" (*yāthāvasarasabhūmi*) means the stage of performing one's own function according to reality.
That is the stage of the true nature of things. "Insight" (*vipassanā*) refers to powerful insight. Some say it begins from the knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅgañāṇa*). Of insight...

And when the jhāna is the basis, mindfulness and the others belong exclusively to the side of the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*), because they are factors conducive to enlightenment in a figurative sense (*pariyāya*). The passage beginning with "Therein" and so forth is a demonstration of the classification of the planes for the fourfold enlightenment factors. 76.
"In the midst of them" means in the midst of those bhikkhus. Granted, this [account] is brief by way of having been included in the formal recitation (*saṅgīti*).
The Blessed One, however, expands upon a passage from the Sutta here in accordance with the inclinations of the assembled assembly;
it is with this in mind that it was said, "There will be a great teaching.

It is said that there is no talk of villages, market towns, and so forth, because such talk constitutes a form of frivolous chatter (*tiracchānakathā*). For indeed, previously, that [talk] had many relatives and many factions.
Now, by way of impermanence, that which is "without faction" and "without party" has become part of the side leading to liberation. "By this" refers to the aforementioned decline.
"Lowest" means inferior. "In my teaching"—this is indeed a qualification for both the meditation on the ownership of one's own actions (*kammassakatā*) and wisdom (*paññā*).
For both of these are far superior to the two kinds of wisdom held by outsiders; such is the case for all omniscient Buddhas.
Because of the distinction gained through his teaching and because it serves as a necessary condition for turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*). 77.

Regarding the phrase "having known their mental disposition": having approached those monks who were speaking in that manner, he knew the movement of their minds, which had become fit vessels for his teaching.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the expression "the ownership of kamma and so forth," [meditative absorption, wisdom, and other qualities] are included.
This is the inclusion of all four types of wisdom.

(Verses 78–80) Regarding the eighth and subsequent verses, it is "in the same manner as stated above," namely, in the manner stated above starting with the words, "Whoever in my teaching... and so forth. The rest here is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the Chapter on Good Friends and the Others is concluded.
81–82. There is nothing to be said regarding the ninth chapter.
10. Commentary on the Second Chapter on Negligence, etc. (Pamādādivagga): 98–115.
In the tenth chapter, that which exists within the internal continuum is "internal" (*ajjhattika*). That which is outside of the internal continuum is...
The external state. By the method of the opposite of what was stated: the meaning should be understood through such expressions as "for the sake of non-destruction" and so forth.

Regarding the fourfold alternative (*catukkoṭika*): having taken the method as it appears in the *Pariyosāna-sutta*—namely, "devotion to the unwholesome, non-devotion to the wholesome; devotion to the wholesome, non-devotion to the unwholesome"—[the Buddha said]: "Monks, I do not see even a single thing other than this..."
The designation "Sutta" arose for those discourses introduced with such phrases as "I perceive," and so forth.

130. In the method of the Suttas, it refers to the inversion of the phenomena of defilement according to their exhortation, the proclamation of the deficiency or excess of various categories of phenomena, and the presentation of what is non-dhamma as dhamma; however, it also refers to the non-inversion of those very same things.

Proclamation according to what is neither deficient nor excessive is the illumination of the Dhamma as "Dhamma. Likewise, proclaiming the practice of the Vinaya contrary to the prescribed method is the illumination of non-Dhamma as "Dhamma";
proclaiming it according to the prescribed method is the illumination of Dhamma as "Dhamma.

According to the method of the Suttanta, there are five kinds of restraint-discipline (saṃvara-vinaya) and abandonment-discipline (pahāna-vinaya), which constitute the Vinaya; by contrast, their opposites constitute non-Vinaya (avinaya). This is according to the method of the Vinaya.

Discipline (*vinaya*) is precisely the practice according to the rule by means of the perfection of the subject matter (*vatthusampadā*) and so forth; it should be understood that non-discipline (*avinaya*) is the opposite of that.
Regarding the phrase "thirty offenses entailing relinquishment and confession" (*nissaggiyā pācittiyā*), the word "iti" here has the sense of "beginning.

By this, there is an inclusion of the ninety-two offenses entailing confession (*pācittiyā*), the four offenses entailing acknowledgment (*pāṭidesanīyā*), and the seven methods for settling legal disputes (*adhikaraṇasamatha*). [Thus,] there are thirty-one offenses entailing relinquishment.
Here, it should be stated: "Ninety pācittiya offenses," and so forth. The rest here is easily understood.
It is called *adhigama* (attainment) because it is to be attained; it refers to the paths and fruits. Nibbāna, however, is not included here because it does not undergo disappearance.

It is called *paṭipatti* (practice) because it is the act of practicing, namely, the engagement with the three trainings; or alternatively, it is practice because it is that which is to be practiced. Because it is to be mastered...

The *pariyatti* (the scriptures) consist of the Three Piṭakas. Although the third true knowledge (*vijjā*) and the sixth direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) are already included by the mention of the Path, they are mentioned again as "the three true knowledges and the six direct knowledges" because of their commonality as *vijjā* and *abhiññā*. Following that, regarding "the six direct knowledges":

the intention is that after a thousand years [from the Buddha’s passing], one may be able to produce the six direct knowledges, but not the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*). "From there" means from the time of the direct knowledges.

"Later" refers to the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). Those who, in the preliminary stage, having remained in pure insight (*vipassanā*) due to the absence of attachment to jhāna, attain the supreme fruit, are called "dry-insight practitioners" (*sukkha-vipassaka*).
However, at the moment of the path (*magga-khaṇa*), it cannot be said that "there is no attachment to jhāna," because of the statement:
"He develops serenity and insight coupled together (*yuganaddha*). "Of the last" means of the very last one.
Although the Noble One is by nature incapable of falling away, for a stream-enterer there is no dhamma attained that can be said to have "arisen" after the exhaustion of his life;
yet, as long as the necessary conditions are not complete and he is unable to produce the higher distinctions, the attainment itself remains non-existent.
Thus it was said: "For a stream-enterer... [it] is called... This is stated with reference to the human world.
It should be understood as "it is said.
"They do not reproach" means that even though they know of existing faults in one another, they neither reproach nor bring charges against them.
"They are not anxious" means they do not give rise to remorse (*kukkucca*). Some also read, "they are not careful in their performance," which refers to a state of laxity (*sāthalikatā*).
The meaning is that they are those who practice the trainings without diligence. The phrase "while hundreds or thousands of bhikkhus are living" is stated by way of abundance;

for even when only a few bhikkhus remain who have not violated the final training rule, or even when only a single one remains, the practice is indeed said to be "not lost. Therefore he said: "Until the last... [the practice] is lost."
"To take in pupils" means to gather in pupils. "By way of meaning" means by way of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
"Starting from the top" means starting from above. "Merely the Uposatha Khandhaka" refers to the canonical text of the Vinaya-mātikā.
He says "among humans" because, as in the case of the *Āḷavaka-pañha* and others, the occurrence of the formal study (*pariyatti*) among the devas is not the measure [of its extent].
"Of the color of the teeth of the lips" means the color of the teeth of the lips; it is said that they wear it after dyeing the tooth-stain one or two times to make it the color of the teeth.
"They cause it to adhere to the hair" means that those binding the hair with that piece of saffron robe-material cause it to adhere [to the hair].
They are "those who have transcended their lineage" (gotrabhū) because of their overcoming and destruction of the bhikkhu-lineage.

Alternatively, *gotta* means a common name; the word *matta* is indicated as being elided. Therefore, they are "lineage-bearers" (*gotrabhū*) because they experience—that is, they bear—the mere lineage of "ascetics" (*samaṇa*); the meaning is "ascetics by name alone.

They are "yellow-necked" (*kāsāvakaṇṭha*) because of having the yellow robe around their necks, or because of the sorrow (*soka*) that arises due to the taking up of the yellow robe. "Directed toward the Saṅgha" means with reference to the Saṅgha.
"Because it was given, it belongs to the Saṅgha. "That body" refers to that body of relics.
"By that very [fact]" means precisely because the disappearance of the other [the Dhamma] is rooted in the disappearance of the Pariyatti (the scriptures).
The intention is that Sakka, the king of the gods, made an effort for the monks to go to the opposite shore during a time of famine. "Both of them" refers to the two Paṃsukūlika Theras.
And there were the elders who were preachers of the Dhamma (*dhammakathika-thera*). "Elders" (*therā*) here refers to those elders established therein who acted as witnesses.
When the elders who were preachers of the Dhamma had brought forward this sutta—“As long as the Suttantas endure...

[etc. ...the security from bondage does not perish”—and with these words, “When the Suttanta is protected, the practice (*paṭipatti*) is protected,” the elder who was a wearer of rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika-thera*) remained speechless.

[They] performed [these acts]. Now, in order to clarify through similes—both by way of contrast (*vyatireka*) and by way of agreement (*anvaya*)—the fact that the non-disappearance of the *pariyatti* (the scriptures) is itself the cause for the non-disappearance of the others, the passage beginning with "Just as" (*yathā hi*) was stated. That is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the second chapter, the *Pamādādivagga*, is concluded.
140–150. The eleventh and twelfth chapters are indeed easy to understand. 13.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Single Person (Ekapuggalavagga). 170.
"Of the single person" means of the chapter on the single person. Therefore he said, "In the first. "One" is a numerical limit.

For that very reason, it has the sense of excluding a second and so forth. Since the word *eka* (one) can also mean "without a companion" (*padhānāsahāya*), he said "delimitation by number" in order to exclude that meaning.
"Teaching of the conventional" (*sammutidesanā*) is teaching regarding the conventional; "teaching of the ultimate" (*paramatthadesanā*) is teaching regarding the ultimate.
"Therein" refers to the teachings of the conventional and the ultimate, not to the conventional and ultimate meanings themselves. Therefore he said: "Such is the teaching of the conventional..."
“Such is the teaching on the ultimate meaning (paramattha). Herein, this is the characteristic of the conventional (sammuti) and the ultimate:
that which, when broken or when its parts are analytically separated by the intellect, no longer retains its conventional designation—such as the various kinds of pots and cloths—is the conventional;
the opposite of that is the ultimate. For that method does not apply to the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of hardness, contact, and so forth. In this regard:
The conventional teaching of "person" (puggala) is based on the designation "person" applied to the collection of phenomena such as form, which proceeds by way of a continuity.

This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. He said, "Impermanent" is the ultimate teaching (paramattha-desanā), meaning that phenomena possessing the nature of arising and passing away are not eternal.
This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. [Objection: Is it not the case that the teaching on the aggregates (khandha) is also...?

It is merely a conventional designation (*sammutidesanā*). Is it not the case that the meaning of "aggregate" (*khandha*) is the sense of a "heap" (*rāsa*) or the sense of a "constituent part" (*koṭṭhāsa*)? True, this is so;

however, this designation "aggregate" pertains to contact and the other [mental factors] as a conceptualization (*paññatti*) based on their immediate conditions, and because it relies upon ultimate reality (*paramattha*), it is more proximate to it.

It is not distant like the designation "person" (*puggala*) and so forth; thus, it is described as being included within ultimate reality. Or, by way of the term "aggregate," those phenomena whose intrinsic nature consists in clinging to that [aggregation] are indicated.

[They] are thus grasped. But surely, since all phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) ascend to the teaching only by way of conventional designation (sammutimukha) and not by way of their own [ultimate] face, would it not follow that the entire teaching is merely a teaching of convention?
This is not so, because the distinction of the teaching is intended here according to the distinction of the phenomena to be taught.
For a word does not manifest its meaning without some basis for its application (pavattinimitta).

"Having heard the teaching by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*)": having heard the teaching set forth by way of the conventional door, beginning with "In this case, a certain person is one who torments himself, devoted to the practice of self-torment," through the arising of knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*).

"Having penetrated the meaning": having penetrated, in accordance with that [teaching], the meaning comprised of the Four Noble Truths by means of the path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) together with insight (*vipassanā*).
"Having abandoned delusion" means having abandoned delusion without remainder, together with the defilements associated with it.
"Distinction" refers to the distinction known as the supreme fruit and Nibbāna. "Of those" refers to such disciples who are to be trained.

"By way of the ultimate meaning" means by way of the ultimate phenomena, such as in the passage beginning, "Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. The rest is exactly as stated in the immediately preceding method.

"In that" means in this teaching, both by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*) and by way of ultimate truth (*paramattha*). "Skilled in various local dialects" means proficient in the languages of different regions.
"Of the three Vedas" is merely an illustration; the intended meaning is that he was skilled in the three Vedas as well as the places for learning the crafts (*sippa*).
For this very reason, he will speak later of the acquisition of crafts. Or, the crafts are included within the Vedas by virtue of being branches of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhāna*).

Having stated "of the three Vedas," he refutes the false doctrine beginning with "The cave contains three hidden things that are not to be grasped," by demonstrating that even the Vedas exist only as something to be recited, and not because they exist as accumulated entities anywhere.
Those which have various regional languages are called *nānādesabhāsā*.
The ultimate, supreme goal is the *paramattha* (ultimate meaning), which is the actual nature of phenomena as they truly are (*yathābhūtasabhāva*).

Conventional designation (*sammuti*) is established merely by worldly convention. If this is so, how can conventional discourse be considered true? To this he says: "Because it is caused by worldly convention";

the meaning is that it proceeds by relying upon worldly common usage (*lokasamaññā*). For worldly common usage is to be understood through adherence (*abhinivesa*), not for the purpose of instructing anyone else.
It is not false, like the proclamation of what has been heard, because it does not overstep that [convention]. Therefore the Blessed One said: “One should not insist on local dialects;
one should not overstep common usage. “Of phenomena” (*dhammānaṃ*) means of phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

“True causes” (*bhūtakāraṇā*) means causes as they truly are, because they proceed in dependence upon what is truly so. “While employing conventional designation” (*sammutiṃ voharantassa*) refers to [the term] “person” (*puggalo*).

When [the Buddha] speaks using the worldly convention [of a "being"] by means of the words beginning with “a being,” it is for the purpose of illustrating moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*). For the function of guarding the world consists in the qualities of moral shame and moral dread;
since their function is made manifest specifically within the continuum of a sentient being, this must be explained by way of a discourse focused on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).

This same principle applies to the rest as well. For when a kamma has arisen in a particular arising of consciousness, the arising of its fruit within that very same continuum is what constitutes "the ownership of one's own kamma" (*kammassakatā*).
Thus, there is neither the destruction of a consciousness already produced nor the acquisition of what was not yet done;

this must be illustrated by a teaching specifically addressed to the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhānā*). The performance of meritorious deeds to be done by those beings is their individual personal effort (*paccattapurisakāra*). That too...

Because it must be brought to completion by way of a continuity [of rebirth], it should be illustrated by a discourse that has the person as its primary focus. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of illustrating the *ānantariya*":

the fruit that occurs immediately after death is called "immediate" (*anantara*); those actions are "immediate" (*ānantariya*) because they are connected to that immediate result, because they have the habit of producing that immediate result, or because they have the purpose of producing that immediate result—namely, the killing of a mother and so forth.
It is for the purpose of illustrating these that [the text says] "those too..."

Indeed, because they must be established by way of a continuum (*santāna*), they should be illustrated precisely through discourse focused on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), such as "one deprives one's mother of life," and likewise, "he dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*mettā*)," and so forth;
and "he recollects his manifold past lives, even one birth," and so forth; and "there is an offering [that bears fruit] from the giver..."

Furthermore, discourses such as those concerning the purification of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), past lives (*pubbenivāsa*), and the purity of offerings (*dakkhiṇāvisuddhi*)— which proceed with the words "it is purified, not from the recipient"—
must be explained as being based on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), because their scope is the continuum of sentient beings (*sattasantāna*). Likewise,

even when explaining the discourse on ultimate reality (*paramatthakathā*) with statements such as "The eight types of persons (*purisapuggala*) are not a person liberated by occasion (*samayavimutta-puggala*)," one does so for the purpose of not abandoning worldly convention (*lokasammuti*).

He speaks on the discourse concerning persons (*puggalakathā*). By this, it should be understood that the purpose of the remaining discourses mentioned—which are based on persons—is included by way of generalization.
Granted, all of this has been stated with reference to those who have not fully understood the bases (*vattu*);
nevertheless, such a teaching is also conducive to ease for those who have fully understood the bases.
"A single person" (ekapuggala) refers to a person who is without equal in distinguished conduct and reliance.

For among the Buddhas, there is indeed no one whatsoever in the world with its devas who is called "distinguished" by virtue of qualities such as morality; likewise, there is none even their equal at the same time. Therefore it was said:
"Neither in this world nor in the next is anyone found superior to or equal to the Buddha. Thus, even an equal...
There is no one else. Even one who serves as a support through inferior qualities does not exist. Therefore it is said:

“A single person devoid of a support consisting of distinguished conduct. Furthermore, those who are equal to the former Perfectly Enlightened Ones in virtues such as morality are called *samā* (equals).
One who is not distinguished from them—like a piece of gold broken in the middle—is a “single person” by way of being equal to the unequaled (*asamasama*).
Because there is no other such person [to compare him with]. Therefore it was said: "In the sense of being without equal," and so forth.

The "world of beings" (sattaloka) is intended here, because he arises within the category of beings. He arises only in the human world, because the worlds of the gods and the Brahmā-world lack the opportunity for Buddhas to arise.
First of all, he does not arise in the sensual-sphere heavens (kāmadevaloka), because of the practice of the holy life (brahmacariya).
Because it is impossible [for them to appear otherwise], and likewise because it is not a matter of mere wonder. For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess qualities that are truly wonderful.
That quality of theirs as beings of wondrous nature is not manifest in the world while they remain in the state of devas, in the same way as it is when they have become human.
Indeed, when a Perfectly Enlightened One is seen in his state as a deva, the majesty of a Buddha is perceived in the world only as the majesty of a deva.
It is not by the power of the Buddha. If that were the case, one would not be resolved upon or confident that "this is a perfectly enlightened Buddha";
one would not relinquish the grasping at the Lord as the creator; and because the state of a deva persists for a long time, one would not be liberated from the doctrine of partial eternalism.
The same principle applies here regarding the statement "one is not reborn in the Brahma-world. For it is for the sake of liberating beings from such grasping that [the teaching is given].
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, arise only in the happy destiny of humans, not in the happy destiny of the devas.
This is because, with this [world-system] as its center, the status of being the field of birth for ten thousand world-systems is demonstrated;
for there is no other place mentioned in the Buddha-word of the Tipiṭaka where Buddhas arise besides this.
Therefore it was said: "He arises in this very world-system (cakkavāḷa).
But why, when arising here, does he arise specifically in Jambudīpa and not in the other continents? Some say:
"Because in Jambudīpa there is the site of the Bodhi-maṇḍa, which is not surpassed by the earth, which is compatible with the state of Buddhahood, and which is an immovable place."
Thus, for this reason, he arises only in Jambudīpa.

By this very [statement], it should be understood that the phrase “he arises only in the Middle Country (majjhima-desa) there” is also explained; for likewise, other places that have not been abandoned are also found right there.
Because of the arising of former Buddhas, Great Bodhisattvas, and Paccekabuddhas, [the place] of the Śrāvaka-bodhisattvas...

The aspiration for disciple-enlightenment (*sāvakabodhi*), as well as the gathering and ripening of the requisites for the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramī*), succeed only here in this Cakkavāḷa, specifically in Jambudīpa, and nowhere else.

Furthermore, the purpose of a Buddha’s appearance is the training of those who are to be trained (*veneyyajanavinaya*); therefore, with regard to the specific individuals to be trained—such as the Chief Disciples and Great Disciples—it occurs in this Jambudīpa.
Thus Buddhas are born [only] here, not on other islands. And this principle is the established custom of all Buddhas;
therefore, the arising of those Supreme Beings in that very place should be understood as being like the mutual dependence of the wheels of a chariot.
Hence it is said in the Commentary: "Buddhas are not born on the three islands; [they are born] in Jambudīpa."
"...thus they are being born; behold the island!
Both of these are indeed incomplete expressions, because the action of arising belongs to the present tense.

Alternatively, "arising" (*uppajjamāno*) means "capable of arising. For this word *māna* has the sense of capability (*satti*); for by whatever degree of capability the Great Bodhisattvas [possess]...

Rebirth in the final existence is to be desired; therein, the meaning is that he is endowed with [the perfections] fully accomplished through the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).
"Distinction" (*bheda*) means specific difference. Indeed, in order to show those three kinds of distinction, it was said:

"For this," and so forth. From the time the Great Being for Enlightenment (*mahābodhisatta*) achieved the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) endowed with the eight factors, for the sake of attaining Buddhahood...

The meaning is that, by virtue of having attained a state of certainty, one who is practicing the path of the accumulations for enlightenment arises through the application of the aforementioned capacity;
this is because arising is an absolute necessity. "Seeking" means investigating.

By the phrase "when knowledge has reached full maturity," it is indicated that prior to this, due to the immaturity of knowledge and because an opportunity had been obtained through the influence of residual kamma, [the path did not arise].

This shows that the Bodhisatta exerted himself in such a great striving (*mahāpadhāna*). That which has arisen at the moment of the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala*) is indeed to be called "arisen.
That it has "come" is because it has been perfectly accomplished through the perfection of its causes.
"For the sake of welfare" means for the attainment of mundane and supramundane welfare. The same principle applies here for "for the sake of happiness" as well.

“Of that” means of that world of beings (*sattaloka*). Showing the very sequence by which this world of beings reached the realization of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*), he says, beginning with “at the Great Seat of Enlightenment” (*mahābodhimaṇḍe*). “As far as today” (*yāvajjadivasa*):

here, by the word “today,” he refers to the period during which the Dispensation (*sāsana*) remains established. “Of gods and humans” (*devamanussānaṃ*): this is an expression used in its highest sense (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*).
To show this, the passage beginning with “not only” was stated. “Of these too” means even of the nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so forth.
By the phrase “this question,” the general nature of the question as a question is shown by the word “which”; it is not shown as a specific [question].
Therefore, in order to make known its status as a specific question, all the questions found in the *Mahāniddesa* are presented according to the method of extracting the meaning (*atthuddhāranaya*).
He shows this by means of the passage beginning with, "And this question... *Adiṭṭhajotanā* (illumination of the unseen): that by which what has not been seen is illuminated.
*Diṭṭhasaṃsandanā* (corroboration of the seen): that by which what has been seen is corroborated. Corroboration (*saṃsandana*) consists in reaching a definitive conclusion through discussion.
*Vimaticchedanā* (resolution of doubt): that by which doubt is severed. *Anumatipucchā* (a question for assent): a question asked for the sake of obtaining consent. "Then what... [and so forth].
In the phrase beginning with “Do you think, monks,” the question “What is your approval? constitutes a question for approval (*anumati-pucchā*).
A question for the desire to speak (*kathetukamyatā-pucchā*) is a question asked out of a desire to speak. A characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) is any intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) that one wishes to know.
“Unknown” (*aññāta*) expresses the state of being unknown by any kind of knowledge. “Unseen” (*adiṭṭha*) [expresses the state of being unseen] by that which consists of vision.
"Unseen as if by direct knowledge" means not seen through wisdom as if it were before one's eyes. "Untoled" means not weighed by means of a scale that would determine, "It is this much;
it is this. "Unexamined" means the completion of the act of knowing has not been performed by means of investigation. "Unclear" refers to the state of wisdom being unmanifest.
"Unclarified" refers to the state of wisdom having been made unmanifest.
It is because these specific qualities serve as the basis that the designation "Tathāgata" is applied to the Blessed One; to demonstrate this, it was said:
"For eight reasons the Blessed One is a Tathāgata," and so forth. Indeed, all the names of the Blessed One are derived solely from his specific qualities.
As it has been said:
“The names of the Great Seer are incalculable according to his qualities;
even from a thousand names, a name should be selected on account of its quality.
Thus, regarding the phrase “come thus” (*tathā-āgata*): here, the word *tathā* serves to provide a simile by way of determining the mode [of arrival]. It is also a general description.

For it abides in distinction. The word *āgata* has the sense of "coming by way of the path" (*paṭipadā*), not the sense of "coming by way of knowledge" as in such phrases as "he has come to the characteristic of suchness" (*tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato*), nor the sense of physical movement as in "the Great Ascetic has indeed arrived at Giribbaja of the Magadhans.
In this context, the word *tathā* has the sense of establishing a simile by way of determining a particular mode; because that [mode] is dominated by compassion...

By way of the gateway of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), showing the path by which previous Buddhas arrived through the method of illustration, he first spoke generally—using the words "yaṃ" and "taṃ" because of their state of absolute connection—in the passage beginning, "Just as [all the world... and so forth, up to "...arrived.
Then, he again described that same path by means of numerous explanations found in such texts as the *Mahāpadhāna Sutta*, for those [Buddhas] who are well-known and proximate.
Pointing to the six Perfectly Enlightened Ones beginning with Vipassī, he said, "Just as the Blessed One Vipassī," and so forth.
Therein, "by that resolution" (*abhinīhāra*) refers to the Great Resolve (*mahāpaṇidhāna*) endowed with eight factors, by way of:

being human, possessing the male gender, the perfection of causes, the meeting with a Teacher, going forth into homelessness, the perfection of qualities such as the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), the subject matter, and the desire. For the bodily resolve of all Buddhas is...

"It is by this very aspiration that it is accomplished. Having thus shown the meaning of the term "Tathāgata" through the distinction of the Great Aspiration, he now spoke the passage beginning with, "Just as the Blessed Vipassī...
[and so on] ...the Blessed Kassapa fulfilled the perfection of giving," in order to show it by way of the fulfillment of the perfections (pāramitā).
And herein, for the purpose of generating proficiency in the practice leading to Great Enlightenment according to the Suttas:

what are these perfections (pāramī)? In what sense are they "perfections"? How many kinds are there? What is their sequence? What are their characteristics (lakkhaṇa), functions (rasa), manifestations (paccupaṭṭhāna), and proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna)?

What is their condition (paccaya)? What is their defilement (saṃkilesa)? What is their purification (vodāna)? What is their opposite (paṭipakkha)? What is their practice (paṭipatti)? What is their classification (vibhāga)? What is...

The inclusion [of the perfections], the means of accomplishment, the time required for their accomplishment, the benefits, and what constitutes their fruit—this detailed exposition regarding the perfections (*pāramīs*) should be understood.
Furthermore, this should be understood by one who desires it according to the method set forth in the *Dīgha-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā*, and is not shown here.
Regarding the perfections divided as previously described, according to the practice as previously described...
With reference to the state of being fulfilled, it says: "having fulfilled the thirty perfections.

Although the great renunciations are indeed included within the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*), they are mentioned separately from the great renunciations for the purpose of showing their specific nature as renunciation and to demonstrate their extreme difficulty.
For that very reason, the renunciation of the eyes is mentioned separately from the renunciation of limbs.
Although there is a commonality in the nature of relinquishment, the inclusion of the relinquishment of wife and children is made alongside the relinquishment of wealth and kingdom.

The "prior application" (*pubbayoga*) consists of the accomplishment of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), together with the preliminary practice known as the "conduct of going and returning.
The "prior conduct" (*pubbacariyā*) is the accomplishment of especially distinguished practice in giving and so forth, or that conduct which is comprised within the *Cariyāpiṭaka*.
"‘The aspiration (abhinīhāra) and prior application (pubbayoga), or the practice of giving and so forth, or solitary wandering by way of physical seclusion—

these constitute the ‘prior conduct’ (pubbacariyā),’ say some. The proclamation of the Dhamma (dhammakkhāna) is the discourse that proceeds by way of making manifest the defects of saṃsāra and the benefits of Nibbāna regarding both giving and so forth,
as well as fewness of wishes and so forth, and which establishes and matures beings for the three types of enlightenment."

"Conduct for the welfare of relatives" (*ñātatthacariyā*) means acting for the benefit of one's kin; that too occurs solely by way of exercising compassion. By the word "etcetera," conduct for the welfare of the world and so forth are included.

"Course of knowledge" (*ñāṇacāro*) or "conduct of the intellect" (*buddhicariyā*) consists of: the knowledge of the ownership of kamma; familiarity with blameless spheres of action, spheres of craft, and branches of science;
familiarity with the aggregates, bases, and so forth; and the investigation of the three characteristics.

In its essential meaning, however, that is simply the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*); it is mentioned separately for the purpose of showing the equipment of knowledge (*ñāṇasambhāra*). "Culmination" (*koṭi*) means the limit; the sense is "the highest point.

"Having developed the four foundations of mindfulness" (*cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāvetvā*) is the connection [to the following]. Therein, "having developed" (*bhāvetvā*) means having produced; "having increased" (*brūhetvā*) means having expanded.
By the mention of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, one has brought the path of arrival to its ultimate consummation.
[The text] shows this. Alternatively, the foundations of mindfulness and so forth should be understood as being accompanied by insight (vipassanā).

Furthermore, it should be understood that here, the beginning of the path of approach is shown by the passage beginning with "by which resolution," the middle by the passage beginning with "the perfection of giving," and the conclusion by the passage beginning with "the four foundations of mindfulness."
"Sampatijāto" means one who has just been born, having just emerged. For as soon as the Great Being had emerged, first the Brahmās received him with a golden net;
from their hands, the Four Great Kings received him on an antelope-skin rug;
from their hands, humans received him on a fine linen swaddling cloth; and when he was released from the hands of humans, he fell upon the earth.
"He is established. By the words beginning with "As it was said," he points to the statement spoken in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta*. "In the white parasol" means in the divine white parasol.

"While being carried" means while being held aloft. And here, it should be understood that by the mention of the parasol alone, the five insignia of royalty (*kakudhabhaṇḍa*), such as the sword and so forth, are already implied. These include the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the elephant goad, the horse-tail whisk, the betel-box, and the turban.
For at that time, they stood waiting together with the parasol. Only the parasols and such were visible then, not those who held the parasols and so forth.
"All directions" means the ten directions; this surveying of all directions did not take place after the seven strides.
For the Great Being, having been released from the hands of men, looked toward the eastern direction, where gods and humans—
Honoring him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they said, “Great Being, there is no one here even equal to you; how much less anyone superior?

Thus, having surveyed all directions—the four cardinal points, the four intermediate points, below, and above—and seeing no one anywhere who was his equal, he took seven strides toward the northern direction.
“Pre-eminent” (*āsabhin*) means supreme. “Foremost” (*agga*) means the very first. “Eldest” (*jeṭṭha*) and “best” (*seṭṭha*) are synonyms for that same term. With the words, “This is my last birth;
now there is no more becoming,” he prophesied the state of *arahantship* to be attained in this very existence.
The meaning stated briefly as “by way of being a precursor to many distinguished attainments” is explained in detail starting with the words “For indeed... (*yañhi*).
It shows this. In that context, "here" refers to:
"The gods held aloft in the sky a parasol with many branches and a thousand circles."
"Golden-handled yak-tail whisks fly about,
yet those who hold the whisks and the parasols are not seen"—
this is the meaning of this verse. Omniscient knowledge itself is called "unobstructed knowledge" because its range is unimpeded everywhere.
He said: "For the attainment of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience. Likewise, this Blessed One also went... [as before] ...by way of being a preliminary sign;
by this he shows that the specific qualities arising by way of natural law at the time of the birth [of enlightenment] are common to all Bodhisattvas.
For those are the outflows of the perfections (pāramitā).
*Vikkami* means he went. *Marū* means gods. *Samā* means equal; they were equal and similar because of the equality of his surveying.
For just as the Great Man surveyed one direction, so too did he survey the remaining directions; there was no obstruction whatsoever in his surveying.
Alternatively, *samā* means fit to survey. For at that time, there were no forms for the Bodhisatta that were deformed, hideous, or repulsive.
“They appear in the directions as unsuitable things to behold.

Having thus explained the term *tathāgata* by means of the word *gata* in the sense of bodily movement, he now says “Or else,” and so forth, in order to demonstrate it in the sense of the movement of knowledge.
Therein, “by renunciation” (*nekkhammena*) means by that which has non-greed as its primary factor.
By means of a wholesome state of consciousness (*kusalacittuppāda*). For here, wholesome states (*kusala-dhammā*) are renunciation (*nekkhamma*), not the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and so on;

some even say it is by means of the first *jhāna*. "Having abandoned" (*pahāya*) means having relinquished. "Gone" (*gata*) means attained (*adhigata*), entered upon, or directed toward a further distinction—this is the meaning.

Alternatively, "having abandoned" (*pahāya*) refers to the cause of abandoning or the characteristic of abandoning. For this word *pahāya* has the sense of cause and characteristic. Indeed, [the path] has the cause of abandoning lust for sensual pleasures (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth as its basis.

In the phrase "gone" (*gato*), what is stated as "going" refers to realization or, alternatively, to practice itself, which is characterized by the abandoning of sensual desire and the other hindrances.
This same method applies to the phrases "having split open" (*padāletvā*) and so forth. "By non-ill will" (*abyāpādena*) means by loving-kindness (*mettā*).

"By perception of light" (*ālokasaññāya*) means by the cognition of light that has become manifest through mental attention. "By non-distraction" (*avikkhepena*) means by concentration (*samādhi*). "By the definition of phenomena" (*dhammavavatthānena*)...
By means of determining wholesome and other states as they truly are. Some also say: "By means of the discernment of name-and-form together with its conditions.

Having thus shown the Blessed One’s state of being a Tathāgata through the preliminary practice for the first jhāna—as described in the passage beginning, "Having abandoned covetousness for the world"—by means of the abandoning of the hindrances such as sensual desire, [the text now proceeds] with the eight [factors] along with their methods.
To demonstrate that [attainment] by means of the eighteen great insights (mahāvipassanā) together with the meditative attainments (samāpatti), he said, "By knowledge" (ñāṇena), and so forth.

For when delusion—which acts as an obstruction to the discernment of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and the overcoming of doubt—is removed, the perceptions of impermanence (aniccasaññā) and the rest are accomplished for one who stands in the full understanding through knowledge (ñātapariññā).

Likewise, when dissatisfaction regarding those [attainments] is dispelled by means of gladness (pāmojja), which has the characteristic of delighting in the meditative absorptions (jhāna-samāpatti), [the perceptions are accomplished].
The "attainment of jhāna and so forth" refers to the means for dispelling discontent and shattering ignorance through meditative absorption (samāpatti) and insight (vipassanā).

It should be understood that the presentation [of the hindrances] out of their sequential order is intended to show that ignorance—which has the nature of a hindrance—is included even among the hindrances listed below.
Because they obstruct entry into the dwelling of meditative absorption, the hindrances are like door-bolts; thus it is said: "having thrown open the bolt of the hindrances."
In the passage, “Having thought and examined by night, one applies oneself to work by day,” it is intended that applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are like smoke;

thus he says, “the smoke of applied and sustained thought. Although suffering is abandoned precisely in the vicinity of the first jhāna, and pleasure is abandoned precisely in the vicinity of the fourth jhāna, he speaks [here] with reference to their excessive abandonment.

“Having abandoned pleasure and pain by means of the fourth jhāna. By the term *rūpasaññā* (perception of form), both the fine-material-sphere jhānas and their objects are expressed under the heading of “perception.

For even the fine-material-sphere jhāna is called “form” (*rūpa*) through the elision of the latter member of the compound, as in such passages as “one possessing form sees forms. Its object, the kasiṇa-form, is also called “form” through the elision of the former member of the compound.

“In ‘he sees external forms, beautiful and ugly,’ and so forth. Therefore, here, in the context of form and form-jhāna, the term *rūpasaññā* (perception of form) refers to the perception associated with that [jhāna];
thus the fine-material-sphere jhānas are stated by way of their perception. Alternatively, it is called *rūpasaññaṃ* because its perception is form;
what is meant is that it is the name for form. Thus, this is a designation for the object of those [jhānas], which is divided into the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.

It should be understood as follows. "Perception of resistance" (*paṭighasaññā*) refers to the perception arising from the impact or striking together of the bases, such as the eye, and their objects, such as visible forms, when the subject and object meet; it is the perception associated with the two sets of fivefold consciousness.
"Perceptions of diversity" (*nānattasaññā*) means perceptions occurring in relation to diverse objects, or perceptions that are themselves diverse; these are the eight [perceptions].

This is a designation for these forty-four perceptions: the wholesome perceptions of the sense sphere, the twelve unwholesome perceptions, the eleven wholesome-resultant perceptions of the sense sphere, the two unwholesome-resultant perceptions, and the eleven functional perceptions of the sense sphere.
For these indeed proceed toward objects that are diverse in their distinctions—such as the perception of form—and diverse in their intrinsic nature.
And because they are diverse, of various natures, and dissimilar from one another, they are therefore called "perceptions of diversity" (*nānattasaññā*).

Contemplation of the impermanent as "impermanent" is the "contemplation of impermanence" (*aniccānupassanā*); this is the name for the contemplation that proceeds by grasping the impermanence of the phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.
"Perception of permanence" refers to [the view] that conditioned phenomena are "permanent and eternal."
It is the occurrence of wrong perception. By the term "perception," one should understand that views and consciousness are also included. This same method applies to the following cases as well.
"By means of contemplation of disenchantment" means by means of the contemplation occurring in the mode of becoming disenchanted with formations (*saṅkhāra*).

"Delight" (*nandi*) refers to craving accompanied by rapture. "By means of contemplation of fading away" means by means of the contemplation occurring in the mode of becoming dispassionate toward formations.
Regarding "contemplation of cessation": it is the contemplation of the cessation of formations.
Alternatively, the contemplation that "those formations simply cease and do not arise again in the future by way of origination" is the contemplation of cessation.
For this very reason it was said: "By means of the contemplation of cessation, one causes cessation, not origination. For this is the desire for liberation.
"Attained to strength": contemplation that proceeds by way of relinquishing is "contemplation of relinquishment. For this is reflective discernment and stabilization.
"Grasping" is apprehension by way of [notions such as] permanence and so forth.

"Perception of compactness" is the grasping of unity by way of continuity, collection, function, and object. "Accumulation" is volitional formation. "Alteration" is the reaching of a particular state of change.

"Perception of permanence" (*dhuvasaññā*) is the grasping at a state of stability. "The sign" (*nimitta*) is the grasping at formations as having a composite form, due to their density as a collection and so forth, and due to their being delimited by their own functions.
"Inclination" (*paṇidhi*) is the inclination toward passion and so forth; in its actual meaning, however, it is delighting in formations by way of craving.
"Adherence" (*abhinivesa*) is the view of self (*attānudiṭṭhi*).
The examination of all phenomena by way of their impermanence, suffering, and so forth, is higher wisdom-insight into phenomena (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*).

The adherence to grasping at the essential is the perversion of perceiving the non-essential as essential. The adherence that the world arose through the creation of a Lord (Īśvara) and so forth is the adherence of delusion (*sammohābhinivesa*).
Some, however, maintain that the adherence of delusion is the occurrence of doubt, such as: "Did I exist in the past? and so on.
They say: the grasping at formations as a shelter and a refuge is *ālayābhinivesa*.

According to the statement, "Delighting in the *ālaya*, rejoicing in the *ālaya*," the *ālaya* is craving (*taṇhā*); some maintain that this very craving, by way of its occurrence through adherence (*abhinivesa*) to the eye and so forth, and to forms and so forth, is called *ālayābhinivesa*.
The knowledge that occurs as "Such formations are to be relinquished" is *paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*.

Because it is free from the round (*vaṭṭa*), it is the "unrolling" (*vivaṭṭa*), namely Nibbāna. Therein, *vivaṭṭānupassanā* (contemplation of the unrolling) is the state of proceeding by means of contemplation (*anupassanā*)—defined as taking that [Nibbāna] as its object;
it is the stage of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*). "Adherence through conjunction" (*saṃyogābhinivesa*) is the adherence to volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) by way of being conjoined with them.
"Associated with views" (*diṭṭhekaṭṭha*) refers to those things that are co-nascent with views and those that are to be abandoned together with views. "Coarse" (*oḷārika*)...
This was said with reference to the defilements removable by the higher paths; otherwise, even those to be abandoned by seeing would be coarser than those removable by the second path.
"Subsisting as a subtle residue" means existing in a minute state. This was said with reference to what is removable by the lower paths.
"All defilements" refers to all remaining defilements, for defilements already abandoned by the first and subsequent paths are not abandoned again.

Hardness is the state of being rigid. Oozing is the state of being fluid. That by which a particular group [of elements] becomes distended or stiffened, like a bellows by means of worldly air, is expansion (vitthambhana).

Space is the limit of form, defined as the distinctness of each respective element from the others, even though there is contact between those belonging to different groups. As for those who hold this view...

That which is the delimitation is itself untouched by those [great elements]; otherwise, there would be no state of delimitation for the great elements because they would attain a state of pervasiveness.
The state of being untouched by those elements within the group (kalāpa) in which the great elements are delimited is the characteristic of non-contact.
Therefore, the Blessed One said in the description of the space element: "It is untouched by the four great elements."
“Rūpaṇā” (being affected) is the arising of something dissimilar when there is a concurrence of opposing conditions.
Because volition is predominant among the phenomena of the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), this is stated by way of volition as: “The characteristic of formations is the act of forming.

For indeed, in the *Suttantabhājanīya* of the *Vibhaṅga* on the aggregate of formations, it is volition alone that is analyzed, beginning with: “Volition born of eye-contact,” and so forth. Thus, they have the characteristic of forming.
And it is volition (*cetanā*). As it is said: "In this context, what is the formation of merit? It is wholesome volition pertaining to the sense sphere," and so forth.

"Pervasion" means the state of being expansive. "In lack of faith" means for the sake of lack of faith; the locative case is used here in the sense of a cause. This same method applies to the terms "laziness" (*kosajja*) and so on.
"Characterized by tranquility" means characterized by the subsiding of the feverish distress of body and mind. [It is] free from sluggishness and agitation.
When higher consciousness is proceeding, equanimity consists in reflection through the cessation of partiality,
due to non-engagement in exertion, restraint, and encouragement;
it is of a nature that embraces [the object], because its opposite— false speech and so forth— is harsh, characterized by deception, and non-embracing.
Right speech, because of its affectionate nature, embraces both the associated states and the person who hears the well-spoken words conditioned by right speech;
thus, it has the characteristic of embracing (*pariggaha*). Bodily activity originates whatever is to be done, and itself constitutes an arising and an effort;
thus, even the abstinences termed right action have the characteristic of originating (*samuṭṭhāna*).
It is to be seen as the lifting up or the arousing of associated states, like the lifting of a burden by means of physical action.
It is the purification or cleansing of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of a living being, or of associated states, or of livelihood itself.
It is said that "formations" (*saṅkhārā*) here refers to volition (*cetanā*), hence it is stated: "the characteristic of formations is volition."
Bowing is the state of being directed toward the object. The base (āyatana) is the process of occurrence;

for it is by way of the bases that the mind and mental factors—termed "the moving" (āya)—occur. "The characteristic of craving as a cause" refers to its status as the productive cause of the round of existence (vaṭṭa), whereas for the Path, it is its quality of leading to Nibbāna;
this is the distinction between them.

The characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*) is its non-erroneous intrinsic nature. Its single flavor (*ekarasa*) is the state of not exceeding one another and being neither deficient nor excessive.

It is indeed serenity and insight joined together (*yuganaddhā*); some also say it is "faith and wisdom, exertion and non-distraction. "Destruction" (*khaya*) is the path, which is the destruction of the defilements.
"Non-arising" (*anuppāda*) is the fruit, because its culmination is non-arising. "Tranquility" (*passaddhi*) is the subsiding of the defilements. "Of desire" (*chandassa*)...
[It is] the desire characterized by the wish to act. Its characteristic as a root is its state of being a foundation.

Its characteristic as an origination is its being the cause for the arising of associated states by way of presenting an object. Its "conjunction" (*samodhāna*) is the mode to be grasped through the meeting of the sense-object and so forth;
it is what is called "convergence. Alternatively, it is "conjunction" because associated states "conjoin together" (*samam odahanti*) by means of it.

Contact (*phassa*). It is called a "convergence" (*samosaraṇa*) because things converge and assemble therein. Since associated states do not function without feeling, they are said to be as if converged for the purpose of experiencing feeling.

The characteristic of being foremost (*pamukha-lakkhaṇa*) is the state of being the leader of the associated states, like the ridge-pole among rafters. Therefore, [it is contact] or rather, of those associated states...
"Exertion beyond that" means beyond that. For wholesome states have wisdom as their supreme excellence. "By means of liberation" refers to the fruit;
for that [fruit] is the essence by virtue of being the ultimate pinnacle of the essence consisting of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.

It should be understood that this analysis of characteristics was made according to the various sūtra passages concerning the six elements, the five jhāna factors, and so on, following the method transmitted in the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*). Likewise...
For indeed, even though some teaching has already been stated previously, it is shown again for the purpose of explaining it from another perspective; and for that very reason, it is said:
“Wholesome states have desire as their root, attention as their source, contact as their meeting point, and feeling as their convergence”;
“Wholesome states have wisdom as their supreme”; “This holy life has liberation as its essence”; and “Nibbāna is its ultimate goal.”
Based on such scriptural passages as, "Friends, the holy life has Nibbāna as its consummation," it is said that "desire has the characteristic of being the root," and so forth.
The "suchness of phenomena" refers to the Four Noble Truths because their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is non-erroneous. They are "such" (*tathā*) because they possess that nature;

they are "not otherwise" (*avitathā*) because they do not have a different nature than that; they are "not otherwise" (*anaññathā*) because they are devoid of any other mode of appearance. The meaning is that they have arisen and come to be with birth as their condition.
The meaning of "arising" (*sambhūta*) is the state of having come forth higher and higher, in accordance with its own conditions, once it has been produced through birth as a condition;

this is the sense of "occurring in succession. Alternatively, the compound *sambhūtasamudāgata* means both the sense of being produced (*sambhūta*) and the sense of having fully come about (*samudāgata*).

Birth does not exist without aging-and-death, nor does aging-and-death arise from anything other than birth; thus, it is the sense of being produced through birth as a condition (*jātipaccayasambhūta*).

And thus, because it arises from birth, it has the sense of being "arisen with birth as its condition. The meaning is that whatever birth serves as a condition in whatever manner, there is a manifestation corresponding to that.

Regarding the phrase "ignorance is the condition for volitional formations," here too it is not that ignorance is not a condition for volitional formations, nor do volitional formations arise without ignorance. Whatever...
In whatever way ignorance is the condition for whichever formations, this is the meaning of ignorance as the condition for formations;
that is to say, its state of being a condition.
"The Blessed One knows and sees that" is the connection. "By him" means by the Blessed One. This should be construed with the phrase "analyzing that."

That is the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "desirable, undesirable, and so forth," it includes the neutral; likewise, it includes the various divisions such as past, future, present, limited, internal, external, both, and so on.

Regarding the phrase "by way of the terms actually occurring": because of the statement, "The visible-form base is seen, the sound base is heard, the odor base, taste base, and tangible-object base are sensed, and all form is cognized by the mind," there is also the term "seen."
And the term "cognized" (viññāta) is obtained with respect to the visible-object base. By many names:

"visible-object base, desirable, undesirable, neutral, limited, past, future, present, internal, external, seen, cognized, form, visible-form base, visible-form element, appearance of color, with visibility, with resistance, blue, yellow," and so forth.
“By such numerous names” means by these and others. “In thirteen sections” refers to the thirteen expository sections (niddesa-vāra) found in the *Rūpakaṇḍa*.
“By fifty-two methods” means by fifty-two methods consisting of four methods of determination for each section.
“Just so” means exactly as it is, because of its unerring vision and its irrefutable teaching.

"I know; I have directly known"—by this demonstration of the occurrence of knowledge in the present and the past, it should be understood that the occurrence of knowledge in the future has also been stated.
The word *vidita* (known) should be understood as not specifying a particular time, as in the expression "seen, heard, sensed" (*diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ*).
"It did not appear" means it did not approach [him] by way of being a self or belonging to a self, just as visible objects and other sense-objects do not.

The etymology of the word *tathāgata* should be understood as follows: he is the "Tathāgata" because he sees, knows, and goes (*gacchati*) in accordance with (*tathā*) the true nature (*yamsabhāva*) and the specific modes (*yampakāra*) of phenomena (*dhammā*).

Some, however, explain it by means of grammatical derivation (*niruttinaya*), either through the elision of the suffix *-ī* in the word *dassī* (from *darśin*) or through the addition of the prefix *ā-* to the word *āgata*, thus forming *tathāgato*.
"Yaṃ rattim" means on which night; this is the accusative case used here to denote continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).

"Tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ" means of the three Māras, namely those designated as the defilement-māra (*kilesa-māra*), the formation-māra (*abhisaṅkhāra-māra*), and the devaputta-māra. "Anupavajjaṃ" means blameless because of being faultless.
"Anūnaṃ" means not deficient because there is nothing to be added. "Anadhikaṃ" means not excessive because there is nothing to be removed.
"Exceedingly. "Complete in every aspect" means complete in all respects through the perfection of meaning, phrasing, and so forth.
"Not otherwise" establishes, by way of contrast, the very meaning already stated as "just so.
By this, he shows the non-perverted nature of the teaching: that it is "just so" as spoken by the Blessed One, because it accomplishes the purpose for which it was spoken, exactly as it was spoken.
By the phrase *gad-attho*, it is shown that it is stated according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*) by changing the letter *da* to *ta*, as in:

"He speaks thus (*tathā gadati*), therefore he is a *Tathāgata*. Alternatively, "That which has gone thus (*tathā gataṃ assa*) is a *Tathāgata*. Here, "gone" (*gata*) means the activity of either body or speech.
And when "thus" (*tathā*) is said, because of the inseparable connection between the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ*, the meaning is "in this way" (*yathā*).

He is indeed established. To show the meaning that bodily and vocal actions stand in mutual conformity—with speech following the desire for speech, and the body following speech, and speech following the body—by way of their state of connection, he said, "For the Blessed One," and so forth.
Furthermore, in this sense, the etymology of *tathāgata* as "one who speaks thus" (*tathāvādita*) is also established.
But since this has already been shown by another method of exposition, he said: "Thus, because of acting accordingly, he is the Tathāgata.
By the phrase "horizontally in immeasurable world-systems," he refutes those who claim that "just as there are world-systems horizontally, so too there are world-systems above and below.
The expression "consisting of the splendor of the teaching" means simply the splendor of the teaching itself.

In such passages as “consisting of merit” (*puññamaya*) and “consisting of giving” (*dānamaya*), because particles function by manifesting the meaning of a word when placed in proximity to it, the word *gata* itself expresses both the sense of "understood" (*avagata*) and the sense of "past" (*atīta*). Thus he said: “*Gata* means understood and past.

Alternatively, from the initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*) up until full enlightenment (*sambodhi*), throughout this interval of the practice of the Great Vehicle of Awakening (*mahābodhiyānapaṭipatti*),...
Because there is an absence of falling away, of defilement, and of turning back, he has gone according to his resolve; thus, having practiced in accordance with his aspiration, he is the Tathāgata.

Alternatively, because of his great psychic power, his attainment of the excellence of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and his possession of unobstructed knowledge, there is no obstruction anywhere;
thus, his movements—of body, speech, and mind—proceed exactly as he desires.
He is a *tathāgata* because his modes of conduct (*pavatti*) are such [as they truly are].

Furthermore, since in the world the words *vidha*, *yutta*, *gata*, and *pakāra* are seen to have synonymous meanings, this Blessed One is a *tathāgata* because he is of the same kind (*tathāvidha*) as the Blessed Ones such as Vipassī and others, who were of that same kind.
And because those Blessed Ones were endowed with such qualities (*yutta*), this Blessed One is also endowed with them in that same way; thus he is a *tathāgata*. Alternatively, because...
“Truth, reality, suchness, thusness”—this is a designation for knowledge. Therefore, because he has come by means of such knowledge (*tathā-ñāṇa*), he is the Tathāgata;
in this way also the meaning of the word Tathāgata is to be understood.
“Having abandoned the stains of sense-desire and so forth, just as they have gone...”
Vipassī and the other Great Seers, as well as the Sakyan Sage who bears radiant glory,
are considered Tathāgatas because of their knowledge of meditative absorption.
“Thus has this Victor arrived, by means of his self-born knowledge,
at the characteristics of the elements, bases, and so forth,
through their distinctions of intrinsic nature, commonality, and classification.”
The Bull of the Sakyas is called the Tathāgata.
With his all-encompassing eye, he has seen the truths as they truly are,
and likewise the conditionality of this world in its entirety.
Because he has manifested [the truth] through that which is not to be led by others,
he is the Victor, the Tathāgata, in accordance with reality.
Even throughout world-systems of manifold divisions...
Regarding the diverse varieties within the range of the Victor’s sense-sphere of visible forms and so forth, his vision is exactly as it is;
therefore, the Tathāgata is "All-Seeing."
But when one speaks of the Dhamma exactly as it is,
and acts in accordance with one’s own words,
one proceeds having surpassed the world by means of one’s virtues.
The Tathāgata, the Leader of the World,
likewise [responded]: "According to his initial aspiration and according to his inclination,
his speech proceeded from the state of his subtle mind and being."
“In whatever manner and by whomsoever the Great Seers were formerly [described], in that same manner is the Conqueror, the Tathāgata.”—Why is this merely a summary verse (*saṅgahagāthā*)?

Because, like the term "heedfulness" (*appamāda*), it encompasses all the qualities of a Buddha through the practice of all wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). For this very reason, he said: “In every aspect,” and so forth. The rest here is of plain meaning.

171. Regarding the second [verse], the phrase "arising" (*uppatti*) refers to the manifestation in the first birth; whereas, in order to show the manifestation in a noble birth, he said "accomplishment" (*nipphatti*).

For at that time, there is the accomplishment of Buddhahood. Having stated "hard to find" (*dullabho*) and so forth, and because the causal equipment for that state is remote, he spoke the words beginning with "once" (*ekavāraṃ*) to demonstrate the cause therein. This is what is meant:
In this context, "reckoning of time" refers to the calculation of months, years, aeons (*kappa*), and so forth.
Even after fulfilling the perfections (*pāramī*) for one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya*), two incalculable aeons, or even three incalculable aeons, it is not possible to become a Buddha;
however, at the very least, one must practice the ten perfections continuously for four incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons.
Because it is possible to attain the state of a Buddha by fulfilling [the perfections], and not otherwise than this, for this reason the manifestation of Buddhas is rare.
172. Regarding the third [verse], "it is not constant" means that it does not occur frequently, since it happens only at certain times.
It was said with reference to the fact that most people clap their hands when they see something wonderful: "having clapped their hands..."
“It should be seen. By the phrase “because he is endowed with,” he shows that this person is called “wonderful” (acchariya) because wonderful qualities and dharmas exist within him.

Furthermore, he says he is “wonderful” because from the very beginning he brought about the resolution (abhinīhāra), and thereafter he practiced those qualities and dharmas that are not shared by others—“a person of practiced conduct is also a wonderful person,” and so forth. [The term refers to] the knowledge of Great Enlightenment itself.
The Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa) is the essence of the mandala. For path-knowledge has omniscience as its proximate cause, and omniscience has path-knowledge as its proximate cause;

thus, it is called "Great Enlightenment" (Mahābodhi). "By one who does not turn back" means by one whose nature is non-retrogression due to having attained the state of certainty regarding enlightenment and the status of a Mahābodhisatta.
Furthermore, the fulfillment of the qualities that constitute a Buddha belongs to no other.

By the phrase "the habituation of anyone," etc., he shows that the Lord of the World is called a "wonderful person" because of his habituation (*āciṇṇatā*) to qualities and dharmas that are not shared by others, across three states: the state of cause, the state of fruit, and the state of benefiting sentient beings.
173. "Action at the time of death" (*kālakiriyā*): this refers to the action performed at the time of death. At what time, and of what kind, is the action? This is a general definition.
For one remains fixed upon a distinction, and a distinction must not be applied by one who seeks a distinction; thus he said:
“At one time, the activity is manifest. But at which one time, and in what way, is it manifest?
Having advanced through many incalculable aeons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus a hundred thousand aeons, it is attained by way of the complete fulfillment of one’s intended desires.
At one time, it was extremely well known throughout the world including the devas that the Parinibbāna of the Most Wondrous Man had occurred.

It was "causing remorse" in the sense that it brought mental anguish. The phrase "in ten thousand world-systems" is stated because [the Buddha-field] is delimited as such, and because it is not within the range of others.
174. Regarding the phrase "of the second Buddha" in the fifth [verse]: it is because there is no second omniscient Buddha (*sabbaññubuddha*).

One called a "Buddha by learning" (*sutabuddha*) is so named because he has awakened through knowledge consisting of what has been heard. One called a "Buddha of the Four Truths" (*catusaccabuddha*) is so named because he has awakened to the four noble truths without exception.
One called a "Paccekabuddha" is so named because his awakening to the Four Truths is individual (*pacceka*), occurring only for himself.

It is because of this that he is a Buddha. For it is only as a Sammasambuddha that he fully awakens to the Truths in such a way that there is the awakening to the Four Truths for the world including the devas.

As for the statement "four, eight, or sixteen," this is said according to the distinction between those Great Bodhisattvas who have made great resolves (*abhinīhāra*) and who are predominant in wisdom, predominant in faith, or predominant in energy. For among those predominant in wisdom...
"Faith is dull and wisdom is sharp. For those in whom faith predominates, wisdom is middling. For those in whom energy predominates, wisdom is dull;
yet it is by the power of wisdom that full enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) is to be attained"—thus it is said in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
However, without distinction, these three types of individuals are differentiated according to the sharp, middling, or dull state of the qualities that ripen liberation (vimuttiparipācanīyadhammā).

They say it is appropriate. For Bodhisattas at the moment of making their aspiration (abhinīhāra) are of three kinds, distinguished as those who understand by a brief indication (ugghaṭitaññū), those who understand by elaboration (vipañcitaññū), and those who must be guided (neyya).

Among them, one who understands by a brief indication possesses the necessary potential (upanissaya) to attain Arahantship together with the six direct knowledges (abhiññā) and the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) while hearing a four-line verse from the presence of a Perfectly Enlightened One, even before the third line has been finished.

The second had the necessary potential to attain Arahantship by means of the six higher knowledges while hearing a single verse from the Teacher’s presence, even before the fourth line was finished. The other, having heard a four-line verse from the Blessed One’s presence,
had the necessary potential to attain Arahantship by means of the six higher knowledges once the verse was completed.

Having made their resolutions and received their prophecies, those who are endowed with these three qualities fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) according to the sequence and the aforementioned divisions of time,
thereby attaining perfect enlightenment. However, as long as those respective divisions of time are not yet complete,

even if those Great Beings were to give day after day a gift like that of Vessantara, they would still [require] the remaining perfections such as virtue (sīla) and so forth, corresponding to that [generosity].
It is not the case that Buddhas will arise in the interval even for one who is accumulating [merit]; why? Because knowledge has not yet reached maturity.

For just as a crop produced at a specific time cannot be obtained with all one's effort and exertion in the interval between when it was produced, so too Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) cannot be attained in the interval between the fulfillment of the perfections (pāramipūrī) and the specific time already mentioned.
"It is to be understood that it 'is accomplished' (*sampajjati*).

'Together' (*saddhiṃ*) means at the same time. 'Without a companion' (*asahāyo*) is stated in the primary sense (*nippariyāyato*). For the meaning of 'companion' (*sahāya*) is the sense of 'going with' (*saha-ayana*).

Indeed, there is no such thing as 'going together' (*samaṃ ayanaṃ*) with the Blessed One in terms of the practice (*paṭipatti*), because [he is] to be measured individually (*paṭi paṭi*) according to his limbs, such as the hands."
“Image” (*paṭimā*) refers to the personal existence (*attabhāva*). “There is no one capable” means there is no one at all—whether a deva, Māra, or Brahmā—who is capable.
“Equal” (*paṭisama*) means equal by way of being a counterpart (*paṭinidhi*).

“To give a counterpart portion” means to make a portion or division that serves as the opposite of the portion of Dhamma—the section of the Dhamma spoken of in such passages as “the four foundations of mindfulness.”

There is no one capable of giving him an answer; there is no person who is his equal in qualities such as virtue, hence he is "matchless" (*appaṭipuggala*). Therefore, he said: "No other," and so forth.
The classification of the three thousandfold great thousandfold world systems will be made clear later on. The rest here is easily understood.
175. Regarding "in that person" in the sixth verse and those following: it refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). "That" refers to the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*).

It is said to have "manifested" because it arises together with him. "Arising" (*uppatti*) means the act of coming into being. "Accomplishment" (*nipphatti*) means full development. "Of what kind? means of what sort.
The eye of wisdom that has come into the hands of disciples belongs only to the two Chief Disciples (*aggasāvaka*).
He said: “Of the Elder Sāriputta,” and so forth. “Concentration-wisdom” (samādhipaññā) means wisdom accompanied by concentration.
Some say it is “wisdom that leads to concentration and brings about specific qualities such as swift penetration. “Light” (āloka) is simply the light of wisdom;

likewise for “radiance” (obhāsa). “The three” refers to the three suttas. They are described as being “mixed mundane and supramundane” because they are intended to refer to the wisdom of the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga-paññā).
"Of the supreme dharmas" means of the most excellent dharmas, owing to the absence of anything superior to oneself. "Seeing" is so called because it is that which is seen;
it refers to the Blessed One’s material body (rūpakāya), and specifically therein, the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana). Therefore he said: "One obtains to see with eye-consciousness.
"Anuttara" means there is nothing higher than this; that itself is the "anuttariya" (unsurpassed state). It is both seeing and that unsurpassed state.
The unsurpassed vision. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. However, there is this distinction between the words:

it is "heard," thus it is hearing (*savana*), namely, the word of the Blessed One. It is "obtained," thus it is gain (*lābha*), namely, faith in the Blessed One. It is to be trained in, thus it is training (*sikkhā*).

The cultivation of virtue, concentration, and wisdom is service (*pāricariyā*), that is, attendance. Recollection is mindfulness (*anussati*), namely, the recollection of the Teacher’s qualities. "Of these" refers to those already mentioned.

Of the six unsurpassed things. "The manifestation occurs" means that through the manifestation of the Tathāgata, [these things] manifest because they are dependent upon him and have him as their object.

Furthermore, by the phrase "the unsurpassedness of seeing," it is not intended merely the sight of the Blessed One’s physical form—which is unsurpassed in the world with its devas—but rather, by way of seeing that form, [it refers to] unwavering confidence (*aveccappasāda*).
