Having placed one’s confidence in the qualities of the Buddha and having plunged into them, the vision must be seen. Therefore he said, “The Venerable One,” and so forth.
This too is called the unsurpassed vision because it is without distinction from what was stated previously.

“Having obtained the sight of the Ten-Powered One” means, like the Elder Ānanda, having obtained the sight of the Ten-Powered One preceded by serene confidence, devotion, and loving-kindness. Vision...
"Having increased" means having increased the practice of insight (vipassanā-cāra) that proceeds by way of seeing.

Having increased the practice of insight by way of seeing up to the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa), one who subsequently enters the great plane of the eighth person (aṭṭhamaka-mahābhūmi) is said to "bring seeing to the attainment of the stream-entry path" (sotāpatti-magga).
Herein, the seeing that proceeds from this point onward is simply called "seeing."

Furthermore, the vision of the root is called the "unsurpassed vision" because it serves as the cause for the vision of the Truths. This same principle applies to the other unsurpassed qualities as well.
"He acquires faith in the Ten-Powered One" means he acquires faith in the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"Having trained in the three trainings" means having trained in the three preliminary trainings. "He attends upon" means he performs service.

Having generated the jhāna of recollection by means of the recollection of the Buddha through the formula beginning with “Such indeed is the Blessed One,” and having made that the proximate cause (padatthāna), one increases insight; thus it is said, “having increased the recollection.
“Direct realization occurs” means there is a making manifest to direct perception. For the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are obtained at the moment of the Path.
At the moment of fruition (phalakkhaṇa), it is said to be "realized" because thereafter it is capable of being applied as one desires among the meanings and so forth.
"Four" is the delimitation by number. "Analytical knowledges" (paṭisambhidā) means "divisions. Of what, then, are these divisions?
From the statement, "Knowledge regarding meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning," and so forth, these are divisions of knowledge. Therefore, "the four analytical knowledges."
The meaning is "fourfold differentiation of knowledge. Regarding *atthapaṭisambhidā*: it is analytical insight (*paṭisambhidā*) with respect to meaning;
the meaning is "knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding meaning, capable of defining, clarifying, and establishing the specific characteristics of the differentiation of meaning.

Likewise, [it is] knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding phenomena (*dhamma*), capable of defining, clarifying, and establishing the specific characteristics of the differentiation of phenomena.
Knowledge of phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*).

Knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding verbal expression, capable of defining, clarifying, and establishing the distinctions of linguistic terminology, is the analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*).

Knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding inspired eloquence, capable of defining, clarifying, and establishing the characteristics of inspired eloquence, is the analytical knowledge of inspired eloquence (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).
Regarding the phrase "knowledge of meanings" (*atthesu ñāṇaṃ*) and so forth: "meaning" (*attha*) is, in brief, cause-and-result.
For that is to be sought, to be reached, and to be attained by way of the cause; therefore it is called "meaning. In detail, however, these five phenomena should be understood as "meaning":
whatever is conditionally arisen, Nibbāna, the meaning of what has been spoken, kamma-result, and functional (neither-good-nor-bad) states. For one who reflects upon that meaning...
The knowledge that has reached such differentiation is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*). "Dhamma" is, in brief, a condition.
For it is called "dhamma" because it bears, carries along, causes to proceed, brings about, and establishes the continuity; therefore, it is called "dhamma.
In detail, however, it refers to any cause that produces a fruit, whether it be the Noble Path, speech, the wholesome, or the unwholesome.

It should be understood as fivefold; for one who reflects upon that phenomenon (dhamma), the knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding that phenomenon is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā).
"Knowledge regarding the meaning, the phenomenon, and the expression of language" refers to the sound of the natural language used for that meaning and that phenomenon.
For one who reflects by taking that as an object, there arises a knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding that expression of conventional terminology (*sabhāvanirutti*).
Thus, this analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*) is said to have sound as its object, not conceptual designation (*paññatti*) as its object.

Why? Because, having heard a sound, one understands: "This is conventional terminology; this is not conventional terminology. This is for one who has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidāpatto*).

For when "contact" (*phasso*) is stated, one knows, "This is the conventional designation of its own nature"; but when "contacts" (*phassā*) or "contact" (*phassan*) is stated, one knows, "This is not the conventional designation of its own nature.

The same method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors]. Furthermore, because he knows the conventional designation of its own nature exactly as it is, he also understands nouns, verbs, prefixes, and indeclinables.
Among types of knowledge, "knowledge" refers to the all-pervading knowledge (*sabbatthakajāṇa*), which has the object as its domain.
This is the knowledge that has reached its differentiation for one who is reviewing [the path] after having performed it.
These four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), moreover, reach their differentiation in two places: on the plane of the trainee (*sekkha*) and on the plane of the adept (*asekha*).
By means of these five causes—attainment, mastery of the scriptures, hearing, inquiry, and prior practice—they reach their differentiation.
They become clear. "Attainment" (adhigama) refers to the penetration of the Truths. "Mastery of the scriptures" (pariyatti) refers to the word of the Buddha;

for one who grasps that, the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) become clear. "Hearing" (savana) refers to hearing the Dhamma; for even one who hears the Dhamma with careful attention, the analytical knowledges become clear.
"Inquiry" (paripucchā) refers to the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā). Regarding the text already learned...
For even in one who explains the meaning, the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) become clear. "Prior application" (*pubbayoga*) means being engaged in prior practice.

Even for one whose meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) has been made manifest by way of taking up and bringing back [the text], the analytical knowledges become clear. Regarding the phrase "both mundane and supramundane":
here, three of the analytical knowledges are mundane; the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) may be either mundane or supramundane.
The meaning should be understood by analyzing it in this way.

By the restrictive phrase "only when a Buddha has appeared," what is intended is a penetration that is not shared with others, since it is obtained only when a Buddha has appeared and is not obtained when no Buddha has appeared.
And having established this, [the terms] such as "of the great eye" and so forth also refer to the greatness of wisdom and the rest.

It should be understood that only what is not shared with others is intended. Likewise, the realization of the fruits of clear vision and liberation, and so forth, should also be seen as bringing about those states for others.
Whatever elements there may be, whether mundane or supramundane, they are all included within these;
they are contained right here. Thus it is said: "These eighteen elements are 'various elements' because of their diverse intrinsic natures."

This same meaning is to be illustrated by the *Vibhaṅga* on the knowledge of the many and various elements (*anekadhātunānādhātuñāṇa*). Because it is stated as "realization" (*sacchikiriyā*), it is said that "clear vision (*vijjā*) is knowledge regarding the fruit. 187.
Since it moves (*cakati*) and revolves again and again, it is called a "wheel" (*cakkam*); therefore, even the postures (*iriyāpathā*) [are wheels] because they revolve again and again.
They are called "wheels" (cakkāni) because they resemble wheels in the sense of revolving; likewise, so too are the perfections such as dwelling in a suitable locality.
From that point onward, it is said that "he brings forth the Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakkaṃ abhinīharati*);

here, at that time, the Great Being, applying himself to the practice of bringing forth [the aspiration], is described as "bringing forth the Wheel of Dhamma," because from then on there arose no further states that would obstruct the bringing forth of the Wheel of Dhamma.
Regarding the phrase "it is called 'brought forth'": here too, the same principle applies.
Even when one penetrates the path of arahantship, it is indeed said that "the Wheel of Dhamma is set in motion," because one brings the knowledge for that purpose to maturity.

At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, it is said that "the Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion," because at that moment there is no further task to be performed for the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma.
For here, it is the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*) that is intended by the term "Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*).
Now, in order to show the Wheel of Dhamma by way of the knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*), he said: "When does it set in motion? and so forth.
Not only for the Elder, but for all followers of the Dispensation (*sāsanika*), the discourse on Dhamma is the Blessed One’s teaching of Dhamma regarding the four Noble Truths and the four...
In order to show that there is no violation of the methods beginning with "oneness" (*ekatta*), the passage beginning with "Whatever monk... has been commenced.
The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the Chapter on Single Individuals is finished.
14. Etadaggavagga (14) 1.
Paṭhama-etadaggavagga: Commentary on the Words "Foremost" (Etadagga)
188. Regarding the phrase *etadaggesu*, one should supply the word *agga* (foremost) and connect it as follows: "It is seen at the beginning of the first section of the first chapter.
*Ajjatagge* means "starting from this very day. *Aṅgulaggena* means "by the tip of the finger. *Ambilaggaṃ* means "a portion of sour [fruit].
*Koṭibhūtā* means "having reached the ultimate limit," because in that place there are no others like them.
Because they are non-existent [in others], they are "foremost" (*agga*) precisely because they have become supreme.

"The designation of this as foremost" (*etadagga-sannikkhepo*) refers to the placing [of a person] among those who are foremost by means of four reasons, beginning with the origin of the discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*). In order to demonstrate in detail how the Elder attained the status of being foremost due to his great wisdom, he said, "How...
and so forth. "Two intermediate phrases" refers to [the locations] at the foot of the *kaṇḍamba* tree and on Mount Yugandhara.
Having shown two phrases in two places. Regarding "Muṇḍapīṭhaka": this was said with reference to that which is neither seven-limbed nor five-limbed, but is merely a plain, shaven seat.
"He sat covering it" means he sat having completely overspread it through the power of the Buddha.
Therefore he said: "Sitting thus," and so forth. "Making him a body-witness" means by means of the mental body (*nāmakāya*).

Having made [the audience] witnesses by way of their acceptance of the teaching. In the phrase “wholesome states, unwholesome states, indeterminate states,” the word *iti* has the sense of “beginning with”;
by this, it includes the entire Abhidhamma teaching.
In the phrase “at the place of the miracle,” this refers to the location where the Twin Miracle was performed. “Behold” is said with reference to their great number.
It is said. *Assā* means of the multitude of humans, as a single entity. *Ākappaṃ* means appearance. *Mahājano* means all people in the world including the devas.
Just as the vision of hell is for the purpose of generating spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), so too is the vision of the heavenly worlds for the very same purpose of generating spiritual urgency:
"In this gradual discourse, just like the talk on heaven, even though one is thus endowed with all perfections..."
"Heaven is impermanent, unstable, and subject to fall. "Having prepared" means having prepared it so that it could be played upon with fifty strings according to one's desire.

"The pentad of questions on worldlings" means starting from the questions concerning worldlings and proceeding until the end of the questions concerning those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
The pentad of questions. First... [as before] ...he asked; he asked a question concerning the domain of the worldling (*puthujjana*).

It is said that "they spoke, each remaining within the domain of their own analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidā*)," because the analytical knowledges functioned within their respective domains according to the specific application of insight (*vipassanā*), just as in the case of the first stage and so forth, in accordance with the manner in which they were directed. He asked a question concerning the domain of the Buddha.
“Those who have fully understood the Dhamma, and those many here who are still in training—being asked, O dear sir, please tell me, being wise, about their conduct.
Thus he asked this question. In that context, “those who have fully understood the Dhamma” means those by whom the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths has been fully analyzed and known. And those...
"Those who have analyzed the Dhamma" means those who have penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Truths by means of the four paths; by this, the *asekkhas* (those beyond training) are described.
The word "puthu" (many/various) should be applied in both instances: "those many who have analyzed the Dhamma, and those many who are *sekkhas* (those in training).
Regarding "of them," it should be connected as "I have asked these two types of persons, the *sekkhas* and the *asekkhas*"; that is, "I have asked."
The meaning is as follows: they move (*iriyanti*) along the path of arrival upon the plane of the trainees (*sekkha*) and the adepts (*asekkha*).

It is called "movement" (*iriya*) because by means of it one moves—that is, goes—to the plane of the trainees and the plane of the adepts. The sense is: "Being asked by me, explain—speak of—that movement, their path of arrival.
Thus, having asked a question regarding the domain of the Buddha, [the Blessed One said]: "Sāriputta, regarding this..."
“How is the meaning of what was spoken in brief to be seen in detail? he asked.

The Elder, having examined the question, thought, “The Teacher asks me about the path of arrival for bhikkhus who are both in training and beyond training. Free from doubt regarding the question, he considered:
“The ‘path of arrival’ can be explained by way of many approaches, such as the aggregates (khandhas) and so forth; in which manner [should it be explained]?”
Thinking, "Will I now be able to grasp the Teacher’s intention while speaking?", he was doubtful regarding that intention;

it is with reference to him that it is said: "The Dhamma-General... [etc. ...was not able. When there is no inspired eloquence to answer the question asked, showing that looking toward the quarters is the natural disposition of beings, he said: "To the east... [etc. ...he was not able."
In this context, "the basis for the arising of a question" means the cause for the arising of a question.
"Having known the elder’s state of weariness" means having understood the elder’s weariness by thinking: "Sāriputta is free from doubt regarding the questions;
it is because he has doubt regarding my intention that he is weary. "The comprehension of the body composed of the four great elements" refers to this [following passage].

The discernment of name-and-form has been explained by way of the aggregates. For when the Blessed One said, "Sāriputta, do you regard this as 'this has come to be'?", he showed the discernment of name-and-form by way of the aggregates. It occurred to the Blessed One:
"If I do not provide a method, Sāriputta will not be able to explain; but if I provide a method, he will be able to explain according to my own intention."

“Having grasped it, he will explain it by way of the categories (khandha). As soon as the Elder was given the method, that question presented itself to him through a hundred methods and a thousand methods.
Therefore he said: “Understood, Blessed One; understood, Sugata.
It is stated that there is no rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the formless realm because there is no opportunity for the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra).
Therefore he said, "Because it is an impossible place" (*abhabbaṭṭhānattā*); the meaning is that it is a land where the arising of Bodhisattvas who have received their prophecy is impossible.

"He was reborn in the realm of form" (*rūpāvacare nibbatti*) means that because of the impossibility of mastery over karma [in other realms], he did not arise in the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*), but arose in the realm of form.
By the phrase "more than a thousand," etc., he shows the *Parosahassa-jātaka*. In that context, "even more than a thousand" (*parosahassampi*) means even exceeding one thousand.
"Of those who have gathered" means of those fools who have assembled and are unable to understand the meaning of what has been spoken.

"They might cry out for a hundred years, being without wisdom" means that these fools, having thus assembled, because they lack wisdom, would weep and lament like cranes for a hundred years or even a thousand years.
Yet, even while weeping, they would find neither the meaning nor the reason.

He explains [the verse] as meaning "one should know. "A single wise man is better" means that even compared to more than a thousand such fools, a single wise person is better—that is, more excellent. As to what kind of person is "wise," he says:
"One who understands the meaning of what is spoken. This refers to one who knows the meaning of what is spoken, like the senior pupil; such a person is of this sort.

The meaning is that one who possesses wisdom is superior. In the second *Parosata-jātaka*, "they should meditate" means they should reflect, having become concentrated in order to know the meaning as it truly is.
The rest here is exactly according to the method already stated.
In the third *Jātaka*, "those who are percipient" refers to all sentient beings possessing consciousness, excluding those who have attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

He shows this. "Those too are miserable" means that because they have not attained that attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they too are miserable and have encountered suffering within the realm of perception (*saññā-bhava*).
For they see the danger in perception, thinking: "Perception is a disease, perception is a tumor, perception is an arrow.
"And those who are non-percipient" refers to the mindless beings reborn in the realm of non-perception (*asaññī-bhava*). Those too...

She is indeed miserable because of her failure to attain this very meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). The bliss of *jhāna* is "without blemish" (*anaṅgaṇa*) because of the absence of the aforementioned defects.
It is also called "without blemish" by virtue of its nature as powerful one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*). He said, "neither percipient nor non-percipient.
It is said that in the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was passing away in a forest wilderness.
When questioned by his pupils, he replied, "Neither percipient nor non-percipient. Just as described in the previous birth story (*jātaka*), the ascetics did not accept the words of the senior pupil.
The Bodhisatta, having come from the Ābhassara realm and standing in the air, spoke this verse.
Therefore it is said: "The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated."
In the *Catutthajāta*ka, "having a radiance like that of the moon" (*candābha*) refers to the white-kasiṇa.
"Having a radiance like that of the sun" (*sūriyābha*) refers to the yellow-kasiṇa.
"Whoever here finds a foothold through wisdom" means that person who, in this world of beings, finds a foothold in these two kasiṇas—that is, they enter into them by making them their object.
Or he is established therein. "By means of the second jhāna, free from applied thought, he goes to the Ābhassara realm":
having acted thus, that person, by means of the second jhāna attained [thereby], goes to the Ābhassara Brahma-world.
"The rest should be understood in the same manner as before"—by this he shows the following: in the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta...
While dying in a forest region, he was asked by his pupils and, having said, "The radiance of the moon, the radiance of the sun," he was reborn among the Ābhassara devas.
The ascetics did not believe the senior pupil. The Bodhisatta, having arrived and standing in the sky, spoke this verse:
"One should indeed hope" means that one should maintain hope in one's own kamma without destroying hope; one should not become despondent.
The meaning is: "He would not give rise to world-weariness; he would not become despondent. *Vā* is a mere particle.
By saying "I desired," he illustrates: "For I desired emergence from the sixty-cubit hell, and I was born exactly thus; I have indeed emerged from there.
It is said that in the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a sarabha deer.
He lived in the forest. The king was a skilled hunter, endowed with great strength. One day, having gone out, he said to his ministers:
"Whichever side the deer escapes by, that person must pay for it.
Then one day, a sarabha deer rose up and fled by the very path where the king was standing. Thereupon, the ministers mocked him. The king thought: "These..."
“They mock me; they do not know my measure,” he thought. So, putting on his lower garment tightly and taking his sword, he rushed forward with great speed, thinking, “I shall catch the sarabha.
Seeing him, the animal pursued him for three *yojanas*.
The sarabha entered the forest, and the king followed right after it. There, along the path where the sarabha deer traveled, a pit measuring sixty cubits in depth—
There was a pit of the Mahāpūtipātana hell, filled with water to the depth of thirty cubits and covered over with grass.
As soon as the hare smelled the odor of the water, he recognized it as a pit, retreated a short distance, and escaped.
But the king, coming straight forward, fell into it.
Not hearing the sound of his footsteps, the Sarabha turned back; not seeing him, he realized, "He must have fallen into a pit of hell.
Coming back and looking down, he saw him struggling in deep water where there was no footing.
Without taking to heart the offense committed by the other, the Sarabha, moved by compassion, thought, "While I am watching, let this poor creature not perish; from this suffering..."
Saying, "I shall release you," he stood by the edge of the pit and said, "Do not fear, Great King; I shall release you from this suffering.
As if exerting himself to rescue his own beloved son, he prepared a stone for the purpose of lifting him out.
Then, having pulled the king—who had come thinking "I shall pierce [the rock]"—up sixty cubits from the hell, he comforted him and [rested him] upon his back.
Having mounted him, he brought him out from the forest, set him down not far from the army, gave him instruction, and established him in the five precepts.
The king, surrounded by his military forces, went to the city and caused the drum of Dhamma to be beaten, proclaiming:
"From this day forth, let all the inhabitants of the kingdom observe the five precepts. As for the Great Being, he [reflected upon] the merit he had performed himself...
Without telling anyone, she partook of a meal of various exquisite flavors in the evening and lay upon her decorated bed.
At dawn, recollecting the virtues of the Great Being, she rose and sat cross-legged on the surface of her bed.
With a heart full of rapture, she uttered this inspired exclamation (*udāna*) in these six verses beginning with, "A man should indeed aspire... and so forth.
In this context, "harmful" and "beneficial" refer to painful contact and pleasant contact, or alternatively, to the contact of death and the contact of life.
For beings, the contact of death is harmful, while the contact of life is beneficial. He shows that for them, the contact of death arrives unexpectedly. "Unexpectedly" means:
it was not thought by me, "I shall fall into a pit," nor was it thought, "A sarabha..."
"I shall kill him"—this was what he thought. But now my thought has been lost; it has become something unintended.

He speaks thus as an expression of spontaneous utterance (*udāna*). "Wealth" means fame and its retinue; these do not arise from mere thought. Therefore, he says that one possessed of wisdom should exert effort alone.
For indeed, even that which was unintended comes to pass for one who possesses effort.
As he was uttering this inspired utterance, dawn broke. The chaplain, having come early in the morning to inquire after his well-being, stood at the door;
hearing the sound of the king’s song of inspiration, he thought: "The king went hunting yesterday;
he must have wounded a sarabha deer there, and it is because of that, I suppose, that he utters this inspired utterance. Thus [it was] for the brahmin.
Having heard the king’s inspired utterance (udāna) with its perfected phrasing, it became as clear as the reflection of one’s own face in a well-polished mirror;
thus, the reason for what had been done by both the king and Sarabha became manifest. He struck at the door with his fingernail.
The king asked, “Who is this? “I am the royal chaplain, Your Majesty. Then, having opened the door for him, [the king said], “Come here, teacher.”
He said: "Having entered and offered greetings of victory to the king, he stood to one side and said:
'Great King, I know the deed you performed in the forest. While pursuing a single sarabha deer, you fell into a pit;
then that sarabha, having fashioned a bridge with a stone, rescued you from the pit. Remembering his virtue, you uttered this inspired exclamation:'"
Having said, "He uttered [this]," he spoke two verses beginning with "In the mountain fastness of Sarabha.
Therein, *anusarī* means he followed after. *Vikkantaṃ* means the effort made for the purpose of pulling out [the elephant].
*Anujīvasi* means you live off it; the meaning is that by its power you have obtained your livelihood. *Samuddharī* means he performed the act of pulling out.
"Having made the stone fit for the Sarabha" means having made it suitable for lifting [the beast] out of the pit, like a staircase.

"With a heart not cowed" means with a mind that has not fallen into despondency. "You spoke of that deer" refers to the golden Sarabha deer whom you described while reclining here upon this splendid bed.
Having heard this, the king thought, "This one did not come on the hunt with me."
Thinking, "He knows all occurrences; how indeed does he know them? I shall ask him," he spoke the ninth verse:
"What is it like? Therein, "of terrifying form" means: "Is your knowledge of a powerful nature? Is it by that [knowledge] that you know this?
The brahmin replied: "I am not an omniscient Buddha; without defiling the phrasing [of the scriptures], by you..."
"However, the meaning of the verse you have spoken occurs to me," he said, and demonstrating this, he spoke the tenth verse beginning with "And not... (*na ce vāhaṃ*).
Therein, "well-spoken" (*subhāsitānaṃ*) means those spoken well without corrupting the phrasing.

"Bringing forth the meaning" (*atthaṃ tadānentī*) means they bring forth—that is, they investigate—the meaning that belongs to them. At that time, the chaplain was the Dhammasenāpati (the General of the Dhamma).
For this very reason, he said: "In the past as well," and so forth. The remainder has its meaning already explained.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña and others," the phrase "by way of qualities according to their true nature" means by way of qualities according to their actual state (yathāsabhāva).
Long-standingness (*rattaññutā*) is to be understood by way of his going forth, by way of his penetration [of the Dhamma], and by way of his knowing the divisions of day and night;
showing this, he said, "Except for the Fully Enlightened One," and so forth.
"He becomes manifest" means that having attained the fullness of mindfulness and wisdom, he becomes manifest and clear. "Aññāsikoṇḍañña" refers to him who was the very first among the disciples.
The four noble truths were known by Koṇḍañña. "In all those [suttas] on the foremost" means in all the suttas concerning the foremost, or in all instances of designating someone as foremost.
"Foremost leaves" refers to the outer leaves that constitute the front of the leaf-fans. "Ninety cubits long" refers to the height for a man of medium stature.
[He was] ninety cubits in height by hand-measure. He crosses over and traverses each region as if on a lotus; thus he is "Padumuttara" (Lotus-Surpasser), the Blessed One. By the word "etc.

in the phrase "with garlands of perfumes, garlands of flowers, etc.," one includes leaf-garlands and so forth. Among these, a garland made with fragrant perfumes is a "garland of perfumes" (*gandhadāma*);
a garland made with cloves, *takkola*, jasmine flowers, and so forth, is a "flower-garland" (*mālādāma*). [A garland made] with *tamāla* leaves and so forth...
What is the *katamālā* (garland of *kata* flowers)? It is a wreath of leaves. *Vaṅgapaṭṭa* refers to a thick, fine cloth produced in the region of Vaṅga. *Uttamasukhumavattha* refers to Kāsī cloth.
Regarding the phrase "at the conclusion of the *Teparivaṭṭa-dhammacakkappavattana-sutta*":

here, it is [taught] by way of the Truths as in "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering," etc.; by way of function as in "The Noble Truth of Suffering is to be fully understood," etc.; and by way of the Noble Truth of Suffering...
Because it was taught by revolving the four truths in three ways—by way of [the phrases] beginning with "fully understood" and so forth—it has three revolutions;
thus it is *tiparivaṭṭa*. It is *teparivaṭṭa* because it is precisely those three revolutions.
And since it is both that *teparivaṭṭa* and the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakkappavattana*), it is the *teparivaṭṭadhammacakkappavattana*; that itself is the sutta.
"At its conclusion" is the meaning.
"Having split open the rice sheath and taking [it]" means: having split open the rice sheath and taking the milk-like essence found therein.
"Suitable" means: we shall cook milk-rice suitable for the Buddhas. "Braids" [are mentioned] by way of their male nature.

The "bundle-top" (*kalāpagga*) refers to the finest bundle when they have been tied into bundles. The "threshing-floor-top" (*khalagga*) refers to the best [sheaves] on the day the bundles are placed upon the threshing floor.

The "threshing-floor-heap-top" (*khalabhaṇḍagga*) refers to the best [grain] on the day the rice has been threshed and made into a heap. The "storehouse-top" (*koṭṭhagga*) refers to the first grain placed into the storehouses.
"Two destinies" (*dve gatiyo*) means two results; the sense is "two culminations. When that prince had attained omniscience...

Remaining in the very same conviction as the young man Koṇḍañña, the other six men also instructed their sons. At the foot of the Bodhi tree, the eastern side is the immovable place known as “Vajirāsana.
It is said that he was “facing east” because he was facing toward the great eastern world-system, rather than merely facing the east;
for even the fleshly eye of the Lord of the World [is capable of seeing].
"Non-obstructive and of great range. "Endowed with four factors" means endowed with the four factors described in the passage beginning, "Let only skin, sinew, and bone remain.
"But all this," however, refers to that which proceeded in the manner beginning, "To whom, indeed, shall I first teach the Dhamma? and so forth.
All of it indeed. It was merely a reflection, because there was no actual accomplishment of the purpose. "Having made it flower and bear fruit" means:

making it fully blossom with the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*), and making it completely laden with the burden of fruit through the paths and fruits—thus, having made it flower and bear fruit.
"Desiring to depart" refers to [the Buddha] regarding his two chief disciples... himself.
Seeing them performing acts of humble service and highly esteeming their exceptional virtues, he became desirous of departing from the presence of the Buddhas.
"Right there" means right there at the Chaddanta Lake moat.
(The Story of the Elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna)
189–190. Regarding the second and third [phrases], "of those possessing psychic power" (*iddhimantānaṃ*): here, the word *manta* refers to the sense of excellence;

thus, in order to show the elder’s preeminent psychic power, it is said, "of those endowed with psychic power" (*iddhiyā sampannānaṃ*). "They played with dust" means they were playmates from childhood (*sahapaṃsukīḷitā*).
"In this very life" means in the very body pertaining to the present existence (*diṭṭhadhammika-attabhāva*). Sixteen wisdoms.
"Having penetrated [the truth] and remaining [therein]," as stated in the *Anupada Sutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya*:
"Bhikkhus, Sāriputta has great wisdom; bhikkhus, Sāriputta has vast wisdom; bhikkhus, Sāriputta has joyful wisdom;
bhikkhus, Sāriputta has swift wisdom; bhikkhus, Sāriputta has sharp wisdom; bhikkhus, Sāriputta has penetrative wisdom."

Having penetrated and realized these sixteen kinds of wisdom— namely, the six beginning with "great wisdom" as they appear in the passage starting with "Sāriputta," the wisdom of the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling appearing in that same sutta, and the wisdom of the path to arahantship— he stands firm.
He engages in discussion regarding questions by means of both posing inquiries and providing answers for those who seek the truth.
"An acknowledged path"—this is a statement regarding the reason for following behind. For this is what is meant:
"What if I were now to follow closely behind this bhikkhu? Why? Because this act of following closely behind is an "acknowledged path" by those who seek it;
the meaning is that it is a path that is both well-known and entered upon.
Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: "When death is certain for us who desire [the goal], there must exist even an ambrosia (amata).

Thus, it is designated merely as "existing"; having approached it through inferential knowledge, one knows that what is called Nibbāna exists, and one seeks and searches for it—this is how the sense should be seen in this context.
"Of their assembly" means of the assembly that constitutes the retinue of the two chief disciples. "The two chief disciples" refers to the two disciples of great power, Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
"In a position" means he established them in the position known as that of the chief disciples.

But why, in this context, is it said "the two great disciples" instead of "the chief disciples"? [It is because] even other great elders possess specific qualities such as supernormal knowledge (*abhiññā*) and so forth.

They receive the designation "great disciples" (mahāsāvaka); however, it is said "the two great disciples" in order to show that among all disciples, these alone deserve to be specifically called "great disciples" because they possess qualities not shared by others.
The Story of the Elder Mahākassapa.

191. In the fourth [section], because the ascetic practices (*dhuta-dhamma*) and the factors of asceticism (*dhutaṅga*) have their root in what is shaken off (*dhuta*), it is begun with the words, "The ascetic should be understood.

In this context, one who has shaken off (*dhuta*) defilements is called an "ascetic" (*dhuta*); thus, an individual whose defilements have been shaken off, or the state that shakes off defilements, is meant.
Furthermore, the Noble Path together with its preliminary stages should be regarded as "the state that shakes off defilements. That which is designated as "ascetic" (*dhuta*)— [End of excerpt]
He speaks of the quality of shaking off the defilements and establishes others therein; thus he is called a proponent of ascetic practices (*dhutavāda*).
Since a tetrad is possible here, the passage beginning with “But herein” is commenced to demonstrate it. *Tayidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is “this is that.
The qualities belonging to one who has become ascetic are the ascetic qualities (*dhutadhammā*). These are fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) and contentment (*santuṭṭhitā*).
These have already been explained above. It is called *sallekha* because it scrapes away (*likhati*) and polishes away (*tacchati*) the defilements;
it is the loathing of defilements, and its state is *sallekhatā*. One is secluded from both kinds of sensual desires, thus it is *paviveka*;

it is a person who abounds in wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), and its state is *pavivekatā*. By this mere placing of the bones, it is "this bone" (*idamaṭṭhi*); [the *ttha*-sound is used for the *tha*-sound].
Having formed the word *idamaṭṭhita* from the syllable *ṭṭha*, its state (*bhāva*) is *idamaṭṭhitā*. Alternatively, by means of these wholesome states there is a foundation (*atthi*) for this;

that knowledge by which one—thinking, "One who has gone forth must indeed be established in such things as the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice"—both undertakes and maintains the ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*) exactly as instructed, is *idamaṭṭhitā*. Therefore he said: "*Idamaṭṭhitā*."

"It is knowledge itself. Regarding the term "ascetic qualities" (*dhutadhammā*): they are called "ascetic qualities" because they are qualities that assist the ascetic volition (*dhutaṅgacetanā*)—which has acquired the name "ascetic" (*dhuta*) due to its activity of shaking off (*dhunana*) those evil states that are the opposites of the practice of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
They are said to "follow along" because they are included within it and comprised by it; they belong to both of these [the ascetic volition and the ascetic practices].

Because of the difference in their modes of practice. "In the matters to be rejected" means in those matters that must be rejected through the cultivation of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), namely, the matters that are to be abandoned.
The list beginning with the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice (*paṃsukūlikaṅga*) and ending with the sitter’s practice (*nesajjikaṅga*) is shown by way of abbreviation (*peyyāla*).

Whatever needs to be said regarding this has all been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. By the very mention of the "Teacher of Ascetic Practices," the Elder’s state of being an ascetic (*dhuta*) is also implied.
"He has been taken" refers specifically to those "who speak of the ascetic practices.
He is "great" either because of the greatness of his initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*) and so forth, and because of his great service to the Dispensation;
or else this is merely a term of praise for the Elder due to the greatness of his virtues, as in the case of "Mahākassapa," just like "Mahāmoggallāna."

Because he had developed faith through the three instances [of the Teacher’s deeds] during the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma and was established in the status of a lay follower (upāsaka), it is said:
“Having resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha,” and so forth. This should be construed with the phrase “of this preeminence.
“Saccakāra” means an act that brings about the state of truth; or, in the sense of non-deception, it means the accomplishment of that purpose. “Kolāhala” means the spreading out of curiosity.
The Teacher, preaching the Dhamma every seventh year and observing the time most suitable for beings to hear it, taught by day during the evening hours and throughout the entire night.
Therefore he said: “The brahmin said to the brahmin:
‘Sir, will you listen to the Dhamma by night or by day? *Vissāsiko* means the state of being trustworthy. From that...
Or there is the reading “paṭṭhāya so.
Regarding the phrase “having fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable eons,” this was said by him after grasping a meaning that had come down through oral tradition.
“Of ungiven fruition” means of fruition that has not yet ripened. “In a fortunate time” means at a suitable time. “A constellation” means...

A festival marked by a lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*). For those festivals which are to be enjoyed under specific lunar mansions are called "lunar-mansion festivals" (*nakkhattāni*), while others are simply called "festivals" (*chaṇāni*).

It is "leading to liberation" (*niyyānika*) because, by liberating one from suffering that has fallen upon one correctly, it brings about deliverance and causes the attainment of the desired goal. "Of them" refers to those golden lotuses. "Hanging down" means variegated with gold and jewels.
*Ratnadāmā* means "a string of jewels. *Puññaniyāmena* means by the fixed order established through the power of merit.
He had been granted permission to bestow the sovereignty of Bārāṇasī upon him. *Phussaratha* refers to an auspicious chariot.

They say that the white parasol, the turban, the yak-tail fan, the sword, the jewel, and the sandals constitute the fivefold regalia of royalty; however, in this context, the white parasol is mentioned separately.
They say that the lion-throne is the fifth. "The edge of the upper robe" (*pārupanakaṇṇa*) refers to the hem of the cloth used for covering.
Urged by the power of the merit of those who gave divine garments, he said, "Is it not thick, father? "Oh, what an ascetic! means "Oh, what a wretched king I am.

"Having faith in the Buddhas" means having faith in the teaching (*sāsana*) of the Buddhas. "Hundreds of walking-places" (*caṅkamanasatāni*): here the word *iti* has the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*). By this, [it includes] fire-halls and other such structures.
She gathered together places suitable for those who have gone forth.
"Well-played" refers to the honor that should be rendered at the place where the Noble Ones have attained final Nibbāna. "She did not neglect [her duties];
the noble lady is free from illness" shows the manner in which she was questioned. "The goddess has attained final Nibbāna" was the reply given by the goddess. "Having prepared... [end of fragment].
"Having handed over. "The going forth as a recluse" (*samaṇakapabbajjā*) means the going forth to be practiced by the Noble Ones who have stilled their evil.
For that king, having seen the appearance of the Paccekabuddhas, thought, "This alone is excellent," and thus he took up exactly such a mark.
"Right there" means in the Brahmā-world itself. The connection is made by bringing forward the phrase, "when the twentieth year had arrived. From the Brahmā-world...
Because [the child] was born from a cave and because the undertaking of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) had been established for a long time, he said, "Do not speak such words.
They say that twenty *dharaṇas* constitute a *nikkha*, while others say five *palas* constitute a *nikkha*.
*Itthākara* means the place of origin of the Woman-Jewel (*itthiratana*). *Ayyadhītā* means our noble master’s daughter; *Bhaddakāpilānī*—
The meaning is as follows: *Samānapaṇṇaṃ* means a similar letter, a correspondence suitable for the prince and the princess.

Those men, departing from the place where they had met toward Mahātittha village in the kingdom of Magadha and Sāgalanagara in the kingdom of Madda, were said to be "sending each other off" (*aññamaññaṃ vissajjantā*) because they were told, "Send [them] this way and that way."
"A garland of flowers" (*pupphadāma*) refers to a flower garland measuring the length of an elephant's trunk. "Those two" refers to those two flower garlands woven together by both of them.
"Both of them" refers to Bhaddā and the youth Pippali. "By worldly bait" (*lokāmisa*) means by the gratification of sensual desire.
"Unassociated" (*asaṃsaṭṭhā*) means not conjoined; they were like a lamp burning inside a jar, for their seed of liberation was blazing within their own disposition.
Because his mind was stirred up. "Fastened with machines" means buckets for drawing water that have been bound here and there by means of attaching door-panels for the purpose of producing crops.
"Workplace" means a place for performing agricultural labor. "Villages of slaves" means villages where slaves reside.
"Having let out" means having poured in. "By way of gesture and movement" means by way of appearance and by way of action.
“*Ananucchavikaṃ*” means unsuitable for the state of one who has gone forth. “*Tassa matthake*” means at the point where the path bifurcates.
The connection is: “It was fitting to gather them [there], so he sat down.

To show that the Teacher’s sitting there was of such a nature, it is said: “But as he sat down,” and so forth. Therein, that which was produced by the accumulation of the stores of merit—immeasurable in time, inconceivable, and beyond full comprehension—belonging to the Buddhas...

The splendor of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), illuminated by the radiance of the Buddha’s qualities, blazing with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, adorned with a halo of fathom-wide light and a garland of rays, is inherently perfect and beyond description;
yet, in order to increase Mahākassapa’s faith—which he had not previously seen—the Blessed One sat without concealing it, having assumed the appearance of a Buddha... [and so forth].
When it was said, "He sat down," [the area] was said to be eighty cubits because it extended over a space of eighty cubits due to its occurrence.
"With a hundred branches" means having many branches, numerous branches. It was indeed golden-colored because it was completely covered on all sides by the rays of the Buddha.
"In three places" means in three locations: from afar, not too far, and nearby. "With three exhortations" means: "Therefore, then, for you..."
“Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: ‘A keen sense of shame and moral dread shall be established in me toward elders, juniors, and those of middle standing.
In this way, Kassapa, you should train yourself. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus:
‘Whatever teaching I hear that is connected with the wholesome, I will take it all to heart.’”
‘Having taken it to heart and having applied my whole mind, I will listen to the Dhamma with an attentive ear’—in this way, Kassapa, you should train yourself.
Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus:
‘May mindfulness directed to the body, accompanied by pleasure, not be abandoned by me’—in this way, Kassapa, you should train yourself. With these three [instructions].
"Give him exhortation. For here, the Blessed One first gave exhortation to the elder for the sake of abandoning pride regarding his birth, since he was of brahmin lineage;

secondly, for the sake of abandoning the conceit that arises based on great learning; and thirdly, for the sake of abandoning self-attachment that arises based on the excellence of his physical requisites.
"Gentle indeed is this [speech] of yours" means: "Gentle indeed is this [instruction] of yours."
But why did the Blessed One speak thus? Because he desired to exchange robes with the Elder.
Why did he become desirous of exchanging them? Because he wished to establish the Elder in his own place. [The Buddha asked: "Are Sāriputta and Moggallāna not there?
[The answer was: "They are. However, this thought occurred to him: "These two will remain for a long time; but Kassapa has a lifespan of two hundred years, and he—[in my absence]..."

"Thinking, 'After the Parinibbāna, having resided in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave and performed the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, he will ensure that my teaching remains in operation for a period of five thousand years,' he established him in his own position.
Thus, the monks will think that they must listen to Kassapa. That is why he spoke thus.
"Like the moon" means being similar to the moon. Not merely by way of roundness; rather, it is because just as the moon [illuminates] the vault of the sky...
Entering [the assembly], he forms no intimacy, affection, or attachment with anyone; yet he is not unloved or displeasing to the multitude.

Thus, by refraining from forming intimacies with anyone, he becomes beloved and pleasing to many people, like the moon, as he approaches the four classes of society, beginning with the kṣatriya families.
The meaning [of the phrase] is as follows: "Drawing back the body and drawing back the mind" means that by not engaging in intimacy with them, one draws away and removes both body and mind;
this is the meaning. "Always new" (*niccaṃ nava*) means always like a newcomer; the sense is that he should act like a guest.
For a guest, having entered a house reached in due order, if the master of the house...
Seeing them, she thinks with compassion, "Our own sons and brothers have gone away from home and wandered about in this way," so she has them sit down and feeds them.
As soon as they have finished eating, she says, "Take your bowls," and rising up, she departs;
she neither forms an intimacy with them nor arranges for their business or duties. In this same manner, she proceeds in succession.

It explains that having entered a house where he has been invited, he takes whatever people give him out of confidence in his deportment, and then departs, having severed his social ties with them and no longer being occupied with their business and duties.
"Appagabbho" means not impudent; [this refers to] bodily impudence in eight ways and verbal impudence in four ways.
The meaning is that he is devoid of immodesty of mind in its many forms. Immodesty of body (*kāyapāgabbhiya*) consists of eight points:
acting in an unbecoming manner with the body when entering among the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, a dining hall, a sauna, a bathing place, on the path for alms-round, or into a private house.
Immodesty of speech (*vacīpāgabbhiya*) consists of four points: [acting in an unbecoming manner] among the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, or in a private house.

The utterance of improper speech. "Mental impudence in various matters" means that even without committing transgressions through body or speech in those various instances, one mentally entertains thoughts of sensual desire and so forth.

The meaning is that he approaches families having become free from impudence (*appagabbha*) by the absence of all these forms of impudence. And [this is illustrated] by the Elder Candūpamappaṭipada in the *Kassapa-saṃyutta*.
Because he realized the state of preeminence among those who advocate the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), it is said: "Taking precisely this Kassapasamyutta as the occasion for the discourse.
192. The Story of the Elder Anuruddha.
In the fifth [section], "merely the elaboration regarding food" refers to the perception of partaking in food while wandering for alms in the village of one's resort.
"Merely for the sake of food. "Of lamp-trees" means of large lamp-trees made of iron or tooth-stick wood;

for even though those lamp-stands are made of iron, the conventional term "lamp-tree" should be understood as applied to them. "Other lamps" refers to hanging lamps, circular lamps, moving lamps, and so forth.
"He went around" means by way of circumambulating to the right. "I [invite] with that which you need": I invite you with that which is required by you.
Therefore, there is a purpose in having him fetch it and take it. His meal appeared in the golden bowl itself;
it arose through the power of the deities, and there was no need for any cooking.
He reflected upon the seven thoughts of a Great Man (*mahāpurisavitakka*), beginning with: "This Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of great desire. Regarding the eighth:
“This Dhamma is for one who delights in the unproliferated (nippapañca), not for one who delights in proliferation (papañca)” — regarding this thought of a man.

“Knowing my intention” means: knowing my intention which, by way of the thoughts of a Great Man (mahāpurisa) such as “This Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of great desires,” remained unable to reach its ultimate conclusion merely because it had been undertaken. “By the mind-made (manomaya)”... [text fragment] ...means: by means of a form produced by the mind.

“By mind-made” means by a mind fashioned as if it were [the body] itself; the sense is “by transformation. “By psychic power” (iddhiyā) means by the psychic power of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi) that proceeds thus: “Let this body become like this mind.
“When my intention arose” (yadā me ahu saṅkappo) refers to the time when [I thought], “What indeed is the eighth Great Person’s reflection? (mahāpurisa-vitakka).

The construction is as follows: "When a reflection arose in me, and when a thought occurred to me, then, having understood my thought through his psychic power (*iddhi*), he approached and taught what was further.

Regarding "he taught what was further": fulfilling this eighth thought of a Great Man (*mahāpurisavitakka*)—namely, "This Dhamma is for one who delights in the unproliferated (*nippapañca*), for one who finds pleasure in the unproliferated; this Dhamma is not for one who delights in proliferation (*papañca*), for one who finds pleasure in proliferation"—he taught it.
He taught above [the world]. Showing that which was thus taught, he said: “The Buddha, delighting in the unproliferated (nippapañca), taught the unproliferated.

Proliferation (papañca) refers to the defilements such as lust and so forth; because they are pacified and because of the absence of those [defilements], supramundane states are called “unproliferated.
He taught the Dhamma in such a way that one might reach that state; the meaning is that he taught the exalted teaching of the Four Noble Truths.
"Having understood his Dhamma" means having known the Dhamma taught by that Teacher. "I dwelt" means I lived practicing according to the instructions.
"Delighting in the teaching" means being devoted to the teaching comprised of the three trainings.
"Attained the three knowledges" refers to these three knowledges: the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
"By me attained and realized. Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished; the meaning is that the instruction and exhortation have been carried out.
(The Story of the Elder Bhaddiya, 193).
Regarding the sixth [verse], since the word *ucca* has the same meaning as *uccā*, he said: "Of those from high families" (*uccākulikānaṃ*) means "in high families" (*ucce kule*).
“Of those who were born. As for “that queen Kālī,” she was called Kālī because of her dark complexion.

Regarding the statement, “And he alone,” etc., it is said that the attainment of sovereignty follows the succession of one’s own family, and thus belongs only to one of great lineage. This is the story of the Elder Lakura-Bhaddiya.
194. "Empty" (*rittako*) means devoid of a gift to be given. "Having adverted to his qualities" means:

having adverted to the qualities such as the Blessed One’s physical beauty, his perfection of deportment, and so forth—having understood his own intention [regarding] the acceptance and consumption of the mango fruit, and other such qualities as they presented themselves.
The Story of the Elder Piṇḍolabhāradvāja 195.

In the eighth [verse], "lion's roar" (*sīhanāda*) refers to a roar like that of a lion due to its fearless nature; those who possess this are "those who roar like lions" (*sīhanādikā*), and it is of them that it is said.
Censure occurs only for one who knows, as they truly are, the qualities that are to be censured and those that are to be praised.

And because praise is appropriate [in this context], he said: “The Buddhas indeed,” and so forth. By the words “Birth is destroyed,” etc., he shows the ground of the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*).
For by means of that knowledge, the noble disciple, while reviewing, understands: “Birth is destroyed,” and so forth.
But which birth of his is destroyed, and how does he understand it? First of all, past birth is not destroyed for him, because it was already destroyed previously.
It is not future [birth], because there is an absence of effort regarding the future; nor is it present, because it already exists.

However, that birth—which is distinguished by one, four, or five aggregates within the one, four, or five-aggregate existences (bhava) and which would otherwise arise due to the non-cultivation of the Path—has been exhausted through the attainment of the state of non-arising by virtue of the cultivation of the Path.
He [the noble one] [regards] that [birth] as having its defilements abandoned by the cultivation of the Path...
Having reflected, one knows and understands: "In the absence of defilements, even existing karma will not lead to rebirth in the future.

"Lived" (*vusita*) means dwelt, fully dwelt; the meaning is that it has been performed, practiced, and brought to completion. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*).

For, together with the virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), the seven types of trainees (*sekkha*) are said to be living the holy life of the Path, while the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*)...
The dwelling has been completed. Therefore, when a noble disciple reviews his own life of purity (*brahmacariya*), he understands: "The life of purity has been lived.

"What was to be done has been done" means that the sixteenfold task—by way of the clear comprehension, abandoning, realization, and development regarding the four truths through the four paths—has been brought to its conclusion.
For it is the virtuous worldlings (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*) and others who perform that task.
One whose taints are destroyed has done what was to be done. Therefore, when a noble disciple reviews his own task, he understands:

"What was to be done has been done. He understands: "There is nothing further to be done for this state," meaning that there is no further task for him regarding this sixteenfold state of function, or regarding the destruction of the defilements through the cultivation of the path. Alternatively, "itthattāya" means...
He understands: "In this state, from this very continuity of the present aggregates of such a kind, there is no further continuity of aggregates for me;
these five aggregates, however, remain with their roots cut, like trees whose bases have been severed, and they will go out like a fire without fuel through the cessation of final consciousness."
Regarding the story of the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta (196):
because he had attained mastery in all eighteen branches of learning, it is said that "he became skilled in all arts.
Since the Dhamma that brings about higher knowledge and direct realization is found therein, it says "without seeing the Dhamma of liberation."
Thus it was said. Therefore he said: “This is what is called the triad of knowledges,” and so forth.

For by this [knowledge], even liberation from an unhappy rebirth is difficult to attain; and because he is one who has obtained the eight meditative attainments accompanied by direct knowledge, he honors the Blessed One—who is himself partially pacified, who has reached the ultimate pinnacle, who possesses the supreme taming and tranquility, and who is not shared by others.
He said, “This man,” and so forth. “Coming with baskets” means coming with fruit containers, that is, coming unaccompanied by a master.
The plural number used for “of the Buddhas” is employed out of reverence.
“He consumed” means he consumed forest roots and fruits containing divine nutritive essence (ojā) placed there by deities. Immediately upon being set down in the bowl...
For the deities there had added divine essence to it. "Having comprehended" means having reflected upon it;

they also say it means having turned it over in the mind. "They attained arahantship" means that, with the continuum of their minds thoroughly purified by the sequential discourse on the words of thanksgiving for the Elder Mahādeva, they attained arahantship.
"By means of the ten topics of discourse" refers to these ten topics of discourse:

the discourse on fewness of desires, the discourse on contentment, the discourse on seclusion, the discourse on non-association, the discourse on the arousal of energy, the discourse on the perfection of virtue, the discourse on the perfection of concentration, the discourse on the perfection of wisdom, the discourse on the perfection of liberation, and the discourse on the perfection of the knowledge and vision of liberation. "Those who dwell in the country of his birth" means...
“Those dwelling in the same country and region as the Teacher” means those who dwell in the same country and region where the Teacher was born.
“Looking at the head” means looking repeatedly at the head of one who is walking ahead. “Having observed the opportunity” means having observed the occasion for discussion.
He asked about the sequence of the seven purifications by saying, “Friend, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One for the sake of purification of virtue? and so forth.

He asked about the seven purifications. He placed him in the foremost position among those who preach the Dhamma, specifically because of his attainment of the ten bases of discourse (*dasakathāvatthu*).
[This concludes] the story of the Elder Mahākaccāyana (197).
Regarding the phrase "of the Dhamma briefly spoken in the tenth": it refers to the teaching in brief, as in the *Madhupiṇḍika-sutta*.
"Of the Dhamma taught": having expanded that brief teaching by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*) and so forth.
"Expounding the meaning": for those who speak after having analyzed the meaning of that brief teaching. "Or by way of the meaning":
they are able to fulfill the teaching by way of the meaning, [thinking] "this many are its meanings. Or by way of the phrasing (*byañjana*).
Others are able to fulfill [the teaching] according to the phrasing, thinking, "So many syllables must be spoken here by way of the teaching.
However, this Elder Mahākaccāna is able to do so even by way of both;
because he teaches in detail, in accordance with the Teacher’s intention, that which was briefly indicated by him, he is therefore called the foremost therein. "In the manner already stated" means...
“Having eaten a good meal early in the morning and having resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha,” and so forth, according to the method explained below.
“By others” means that her hair is much longer than that of other women. And it is not only long;
moreover, it is glossy, dark blue, and soft. “Nikkesī” means having little hair, just as in the expression “a girl with no hips.”
"Merchandise" refers to goods that ought to be sold. "Having reflected" means having reflected upon the supporting conditions and the attainment of the natural state of the hair.
"With respect" means that even those with shaven heads came with a single voice out of respect for the elders.
"Having invited" means having invited them for the following day. "Of this woman" refers to the daughter of the aforementioned merchant. "Pertaining to the present life" (diṭṭhadhammika) means...

The restriction is applied to the impossibility [of other results]; the meaning is that there was only the attainment of fame pertaining to this present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*). "Attainment of fame" means the attainment of success in existence (*bhavasampatti*).

For among the seven impulsive volitions (*javanacetanā*), the first has its fruit to be experienced in the present life, the last has its fruit to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), and the five in between have their fruits to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariyavedanīya*); therefore, the first...
With the exception of one volition, the remaining ones yield their respective full fruits;
however, from the first volition, there was only the attainment of fame in this very life.
The commentary on the first group of foremost disciples is concluded.

14. Etadaggavagga (14) 2. Commentary on the Second Etadaggavagga: The Story of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka The Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, this is the foremost among my disciples who are slow-witted yet have become wise. At that time, the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him. Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka: "Cūḷapanthaka, you too are foremost among my disciples who are slow-witted yet have become wise. When the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka heard this, he thought: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! The Teacher himself has declared me to be foremost among his disciples who are slow-witted yet have become wise. Having thought thus, he attained a state of rapture and joy born of that thought. Then, as he was walking back and forth and sitting, he developed concentration through the practice of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasati*). With the mind concentrated, he attained the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) right then and there. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was seated not far from the Blessed One. He considered the minds of the five hundred bhikkhunīs who were living with the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, and he saw that they had fallen into a state of negligence. Seeing this, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, sat down to one side, and said: "Venerable sir, the minds of the five hundred bhikkhunīs living with the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka have fallen into negligence. May the Blessed One please exhort them. The Blessed One consented by silence. Then the Blessed One rose from his seat and went to the place where the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka was staying. The Venerable Cūḷapanthaka saw the Blessed One coming from afar and prepared a seat. He took water for washing the feet and a footstool, and he arranged a lamp. When the Blessed One had arrived, he paid homage to him and sat down to one side. The Blessed One washed his feet; the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka poured the water. After the Blessed One had washed his feet, he sat down on the prepared seat. The Venerable Cūḷapanthaka also washed his feet and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka: "Cūḷapanthaka, go to the nuns' quarters and exhort the bhikkhunīs. "Venerable sir, those bhikkhunīs are difficult to deal with and prone to anger. They might strike me with their fists, or with stones, or with sticks, or even with weapons. "Cūḷapanthaka, do not worry; go and exhort the bhikkhunīs. "Very well, venerable sir," the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. The Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, thinking, "I am not fit to exhort these bhikkhunīs face to face," went to the dwelling of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana and said to him: "Venerable sir, I am not fit to exhort these bhikkhunīs face to face. Please exhort them yourself. "Cūḷapanthaka, what is the reason for this? "Venerable sir, those bhikkhunīs are difficult to deal with and prone to anger. They might strike me with their fists, or with stones, or with sticks, or even with weapons. "Cūḷapanthaka, do not worry; go and exhort the bhikkhunīs. "Very well, venerable sir," the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka replied to the Venerable Mahākaccāyana. Then the Venerable Mahākaccāyana dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having finished his almsround in Sāvatthī, he returned, ate his meal, and approached the Blessed One. He paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side, and said: "Venerable sir, I shall go to the nuns' quarters and exhort the bhikkhunīs. "Kaccāyana, go and exhort the bhikkhunīs according to the Dhamma. "Very well, venerable sir," the Venerable Mahākaccāyana replied to the Blessed One. He rose from his seat, took his bowl and robe, and went to the nuns' quarters. He exchanged greetings with the bhikkhunīs and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana exhorted the bhikkhunīs with a discourse on the Dhamma. When the Venerable Mahākaccāyana had finished exhorting the bhikkhunīs with a discourse on the Dhamma, he rose from his seat and departed. The bhikkhunīs followed after the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, saying: "Wait, Venerable sir, until we have finished our chores. But the Venerable Mahākaccāyana did not wait. Then the bhikkhunīs thought: "We have been exhorted by the Venerable Mahākaccāyana with a discourse on the Dhamma, yet he did not wait for us. Who else can exhort us? Then the bhikkhunīs approached the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka and said: "Venerable sir, we have been exhorted by the Venerable Mahākaccāyana with a discourse on the Dhamma, yet he did not wait for us. Please exhort us. "Sisters, I am not fit to exhort you face to face. The Blessed One himself will exhort you. "Venerable sir, we have been exhorted by the Venerable Mahākaccāyana with a discourse on the Dhamma, yet he did not wait for us. Who else can exhort us? Venerable sir, please exhort us. "Sisters, if you say, 'Venerable sir, we are your daughters,' then I shall exhort you.

"Venerable sir, we are your daughters; please exhort us. "Very well, sisters," the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka replied to the bhikkhunīs. Then the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: "Venerable sir, I have exhorted the bhikkhunīs. "Cūḷapanthaka, how did you exhort the bhikkhunīs? [He then related the entire conversation. "Cūḷapanthaka, you have exhorted the bhikkhunīs well. Cūḷapanthaka, if you had exhorted the bhikkhunīs with this very discourse, they would have attained the destruction of the taints right then and there. However, because they were negligent, they did not attain the destruction of the taints. Nevertheless, Cūḷapanthaka, you have exhorted the bhikkhunīs well. Then the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, he departed. The Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, this is the foremost among my disciples who are slow-witted yet have become wise. When the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka heard this, he thought: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! The Teacher himself has declared me to be foremost among his disciples who are slow-witted yet have become wise. Having thought thus, he attained a state of rapture and joy born of that thought. Then, as he was walking back and forth and sitting, he developed concentration through the practice of mindfulness of breathing. With the mind concentrated, he attained the destruction of the taints right then and there. When the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka had attained the destruction of the taints, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: "Venerable sir, I am one who has attained the destruction of the taints. "Cūḷapanthaka, you are one who has attained the destruction of the taints. Then the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, he departed. The Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, this is the foremost among my disciples who are slow-witted yet have become wise. When the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka heard this, he thought: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! The Teacher himself has declared me to be foremost among his disciples who are slow-witted yet have become wise. Having thought thus, he attained a state of rapture and joy born of that thought. Then, as he was
198–200. Regarding the second [section], "produced by mind in the first": this means generated by the mind of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-manas*).
"A body made by mind" refers to a body that has reached another location by means of the mind of direct knowledge.

"A body produced by mind" refers to a body fashioned by the mind of direct knowledge, as in such passages as "he creates another body. "Exactly similar" means exactly like oneself. "Of only one kind" means...
[He created] exactly the kind of form he himself had made. For this is generally the limit of the method for disciples regarding the manifestation of psychic power (*iddhi-nimmāna*).
He is called "foremost" because he partially conformed to the Teacher’s manifestation of psychic power.
Regarding the term "possessor" (*lābhin*): here, the vowel *ī* in *lābhī* has the sense of excellence. By that, [it is shown] that the Elder possessed the four fine-material-sphere jhānas.
This shows that he has attained it with excellence and distinction. The same principle applies here as well regarding "the attainment of the immaterial-sphere jhānas.

To show that this skill in the turning away from perception of mind is not due solely to the attainment of the fine-material and immaterial jhānas, but rather through these other causes as well, it is said:
"And Cūḷapanthaka," and so forth. And here, "mind" (*ceto*) refers by way of the head-term for "consciousness" (*citta*).
Concentration has been explained; therefore, the turning away of the mind from concentration is the "turning away of the mind" (*cetovivaṭṭa*).

One who attains fine-material-sphere jhāna is called "skilled in the turning away of the mind" because, having turned the concentrated mind away from a single object, they cause each successive lower state to fall away in favor of the one immediately above it.

This refers to one who, having transcended the perceptions described in the passage beginning with "entirely surmounting perceptions of form," dwells in the attainment of the base of infinite space... [and so on].

One who is skilled in the turning away from perception is one who is skilled in the jhānas described under the heading of "perception" as "accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception";

likewise, one who is skilled in the turning away from perception is one who, having turned the mind away from perceptions of woman, man, and so forth, as well as from the perception of permanence and the like,

is preeminently devoted to the contemplation of voidness regarding the mere conditioned phenomena of form and formlessness, as well as the unconditioned Nibbāna, and in terms of turning away from the round of existence.

Through skill in concentration (*samādhi-kusalatā*), there is skill in the turning away of the mind (*ceto-vivaṭṭa-kusalatā*) by virtue of dwelling frequently therein. Likewise, through skill in insight (*vipassanā-kusalatā*), there is skill in the turning away of perception (*saññā-vivaṭṭa-kusalatā*).

"One" refers to the Elder Cūḷapanthaka. Regarding the "characteristic of concentration" (*samādhi-lakkhaṇa*), this refers to the essential nature (*sabhāva*) of concentration such as that accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*).

Again, "one" refers to the Elder Mahāpanthaka. Regarding the "characteristic of insight" (*vipassanā-lakkhaṇa*), this refers to the essential nature of insight such as the seven contemplations (*anupassanā*) and the eighteen great insights (*mahā-vipassanā*).
*Samādhigāḷho*: having plunged into concentration, with a mind that has immersed itself in concentration due to the well-cultivated state of meditation.

*Aṅgasaṃkhitte*: in the contraction of the factors of jhāna by way of the fourfold, fivefold, and so forth. *Ārammaṇasaṃkhitte*: in the contraction of the objects of focus such as the kasiṇas, by means of producing space through the removal of the kasiṇa, etc.
*Aṅgavavatthāpane*: in the defining of the jhāna factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*), etc. *Ārammaṇavavatthāpane*: in the defining of the objects of focus.
In the discernment of the objects of jhāna such as the earth-kasiṇa and others.

"By means of jhāna-factors" means by means of the fine-material-sphere jhāna-factors; the jhāna-factors themselves are the jhāna. Again, "by means of jhāna-factors" refers to the immaterial-sphere jhāna-factors.
"Brother" means the elder brother. "His" refers to the householder. "A golden offering" means an offering of flowers made of gold.
Having done so. "In the city of the gods" means in the great city of Sudassana within the realm of the Thirty-three.
"By the main gate" means having gone out on that day through the principal gate, which was opened first of all.
"Kokanada" is a specific type of lotus, just as one says "kokāsaka. It is said that it has many petals and is endowed with exquisite color.
And it is exceedingly fragrant. Some say that "kokanada" refers to the white lotus. "In the morning" means early indeed.

This is the meaning here: just as the lotus known as the *kokanada* would be in full bloom, opened wide, its fragrance not yet dissipated, and shining at the time of sunrise in the morning, so too [the Buddha] was fragrant with the scent of his body and the scent of his virtues during the autumn season.
One sees the Perfectly Enlightened One, Aṅgīrasa, blazing with his own splendor like the sun in the sky, emitting radiance from his limbs.
It is said that Cūḷapanthaka, having gone forth during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, was wise; [and] of a certain...
At the time of receiving the recitation (*uddesa*), he mocked and joked with a certain slow-witted monk.
That monk, being ashamed because of that mockery, neither received the recitation nor practiced its recitation (*sajjhāya*). Due to that karma, this [monk] became slow-witted even after going forth;
therefore, as he attempts to grasp each successive word, what he has already grasped is lost. Having prepared it through supernormal power (*iddhi*),...
Seeing his past cause—namely, that he had given a pure piece of cloth—he assigned him a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) corresponding to that deed, saying, "He gave a pure piece of cloth.
It is said that in the past, when he was a king, while performing a circumambulation of the city, sweat broke out from his forehead;
he wiped his forehead with a perfectly clean garment, and the garment became soiled. He [thought], "This..."
“Depending on this body, such a pure cloth, having abandoned its natural state, has become soiled;
impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena!”—thus he acquired the perception of impermanence. For that reason, the dust-remover itself became his requisite.
By “hairs” he means the fine threads of the cloth-pieces. “With soiled elements” means having a soiled nature.
