“Having such a destination” means that this mind is naturally bright and pure by way of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), but has become defiled through association with states such as lust.
“Having brought together the constellations” means having directed the mind toward them, having adverted to them;
this is the meaning. “For the sake of the cat” means for the sake of the cat’s range of activity. “By one who works on the water-way” means by one who works on the ocean.
They graze upon grass that is fit to be eaten. "Saccakāra" means an act that brings about truthfulness;
it is said to be a pledge to be given after stating, "The goods taken by oneself must not be given to others. "By the third reply" means by the third instruction.
"Having become owners" means having become masters.

"Even by a little" means even by a small amount or a trifling amount. "The wise one" means one possessed of wisdom (*paññā*). "By his capital" means by the cost-price of his merchandise. "Discerning" means skilled in trade.
"He raises himself up" means that by generating great wealth and fame, he establishes and settles himself therein. How so? Like a tiny spark when it is fanned; just as—
Just as a wise man gradually throws cow-dung powder and other materials into a small fire,
fanning it with his breath, causes it to arise, increases it, and makes it into a great mass of flame; even so, a wise man,
having obtained even a small amount of wealth, employs various means to increase both his riches and his fame, and having increased them, once again—
Therein, he establishes himself. Or rather, by means of that very greatness of wealth, he elevates himself;
the meaning is that he makes himself well-known and famous.
The story of the Elder Subhūti.
201–202. In the third [explanation], it is said that "afflictions" (raṇa) refers to the defilements such as lust;
thus, in passages such as "states with affliction" (saraṇā dhammā), the defilements like lust are called "afflictions. They are called "afflictions" because beings are afflicted by them.
Overcome by these, beings cry out and lament in various ways; therefore, those [defilements] such as lust are termed "afflictions. "Without deviating from the prescribed order" means...
"Teaching without departing from the manner taught" means that he teaches the Dhamma by making it non-specific, following exactly the method taught by the Teacher.
"Thus, when emerging from the jhāna of loving-kindness, if there is the taking of alms,
it will be of great fruit for those who give the alms"— this is to be illustrated by the Cūḷaccharāsaṅghāta Sutta.
For when a bhikkhu cultivates a mind of loving-kindness for even as long as the snap of a finger, the gift given to him becomes of great fruit and great benefit;
and by that means, he consumes the alms of the kingdom not in vain—this meaning is already established therein.
"Having grasped the sign" means having observed the characteristic form.
The Story of the Elder Revata of the Khadiravana Forest (203).
In the fifth [verse], "a forest that is congenial" (*sabhāga-vana*) means a forest that is suitable; "congenial" (*sabhāga*) has the sense of being appropriate.
For that which is not naturally opposed and not opposed by disease is called "congenial. This also applies to expressions such as "water that is congenial" (*udaka-sabhāga*), and so forth.
The meaning should be understood by this same method. "The moment of accumulating wholesome karma" refers to the opportunity for the amassing of wholesome karma.
"Of the three brothers" refers to these three elder brothers: Upatissa, Cunda, and Upasena.
"And of the three sisters" refers to these three elder sisters: Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā.
And here, after the Elder Sāriputta himself had gone forth, he ordained the three sisters—Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā—as well as his brothers Cunda and Upasena;
thus, only the young man Revata remained at home. Therefore it was said: “They are ordaining us...,” and so forth.
“The older ones” means those who are more advanced in age. And this refers to the long life of the girl.
Desiring [to do so], they said. It is said that his grandmother was two hundred years old, with broken teeth, grey hair, wrinkled skin, limbs covered in moles, and a body bent like a rafter.

"Running about" (*vidhāvanikā*) refers to the game of running about. By the phrase "the three attainments," he speaks with reference to human, divine, and liberation-attainments based on oral tradition; [alternatively,] human, divine, and Brahma-attainments.

Or rather: "We shall examine the merit of Sīvali. Having understood, "This is the place where the ripening of the merit performed by Sīvali is bestowed," he spoke thus. "A level spot" means an even place.
Regarding "that ground is delightful": although Arahants do not obtain physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) in a village, they do obtain mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*).
But they certainly do obtain them. For even objects resembling those of the divine realms cannot disturb their minds;
therefore, whether it be a village or any other place such as a forest, "wherever Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful"—the meaning is that such a region of earth is indeed beautiful.
The Story of the Elder Kaṅkhārevata (204).
Regarding the sixth [point]: "Friends, sugar is not allowable. One day, while on his way, the elder entered a sugar-refining factory;
seeing that flour and ashes had been added to the sugar, he thought, "Sugar is not allowable; sugar mixed with meat-products is not permitted."
He spoke thus because he was apprehensive, thinking, "I might eat at an improper time.
Regarding "beans are unallowable," one day, seeing beans growing by the roadside on his way, he became apprehensive, thinking, "Beans are unallowable;
even when cooked, beans grow [from seeds]," and so he spoke thus. Everything else here is self-evident.
The Story of the Elder Soṇakoḷivisa 205.
In the seventh [case], there was indeed a failure due to over-exertion of energy (*accāraddhavīriyatā*).
"Heaped up with water" means having raised the dry land with water and piled it up here and there. "Smeared with green" means having been plastered with cow dung.
“They nourish with three kinds of water” means they nourish and sustain with these three kinds of water: milk-water, scented water, and pure water.
“Having strained” should be construed as “having taken rice grains that have been thoroughly cleansed.
“I think it is like a god” means it is like a god. “By way of the simile of the lute”: “What do you think, Soṇa, when the strings of your lute are too tight?”
“Would that lute, at that time, be resonant or serviceable? “Certainly not, venerable sir.
“In the same way, Soṇa, over-exerted energy leads to restlessness, and overly slackened energy leads to laziness.
Therefore, Soṇa, you should resolve upon evenness of energy and evenness of the faculties.”
"Penetrate [this]"—thus, by means of the "Discourse on the Simile of the Lute," which was delivered using the lute as a simile.
"For the purpose of joining energy with serenity" means for the purpose of joining energy with serenity.
The story of the Elder Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa.
206. Regarding the eighth [verse], it is said: "He is called Kuṭikaṇṇa. Although he should be called "Koṭikaṇṇa" (Point-Ear), he is conventionally designated as "Kuṭikaṇṇa" (Hut-Ear).
"Kulagharikā" means one who belongs to a noble family. She, it is said, was the wife of a very wealthy merchant in a prominent family in the kingdom of Avantī.
Having heard the Dhamma discourse of the One Possessed of Ten Powers and having established herself in the fruit of stream-entry, she reflected—this is [the context].
This is stated according to the opinion of the Aṅguttara reciters. However, in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, it says:
“The Blessed One approached with his retinue and heard the teaching of the Dhamma, yet he did not attain any distinction. Why was that?
For while listening to the Dhamma, he recalled Hemavata and, looking around in all directions, wondered, ‘Has my companion arrived or not?’”
"Not seeing him, [Sāriputta] became distracted in mind, thinking: 'My companion has been deceived, he who does not hear such a teaching of the Blessed One, so full of varied eloquence,'" it is said.
For it is only at the moments of rebirth-linking, birth, the Great Departure, the Enlightenment, and the Parinibbāna that these thirty-two portents appear.

Having offered [the sacrifice], they vanish immediately and do not remain for long; however, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, those [trees] become especially magnificent and, having remained for a much longer time, they cease.
Therefore it was said: "Having seen the Himalayas, three thousand yojanas in extent, flowering out of season," and so forth.
"The vanguard of the army" means the troops that march at the very front. By what means did they reach the state of flowering?
"Do you know? means: for what reason do you know the state of the Himalayas being in bloom? It is said: "Do you know the reason why this miracle of untimely blossoming has occurred?
"The fact that it has been set in motion" means the fact that the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion by the Blessed One.
"He took up a sign in the sound" means he perceived the characteristic form within the sound. "From that... [refers to] "I [thought]: 'This...'"
The meaning of the statement, "I have come into your presence because I thought, 'I shall make him know that Dhamma which is the Deathless,'" is that it occurred immediately thereafter.
Having spoken to Hemavata about the appearance of a Buddha, Sātāgira, desiring to bring him into the presence of the Blessed One, recited the verse beginning with "Today is the fifteenth.
In that context, "today" refers to this very day and night, which is the fifteenth according to the counting of the fortnight.

It is called *uposatha* because it is to be observed (*upavasitabba*). Or, among the three types of *uposatha*, today is the fifteenth-day *uposatha*, not the fourteenth-day *uposatha*, nor the *uposatha* for communal harmony.
"Celestial" (*dibba*) means existing in the heavens; they are called celestial because they exist therein.

What are they? They are forms (*rūpa*). For on that night, due to the radiance of the bodies, garments, ornaments, and palaces of the deities who have assembled from ten thousand world-systems, [the place] is illuminated.

Just as the entire Jambudīpa was adorned by the moonlight free from such defilements as clouds and mist, it was even more exquisitely adorned by the bodily radiance of the Blessed One, the utterly pure deity. Therefore he said: "A divine night has arisen.
Thus, by means of this description of the qualities of the night, he spoke of the appearance of a Buddha, generating confidence in the mind of his companion.

He said: “Come, let us see the Teacher of peerless name, Gotama. In this context, he is called “of peerless name” (*anomanāma*) because his name is derived from qualities that are peerless, stainless, and perfect in every respect.
For instance, according to such methods as “he is a Buddha because he has awakened to the truths, he is a Buddha because he awakens the world,” his name is “Buddha” due to his peerless qualities.
Furthermore, “he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he has destroyed passion (*rāga*), he has destroyed hatred (*dosa*),” and so forth.

By the method beginning with “the Blessed One” (*bhagavā*), the name “Blessed One” is [given] because of his peerless qualities. This same method applies to such passages as “the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, perfected in knowledge and conduct.

He is the Teacher (*satthā*) because he instructs gods and humans in matters pertaining to the present life and so forth, saying, “Abandon this; having undertaken this, proceed. To that Teacher of peerless name. The word *handā* is used in the sense of an exhortation.
*Nipāto* (is a particle). *Passāma* (let us see) is the present plural form used by including himself along with [the others].
*Gotama* refers to the Gotama clan. This is what is meant: "Do not entertain doubt as to whether he is the Teacher or not;
being resolutely determined, come, let us see, O Gotama."
When this was said, Hemavata thought: “This Sātāgira, by speaking of the Teacher as ‘one of no inferior name,’ reveals his omniscience;
and omniscient ones are rare in the world, for the world is afflicted by those who claim omniscience while being like Pūraṇa and others.
But if he is indeed omniscient, he must certainly have attained the characteristic of a Tādin (the Tranquil One). Therefore, thus...”
Thinking, “I shall grasp it,” he asked about the characteristic of suchness (tādilakkhaṇa), saying, “Is the mind...? and so forth. Therein, *kacci* is an interrogative particle.
*Mano* means the mind (*citta*). *Supaṇihito* means well-placed, immovable, and unshakable. *Sabbesu bhūtesu* means among all beings.
*Tādino* refers to one who has attained the characteristic of suchness. Or rather, this is a question [addressed] to you: “That [mind] of yours...”
"Is the Teacher equanimous toward all beings, or not?"—regarding such objects as "the desirable" and "the undesirable.
"Intentions" means thoughts (*vitakka*). "Bringing under control" means having brought them into one's power. This is what is meant:
regarding that Teacher you speak of, has his mind been well-directed toward all beings while he possesses the characteristic of equanimity, or not?
As long as he does not receive the necessary conditions, he appears to be well-directed.

You should consider whether that teacher is impartial toward all beings and creatures, or not; and whether those intentions that might arise through passion and aversion toward desirable or undesirable objects have been brought under his control, or whether he is sometimes still subject to their influence.
"Three years" means three years from the day Soṇa went forth.
At that time, it is said, the bhikkhus mostly resided in the Middle Country; therefore, there were only a few there.
And they lived separately, one or two in a single town. Then, having brought several bhikkhus from elsewhere for the elders...
When those who had been brought forward departed for some business, and after waiting for a time, when they were being brought back again, others departed;
thus, through this repeated bringing and going, the assembly took a long time to form, and at that time the Elder was living alone.
Therefore it is said: "Having sought a group for three years."
“Three years” is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous duration (*accantasaṃyoga*).

“Having understood the Teacher’s intention” means that by his very act of commanding, he understood the Teacher’s intention, thinking, “The Blessed One wishes to dwell in the same fragrant cell with this person.
For it is said that the Blessed One, when wishing to dwell in the same fragrant cell with someone, [would have] the assignment of lodgings made for that person.
He instructs the Elder Ānanda.
"Having spent the time in the open air" means having spent the time by sitting in the open air.

For the Blessed One, while providing a hospitable welcome to the Venerable Soṇa through his attainment of meditative absorptions, [taught] all the absorptions common to disciples in direct and reverse order.
Entering [the meditative attainments], he spent most of the night sitting in the open air; having washed his feet, he entered the monastery.

Therefore, the Venerable Soṇa, understanding the Blessed One’s intention, likewise entered all those attainments accordingly, and having spent most of the night sitting in the open air, he washed his feet and [entered] the monastery.
They say he entered. Having entered, and being permitted by the Blessed One, he made a screen for his robe and spent the time sitting at the side of the Blessed One’s feet.
"Exhort" means he commanded. "May the Dhamma occur to you, monk, to speak" means: may the Dhamma present itself to you, O monk, to be spoken;
may the gateway of knowledge come to you, according as it was heard and according as it was mastered.
The meaning is: "Speak the Dhamma. "The Aṭṭhakavagga" refers to the sixteen suttas beginning with the *Kāmasutta*, which constitute the Aṭṭhakavagga. "Well-mastered" means correctly mastered.

"He requested all the boons" means he requested these five boons: ordination by a group consisting of a quorum of five including a master of the Vinaya, permanent bathing, a skin rug as a spread, sandals for moving from place to place, and being allowed to be separated from one's robes.
"Only as it has come down in the Sutta" refers to the discourse found in the Udāna-pāḷi.
Regarding the story of the Elder Sīvalī (207):
"Having conversed again and again" in the ninth [case] means by way of repeatedly contending with the king.
Having held a discussion. "Hard sugar-curd" (*guḷadadhi*) means hard curd resembling solidified sugar.
"To pull too much" means to draw excessively. "Having drained the whey" means having caused the liquid from the curd to flow out; the meaning is "having strained it. There is also a reading:
"Having taken the whey from the curd. "Her" refers to Suppavāsā. "Causing her to touch the seed-tray" means...
This is the connection. "Until they do not draw it out" means until they are not drawn out toward giving;
the intention is that they simply desire to give. "You experienced great suffering" means you experienced the great suffering caused by childbirth.
"Having addressed her husband" means that for seven days, being obstructed in her womb and afflicted by intense, harsh sensations of pain, she [thought], "The Perfectly Enlightened One..."
“Ah, that Blessed One, who teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of such suffering as this!
Ah, well-practiced is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, who has set out for the abandoning of such suffering as this!
Ah, truly blissful is Nibbāna, wherein such suffering as this is not found!”—with these three thoughts...
Enduring that suffering, because she desired to send [her husband] into the presence of the Teacher, she addressed her husband. "Before death" means precisely prior to death.
"A sign" means a gesture. "Food for life" means food to be given when there is a danger to one's life.
"He became capable of all tasks" means he was able to perform whatever task was to be done by children of seven years of age.

Because of his capability, he was able to perform all the duties. For that very reason, while the great almsgiving was being distributed for seven days, starting from the day of his birth, he took a water-vessel (*dhammakaraṇa*), strained water for the Saṅgha, and gave it to them.
By means of the verse beginning with "Yo mañ" (*Whoever...*), [he showed how] the monk [crosses] this path of passion, this difficult ford of defilements, and this cycle of saṃsāra.
The meaning is: "I call him a brahmin who has transcended the delusion that does not penetrate the Four Truths, who, having crossed the four floods, has reached the further shore;
who meditates with the two kinds of jhāna; who is unshaken due to the absence of craving; who is free from doubt due to the absence of indecision;
who, by the absence of clinging, does not cling, and who is extinguished through the extinction of defilements."

Furthermore, by the statement, "The shaving of all his hair and the realization of Arahatship occurred simultaneously, neither before nor after," it is shown that the Elder attained Arahatship at the very moment of the razor's edge. However, some teachers say this:
"When the General of the Dhamma had given him exhortation according to the method stated above, [the Elder thought], 'I shall know what is possible for me to do.'"
Having gone forth and taken up the meditation subject of insight (vipassanā), on that very day he saw a certain variegated hut;
entering it, he recollected the suffering he himself had experienced within his mother’s womb for seven years.
Following that recollection, as he directed his knowledge toward the past and the future, the three realms of existence appeared to him as if they were ablaze. This was the ripening of his knowledge.

"Having reached [the stage of] *gotrabhū*, he descended into the path of insight (*vipassanā-vīthi*) and, at that very moment, by means of the sequence of the paths (*magga-paṭipāṭi*), exhausting all taints (*āsava*), he attained *arahantship*.
Thus, in both cases, it is shown that *arahantship* arose for the Elder;
moreover, the Elder became one who had mastered the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and possessed the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiñña*).
The Story of the Elder Vakkali (208).

"At the time for taking food" means at the time for the meal. "He would attain the peaceful state" means he would attain Nibbāna, which is called the "peaceful state" because it is the bliss resulting from the subsiding of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*).
By the first line, it is implied that he would have attained it while still standing on the mountain.
By the first foot, he was already standing on Mount Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa). The rest here is easy to understand.
The commentary on the second *Etadagga-vagga* is finished.
14. *Etadagga-vagga*.
(14) 3. Commentary on the Third Division on the Foremost:
The Story of the Elders Rāhula and Raṭṭhapāla, 209–210.

Regarding the first and second [suttas] of the third division, the "Three Trainings" refers to those comprised of higher virtue (*adhisīla*), higher mind (*adhicitta*), and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*).
The three trainings. "Having made fourteen meal-interruptions" means having made fourteen meal-interruptions by means of two meal-interruptions each day for seven days due to being without food.
"Of them" refers to those ascetics. "Having provided the requisites such as gourd vessels" refers to the ascetic requisites such as gourd vessels.
"Having placed together. "The bodily element accompanied by fever" (*sapariḷāha-kāyadhātu*) refers to the nature of the body being accompanied by fever due to an excess of bile.
"A hundred thousand" means measuring one hundred thousand. They have a hundred thousand as their measure, thus they are "hundred-thousanders" (*satasahassā*);

this is formed by the elision of the final member of the compound, just as "existence in the realm of form" (*rūpabhava*) is called "form" (*rūpa*). Alternatively, the suffix *-aka* should be understood in the sense of existence (*atthiattha*), as in "that which has a hundred thousand as its measure. [This refers to] that which is reckoned as the manifestation of unwholesome states such as the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*).
They are "free from raw stench" (*nirāmagandha*) because they have no raw stench or corpse-odor;
the meaning is that they are devoid of the manifestation of the defilements as previously described. Here, the manifestation of defilements is called "raw stench. For what reason?

Because it is unpleasant, because it is mixed with the impurity of defilements, because it is loathed by the virtuous, and because it brings about an extremely foul state of being. Thus, those who have defilements in excess...
Sentient beings (*sattā*) are each exceedingly foul-smelling. For that very reason, even the corpse of one free from defilements (*nikkilesa*) does not have a foul odor.

"Carrying the burden of the gift-offering site" (*dānaggaparivahana*) means carrying the duty of the gift-offering site. "Measurer" (*māpaka*) refers to one who measures grain by giving a fixed daily allowance.
"In the Canon" (*pāḷiyaṃ*) means in the Vinaya Canon. He spoke after recounting the *Migajātakam*; it is said that in the past, the Bodhisatta was born in the womb of a deer.
Having been reborn, he lived in the forest surrounded by a herd of deer.
Then his sister brought her own son to him and said, "Brother, please train this nephew of yours in the art of hunting. The Bodhisatta consented, saying, "Very well," and added, "Go, dear child;
you should come at such-and-such a time and receive your training. He [the nephew] then waited for the time appointed by his maternal uncle.

Without overstepping [his instructions], he approached him and learned the art of the deer-trap. One day, while wandering in the forest, he was caught in a snare and cried out with the cry of a trapped animal.
The herd of deer fled and informed his mother, saying, "Your son has been caught in a snare.
She went to her brother and said, "Brother, your nephew has been taught the art of the deer-trap."
He asked. The Bodhisatta said, "Do not suspect your son of any evil;
he has mastered the art of the deer-trick well, and now he will come back making you laugh," and then spoke the words beginning with, "The deer lies down on three sides.
Therein, "the deer" refers to his nephew, the deer. "Tipallatthaṃ" means a bed; it is so called because [the body] is straight on both sides.
It would be "stretched out" (pallatthaṃ) in three ways by way of its lying down; or, it would have three stretches, thus it is "three-stretched" (tipallatthaṃ).
"Possessing many wiles" (anekamāyaṃ) means having much deceit and much guile.
"With eight hoofs" (aṭṭhakkhuraṃ) means being endowed with eight hoofs, two on each foot. "Passing away at midnight" (aḍḍharattāpapāyiṃ) refers to the first watch of the night.
Having passed through the middle watch and come from the forest to drink water, he drinks water at the hour of midnight; thus he is called "one who drinks water at midnight" (*addharattāpapāyī*).
There is also a reading: “*addharatte āpapāyī*. I had my nephew, the deer, thoroughly train in the art of hunting.
How so? Just as he would inhale through one nostril while on the ground for six *kalās*.
"The nephew surpasses [the uncle]. This is what is meant:

for I have had him train your son in such a way that, by restraining the wind in one upper nostril and remaining fixed to the ground, he surpasses the hunter with six skills while breathing right there on the earth through a single lower nostril; he overwhelms him with six divisions.
The meaning is "he deceives. By what six [means]? By lying on his side with four legs stretched out;
by scratching grass and dust with his hooves; by thrusting out his tongue; by causing his belly to distend; by discharging excrement and urine; and by suppressing his wind.
Or else, he taught him in such a way that [the horse] would [discharge] onto the ground through one ear.
"Breathing in. "By six" means by the six reasons mentioned below. "He will deceive" (kalāhī) means he will deceive; the sense is that he will outwit the hunter.
"Lady" (bhōtī) is a way of addressing a sister. "Nephew" (bhāgineyya): thus, by these six reasons, he points to the nephew as a deceiver.
Thus the Bodhisatta comforted his sister, telling her that her nephew had thoroughly mastered the art of the deer-trick.
That young fawn, though bound by the snare, remained unbound;
he lay on the ground with his legs stretched out along his broad flank, and striking the earth near his feet with his hooves, he kicked up dust and grass.
Having torn it out, having discharged excrement and urine, having lowered the head, having protruded the tongue,
having made the body slick with saliva, having caused the belly to swell by taking in air, having rolled the eyes,
and causing wind to circulate through the lower nostril while suppressing the wind through the upper nostril, [he brought] the entire body to a state of rigidity.
Having had it hoisted up, he made it appear as if dead; blue flies swarmed around it, and crows perched in various places upon it.
The hunter returned, struck its belly with his hand, and thinking, "It must have been caught early this morning;
it has become putrid," he untied its binding rope and said, "Now, having cut it open right here and taken the meat..."
“I shall go,” he said, and becoming free from fear, he began to grasp the branches and foliage.
The young fawn also stood up, planted its four feet firmly, shook its body, stretched out its neck, and with great speed—like a cloud torn asunder by a mighty wind—rushed toward its mother.
The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that Rāhula is desirous of training; even in the past he was so.”
"Only one who desires training [is a true ascetic]. Having thus related the Migajāta Jātaka, he spoke.
He gave the Ambalaṭṭhika Rāhulovāda: "Do you see, Rāhula, this small remnant of water left in the water-drawer?
Yes, venerable sir. Even so small, Rāhula, is the asceticism of those [who lack training]."
“Those who have no shame in conscious lying,” with these and other words he delivered the Ambalaṭṭhika-Rāhula-vāda.

Regarding the phrase “while thinking thoughts connected with the household life”: it is said that while the Venerable Rāhula was walking behind and behind the Blessed One, he looked at the Tathāgata from the soles of his feet up to the hairline on his head; he [beheld] the Blessed One’s splendor in the guise of a Buddha.
Having seen him, [he thought]: "The Blessed One shines, his body variegated with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
because he is encircled by a fathom-wide radiance, he is like a mountain of gold surrounded by scattered golden dust, or like a golden mountain encircled by streaks of lightning;
though covered by a robe of rags from the dustheap, he is like a golden mountain encircled by red woolen cloth, or like a golden casket adorned with coral creepers."
He thought: "Oh, how great is the splendor of this physical form, adorned by the power of the thirty pāramīs! It is like a golden cetiya anointed with Chinese lacquer powder;
it is like a golden pillar smeared with liquid lac; it is like the full moon that has just risen, set within a mass of red clouds.
Then, looking at himself, he thought: "I too am radiant, if only the Blessed One [were present] in the four..."
"Having ruled as a wheel-turning monarch over the great islands, he did not grant me the position of his chief counselor;
were that so, the surface of Jambudīpa would be exceedingly beautiful. Thus, based on his own physical form, he gave rise to sensual desire rooted in the household life.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "Having seen the excellence of both the Teacher’s and his own physical beauty, while entertaining thoughts rooted in the household life."
The Blessed One, as he was walking ahead, thought: "Rāhula’s physical form is now full of skin, flesh, and blood;
the time has come for his mind to leap toward alluring objects such as visible forms. Is Rāhula passing his time fruitlessly?
Then, with the mere act of turning his attention, [the Buddha saw him] like a fish in clear water, in a state of utter purity.
And just as one sees the reflection of a face in the circle of a mirror, he saw that arising of consciousness; and having seen it, [he thought]:
"This Rāhula, though being my own son, as he follows behind me, gives rise to sensual desire based on his own person, thinking, 'I am beautiful;
my field of color is clear. He is leaping across a place where there is no ford; he has entered upon a wrong path."
He wanders in what is not his proper domain; like a traveler who has lost his way, he goes toward a direction that should not be gone toward.
Furthermore, this defilement of his, increasing within, will not allow him to see even his own welfare as it truly is, nor the welfare of others, nor the welfare of both;
moreover, it will cause him to take rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, and in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
He will cause [the being] to fall into the cycle of existence that has no known beginning, into the crowded realms of the asuras and into the mother’s womb.
Just as a great ship filled with many treasures, taking on water through a breach in its planking,
must not be neglected for even a moment, but requires the gap to be closed with ever-increasing speed, so too is this [being].
“It must not be overlooked. As long as this defilement does not destroy the jewel of virtue and the other virtues within me, I shall suppress it right now.
Having formed this resolve, he then addressed Rāhula:
“Rāhula, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or...”

“Whether gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—every form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “But, Blessed One, is it only form?
Is it only form, O Sugata? “Rāhula, it is not only form; feeling also, Rāhula, perception also, Rāhula, mental formations also...”
"Rāhula, consciousness too, Rāhula," he spoke thus in the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta. To show that, it is said: "Whatever [feeling], Rāhula... he spoke.
However, in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, they say "the Rāhulovāda" with reference to the Rāhulovāda spoken in the Rāhula Saṃyutta. Therein—

“Venerable sir, it would be well if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, venerable sir, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. When the elder had thus requested, [the Blessed One said]:
“What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But what is impermanent, venerable sir...”
"Is it suffering or is it happiness? "It is suffering, Bhante. "But as for that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus:
'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'? With these words, he began the *Rāhulovāda*.

The intention is that this was the Elder’s own practice of insight (*vipassanā*), and not something spoken for the purpose of cutting off discursive thought (*vitakkūpaccheda*) as in the *Mahārāhulovāda*.
Then, when the Teacher knew that his knowledge had reached maturity, and so forth—in these passages, it is said that while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"Rāhula’s qualities conducive to the maturation of liberation have indeed matured;
what if I were to further train Rāhula in the destruction of the taints? Then, at the time of the morning, the Blessed One...
Having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, he entered Sāvatthī for alms. After his meal, returning from his alms round, he addressed the Venerable Rāhula:
“Take your sitting mat, Rāhula; let us go to the Blind Men’s Grove for the day’s abiding.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Rāhula replied to the Blessed One, and taking his sitting mat, he followed.

Taking him with him, he followed closely behind the Blessed One. At that time, many thousands of deities followed behind the Blessed One after paying homage to him, thinking, "Today the Blessed One will further train the Venerable Rāhula for the destruction of the taints.
Then the Blessed One, having entered deep into the Andhavana forest, at a certain spot...
He sat down on the seat prepared at the foot of a tree. The Venerable Rāhula, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Then, addressing the Venerable Rāhula, [the Blessed One said]: "What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?
"Impermanent, Bhante. "But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness? "Suffering, Bhante."
"Venerable sir, as for that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus:
'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'? It was with reference to this that he gave the Rāhula-Advice. It is said in this regard:
"Seated in the Andhavana forest, he delivered the Cūḷarāhulovāda."

"By hundreds of thousands of millions of deities": these are precisely those deities who made their aspirations together with the Venerable Rāhula when he made his aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara during the time of King Pathavindhara.

Among them, some were earth-dwelling deities, some were sky-dwelling deities, some were reborn in the worlds of the Four Great Kings and other celestial realms, and some were reborn in the Brahma-world. In this...
On that day, however, they all gathered together in one place, in the Andhavana grove itself.
*Ābhidosika* means stale, having become putrid after being kept overnight (*pārivāsika*) and having passed one night.
This is indeed a designation for that which has passed one night, namely, "stale" (*ābhidosika*). The etymological meaning here is: "overcome by the defect of putrefaction."
*Abhidoso*: "not of yesterday"; *ābhidosiko* means "of yesterday. *Kummāsaṃ*: barley-gruel. *Adhivāsetvā*: having accepted;
that is, having been invited by his father with the words, "Well then, dear Raṭṭhapāla, accept tomorrow's meal," the Elder accepted the alms for the following day.
And in this context, the Elder was one who habitually went on his alms-round with a dignified bearing, yet he accepted the alms for tomorrow.
He did not consent; however, he consented out of consideration for his mother.
It is said that as she repeatedly recollected the Elder, great sorrow arose within her, and she became as if pained by the very act of weeping.
Therefore, the Elder thought, "If I depart without seeing her, her heart might break," and so he consented out of compassion. For wise monks [act thus] toward their mothers and fathers.
Those who seek purity through the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) do not become so by neglecting the assistance that should be rendered to their teachers (*ācariya*) and preceptors (*upajjhāya*).
Regarding "women adorned and ready": this refers to women sent by their father.
It is said that on the following day, his father had a great heap of gold and bullion prepared in his own residence and had it covered over with mats.
The venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s former wives were instructed: “Come, you brides;
adorn yourselves with that same jewelry with which you formerly used to be dear and pleasing to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla. Having been thus commanded, they adorned themselves accordingly.
Then, after exquisite food both hard and soft had been prepared, the time was announced, and having arrived, they sat down on the seats that had been laid out.
To him as he sat on his seat, they entreated him, saying: “Ratthapāla, this is your wealth of clay;
there is other wealth from your father, and other from your grandfather. Dear Ratthapāla, it is possible for you to enjoy wealth and perform meritorious deeds.
Come, dear Ratthapāla, renounce the training, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds. Thus they requested.

Having rejected [the teaching] and when the Dhamma had been taught, he brought [him] there, thinking, "I will cause him to be expelled from the order. [The other] thought, "Now he has begun to give a discourse on the Dhamma;
enough, I shall not do as he says," and rising up, he went and caused the door of that man's harem to be opened, saying, "This is your husband; go, and by whatever means necessary, seize him!"
“Exert yourselves! he urged them. The dancing girls, who were in their prime, surrounded the Elder.
Among them, he produced the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*). Therefore it is said: “Having produced the perception of foulness in that company of women adorned and arrayed.
And while standing, he taught the Dhamma.
“Behold this form fashioned by the mind, a heap of diseased members piled together;
it is afflicted, full of many thoughts, and possesses no lasting stability.
Behold this form fashioned by the mind, adorned with jewels and earrings.”
Bones covered with skin, adorned with clothes,
with feet dyed red with lac and a face smeared with powder—
this is enough to delude the fool, but not one who seeks the further shore.
“Hair is fashioned into eight-patterned curls, and the eyes are anointed with collyrium;
this is sufficient for the delusion of a fool, but not for one seeking the further shore.
This putrid body, adorned like a painted box of ointment—”
Enough for the delusion of the fool, but not for one who seeks the further shore:
“The hunter has set his snare, yet the deer did not fall into the trap;
having eaten the bait, I am going, while the deer-catchers wail.”
Having taught the Dhamma with these verses, he "flew up into the air," meaning he leaped into the sky. But why did the Elder go through the air?
It is said that his father, the merchant, had bolts fastened at the seven gate-towers and commanded the Mallas: "If he goes out and departs..."
“Seize him by his hands and feet, strip off his saffron robes, and make him take up the appearance of a householder.
Therefore, the Elder, thinking, “May these people not commit demerit by seizing one such as me, who has destroyed the great taints, by the hand or the foot,” departed through the air.
Migacīra is a pleasure garden of that name. It is adorned with the four kinds of loss.
It is adorned with these four kinds of loss: the loss of youth, the loss of health, the loss of wealth, and the loss of kinsmen.
"Loss" (pārijuñña) means decline. The rest here is easily understood.
This is the story of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna.
211. "Those who take a voting ticket" (salākagāhakā) refers to those taking the third vote. The connection is that even as he was going to the Sunāparanta country, he took the voting ticket first.
"Within six years" means within the interval of six years. "Friendship" (mettī) means the state of being a friend.

"When there is a cause for schism" (bhedake sati) means when there exists a factor that creates division. "From the vicinity of the thicket" (gumbasabhāgatā) means from near the thicket; this is precisely what it means.
Or this is another reading. "Having been a woman" means having appeared as a woman; the meaning is that she assumed the form of a human female.

"Long-lasting" means following for a long period of time. "For such a duration" means for such a length of time. "Come, friend" means "take it, friend. "Having grasped the meaning" means having grasped the true meaning;
or this is simply another reading. "A rogue was born" means a scoundrel was born.
"Do not speak harshly to anyone" means: do not speak harshly to any single individual. "If spoken to, they might retort" means:
if others are told by you that they are immoral, they might likewise retort to you in the same way. "For contentious speech is painful" is the further reason:
this so-called quarrelsome talk is indeed painful. "They might touch you with retaliation" means: [they might strike] another with physical punishment and so forth.
If you strike back, such counter-blows would fall upon your own head.
"If you keep yourself still" means if you are able to remain motionless.
"Like a gong struck" refers to a bronze cymbal placed on its stand after its rim has been trimmed down until it is only a palm's breadth thick; for such a thing, when struck by the hands—
Even when struck with feet or with a staff, it makes no sound. "You have reached Nibbāna":
if you are able to become like this, fulfilling this practice, then even though you have not yet actually attained Nibbāna, you are said to have reached it.
"No provocation exists in you": [this refers to] the thought, "In this way you are immoral, whereas I am virtuous."
The meaning is that for you there exists no such provocation characterized by contentious speech and further disputes, nor will there ever be any.
"By defilement" means by way of the cause of corruption.
(The story of the Elder Vaṅgīsa)
212. In the fourth [verse], "of those possessed of perfect eloquence" (*sampannapaṭibhānānaṃ*) means of those whose eloquence is complete.

"He who knows passing away... [etc. ...in every way": he who knows the passing away and rebirth-linking of beings, making them manifest in every aspect—I call him *Buddha* because he is awakened to the four truths;
*Sugata* because he has gone well by virtue of his excellent practice; and *Asakta* (Unattached) because of his lack of clinging.
The meaning is: "I call him a brahmin. Regarding the phrase "whose destination":

he whose destination these deities and others do not know—I call him a brahmin who, because his taints have been exhausted, is one with taints destroyed (khīṇāsava), and because he is far removed from defilements, is an arahant.
This is the story of the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta.
213. Regarding the phrase "of those who are entirely pleasing" (*sabbapāsādikānaṃ*) in the fifth [section]: it means those who generate complete confidence (*pasāda*).
"What is this? (*kiṃ tāyaṃ*) means "what is this for them? "Too quickly" (*atilahuṃ*) means "too swiftly.

Those for whom there is no proximate cause (*upanissaya*) for the paths and fruits that ought to arise in that particular existence, the Buddhas call them "fools" (*moghapurisa*), as in the case of Ariṭṭha, Lāḷudāyin, and others. Regarding the proximate cause (*upanissaye*):
Even though at that moment there was neither the path nor the fruit, they still called him a "foolish man," just as they did in the case of the Elder Dhaniya and others.
Because this [person] also lacked the path and the fruit at that moment, he said, "a foolish man";
the meaning is "an empty man. "On account of the multitude" means on account of the multitude in the assembly. "In many ways" means by way of many reasons.
“I wish, O bhikkhus,” said the Blessed One; it is said that during that half-month he did not see any being capable of being awakened, and therefore he spoke thus.
Even so, the teaching of the Dhamma ought to have been performed according to the sequence of the discourse. However, it occurred to him:
“When I have granted them leave and am in seclusion, the bhikkhus will establish an unrighteous convention.”
“Upasena will break it; having gained confidence in him, I shall allow the monks to see him.
Then many monks who wish to see me will undertake the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and on account of their discarded sitting mats, I shall lay down a training rule.
It was for this reason that he spoke thus. “Of the elder” means of the Elder Upasena. “Pleasant” (manāpāni).
When he asks, "Monk, are these rag-robes yours? he asks: "Monk, were these rag-robes taken by you according to your own liking and preference?
[The monk replies: "Venerable sir, these rag-robes are not to my liking; venerable sir, they were not taken by me according to my own liking and preference;
rather, I was seized like one by the throat, as if by a blow to the head."
He shows this by saying "mayāti. "It is indeed found in the Pāḷi" refers to the Vinaya-pāḷi.
Regarding the story of Thera Dabba (214):
"In the eighteen great monasteries" refers to those situated all around Rājagaha.
"In the great monasteries. "Upavijaññā" means those whose time of delivery is near. "Rahagato" means having gone into seclusion.
It is said that the Elder, seeing that his own task was accomplished, thought:
"I am maintaining this body, yet it stands at the mouth of impermanence like a lamp placed at the mouth of a draft; its nature is such that it will soon go out."
Thinking, "As long as he has not attained Nibbāna, what service might I perform for the Saṅgha?
he reflected thus: "In foreign lands, many sons of noble family go forth even without having seen the Blessed One;
they come from afar thinking, 'We shall see and pay homage to the Blessed One. Among them..."
The lodgings were insufficient, so they even made their beds on stone slabs.
"But am I not able, by my own power, to create for those sons of good family—according to their wishes—palaces, monasteries, and upper chambers, as well as couches, seats, and rugs, and give them?
On the following day, some among them appeared exceedingly exhausted; out of respect, they...
“Standing before the bhikkhus, they do not even assign the meals, yet I am indeed capable of assigning their meals.
Reflecting thus, he thought: “What if I were to arrange lodgings for the Saṅgha and also assign the meals? Regarding the phrase *sabhāgasabhāgānaṃ*:
it means those who are similar by virtue of qualities such as being experts in the Suttantas and so forth.
It is not out of intimacy with friends. For the Elder, having selected those who are experts in the Suttas, he assigns them suitable lodgings one by one.
The same method applies to those who are experts in the Vinaya, the Abhidhamma, those practicing meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), and those possessing great physical strength.
Therefore it is said in the Pāḷi: “Those bhikkhus who are experts in the Suttas, he assigns lodgings for them all together,” and so forth.
"With a finger burning": having entered the fourth jhāna of the fire-kasiṇa and emerged, he resolved upon the burning of a finger by means of the knowledge of direct higher power (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*).
Thus, with that very flame produced from the attainment of the fire-element, his finger was burning.
Regarding the phrases "this bed" and so forth, even when the Elder speaks such words as "this is a bed," [the emanated being] likewise [speaks for himself].
In the place where they have gone, they say, "This is a bed," and so forth. For this is the nature of those who are created:
"When one speaks, all the created beings speak;
when one remains silent, they all remain silent."
In whatever monastery couches, chairs, and so forth were lacking, he fulfilled them there by his own power;
thus, for those things created by him, there is no statement that they lack a physical basis (*avatthuka*), because couches, chairs, and so forth exist everywhere.
Furthermore, in all monasteries, he resolves upon making the paths leading to them of equal measure. As for the shape of the boundary markers (*katika*) and so forth—
It should be understood that because of their various forms, the rules of agreement (*katikavatta*) for each respective dwelling are to be recited separately.
For it is said that the natural law (*dhammatā*)—such as "when one speaks" and so forth—applies to those created without specific determination.

Thus, those who are created without making determinations based on distinctions such as complexion, age, physical features, equipment, or actions, become identical to the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimant*) precisely because they were created without such determination.
Whether standing, sitting, or otherwise, or whether speaking or remaining silent—whatever the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*) does, they all do that very same thing.
But if he wishes to make them appear in various ways—some in the first stage of life, some in the middle stage, and some in the final stage;

likewise, some with long hair, some half-shaven, and some with mixed hair; some wearing robes that are half-red, and some with yellowish robes; and [engaging them] in reciting words, preaching the Dhamma, eloquent expositions, asking questions, answering questions, dyeing robes, sewing robes, washing robes, and so forth—[then they act accordingly].

Or, wishing to perform other various kinds [of feats], he emerges from the foundational jhāna and performs the preliminary work (*parikamma*) in such a manner as, "Let so many bhikkhus be in their prime," and so forth.

Then, having re-entered attainment and emerged again, when he makes his resolution (*adhiṭṭhāti*), they become exactly of the kind he desired, together with the resolving consciousness (*adhiṭṭhānacitta*). Again, for himself...
"He returns to his own dwelling place" means that instead of sitting down with them to engage in conversation about the countryside, he returns to his own residence at Veḷuvana.
"In the Canon" (pāḷiyaṃ) refers to the Vinaya Canon.
This is the account of the Elder Pilindavaccha.
215. Regarding the phrase *piyānaṃ*: it means "of those who are dear. Regarding *manāpānaṃ*: it means "of those who increase the mind's delight.
As for *Pilinda*, that is his clan (*gotta*); and *Vaccha*, that is his name. However, they also speak by reversing what was stated here, saying: "Pilinda is the name, Vaccha is the clan.
For this very reason, it was stated by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla in his commentary on the *Theragāthā*: "Pilinda is his..."
They gave him a name, and his clan-name was Vaccha. Therefore, at a later time, he became known as Pilindavaccha.
“Having brought together” means having made into one.
“Having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, having gained faith, and having gone forth”—this is according to the reciters of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
This was stated by way of a narrative. Others, however, say: even while our Blessed One had not yet arisen, [the Elder] was born in a brahmin household in Sāvatthī and became known as Pilindavaccha.

Having gone forth as a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka) due to an abundance of world-weariness (saṃvega) within saṃsāra, he mastered the knowledge called Cūḷagandhāra and became a traveler through the air and a knower of others' minds. Then, in Rājagaha...
He lived there, having attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame.

Then, when our Blessed One had attained full enlightenment and gradually arrived at Rājagaha, from that time on, by the power of the Buddha, his knowledge did not succeed and he could no longer accomplish his purpose.
He thought: “I have indeed heard this from the teachers of my teachers as they were speaking: ‘Wherever...’”
“The Great Gandhāra spell succeeds, but the Lesser Gandhāra spell does not succeed there. [He thought:
“Ever since the arrival of the ascetic Gotama, this spell of mine has not succeeded.
Without a doubt, the ascetic Gotama knows the Great Gandhāra spell; what if I were to attend upon him and learn the spell from his presence?”
So, having approached the Blessed One, he said this: “Great Ascetic, I wish to master a certain branch of knowledge in your presence;
grant me the opportunity. The Blessed One said, “In that case, go forth [into homelessness].
Thinking, “Going forth is the preliminary practice for knowledge,” he went forth. “By way of disparaging others” means by way of censuring others.
“Gentle” means not harsh. “Communicative” means communicating the meaning. “Truthful” means having a real meaning.
“One who does not provoke” means that one should not cause another to become angry by means of speech;
one whose taints are destroyed would not speak such speech as that. Therefore, “I call him a brahmin”—this is the meaning.
"Having investigated" means having examined. "Going with a fierce speed" means going with a swift gait.
(The Story of the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya, 216.
Regarding the eighth [case], "having gone by staying for one night" means having gone through the power of a deity; it may also mean "through the power of the Buddha."
They said this. Having thus gone and entered the monastery, he saw many bhikkhus walking in the open air after their morning meal to relieve physical fatigue.
He asked, "Where is the Teacher now? The bhikkhus replied, "He has entered Sāvatthī for alms. They then asked him, "But from where have you come? "I have come from Suppāraka," he said.
“When did you set out? “I set out yesterday evening. “You have come from afar;
wash your feet, anoint them with oil, and rest for a while. When you arrive, you will see the Teacher.
“Venerable sir, I know nothing of danger to the life of either the Teacher or myself; thus, for a single night, I have stayed nowhere and sat nowhere.”
"I have come along a road of two hundred yojanas; having seen the Teacher, I shall rest.

Having said this, he entered Sāvatthī in great haste. Seeing the Blessed One wandering for alms with the incomparable splendor of a Buddha, he thought, "At long last, I have seen the Perfectly Enlightened One," and from the very spot where he saw him, his body bent low in reverence.
Having gone to the very middle of the street, he paid homage with the fivefold prostration, grasped [the Teacher’s] ankles firmly, and said this:
“Teach me the Dhamma, Bhante; teach me the Dhamma, Sugata, which may lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time.
Then the Teacher declined him, saying: “It is not yet the right time, Bāhiya; I have entered among the houses for alms.”
Having heard this, Bāhiya said, "Venerable sir, while wandering through the cycle of existence, I have never before obtained solid food;
I do not know whether there will be an obstacle to the life of either you or myself. Teach me the Dhamma. The Teacher refused him a second time as well.
For it occurred to him: "From the moment he saw me, his entire body..."
"It will be completely overwhelmed by rapture; even if one hears the Dhamma with such a forceful surge of rapture, one will not be able to penetrate it.
Let alone equanimity as the middle state—since he has come from a road of two hundred leagues in a single night, his exhaustion is also great;
let that too subside for now. Therefore, having refused twice, [he said:]
On being requested for the third time, while standing right there in the middle of the street, he taught the Dhamma in the manner beginning with: “Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus:
‘In the seen, there shall be merely the seen’,” and so forth. Presenting this matter in brief, he said:
“The Teacher had entered for alms,” and so on. Therein, *antaraghare* means in the middle of the street.
"Seeking bowl and robes because his bowl and robes were incomplete":

it is said that while he was practicing the duties of a recluse for twenty thousand years, thinking, "It is proper for a bhikkhu, having obtained his own requisites, to eat by himself without looking to others," he did not provide assistance with even a single bowl or robe to another bhikkhu. Therefore, for him—
Knowing that "an alms-bowl and robes produced by supernormal power will not arise," he did not grant him the going-forth by the formula "Come, monk.
And when he was asked for the going-forth at that very moment, having asked, "Is your bowl and robes complete?
and being told, "They are incomplete," he said, "In that case, go and search for a bowl and robes," and then departed. Therefore, while he was searching for a bowl and robes—
He gathers rags from a rubbish heap. "Even a thousand" is a term of limitation;

that is, even if the verses are limited by a thousand—whether one thousand or two thousand—and if they are composed of meaningless words, such as those describing the color of the sky or the color of mountains, which merely illuminate [the world] without pointing toward *nibbāna*.
The meaning is that as long as verses are composed of useless words, however many they may be, they are indeed evil.
"A single verse-line is better" means that even a single verse such as "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless... [as far as] like the dead" is better.
This is the story of the Elder Kumārakassapa.

217. In the ninth [birth], he experiences prosperity for one *buddhantara* (the interval between Buddhas). Because of his certainty regarding *sāvaka-bodhi* (disciple-enlightenment) and the excellence of his accumulation of merit, he does not fall into the lower realms;

instead, experiencing prosperity among gods and humans for one *buddhantara*, it is said that he was "born in the womb of a certain noble maiden. Having stated this, [the text describes] the manner of his birth.
To show [the matter] starting from the very beginning, it was said: “And she,” and so forth. Therein, “she” refers to the girl of good family.
The word “and” (ca) has a sense of contrast; by it, it highlights the distinction that is being stated. “Family home” (kulagharaṃ) means the house of her husband’s family.
“Sign of conception” (gabbhanimittaṃ) means the physical manifestation of the state of having become pregnant. Even though Visākhā belonged to a family residing in Sāvatthī...
The passage beginning with “Visākhā and... was spoken in order to show her preeminence in that regard, just as one might say, “The brahmins have arrived;
Vāsiṭṭha has also arrived. The construction is: “Because she had been given this name by the Blessed One himself.
Since princes are designated in the world as “kumāras,” and because he was the king’s biological son, he said: “The king’s... they recognized him.”

"Having formulated fifteen questions" means: having formulated fifteen questions according to the method found in the Vammika Sutta, beginning with, "Bhikkhu, bhikkhu, this anthill smokes at night and blazes by day. Regarding King Pāyāsi:
[he held that] "there is no other world, there are no beings of spontaneous birth, and there is no result of well-done or ill-done deeds..."

“...the fruit, the result”—this was the view held by King Pāyāsi. For at that time, while not yet consecrated, the king was residing in the city of Setavyā, which had been given to him by Pasenadi of Kosala, and there he adopted this view.
[The Blessed One] adorned [his response] with fifteen questions: “What do you think, royal prince, regarding these sun and moon, whether in this world or in the next...”
Having adorned it with these fifteen questions, beginning with “Are they gods or humans?”—in the *Pāyāsi Sutta*.
The story of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika (218).
The tenth [section] is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the Third Section on the Foremost Ones is concluded.
14. The Section on the Foremost Ones (14). 4.
Commentary on the Fourth Section on the Foremost Ones.
The Story of the Elder Ānanda (219–223).
Regarding the first [story] in the Fourth Chapter, it says "of the dimensions mentioned below":
this refers to the story of the Elder Koṇḍañña told below, which states, "Its main petals were ninety cubits long, the filaments were thirty cubits, and the pericarp..."
It was of the dimensions thus described: twelve cubits [in height], and the area where the feet were set was eleven cubits.
"He sent it to the king" means that he sent it after reporting the state of rebellion among the border regions. However, in the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said:
"Without reporting the state of rebellion among the border regions to the king, he himself pacified it; having heard of this, the king was delighted."
"Having summoned his son, he said, 'Sumana, I give you a boon; take it,'" so it is said.
"Na metaṃ cittaṃ atthī" means "I have no such thought. "Avañjhaṃ" means not empty.
"Aññaṃ varehī" means "choose another," which is to say, "take another. "Udakaṃ adhiṭṭhāyā" means having resolved, "Let there be water."
"By way of going" means by means of walking. "Not with a worldly eye" means they do not look toward material things, such as the requisites consisting of robes and so forth.
"Only in the vicinity of the dwelling place" means precisely near the place where he dwells. "Exclusively beloved" means he is exclusively beloved in the position of an attendant.
"Of this very one" means of this very bhikkhu. "Duplicity of speech does not exist" means speech that has become twofold.

"They do not exist" means that there are no indeterminate discourses. "Unbound" means unsettled. "With blood flowing" is an instrumental expression used to indicate the state of being so characterized; the meaning is "one who is joined with flowing blood.
"Beset" means followed. "Arise, friend Ānanda! Arise, friend Ānanda!"—this is a doubled expression used in haste. [The remainder is] twofold.
"With water" means with both cold water and warm water. "With three kinds of tooth-sticks" means with the three types of tooth-sticks: small, large, and medium.
"He goes around nine times" means that when the Teacher calls him, he goes around nine times in order to give a reply and to dispel sloth and torpor. For this very reason, it was said:
“Thus it occurred to him,” and so forth. The rest here is easily understood.
The story of the Elder Uruvelakassapa (224).
Regarding what must be said concerning the second [case], that has already been given in detail in the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The Story of the Elder Kāḷudāyi (225).
"In the third [verse], *gamanākappa* means the manner of going. The rest here is self-evident.
The Story of the Elder Bākula.

226. In the fourth [verse], *nirābādhānaṃ* means "of those free from affliction. Just as when one ought to say *dvāvīsati* or *dvattiṃsā*, etc., the forms *bāvīsati*, *bāttiṃsā*, and so forth are used;

likewise, when one ought to say *dvikulo* (one who belongs to two families) or *dvekuloti*, it is said *bākuloti*. He explains: "Because he was raised in two families (*dvīsu kulesu vaḍḍhitattā*), he is called *Bākula*."
"Thus named. By "upayogena" is meant by his power or majesty. "At a time of health" means at a time when one is free from illness.
"Even for as long as it takes to milk a cow" (gadduhanamattam) means even for a duration of time sufficient to milk a cow. However, here the entire period of milking a cow is not intended;

rather, it refers specifically to the brief moment required to grasp the cow's udder and extract a single drop of milk. "A hall of health" (ārogyasāla) is a hall constructed for the purpose of restoring the state of health to those who are afflicted.
"By means of diving and surfacing" means by means of diving and surfacing only slightly in water that reaches the knees.
"Having abandoned it, he fled" means having abandoned it right near the mouth of the fish, he fled. "By the power of the child" means by the power of the child’s merit.
"Dying as they were being killed" means they die while being struck with sticks and other weapons; [it does not mean] by means of a net.

"Though bound, he was not killed" means that although he had been bound, he was not put to death. "As soon as he was taken out, he died" means that at the very moment he was removed [from the water], he died.
Therefore, no effort was made to kill him—that effort by which the child might have suffered illness. "That" refers to the fish.
"Entirely" means without deficiency, with all its limbs complete. "He does not sport" means he does not take delight in anything.
She does not conceive [a false notion]. "They tear her back" means they tear her back by the power of the child's merit.
"Having caused a drum to be beaten" means having had a drum beaten with the proclamation, "A son has been obtained. "She declared her true nature" means she spoke of her own status as a mother;
because she had carried him in her womb, she was unable to act as one who was not his mother—due to her state as a biological mother, she could not act as a non-mother.
"It is possible. "Even those who catch fish" means even those who catch them by selling them.
And since those who catch them in that manner are said to be catching everything included therein, he says: "There are none who can catch them while setting aside the scales and so forth.
"This one also cannot be made a mother" means it is not possible because her status as a son has already been given away.
The Story of the Elder Sobhita (227).
The fifth [story] has its meaning already explained.
The Story of the Elder Upāli.
228. Regarding the sixth case, the story of the monk from Bhārukaccha:
It is said that a certain monk residing in the country of Bhārukaccha, having engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife in a dream, thought, "I am no longer a recluse; I shall disrobe.
While traveling toward Bhārukaccha, he saw the Venerable Upāli on the road and reported this matter to him. The Venerable Upāli—
He spoke thus: “There is no offense, friend, because it was in a dream.

Since this occurs precisely because there is no objective reality in a dream, the Elder Upāli, although this case had not previously been adjudicated by the Blessed One, determined it in this way by means of the underlying principle (*nayaggāha*).
A householder had two children: a son and a nephew. Then that householder became ill.
He said this to the Venerable Ajjuka: "Venerable sir, please point out this place to whichever of these boys has faith and confidence.
At that time, the householder’s nephew had faith and confidence.
Then the Venerable Ajjuka pointed out that place to that boy. With that wealth...
He established a family and instituted a tradition of giving.
Then the householder’s son said this to the Venerable Ānanda: “Venerable Ānanda, who is the heir to a father’s inheritance:
the son or the nephew?”—“The son, friend, is the heir to the father.”—“Venerable sir, our noble master Ajjuka possesses wealth.”
“He told us about his sexual misconduct. “He is no longer a *samaṇa*, friend; he is Ajjuka.
Then the Venerable Ajjuka said this to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, give me a legal decision.
They both went into the presence of the Elder Upāli. Then the Venerable Upāli said this to the Venerable Ānanda: “Now, friend—”
“Ānanda, if one is told by the owner, ‘Point out this place to such-and-such a person,’ and he points it out to him, what offense does he commit?
“Nothing at all, Bhante, not even a minor offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
“Friend, this Venerable Ajjuka was told by the owner, ‘Point out this place to such-and-such a person,’ and he pointed it out to him.”
“There is no offense, friends, for the Venerable Ajjuka. When the Blessed One heard this, he said, “Well spoken, monks, by Upāli,” and gave his approval;
it was with reference to this that it was said. The story of Kumārakassapa has already been related above. Regarding “the six nobles”:

these are the six nobles consisting of Bhaddiya the Sakyan king, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimila, and Devadatta. “Adorned” means decorated. “In the Pāḷi” means in the Pāḷi of the Saṅghabhedakkhandhaka.
The Story of the Elder Nandaka (229).
Regarding the phrase "in the seventh, in a single convergence" (*ekasamodhāne*): it means in one convergence, that is, in one assembly. The rest is easily understood.
The Story of the Elder Nanda.

230. In the eighth [case], "he does not look at that direction without delimiting it by means of the four kinds of clear comprehension" means that he does not look at that direction without delimiting it by means of the fourfold clear comprehension—namely, those termed clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of resort, and clear comprehension of non-delusion. For that venerable one thought:
"It was precisely because of my failure to guard the doors of the sense faculties that I fell into such adverse states as lack of delight in the Teaching."
Thinking, “I shall thoroughly subdue that very [mind],” he becomes filled with enthusiasm, possessing powerful moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*).

Because he has performed his duties therein, his restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) has reached the highest perfection; thus, without ever abandoning the fourfold clear comprehension (*catu-sampajañña*), he looks in every direction.
And this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, if Nanda needs to look toward the eastern direction, he looks toward the eastern direction after having fully concentrated his whole mind, thinking:
‘May no covetousness, dejection, or evil unwholesome states overwhelm me as I look toward the eastern direction. In this way, he is clearly comprehending in that regard. If, bhikkhus, ...”
“The western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, above, below, and the intermediate directions must be looked upon by Nanda.
Having brought everything to mind, Nanda looks toward the intermediate directions, thinking: ‘As I am thus looking toward the intermediate directions... [he remains] clearly comprehending.

Regarding the phrase “when the auspicious ceremonies of consecration, entering the house, and marriage are taking place,” three types of auspicious ceremonies are mentioned here; [this is stated] in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*.

However, it is stated: "On that very day, there were five auspicious ceremonies for Prince Nanda: the ceremony of shaving the hair (kesavissajjana), the binding of the turban (paṭṭabandha), the house-consecration ceremony (gharamaṅgala), the umbrella-consecration ceremony (chattamaṅgala), and the marriage ceremony (āvāhamaṅgala).

In this context, the shaving of the hair is the "ceremony of shaving the hair" performed according to family custom. The binding of the turban is the "binding of the turban" as the heir apparent. The great festival of entering a brand-new house is the "house-consecration ceremony."
The house-consecration festival; the marriage ceremony festival is the *āvāha-maṅgala*; the festival of the prince’s parasol is the *chatta-maṅgala*.
The consecration festival of Prince Nanda did not afflict him as much as the words spoken by Janapadakalyāṇī—this phrase must be supplied.
To show that very speech in its actual form, [the text says]: “At the time of taking the bowl and departing,” and so forth.
It is said: "A beauty of the land" (*janapadakalyāṇī*) means one who is beautiful and supreme in her country, free from the six bodily defects and endowed with the five beauties.
For she is neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair;
thus, having transcended the human complexion yet not having reached the divine complexion, she is free from the six bodily defects. [She possesses] beauty of skin and beauty of flesh.

Because she is endowed with these excellences—namely, excellence of skin, excellence of bones, and excellence of age—she is called "one endowed with the five excellences. For she has no need for external lighting;
by the radiance of her own body alone, she creates light within a space twelve cubits around. She is either the color of yellow *piyaṅgu* or the color of gold; this is her excellence of skin.
Furthermore, her four hands, feet, and face are as if treated with lac dye, resembling red coral or red woolen cloth;

this is the excellence of her flesh. Her twenty nails, in the places where they are not detached from the flesh, appear as if filled with lac dye, while in the places where they are detached, they resemble streams of milk; this is the excellence of her sinews. Her thirty-two teeth—
They appear like a row of well-polished, perfectly cleansed diamonds; this is her excellence of bone (*aṭṭhikalyāṇatā*).
Although she is a hundred and twenty years old, she appears as if she were sixteen years of age due to the absence of grey hair; this is her excellence of age (*vayakalyāṇatā*).
Thus, because she is endowed with these five excellences, she is called "the excellence of the land" (*janapadakalyāṇī*). *Tuvaṭam* means quickly.

"He will take it back at this spot; he will take it back at that spot"—thinking thus, it is said, he was unable to say "Venerable Sir, please take your bowl" out of reverence for the Tathāgata, and so he thought: "He will take the bowl at the top of the stairs.
The Teacher did not take it even at that spot. The other [thought]: "He will take it at the foot of the stairs."
He thought, "The Teacher will accept it there. But the Teacher did not accept it even there. He thought, "He will accept it in the royal courtyard.
But the Teacher did not accept it even there. While he was still thinking, "He will accept it here," or "He will accept it there," the Teacher led him to the monastery and ordained him.
The Story of the Elder Mahākappina (231).
Regarding the ninth verse, "one who is rich in learning" means one who loves hearing the Dhamma. "To the attendant" means to the doorkeeper.
"By means of a declaration of truth" means by means of a *saccakiriya* (act of truth). The Teacher thought, "Let Uppalavaṇṇā come. The Elder Nun arrived, and having ordained them all, [she departed].
"She went to the nuns' quarters"—this was said by one who was showing the method of exposition used by the reciters of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
For it is said in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*:
"Having paid homage to the Teacher, they stood to one side and requested the going-forth. When this had been said, the Teacher..."
Some say that he was thinking of Uppalavaṇṇā’s arrival. However, the Teacher said to those female lay disciples, “Go to Sāvatthī and have them receive the going-forth in the nunnery.

Traveling by stages on their journey through the countryside, they received honors and hospitality brought by the great multitude along the way; traveling the entire two-hundred-yojana road on foot, they arrived at the nunnery.
"Having gone forth, they attained arahatship.

Regarding "one who drinks the Dhamma" (*dhammapīti*): it means one who drinks the Dhamma; that is, one who drinks the Dhamma. Now, this Dhamma cannot be drunk from a vessel like rice-gruel and the like;
rather, one touches the ninefold supramundane Dhamma with the mental body (*nāmakāya*) by way of its object.

One who realizes [the truths] by penetrating the Noble Truths of suffering and so forth through the clear comprehension of full understanding (*pariññā*) and the other modes of realization, is said to "drink the Dhamma.
"He sleeps happily" is merely a figurative expression; the meaning is that he dwells happily in all four postures.
"With a serene mind" means with a mind that is untroubled and free from defilements. "Proclaimed by the Noble Ones" refers to the Noble Ones such as the Buddha and others.
Having explained the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth;
"he always delights" means that one endowed with wisdom, dwelling with a mind serene through such joy in the Dhamma (dhammapīti), always delights and finds great pleasure.
He addresses the Elder as "Brāhmaṇa" because of his having banished evil.
The Story of the Elder Sāgata (232).

Regarding the tenth [offense], "by the word of the group-of-six": it is said that the lay followers of Kosambī approached the Venerable Sāgata, paid homage to him, and standing to one side, spoke thus: "Venerable sir, what is both difficult to obtain and pleasing for the masters?"
"What should we prepare? When this was said, the group-of-six monks said to the lay followers of Kosambī:
"Friends, there is a kind of fermented rice-gruel called *kāpotikā*, which is pleasing to the monks and difficult to obtain; you should prepare that.
Then the lay followers of Kosambī prepared *kāpotikā* fermented rice-gruel in every house and [offered it] to the Venerable Sāgata.
Seeing him wandering for alms, they said this: “Venerable sir, let the noble Sāgata drink the clear pigeon-gruel;

venerable sir, let the noble Sāgata drink the clear pigeon-gruel. Then the Venerable Sāgata, having drunk the clear pigeon-gruel from house to house, fell down at the city gate as he was leaving the city. Thus it was said: “Of the group of six...”

"By means of this speech, having prepared *kāpotika* [liquor] with faith in all the houses," and so forth. In that context, *kāpotikā* refers to that which has a color like the feet of a pigeon and a reddish luster.
*Pasannā* is a designation for the scum of liquor (*surāmaṇḍa*). "Arising in the Vinaya" means it is found in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) concerning the drinking of intoxicants.
This is the story of the Elder Rādha.
233. In the eleventh [sutta], it is said that the Teacher gave a sign to the Elder Sāriputta; this means he gave him a sign to ordain the brahmin—he commanded him.
It is said that when the Blessed One saw that brahmin had failed to obtain ordination and had become emaciated, coarse, discolored, and sallow, he addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, who is that?"
“He remembers his debt to that brahmin. When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Blessed One:
“I, Bhante, do remember my debt to that brahmin. “But what, Sāriputta, is the debt you remember to that brahmin?
“In this regard, Bhante, while I was walking for alms in Rājagaha, that brahmin [gave me food].”
“He had me give him a ladleful of alms; it is this service, Bhante, that I remember of that brahmin.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta! For noble persons, Sāriputta, are grateful and mindful of what has been done for them.
