Therefore, Sāriputta, let that brahmin go forth and receive full ordination. Thus he is mentioned in the *Aṭṭhuppatti* (the introductory narrative) of the *Alīnacittajātaka*.

It appears in the context of a specific occasion (aṭṭhuppatti). "Of treasures" (nidhīnaṃ) refers to jars of treasure filled with gold, silver, and so forth, which have been buried and deposited here and there.
"A provider" (pavattāraṃ) means one who, out of compassion for people living in hardship and poverty, says: "Come, I shall provide you with a means of living in comfort."
It is like one who, having led another to the location of a hidden treasure, extends his hand and says, "Take this and live happily," to the one who points it out.

Regarding "one who sees faults" (*vajjadassin*): there are two kinds of those who see faults—the seeker of flaws who thinks, "I will restrain him in the midst of the Saṅgha for this impropriety or this lapse"—and [the other], for the purpose of making known what is not yet known and for the purpose of favoring what is already known.
It is also established by its nature of uplifting through the examination of various faults out of a desire for the growth of one's virtue and so forth;

this is what is intended here. For just as a person in distress does not become angry, but rather becomes joyful, when someone shows him a hidden treasure—even if they threaten or strike him, saying, "Take this!"—in the same way, [one should not be angry] toward such a person regarding what is unbecoming.
Upon seeing a slip or a lapse, one should not become angry; rather, one should simply be pleased. One should even invite them, saying:
"Venerable sirs, you have performed a great service for me by standing in the place of my teacher and preceptor and instructing me;
please speak to me again."

One who does not speak reprovingly: for some, having seen an unseemly act or a lapse on the part of their student or others, thinks, "This person serves me diligently with the offering of mouth-water and other services;
if I speak to him, he will no longer serve me, and thus I shall suffer a loss. Being unable to speak to him because of this, he is one who does not speak reprovingly. He—

He scatters rubbish upon this teaching. But he who, seeing such a fault, reprimands it in accordance with the fault, sends him away, inflicts punishment, expels him from the monastery, and trains him—this one is called a "reprover," just like the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For this was said: "I shall speak, Ānanda, having reproved, having reproved."
“Having threshed it again and again, Ānanda, I shall speak; that which is the essence will remain.
“A wise person” means one endowed with the wisdom born of the Dhamma as nourishment (*dhammaoja*). “One such as this” means one should associate with and attend upon a wise person of this kind.
For a pupil who associates with such a teacher, it is better and not worse; there is only progress, not decline.
The Story of the Elder Mogharāja (234).
Regarding the phrase "in the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana" in the twelfth [story]: it refers to a city that had acquired this name because it was seized by one Kaṭṭhavāhana.
It is said that in the past, there lived in Bārāṇasī a certain carpenter who was peerless in his own craft; he had sixteen pupils.

Each one had a thousand pupils. Thus, those sixteen thousand and seventeen [additional] teachers and pupils, all of them making their living by depending on Bārāṇasī, went near the mountain, took timber from the trees, and right there completed various kinds of palaces.
Then, having constructed a raft and brought it across the Gaṅgā to Bārāṇasī, they...
If the king requires it, they construct and present him with a palace of one or seven stories.
If not, they sell these as well to support their wives and children. Then one day, the teacher reflects:
"It is not possible to live forever by the work of a carpenter; for this craft is difficult when one reaches old age."
He addressed his pupils, saying, "Sons, bring some small-jointed trees such as the udumbara. Having agreed, saying "Very well," they brought them.
He had a wooden bird constructed with them, entered its interior, and filled it with air using a bellows.
The wooden bird leaped into the sky like a golden swan-king and soared above the forest.
He descended in front of his pupils.
Then the teacher said to his students: "Dear sons, by making such wooden vehicles as these, it is possible to seize the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa.
You too, dear sons, make these; having seized the kingdom, we shall live. It is difficult to subsist by the craft of carpentry."
"Let us live. Having done so, they informed their teacher. Then the teacher said to them: "Which kingdom shall we take, dear ones?
"The kingdom of Bārāṇasī, Teacher. "Enough, dear ones; do not let this please you.
For even if we were to take that, we would still not escape the designation 'carpenter-king' and 'carpenter-prince'; it is a great [burden]."
"Jambudīpa; let us go elsewhere. Then, together with their wives and children, they mounted wooden wagons, equipped themselves with weapons, and set out toward the Himālaya.
Having entered a certain city in the Himālaya, they established themselves right in the king’s residence.
Having seized the sovereignty there, they consecrated the teacher in the kingship. He [was known as] Kaṭṭhavāhana.
Because he became famous as "the King," that city received the name "Kaṭṭhavāhana-nagara" (The City of the Wood-Carrier) because it was taken by him.
*Tapacāraṃ* means the practice of asceticism (*tapacaraṇaṃ*). He sat upon a stone slab at the Pāsāṇacetiya;
that is, he sat in the great pavilion built by Sakka on the stone slab which had acquired the common designation "Pāsāṇaka-cetiya. It is said that there, upon a large rock...
Formerly it was a place for deities, but when the Blessed One appeared, it became a monastery;
yet, by virtue of its former designation, it is called "Pāsāṇacetiya.
Having been asked by him, the second [monk] then asked the Teacher a question.
“Bāvari asks concerning the head and the striking of the head;
may the Blessed One explain that, and dispel our doubt, O Seer.
When this question had been thus asked by him, and the Blessed One—
“Know that ignorance is the seal, and true knowledge is that which destroys the seal;
it is joined with faith, mindfulness, concentration, desire, and energy.
When this question had been answered, he became the second [questioner] and asked another question.
Then he... spoke this question:
"How is it that the King of Death does not see one who contemplates the world?"—when this question was asked by him—
“Behold the world as empty, Mogharāja, always mindful;
having uprooted the view of self, thus may you be a crosser of death.
To one who beholds the world in this way, the King of Death does not see.”
He answered the question.

"The rest of the people" means the remaining persons assembled in that gathering. "Are not mentioned" means they are not spoken of by way of such statements as "so many are stream-enterers," and so forth. Thus, this narrative background arose in the Pārāyana section;
it arose within the Pārāyana-vagga. The commentary on the fourth *Etadagga-vagga* is finished.
The commentary on the Therapāḷi is finished.
14. The Chapter on the Foremost (Etadagga-vagga) (14). 5. Commentary on the Fifth Chapter on the Foremost (Pañcama-etadagga-vagga-vaṇṇanā).
The Story of the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
In the commentary on the first verse of the *Therīgāthā*, regarding the phrase "that is, Mahāgotamī," some read it as "that is, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
In that context, "Gotamī" refers to her clan name (*gotta*). However, on the day of her naming ceremony, she received great honor...
The brahmins, having observed the perfection of her marks, prophesied:
"If she obtains a daughter, she will become the chief queen of a universal monarch; if she obtains a son, he will become a universal monarch.
In either case, they declared, "Her progeny shall indeed be great. Therefore, both from the lineage of her sons and the lineage of her daughters...
And because of her great size, they addressed her as “Mahāpajāpatī. Combining both [names], she is called “Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
“Alms-food by turn” means alms-food that should be given in rotation. “They gave her a name” means they gave her a name consisting of her clan-name (*gotra*).
“Maternal aunt” means the younger mother; for a mother’s sister is called a “maternal aunt” (*mātucchā*). “At the conclusion of the *Kalahavivāda-sutta*...”

This was stated according to the narrative tradition of the Aṅguttara reciters at the conclusion of the *Kalahavivāda-sutta* found in the *Suttanipāta*, beginning with the words: “From where do quarrels and disputes arise?
Others, however, say it was at the conclusion of the *Attadaṇḍa-sutta* found in that same *Suttanipāta*, beginning with the words: “Fear has arisen from the rod of oneself.”
Regarding the phrase "those who have gone forth after having left [the world]," they say that these are those who have gone forth by means of the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) ordination.
For this very reason, it is stated in the commentary on the *Attadaṇḍa-sutta* in the *Sutta Nipāta*:

"At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred Sākiyan princes and Koḷiya princes went forth by means of the 'Come, monk' ordination; taking them with him, the Blessed One entered the Great Forest."
The rest here is easily understood.
Regarding the story of the Elder Nun Khemā (236):
"In the second [verse], 'having become included among others' means having become a slave to others. 'He was tawny like liquid gold' means he was as if tawny with liquid gold."

"Like a spider with its web": just as a spider, having spun a thread-web, lies in its center at the navel-circle, and when a grasshopper or a fly falls upon the edge, it goes swiftly, pierces it, drinks its sap, and returning once more, settles down in that very same place;
even so are those beings who are stained by passion and corrupted by hatred.
Deluded by ignorance, they follow the stream of craving they themselves have created; they are unable to transcend it, and thus it is difficult to cross.

"Having cut even this, the wise go on"—the meaning is that the wise, having severed this bond, being without longing and free from attachment, go forth, proceeding by means of the path of arahantship after abandoning all suffering.
The Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā (237).
The third [story] has its meaning already explained.
The Story of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā.

238. "Even with a hundred gatekeepers" means even with a hundred doors. For the word *paṭihāra* is seen to refer both to gates and to doorkeepers. "To one's own family circle" means to the vicinity of one's own home.
"For protection" means for the state of being protected, for the purpose of a refuge. "Relatives" refers to those remaining kinsmen and friends, setting aside sons and fathers.
"Of one seized by the ender" means of one overcome by death. For in the course of worldly existence, sons and the like—

Although they have been a refuge by means of giving food, drink, and so forth, and by rescuing one from arisen misfortunes, at the time of death they are incapable of warding off death by any means whatsoever; therefore, they do not exist as a refuge or a shelter.
For this very reason it is said: "There is no refuge among kinsmen."
Knowing this reason— that they are unable to provide refuge for one another—
the wise person, being restrained and protected by the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*),
should quickly clear the Eightfold Path leading to Nibbāna; such is the meaning.
The Story of the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā (239).
Regarding the phrase "in the fifth state of dependence on others": this refers to the status of a slave to others.
It is said that the Elder Sujāta performed a meritorious deed by selling her own hair and giving the proceeds as an offering to the Chief Disciple named the Elder Sujāta.
He made an aspiration; it is with reference to this that it was said. "When his hand was extended" means when his hand was extended for the purpose of supporting him, according to his former habit.
It is said that he, having become a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), did not come as he used to on other days—looking here and there, smiling, and laughing—but rather came with his faculties calmed.
With a peaceful mind, he departed. Dhammadinnā, having opened the lion-window and looking out at the street, saw the manner of his approach; thinking, "What could this be?
she went to meet him and, standing at the top of the stairs, extended her hand to offer support. The lay follower withdrew his own hand.
She thought, "I shall know at the time of the morning meal. Previously, the lay devotee used to eat together with her;
however, on that day, without having consulted her, he ate alone like a monk devoted to yoga. Therefore it is said:
"Even while eating, he did not speak, saying, 'Give this,' or 'Take this. In this context, "give this" means...
"Give hard food or soft food; take this away"—that is, take away this hard food or soft food.

"On account of intimacy" means on account of intimacy through the defilements. Being urged by a perfection of causes that was nurtured over a long period and shining within like the flame of an oil lamp in a jar, she said: "This being so... [pe] ...for me."
“Grant me the going forth.
Thus, even while remaining in the midst of his home, the merchant brought an end to suffering. For it is said that when [the Buddha] said, “Dhammadinnā, there is no fault in you;
however, from this day forward, because of our intimacy… [and so on] … I shall go to my family home,” she [responded].
She thought thus: “There is no ordinary person who speaks in such a manner; surely he has realized the supramundane Dhamma.
Therefore, this thought occurred to her: “This merchant, while remaining right in the midst of his home, has brought an end to suffering.
However, in the *Madhyamāgama-ṭīkā*, it says: “Then, why [did she think] with me...”
He thought: “One should not even engage in mere conversation as one normally would;
this so-called supramundane Dhamma is weighty and solemn, it should not be disclosed. Yet, if I do not speak of it, she will tear her heart asunder and die right here.
Out of compassion for her, he spoke: “Dhammadinnā, I [have learned] from the Teacher...”
It is said: "Having heard the teaching on the Dhamma, one has realized what is called the supramundane Dhamma; for one who has realized that, such mundane activity is not appropriate.
Thus he asked a question concerning the five aggregates and so forth: "Venerable lady, it is said 'personality, personality'; what indeed is personality?"

“Noble lady, personality (sakkāya) has been spoken of by the Blessed One,” he asked, according to the method set forth in the Cūḷavedalla Sutta. To each question he was asked, he replied according to the very same method given there:
“Friend Visākha, these five aggregates of clinging have been spoken of as personality by the Blessed One,” and so forth.
“Sharpness” means keenness. [This refers to one] who has not yet attained the path of arahantship.
Because the question does not arise there without prior learning (*uggaha*), he said: “By way of learning, he asked even about the path to arahantship.
To turn that back, when it was asked, “But, noble lady, what is the counterpart to liberation?
and it was replied, “Liberation, friend Visākha, has Nibbāna as its counterpart,” [he asked] again: “But, noble lady, what is the counterpart to Nibbāna?”

When questioned, she turned him back and said, “You have overstepped, friend Visākha,” and so forth. Therein, “you have overstepped” (*accasara*) means that by asking what should not be asked, you have gone beyond the limit of the questions.

“She was unable to grasp the limit of the questions” means she was unable to grasp the measure of their boundary. For it is appropriate to grasp the limit of the questions at the point where they ought to end.
Having failed to stop after that, he continued to question and was unable to grasp the limit of the questions.
Furthermore, he asked about a counterpart for that which has no counterpart. This very nibbāna is without counterpart;
it is impossible to show it by making it a counterpart with any other phenomenon, such as saying it is blue or yellow. And yet, you ask about it with this intention.

The meaning is as follows: "Plunged into Nibbāna" (*nibbānogadha*) means having entered into Nibbāna and remaining there; the meaning is that it has penetrated into Nibbāna, being contained within Nibbāna.
"Having Nibbāna as its ultimate goal" (*nibbānaparāyaṇa*) means that Nibbāna is its supreme destination, its final resort; the meaning is that it does not go beyond that.
"Having Nibbāna as its conclusion" (*nibbānapariyosāna*) means that Nibbāna is its end and its limit.
"Pure" refers to the aggregates of the past. "Later" refers to the aggregates of the future. "In the middle" refers to the aggregates of the present.
"Possessing nothing" means one for whom there is no "something"—that is, the grasping of craving—regarding these three;
such a person, being without the "something" of lust and so forth, and being without grasping due to the absence of any seizing, I call a brahmin. This is the meaning.
"Learned" means endowed with wisdom, which is defined as proficiency in the elements, the sense bases, and so forth. For this has been said:

"In what way, venerable sir, is one learned? When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and impossible—it is in this way that one is learned."
“Ānanda, a bhikkhu is wise.
Regarding “of great wisdom”: she is endowed with a wisdom capable of discerning great meanings, great teachings, great linguistic expressions, and great inspired insights.
For this elder nun has attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) of one beyond training (asekha).
The greatness of wisdom through the state of abiding having fulfilled the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). "As it was by Dhammadinnā" means:
"I would answer in exactly the same way as the answer given by the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā. *Taṃ* is a particle used for emphasis.
The story of the Elder Nun Nandā.

240. In the sixth [verse], "not seeing another path" means not seeing another means (*upāya*). "Confident" means free from apprehension. "The sign of a woman" means the beautiful sign of a woman; what is meant is the aspect of beauty. "Having spoken the verse in the *Dhammapada*" refers to:
"A city is built of bones, plastered with flesh and blood, Wherein old age and death, pride and hypocrisy reside."
Having spoken this verse, the intended meaning therein is as follows:

Just as people build an external house known as a "city" by piling up timber for the purpose of supporting the roof-beams of the morning and evening meals, binding them with creepers, and plastering them with clay;
even so, this internal [body] is likewise composed of three hundred bones piled up, bound together by sinews, and plastered with flesh and blood.

This city was built for the purpose of laying out the cloak of skin over that which is covered by the decay characterized by aging, death characterized by mortality, pride characterized by arising in dependence on the attainment of health and so forth, and malice characterized by the destruction of well-done deeds.
For it is precisely such physical and mental affliction as this that has been laid down here. From this...
"There is nothing whatsoever to be grasped above"—
thus he spoke this sutta:
"Whether walking or standing, sitting or lying down..."
“He bends and he stretches—this is the movement of the body.
‘Bound together by bones and sinews, plastered over with skin and flesh, the body is concealed by the outer skin; it is not seen as it truly is.’”
With these words he spoke the sutta.
[The Story of the Elder Nun Soṇā, 241.
Regarding the statement, "In the seventh [chapter], he established all of them individually in the household life," here, "all of them individually" means—
It should be understood that after establishing her in the household life, [the father] thought, "My sons will look after me; what need have I for a separate family estate?

and thus divided and gave away all his property. For it was precisely because of this that from then on they did not even recognize her as "mother" when she came before them, thinking, "What will she do for us? Indeed, such was the case with her...

After a few days had passed, the wife of the eldest son said, "Oh, this man comes to our very house as if he were giving us two shares, saying, 'This is my eldest son! The wives of the other sons spoke in exactly the same way.
When he went to their houses, starting with the eldest daughter, they too spoke to him in the same manner. Thus, she was subjected to humiliation.
Having made this offering, she thought, "What is the use of living in their presence?
I shall live as a bhikkhunī," and having gone to the bhikkhunīs' quarters, she requested the going-forth; they ordained her. Demonstrating this very story, he said:
"Bahuputtikasoṇā, knowing their lack of respect toward herself, thought, 'What will I do with a household life? and having gone forth, she was ordained."
"Going to the monastery" means going to the monks' residence. "The supreme Dhamma" refers to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (*navavidha-lokuttara-dhamma*).

For that which is called the supreme Dhamma is such that even if one lives for a hundred years without seeing it, it is better to live for but a single day or a single moment if one sees and penetrates that Dhamma. "A guest person" (*āgantuka-jana*)...
He speaks with reference to the community of bhikkhunīs who had gone to the monastery. "Without having reflected" means without having carefully considered.
The story of the Elder Bhikkhunī Bakulā (No.
242) is the eighth; its meaning is self-evident.

The Story of the Bhikkhunī Kuṇḍalakesā (243). Regarding the ninth tetrad: it refers to the fourfold sequence of the cognitive process (*vīthicatukka*). A "tetrad" (*catukka*) is a collection of four. "From the prison" means from the jail. "Having raised up" means having lifted out.

"Even for a moment do not think" means that even for a moment, or at that very instant, one should contemplate the meaning appropriate to that occasion by means of *ṭhānuppattika-paññā* (wisdom arising from the situation).

One might be able to reflect upon it. Even a thousand verses that are composed of meaningless words—this verse was spoken by the Blessed One to the Elder Dārucīriya, and here too, this very same verse is presented.

In the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla also spoke this same verse in the account of the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesī. However, in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, in the account of the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesī—
“And though one should recite a hundred verses composed of meaningless words, a single verse of Dhamma is better, hearing which one attains peace.

This is the verse that has come down. Since it was stated in various places according to the narrative methods of different reciters, no contradiction between earlier and later passages by the Teacher should be suspected here.
The Stories of the Elder Nun Bhaddākāpilānī and the Elder Nun Bhaddākaccānā (244–245).
The tenth and eleventh [stories] are already clear in their meaning.
The Story of the Elder Nun Kisāgotamī.

246. "By the three austerities" means by the three austerities known as the austerity of the body (*vatthalūkha*), the austerity of the thread (*suttalūkha*), and the austerity of the dye (*rajanalūkha*). "White mustard seed" (*siddhatthaka*) refers to the seed of the mustard plant.
"Complete with children and cattle" means that having obtained children and cattle endowed with beauty, strength, and so forth, [one thinks]:
"My children are handsome, strong, wise, and capable of all tasks; my ox is healthy, handsome, and capable of carrying heavy burdens."
“‘My cow gives much milk’—thus one who is devoted to children and livestock;

whose mind is distracted (byāsattamanas) means one whose mind is attached precisely to whatever has been obtained among objects perceivable by the eye and so forth, such as gold and silver, or bowls and robes.
‘A sleeping village’ (suttaṃ gāmaṃ) means a body of beings that has fallen into sleep.”

"Like a great flood": just as a vast flood of a great river, in both depth and breadth, carries away everything from such a village—leaving behind not even a dog—so too does Death carry away a person of the aforementioned kind;
this is the meaning. "The deathless state" (*amataṃ padaṃ*): a portion free from death; the meaning is the great Nibbāna, which is deathless. The rest here is self-evident.
The Story of the Elder Nun Siṅgālakamātā, 247.
The thirteenth [story] has its meaning already explained.
(The commentary on the fifth section on "Foremost Among" is concluded.)
The commentary on the Therīgāthā is finished.
14. The Chapter on the Foremost (Etadagga-vagga) (14) 6. Commentary on the Sixth Chapter on the Foremost (Chaṭṭha-etadagga-vagga-vaṇṇanā)
The Story of Tapussa and Bhallika (248).
Regarding the commentary on the *Upāsakapāḷi*, "of those going for refuge first of all" means of those who go for refuge being the very first of all [lay followers].
"From here onwards" means after the seven-day period. "The cessation of the journey."

"Made [them turn back]" means he brought about the cessation of their journey. The meaning is that he acted in such a way that those oxen, having dropped their yoke, would not go forward even when beaten.
"Of them" refers to Tapussa and Bhallika. "Having resolved" means having infused [the intention]. "Yakkhāvaṭṭo" (the turning of a yakkha) is a compound of *yakkhassa* and *āvaṭṭo*.
The same applies to the remaining terms. "He looked to the practice of past Buddhas" means: by whom was the practice of past Buddhas... [observed]?
"Accepting with a vessel"—he looked to the practice established by the Buddhas.

"Having established themselves in the two-fold refuge through speech"—because the Saṅgha had not yet arisen, they established themselves in the two-fold refuge by way of the Buddha and the Dhamma. "Cetiya"—an object worthy of veneration.
"By means of the hair-relic of the living one"—by means of the hair-relic of the Blessed One while he was still alive.
Anāthapiṇḍika the Merchant’s Story 249.
"By that very same quality" means by that very quality known as the state of being a donor.
For he, because of his success in all desires, his freedom from stinginess, and his possession of qualities such as compassion, constantly gave alms to those who were destitute. By that—
Because he provided alms-food for the destitute at all times, he became known by the name Anāthapiṇḍika.
“Having built monasteries at intervals of a yojana” means having constructed one monastery every yojana.
Having said, “He established such a gift as this,” and wishing to analyze and demonstrate that very gift, [the Buddha said]: “Every day, five *salāka*-tickets of food...”
He said, beginning with “there are,” and so forth. In that context: *salākabhatta* is food to be distributed by means of tickets.
*Pakkhikabhatta* is food to be given on one day of a fortnight. *Dhurabhatta* is food to be given after setting aside [a portion] at the main house.
*Āgantukabhatta* is food to be given to visitors. The same applies to the remaining types as well. Five.
"Five hundred seats were always prepared in the house"— meaning that five hundred seats were perpetually arranged for the five hundred bhikkhus who would sit and eat in the house.
(The Story of the Householder Citta)
250. In the third [case], it was deer themselves who took the form of deer. "Having caused him to take alms" means:
having caused him to take them for the purpose of receiving alms by saying, "Venerable sir, please do me this favor; sit here and receive alms.

The proximate cause (upanissaya) was the wholesome state conducive to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya-kusala) accumulated with the aim of turning away from the round of existence (vivaṭṭa). He taught only the Exposition of the Six Sense Bases (Saḷāyatanavibhatti).
He delivered a discourse on the Dhamma connected specifically with the analysis of the six sense bases.
By "the Elder" is meant the Great Elder who was the eldest among all those assembled there. Regarding the phrase "unable to answer the question": this refers to the householder Citta, who [asked]:
"Venerable Elder, as for these various views that arise in the world, such as 'the world is eternal,' or..."

‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘the world is finite,’ or ‘the world is infinite,’ or ‘the soul and the body are the same,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another,’ or ‘a Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘neither...’
“...or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ or these sixty-two views enumerated in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*—
in what, venerable sir, do these views exist, and in the absence of what do they not exist?
When he was thus questioned with such questions, being unable to answer them, [he remained silent]— it is said that this question was asked up to three times.
When questioned, the Great Elder remained silent. Then the Elder Isidatta thought:
"This elder neither answers for himself nor requests another; moreover, this lay devotee harasses the Saṅgha of monks.
I shall answer him and thus provide him with a comfortable dwelling. Having thought thus, he rose from his seat and approached the elder.
Having gone there, he said, "Venerable sir, let me answer this question for the householder Citta.
When this was said, the Elder requested of Isidatta, "Friend Isidatta, please answer this question for the householder Citta.
Thus it is said: "He was requested by one who was unable to answer the question."
"Having answered the question": "Householder, these various views that arise in the world—whether 'the world is eternal' or 'the world is not eternal'...

[and so on]... and these sixty-two positions enumerated in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*—these views, householder, exist when there is the view of a real self (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*); they exist because of the view of a real self."
Having answered the question in the manner beginning with "When there is no [cause], they do not arise," [the Elder spoke].
"Known in his capacity as a lay companion" means that the householder knew the Elder’s status as a lay companion through his mind.

It is said that Citta the householder, being satisfied by the Elder’s explanation of the question, asked, "Venerable sir, from where has the noble Isidatta come? and [the Elder replied], "Householder, I have come from Avanti."
When he was told, "I am coming," Citta asked, "Venerable sir, there is a clansman named Isidatta from Avanti who is a friend of ours though we have not met;
has that venerable one been seen by you? The Elder replied, "Yes, householder.
When asked again, "Venerable sir, where does that venerable one dwell at present? the Elder remained silent. Then Citta...
The householder asked, “Venerable sir, is it our noble Isidatta?
When [the monk] replied, “It is so, householder,” he recognized him as his own lay companion.
Having displayed the miracle of the attainment of fire, on one day Citta the householder said, “It would be well for me...”
“Venerable sir, may the noble one display a miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) that transcends the human state,” he requested of the Great Elder.
The Elder said, “In that case, householder, spread out your upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) on the veranda and scatter a bundle of grass there.
When this had been done by him, the Elder entered his own dwelling, set a time-limit, and performed such a feat of psychic power (*iddhābhisaṅkhāra*).
He directed his mind so that the flame, having escaped through the keyhole and the crack between the door panels, burned the grass but did not burn the upper robe.
Then Citta the householder, having shaken out his upper robe, was moved with emotion and his hair stood on end;
standing to one side, he saw the elder emerging and said, "May you find delight, venerable sir."
“Venerable sir, Ambāṭakavana in Macchikāsaṇḍa is delightful; I shall provide for the Venerable one’s needs regarding robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Thereupon, the Elder, thinking, “It is no longer possible to dwell here,” departed from that monastery. With reference to this, it was said:
“Having displayed the miracle of the attainment of fire, [he thought], ‘Now it is not fitting to dwell here,’ and [departed] at his pleasure.”
“He departed. Regarding the passage beginning with “the two chief disciples,” whatever needs to be said has already been set forth in detail in the Vinaya Piṭaka.
“Faithful” means endowed with both mundane and supramundane faith.

“By virtue” refers to the two kinds of virtue—virtue of the householder and virtue of the homeless; here, the virtue of the householder is intended, meaning one who is endowed with that. “Endowed with fame and wealth”:

The meaning is that he is endowed with the same kind of fame as that possessed by Anāthapiṇḍika and others—consisting of a retinue of five hundred lay followers—as well as the two kinds of wealth: material wealth such as money and grain, and the sevenfold noble wealth.
"In whatever region" means in any direction, such as the east, where such a son of good family resides.
The meaning is that whatever place he frequents, there he is honored with such gains and respect.
[This concludes] the story of Hatthaka Āḷavaka (251).

In the fourth [section], "by means of the four bases of sympathy" refers to what is known as generosity (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*piyavacana*), beneficial conduct (*atthacariyā*), and impartiality (*samānattatā*).

By means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*). In order to make clear the matter already stated—that [the messenger] was to be sent to Āḷavaka along with a meal for the following day—he said: “In this regard, this is the sequential account,” and so forth.
Having gone to the forest for the sake of hunting deer, King Āḷavaka abandoned his various theatrical performances and enjoyments, and for the purpose of warding off thieves...
Going out for a hunt every seventh day for the purpose of suppressing rival kings and for the sake of physical exercise,
he once went to the forest for the hunt with his army, having established a rule that "the side from which the deer flees shall bear the responsibility.
There, he [saw] a single deer— an eni-deer— that had fled from the spot where he himself was standing.
"Having pursued" means having pursued alone for a journey of three *yojanas*. For the king, endowed with great speed, took up his bow and pursued that deer on foot for those three *yojanas*.
"Having killed" means that since the *eṇi* deer possess a speed of exactly three *yojanas*, he killed that deer when its speed was exhausted as it stood having entered the water. "Having cut in two."
"Having lashed it to the tip of his bow and returning," means that even though he had no need for the meat,
he was returning after lashing the deer— cut in two— to the tip of his bow in order to clear himself from the reproach, "He failed to catch the deer.
"Sandacchāyam" means dense shade, with thick leaves and foliage.
"The deity dwelling in the tree" refers to the *yakkha* Āḷavaka.
For he, having received a boon from the Great Kings, dwelt there at midday, devouring living beings who entered the area covered by the shadow of that tree.
"He sat upon the seat-couch where Āḷavaka used to sit" means in that [place] which was well-known...
On auspicious days and such occasions, Āḷavaka would sit and enjoy his glory; he sat upon that very same celestial jewel-couch.
When his own departure was not being accomplished, he reflected, "What indeed is the cause?
At that time, it is said, Sātāgira and Hemavata, having paid homage to the Blessed One right there in Jetavana, [thought], "We shall go to the assembly of yakkhas."
Accompanied by their retinues, they travel through the air by means of various vehicles. However, there is not a path for the *yakkhas* everywhere in the sky;
rather, having avoided the celestial palaces (*vimānas*) situated in the air, the path exists only where the way is clear.
But Āḷavaka’s palace was built on the ground, well-guarded, surrounded by a wall, with its gates, watchtowers, and gatehouses well-arranged, and covered above by a bronze lattice like a casket.
It was three *yojanas* in height, and above it was a path; having reached that place, they were unable to proceed further.
Indeed, no one is able to go from the spot where the Buddhas sit upward as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*);
therefore, when their own progress failed, they reflected, "What now could be the cause?"—such was their conversation.

Having heard this, he thought: "Since a discourse on faith is as ill-suited for one lacking faith as a discourse on virtue is for those who are immoral, therefore, upon hearing the Blessed One’s praise from these *yakkhas*, his heart was set ablaze with internal rage—like salt or gravel cast into a fire—and he thought thus.
'The mountain peak' refers to the peak of Mount Kelāsa."
From this point onward, the battle with Āḷavaka should be related in detail.
It is said that standing on the surface of the emerald with his left foot, he thought, "Behold now whether your Teacher is of great power, or I!
With his right foot, he struck Mount Kelāsa-kūṭa, which was about sixty yojanas away; like a ball of iron struck by an iron hammer, it emitted sparks of flying fire.

Standing there, he proclaimed, "I am Āḷavaka! and his voice resounded throughout the entire Jambudīpa. By the power of the yakkha, even the Himālaya mountains, extending for three thousand leagues, trembled.
Thinking, "By this very means I shall drive the ascetic away," he unleashed a whirlwind;
and from the east and other directions, winds arose measuring half a league, one league, two leagues, and three leagues.

Having split mountain peaks and uprooted forests, thickets, trees, and the like, they rushed toward the city of Āḷavī, pulverizing old elephant stables and other structures, and scattering roof-tiles and bricks through the air.
The Blessed One resolved, "Let there be no harm to anyone.
When those winds reached the One of Ten Powers, they were unable to move even the hem of his robe. Then, a great rain fell.
He raised [the clouds], thinking, "I shall kill the ascetic by drowning him under water.

Through his supernatural power, clouds consisting of layers of hundreds and thousands of folds arose one after another and rained down. By the force of the torrential rain, the earth was rent asunder.
A great flood came over the forest trees and other things, yet not even a drop the size of a dewdrop fell upon the Blessed One’s robe.
He was unable to terrify him. Thereupon, he raised a rain of stones.
Massive mountain peaks, smoking and blazing, came through the air and, upon reaching the One of Ten Powers, turned into divine bouquets of flowers.
Then, he raised a rain of weapons: swords with single edges, double edges, spears, arrows, and the like, all smoking.
Blazing forth, they came through the air and became divine flowers at the feet of the One of Ten Powers.
Then he raised up a rain of embers; embers the color of *kiṃsuka* flowers came through the air and, having become divine flowers, scattered at the feet of the One of Ten Powers.
Then he raised up a rain of hot ashes; the exceedingly hot ashes came through the air...
It fell at the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers (the Dasabala) as sandalwood powder. Then it raised a rain of sand;
the exceedingly fine sand, smoking and blazing, came through the air and fell at the feet of the Dasabala as divine flowers.
Then it raised a rain of mud; that, smoking and blazing, came through the air...
Having become a divine fragrance, it fell at the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers (*dasabala*). Then, thinking, "I shall terrify the ascetic and cause him to flee," he produced a darkness.
Having become like a darkness endowed with four factors, it reached the One Possessed of Ten Powers and vanished, like darkness struck by the radiance of the sun.
Thus, with these nine showers—the wind, the rain, the stones, the blows, the embers, the glowing coals, the sand, the mud, and the darkness—the *yakkha* [attacked].
Failing to frighten the Blessed One away, he himself approached the Blessed One with a fourfold army crowded with various kinds of spirit hosts, their hands bearing many sorts of weapons.

Those spirit hosts performed many kinds of transformations and seemed as though they were coming upon the Blessed One, crying out, "Seize him! Strike him! Nevertheless, [the Blessed One appeared] like a ball of iron that has been thoroughly heated.
Like flies, they were simply unable to approach the Blessed One.
Thus, even after displaying many kinds of terrifying forms throughout the entire night, being unable to move the Blessed One, Āḷavaka thought:
"What if I were to discharge a weapon that is invincible to anyone? For if he...
If an angry person were to discharge that weapon of cloth into the sky, the rain would not fall for twelve years.
If he were to discharge it onto the earth, all trees, grasses, and so forth would wither away and would not grow again for twelve years.
If he were to discharge it into the ocean, it would dry up entirely, like a drop of water on a heated pan. If [he were to discharge it] upon Mount Sineru...
It would release [the bolt] and scatter it into pieces. He released his upper garment as a weapon of such great power and seized it.
For the most part, the deities of the ten-thousandfold world system gathered together with speed, thinking, "Today the Blessed One will subdue Āḷavaka;
we shall hear the Dhamma there. There were also deities who desired to witness the battle.
They gathered together. Thus, the entire sky became filled with deities.

Then Āḷavaka, moving back and forth near the Blessed One, released his cloth and weapons. Like a thunderbolt wheel, making a terrifying sound in the sky, smoking and blazing, it reached the Blessed One;
for the purpose of humbling the yakkha’s pride, it [became] a foot-wiping cloth.

Having offered the sacrifice, he fell at his feet. Seeing him, Āḷavaka became like a bull with its horns broken, like a snake with its fangs pulled out—bereft of splendor, devoid of pride, and with the banner of his conceit cast down. Thus should this battle with Āḷavaka be related in detail.
He asked eight questions:
“What indeed is the wealth of a person that is most excellent?
What indeed is well-practiced that brings happiness?
What indeed is the sweetest of all tastes?”
“How should one live that they call the best way of life?”—with these and other words he asked eight questions. The Teacher replied:
“Faith is the supreme wealth for a person in this world... and so forth.
“Dharma well-practiced brings happiness;
truth indeed is the sweetest of tastes;
they say that a life lived with wisdom is the best.”
He answered with "Ādinā. "Vikkandamānāyā" means while she was wailing excessively.
In the fifth [case], the Teacher did not give a formal undertaking beyond that; this refers to the fact that the formulation of the training rule occurred after one year.

the point here is this: that [offense] is assigned to a worldling (puthujjana) alone, just as the volition to kill...
Even when it has a present object, the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) occurs by taking that object as its support through the process of severing the continuity [of the kamma-result];
the volition of giving (cāgacetanā), however, does not function in this way. For that volition merely consists in the act of giving after having taken the object to be given as its support;
and that "giving" consists in making that object the property of another. Therefore, it is only when the object has been made the property of another that it is truly said to have been "given."

"It flows with blood" means that it becomes accumulated through being agitated by impact. "Larger" means heavier. "As in the case of tending to the body" means as in the case of tending to the physical body of the Teacher.
"Not having assembled" is an indication of concord. "And there is a schism" means there is a schism in the Saṅgha.

"It is permissible" means by way of perception—that is, with the perception that "performing such an act does not lead to a schism in the Saṅgha. Likewise, "from nine [monks] or less in the assembly..."
For one who acts with an assembly of fewer than nine, it should be joined with the word "likewise" (*tathā*).

By this term "likewise," the phrase "it is not an ānantariya-kamma" is drawn forward, but not the phrase "there is indeed a schism. For, at the very least, a schism in the Saṅgha occurs by means of a group of nine.

Those who speak according to the Dhamma are blameless because they do not persist in what is contrary to the Dhamma. The preliminary stage to a schism in the Saṅgha is a "fracture in the Saṅgha" (*saṅgharāji*).
They fulfill the door of the body alone, because they are to be characterized precisely by the nature of bodily action. As for the statement, "By those who remain...
it is released for an aeon (*kappa*)," this does not accord with the *Kappaṭṭha-kathā*. For therein, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said:
"'One bound for the states of misery'—this sutta means that if he were to divide one aeon into eighty parts and should remain for even a single part of that time..."

"It was said with reference to an *āyukappa* (a lifespan-aeon). And as for the phrase "only at the destruction of the *kappa*," since the meaning is "only at the destruction of the lifespan-aeon," there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, in this context, the expression "as it is settling" is also stated by way of an unreal conceptualization (*abhūtaparikappa*), as if saying, "it will be destroyed tomorrow.
[The being] is cooked in hell for only a single day; beyond that, since there is no *kappa*, there is also no lifespan-aeon.
The application of the meaning should be understood by way of non-contradiction. "The others" refers to the other deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*) besides schism in the Saṅgha.

If those [other deeds] are included under the designation of "deeds that have already come to fruition" (*ahosi-kamma*), then how can they be called "of immediate retribution," given that there is no yielding of result immediately after death?
Alternatively, if there is a yielding of a fruit, then the time for their fruit is indeed immediately after death and not otherwise.
Certainty is intended by way of the restriction of the time of the fruit, not by way of the restriction of the giving of the fruit.

If it were otherwise, then certainty would also apply to other [karmas] whose fruit-time is restricted—namely, those to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) and those to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*)—even when they do not ripen due to the deficiency of other conditions and so forth;
therefore, [certainty applies] to those things possessing the nature of ripening (*vipākadhammadhamma*) by virtue of their own intrinsic nature, even when they do not ripen.

Just as the state of being subject to ripening (vipākadhammatā) remains fixed by its own nature even when the fruit is not yet ripening—once the fruit has been given by a powerful immediate karma (ānantariya)—so too the occurrence of immediate karmas, though their fruits have not yet ripened, possesses a fixed nature regarding the giving of the fruit and is of the nature of an immediate karma.

Thus, the state of being an immediate karma (ānantariyatā) should be understood as fixed precisely by the necessity of the giving of its fruit through its own inherent nature. And it must necessarily be of the nature of an immediate karma, and for that very reason, of a fixed nature.
And this must be accepted: that their occurrence [is such] because, in the absence of another stronger immediate (*ānantariya*) karma, they invariably yield their fruit immediately after death.

But would it not follow that, for others as well—namely, those karmas to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*)—if there were no other giver of ripening, they too would necessarily yield their fruit immediately after death?
Does it follow that the process [of kamma] possesses a fixed nature and a nature of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) because it gives its fruit exclusively? It does not so follow;

for its result is to be averted by a volitional aspiration (*cetopaṇidhi*) of a different class or by a counteracting factor, and thus there is an absence of the quality of giving its fruit exclusively in the immediately following [moment].
However, this is not the case for the "immediate" first jhānas and so forth, in relation to the second jhānas and so forth.
There exists no mental aspiration that is dissimilar [to the action] and capable of producing a different fruit, because all *ānantariya* (immediate) karmas have Avīci as their fruit;

nor is there any mental aspiration capable of averting the fruit of an *ānantariya*—which produces rebirth in a higher realm—just as the mental aspiration of a virtuous person seeking rebirth in a lower realm [averts a higher one], because one is cast into Avīci even against one's will; nor is there anything that can destroy the *ānantariya*.
There is some karma; therefore, their immediate succession (*ānantara*) is a state of occurrence whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is to produce exclusively a result.

Furthermore, even when many deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) have been committed, because they possess an intrinsic nature fixed toward a result exclusively, and because there is no possibility of their ceasing to ripen, they are determined by their very nature to be fixed.
Among those [deeds] which share a common nature, once the result has been given by one, the others—
Because the task that ought to be performed by oneself has already been accomplished by that very act, they do not produce a second or even a third rebirth-linking;
nor is it due to a failure of capacity. Thus, there is no cessation of their status as having committed an immediate offense (*ānantariya*);
however, since a state of being increasingly grave is indeed applicable to them, he said, "by which... [it] ripens," in order to show that schism in the Saṅgha may be even more grave.
Furthermore, it should be understood that for one [type of kamma], others serve as supporting conditions.
By the statement "it ripens by way of rebirth-linking," it appears as if the giving of result during the course of existence (pavatti) for the others is thereby permitted.
The construction is: "Or she is not virtuous in the same way" means that she is not virtuous in the same manner as her father was virtuous. If the mother is virtuous, [then] matricide...
The construction is: “it ripens by way of rebirth-linking. “A regular monk” (*pakatatta*) means one who has not been suspended.
“Belonging to the same communion” (*samānasaṃvāsaka*) means one who is not guilty of a defeat (*pārājika*). “Within the same boundary” (*samānasīmāyaṃ*) means within a single boundary. 276.

“Unable to perform the Teacher’s duty” means unable to perform that which is the Teacher’s duty to do, such as instruction and so forth; thus, having rejected the Blessed One. “Another founder of a sect” (*aññaṃ titthakaraṃ*) means another teacher. For this has been said:
“The ford must be known; the founder of the ford must be known; the followers of the ford must be known; the disciples of the followers of the ford must be known.
In this context, ‘the ford’ refers to the sixty-two views. For here, teachers cross over, float, and perform the act of emerging and submerging;
therefore they are called ‘fords. One who gives rise to such views is called a ‘founder of the ford,’ such as Pūraṇa Kassapa and others.”
"Those who have gone forth having adopted his doctrine are called 'titthiyas. For they are called *titthiyas* because they were born on a 'ford' (*tittha*).
Alternatively, they are called *titthikas* because this 'ford,' which consists of the aforementioned wrong views, belongs to them; and *titthikas* themselves are *titthiyas*.
Those who provide their requisites should be understood as 'titthiya disciples.'"

277. Regarding birth and so forth: the "birth-field" (*jātikhetta*) consists of ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), which are capable of being affected by such events as the shaking [of the earth] or the approach of deities. The "command-field" (*āṇākhetta*) is the sphere where his command operates by its mere power. The "range-field" (*visayakhetta*) is the sphere that constitutes his objective range. Together with this world-system known as the "ten-thousandfold world-system" (*dasasahassī lokadhātu*)— [The text continues: ...the Buddhas, having attained omniscience, do not know all things simultaneously; rather, they know them through the power of their knowledge. For it is said: "O monks, the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the past is unobstructed and unimpeded throughout the entire extent of the past. And so on, up to: "O monks, the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the future is unobstructed and unimpeded throughout the entire extent of the future. And: "O monks, the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the present is unobstructed and unimpeded throughout the entire extent of the present. Furthermore, it is said: "O monks, the Tathāgata knows the minds of beings as they truly are: he knows the mind with lust as a mind with lust, and the mind without lust as a mind without lust; the mind with hatred as a mind with hatred, and the mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; the mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, and the mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; the contracted mind as contracted, and the distracted mind as distracted; the great mind as great, and the small mind as small; the surpassable mind as surpassable, and the unsurpassable mind as unsurpassable; the concentrated mind as concentrated, and the unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated; the liberated mind as liberated, and the unliberated mind as unliberated. Thus, the Blessed One knows the minds of beings as they truly are. Moreover, it is said: "O monks, the Tathāgata knows the various elements as they truly are: he knows the element of earth as the element of earth, the element of water as the element of water, the element of fire as the element of fire, and the element of air as the element of air; he knows the element of the infinite space as the element of the infinite space, and the element of the infinite consciousness as the element of the infinite consciousness. Thus, the Blessed One knows the various elements as they truly are. Furthermore, it is said: "O monks, the Tathāgata knows the various dispositions of beings as they truly are: he knows the disposition of beings who have low dispositions as a low disposition, and the disposition of beings who have noble dispositions as a noble disposition; he knows the disposition of beings who have inferior dispositions as an inferior disposition, and the disposition of beings who have superior dispositions as a superior disposition; he knows the disposition of beings who have dark dispositions as a dark disposition, and the disposition of beings who have bright dispositions as a bright disposition; he knows the disposition of beings who have mixed dispositions as a mixed disposition, and the disposition of beings who have purified dispositions as a purified disposition. Thus, the Blessed One knows the various dispositions of beings as they truly are. Also, it is said: "O monks, the Tathāgata knows the various inclinations of beings as they truly are: he knows the inclination of beings who have low inclinations as a low inclination, and the inclination of beings who have noble inclinations as a noble inclination; he knows the inclination of beings who have inferior inclinations as an inferior inclination, and the inclination of beings who have superior inclinations as a superior inclination; he knows the inclination of beings who have dark inclinations as a dark inclination, and the inclination of beings who have bright inclinations as a bright inclination; he knows the inclination of beings who have mixed inclinations as a mixed inclination, and the inclination of beings who have purified inclinations as a purified inclination. Thus, the Blessed One knows the various inclinations of beings as they truly are. Moreover, it is said: "O monks, the Tathāgata knows the various faculties of beings as they truly are: he knows the faculty of faith in beings who possess the faculty of faith as the faculty of faith, and the faculty of wisdom in beings who possess the faculty of wisdom as the faculty of wisdom; he knows the dull faculty in beings who possess a dull faculty as a dull faculty, and the sharp faculty in beings who possess a sharp faculty as a sharp faculty; he knows the inferior faculty in beings who possess an inferior faculty as an inferior faculty, and the superior faculty in beings who possess a superior faculty as a superior faculty. Thus, the Blessed One knows the various faculties of beings as they truly are. Furthermore, it is said: "O monks, the Tathāgata knows the path leading to the attainment of all things as it truly is: he knows the path leading to hell as the path leading to hell, the path leading to the animal realm as the path leading to the animal realm, the path leading to the realm of hungry ghosts as the path leading to the realm of hungry ghosts, the path leading to the human realm as the path leading to the human realm, and the path leading to the heavenly realms as the path leading to the heavenly realms. Thus, the Blessed One knows the path leading to the attainment of all things as it truly is. Also, it is said: "O monks, the Tathāgata knows the destruction of the taints as it truly is: 'This is suffering,' 'this is the origin of suffering,' 'this is the cessation of suffering,' 'this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering'; 'these are the taints,' 'this is the origin of the taints,' 'this is the cessation of the taints,' 'this is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.

Knowing thus, seeing thus, my mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, my mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and my mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance. Being liberated, the knowledge arose: 'It is liberated. I directly knew: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. Thus, the Blessed One knows the destruction of the taints as it truly is. Furthermore, it is said: "O monks, the Tathāgata possesses these ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessing which, and relying upon which, he claims his place as the Bull of Men, utters his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel of Brahmā. Thus, the Blessed One possesses these ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessing which, and relying upon which, he claims his place as the Bull of Men, utters his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel of Brahmā. Also, it is said: "O monks, the Tathāgata possesses these four grounds of self-confidence, possessing which, and relying upon which, he claims his place as the Bull of Men, utters his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the supreme wheel of Brahmā. What four? O monks, regarding the claim: 'I am fully enlightened,' if any ascetic or brahmin, or any god, Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone in the world, should challenge me with a valid reason, saying: 'You do not possess full enlightenment in these things,' then let that be the basis for my fear, trembling, or horripilation. But since I see no such ground, I dwell secure, fearless, and untroubled, claiming my place as the Bull of Men, uttering my lion's roar in the assemblies, and setting in motion the supreme wheel of Brahmā. O monks, regarding the claim: 'I have utterly destroyed the taints,' if any ascetic or brahmin, or any god, Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone in the world, should challenge me with a valid reason, saying: 'These taints are not destroyed in you,' then let that be the basis for my fear, trembling, or horripilation. But since I see no such ground, I dwell secure, fearless, and untroubled, claiming my place as the Bull of Men, uttering my lion's roar in the assemblies, and setting in motion the supreme wheel of Brahmā. O monks, regarding the claim: 'These are the obstacles, and when one dwells with these obstacles, one cannot realize the supreme knowledge and vision, the higher knowledge and awakening, in this very life,' if any ascetic or brahmin, or any god, Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone in the world, should challenge me with a valid reason, saying: 'When one dwells with these things, one can still realize the supreme knowledge and vision, the higher knowledge and awakening, in this very life,' then let that be the basis for my fear, trembling, or horripilation. But since I see no such ground, I dwell secure, fearless, and untroubled, claiming my place as the Bull of Men, uttering my lion's roar in the assemblies, and setting in motion the supreme wheel of Brahmā. O monks, regarding
The ten-thousandfold world system stands surrounding this world-system.
That these alone constitute the field of birth [for a Buddha] is to be understood by way of the nature of things (*dhammatā*).

Some say it is "by way of its being encompassed," and they further state: "For all Buddhas, the field of birth is exactly that much; and only for the deities dwelling therein does there occur the realization of the Dhamma. [Regarding the phrase] "in the mother's womb":

The mention of only the six periods, such as the time of descent [into the womb], is merely by way of illustration, because that trembling is also obtained at times such as the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*).
What is called the "field of authority" (*āṇākhetta*) is that which contracts and expands all at once;
it is where the command prevails through the head-honored acceptance of the deities dwelling therein by that command—and this belongs exclusively to the Buddhas.
It is by its very power alone, not by way of intention. However, by way of intention, because of the statement, “Or as far as he might wish,” the command would indeed continue even beyond that.
But as for the statement, “They do not arise,” meaning “they exist,” it refers to such passages as, “I have no teacher; one like me is not found.”
Standing in the world-system and speaking, the Blessed One said:
"But, friend Sāriputta, are there now any other recluses or brahmins who are equal to the Blessed One in perfect enlightenment?
When asked thus, "Venerable Sir, I would say 'No,'" he spoke this in order to show the reason for it: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that in one [world-system]..."
The intention [of the Dhammasenāpati] who cited this sutta— “In a single world-system, two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones,
might arise neither before nor after one another”— is that, having set aside this world-system which constitutes a Buddha-field,
non-arising elsewhere is stated.
“Ekatā” means together; the meaning is “at one time. But how is that time delimited?
Showing that it extends from the moment of taking rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in the final existence until the Parinibbāna of the elements, he says, “Therein,” and so forth.
“Because of there being nothing wonderful” means because there is an absence of wonder even when both [Buddhas] arise. When both arise...
Showing that this is not surprising, let alone when it occurs among many, he said, "And if," and so forth. Buddhas are like gold broken into pieces, all identical;
thus their teaching is also of one flavor and one kind. He said, "Because there is no distinction in the teaching," thereby establishing its lack of surprise.
By the phrase "because of the absence of dispute," he indicates the purpose of the absence of dispute.
It shows that two Buddhas do not arise simultaneously. "This reason" refers to this reason consisting of non-rarity and so forth.
"Therein" means in the *Milindapañha*.
"Bearing only one Buddha" means being the support for a single Buddha (*ekabuddhadhāraṇī*). By this it is shown that these qualities of a Buddha are of such a nature that—
This shows that this world-system is incapable of bearing the second set of Buddha-qualities.
Indeed, it can be understood that the extraordinary weight of the specific qualities produced by particular conditions is difficult to bear even for the great earth.
For instance, at the time of his full enlightenment, the great earth could not sustain the burden of the qualities of the Lord of the World who had approached the Bodhi tree from three directions.

He was unable [to hold it]. Therefore, having stated "one should not hold it," he spoke the passage beginning with "it might move" (*caleyya*) and so forth, explaining that very non-holding through various synonyms.
Therein, "it might move" (*caleyya*) means it would quiver; "it might shake" (*kampeyya*) means it would tremble;

"it might incline" (*nameyya*) means it would lean to one side; "it might sink down" (*onameyya*) means it would subside; "it might bend in various ways" (*vinameyya*) means it would bend here and there in diverse manners.
“Vikireyya” means he would scatter it about like a handful of chaff by the wind. “Vidhameyya” means he would cause it to perish. “Viddhaṃseyya” means it would become completely shattered.
And being in such a state, it would not remain anywhere; thus he said, “it would not find a place to stand.
Now, showing an illustration for that, he said, “Just as, O Great King,” and so forth. In that context, “some men” refers to—
In one man. *Samupādikā*: it goes forth (*pajjati*) and proceeds (*pavattati*) equally upward, thus it is *samupādikā*;
the meaning is that it moves level across the surface of the water. They also read *samuppādikā*, which has the same meaning. *By color* means by shape. *By measure* means by height.
*By thinness or stoutness* means by the state of being thin or stout; the meaning is by circumference. *Of both as well*.
"Of both" means either two [people] or the weight of the bodies of both.
"Covering" means finding pleasure in it, generating a relish for it. "Become languid" means having become sluggish due to that food.
"Becoming like a non-bending staff" means becoming like a staff that cannot be bent because one is unable to bend over due to eating as much as one desires. "Eaten once"—
“Vameyya” means that having swallowed even a single morsel of food, one should vomit it up;
this is the meaning. “The earth trembles from the excessive burden of Dhamma”:

[the Elder asks] with the intention of questioning whether the earth, which indeed stands by means of Dhamma, would tremble and perish because of that very same Dhamma. Again, the Elder said: “In this world, a ‘jewel’ is that which sustains a household...”
And that which was seen by the world as the cause of the cart’s breaking— the excessive weight due to its own heavy nature—
was likewise esteemed by the wise for its excellence of benefit and happiness while supporting those who possess it; yet,
because of its heavy nature through its profound and immeasurable state, it became the cause of the earth’s quaking as an excessive burden.”
Showing this, he said, "In this case, Great King, there are two carts," and so forth.

By this very statement, it should be understood that the reason for the earthquake at the time of the Tathāgata’s descent into his mother’s womb and other such occasions has been described. "Of one" means from one;
the meaning is: having taken a jewel from one cart, from that cart.
*Osāritaṃ* means uttered; the sense is that it has been spoken. *Aggo* means the foremost among all beings.
*Jeṭṭho* means the eldest. *Seṭṭho* means the most praiseworthy. He is *visiṭṭho* because he is endowed with distinguished qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
*Uggatatamo* means the highest. *Pavaro* is a synonym for that same quality. *Asamo* means there is no one equal to him. The previous Buddhas were unequalled (*asama*).
"Equal to them" means equal to the unequaled (*asamasama*). "Without an equal" means there is no person who is his counterpart (*paṭisama*).
"Without a counterpart" means there is no one who is his match (*paṭibhāga*). "Without a rival" means there is no person who is his rival (*paṭipuggala*).
"Natural disposition" (*sabhāvapakati*) refers to a natural state that is intrinsic and beyond description. "Due to the greatness of the cause" means because of the magnitude of the causal factors.
It is said that the qualities of a Buddha are produced by great causes known as the *pāramīs*, which are the factors that constitute the state of a Buddha.

Just as the earth and other such things are vast entities, and as the great world-systems (*cakkavāḷas*) and so forth are each singular within their own respective domains, so too the Perfectly Enlightened One is great and singular within his own domain. And who is he?

What is its object? It is the Buddha-ground, or as much as there is to be known. By saying, "The Blessed One alone has an infinite range like space," he demonstrates that there is no second Buddha even in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
"By this very phrase" means by this very phrase, "of a single world-system. Ten thousand world-systems.
"Taken" means taken with reference to birth and field. "By this very single world-system" means by this very one, not by any other.

Just as when it is said, "They arise in this very world-system," it is appropriate to delimit it as being in Jambudīpa within this world-system, and even there, specifically in the Middle Country; so too [is it with] "of a single world-sphere."
Even when the "field of birth" (*jātikhette*) is intended, it is appropriate to delimit it by this very world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
The commentary on the first chapter is concluded.
15. The Text on the Impossibility (Second Chapter).
(15) 2. Commentary on the Second Chapter of the *Aṭṭhānapāḷi* 278.

"By way of the cessation of disputes" means by way of the causes that bring about the cessation of disputes. When two [parties] have arisen, whatever dispute might occur, the very non-arising of that is here what is meant by the "cessation of disputes.
By the phrase "in one island," etc., it is shown that even in another island, they do not [arise] together.

It arises; how much more so when it is shown by means of a single lamp. "He too would decline" means that he would decline because [the light] must function only within the region of a world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). 279–280.

"Human state" (*manussatta*) means the human condition, because it is the state suitable for the qualities such as going forth (*pabbajjā*). "Perfection of gender" (*liṅgasampatti*) means the male state.
"Cause" (*hetu*) means the perfection of causes preceded by the mental and verbal aspiration. "Seeing the Teacher" (*satthāradassana*) means being in the presence of the Teacher.

*Pabbajjā* (going forth) refers to the going forth among ascetics who profess the efficacy of ritual action (*kammakiriyavādī*) or among the monks (*bhikkhu*). *Guṇasampatti* (perfection of qualities) refers to the attainment of qualities such as the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
*Adhikāra* (service) means superior service rendered toward the Buddha; it is said to be a distinguished act of assistance, a superior honor (*sakkāra*).
*Chanda* is simply the state of desire (*chandatā*); it is the wholesome desire characterized by an exceptional eagerness to act for the sake of perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
"By the combination of eight factors" means by the conjunction of these eight qualities. "Resolution" (abhinīhāra) means the aspiration of the body.

"Succeeds" (samijjhati) means it is accomplished. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Paramatthadīpanī* commentary on the *Cariyāpiṭaka*.
"In every way complete" refers to the perfection of the characteristics [of a Great Man], such as being the supreme among beings and so forth.
It is indeed endowed with every aspect. For it is not possible for a woman to possess such things as the male organ being concealed within a sheath;
moreover, the second nature is indeed inferior to the first nature. Therefore he said in the subsequent section, beginning with "because," etc.
281. "In this world, for a man to be reborn there" means: for one who has become a man in this human world, to be reborn there.

Because they are reborn in the Brahma-world with the personal existence (attabhāva) of a Brahmā. By this, he shows that although the male sexual organ is absent, the Brahmās possess the appearance of males.
And it is with reference to that very male appearance that the Blessed One said: "If a man were to exercise the status of a Brahmā. For this very reason, he says:
"Even though [the organs] are the same," and so forth. If this is so, would not women fail to arise in the Brahma-world?
He said: “The state of a Brahmā,” and so forth (290–295).
By the Pāli passage beginning with “Of bodily misconduct,” the determination of kamma is explained. *Samañjanaṃ* means *samaṅgo*, which is *samannāgamo*;
one who possesses this is *samaṅgī* or *samannāgato*. Alternatively, one whose nature is to associate (*samañjanasīlo*) is *samaṅgī*; [this refers to] the prior stage.
From the collection of requisites onwards, there is possession of accumulation by way of the act of accumulating;

there is possession of volition by way of the volition that brings [the action] to completion. Alternatively, there is possession of accumulation by way of the continuum of volition, and possession of volition by way of each respective moment of volition.
There is possession of kamma by way of kamma that has been performed and accumulated, the result of which has not yet matured.
When karma has begun to ripen, there is "possession of fruition" by way of the occurrence of the result. There is "possession of presence" by way of the time when karma and so forth are present.
"At the moment of accumulating wholesome and unwholesome karma" means at the moment of striving toward wholesome and unwholesome karma.
By the word "thus" (*tathā*), the phrase "wholesome and unwholesome karma" is drawn forward. "As the karma was performed..."
It becomes capable of yielding fruit; thus it is "done" (*kata*) and "accumulated" (*upacita*). "Worthy of ripening" (*vipākāraha*) means worthy of ripening in the second existence and so forth.
The construction is: "the sign of rebirth (*upapattinimitta*) appears to those being reborn.

The "sign of rebirth" (*upapattinimitta*) is the cause or reason for the arising of rebirth—namely, karma, the sign of karma (*kammanimitta*), and the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*). [As stated] in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
However, the application has been shown by way of the sign of the destination alone. The appearance of both kamma and the signs of kamma should also be understood according to what is appropriate.
For it is said: "Those kamma-formations which were performed by him in the past, at that time they hang over him, hang down toward him, and dangle before him.
Thus, for one whose death is near, they appear like the shadows of great mountain peaks in the evening.
For a being, karma that has been given the opportunity to ripen in the mind—like in a dream—has its sign, the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*), standing before it.

"It moves" means it turns over. For when one kind of sign has appeared due to a particular karma, the appearance of another sign due to another karma by way of a specific condition is what constitutes this "turning over. The rest are motionless; that is, the remaining ones.
The fourfold possession (*samaṅgitā*) is immovable because it does not change.
"Dog-rider" (*sunakhavājika*) means one whose habit is to ride by means of dogs for the sake of hunting deer; the meaning is "dog-hunter.

"Flower-strewn worship" (*tala-santharaṇa-pūjā*) refers to the worship consisting of the covering of the ground's surface with flowers. "Volition of undertaking" (*āyūhana-cetanā*) is by way of the possession of kamma, namely, bodily misconduct.

By means of the volition that brings about completion through successive effort, by not being shaken from the very planning [of that action] due to the knowledge that brings about the destruction of karma, and by way of being possessed of the karma as it has been accumulated.
"Karma" refers to unwholesome karma. "At that very moment" means at the very moment of the effort. "Of that" refers to one who possesses the karma.
Heaven is barred for that person, meaning that if that karma were to obtain the opportunity for its fruition—that is the intended sense.
And the phrase "heaven is barred" is merely an illustration; his human world is also barred, so they say.

However, others—because the obstruction to fruition (*vipākāvaraṇa*) was not mentioned by the preceding [teachers], and because it was stated without qualification as "at that very moment"—in order to avoid that fault, [they explain] "accumulated karma..."

He said, beginning with the words, "By name," and so forth. The statement, "When karma obtains an opportunity for fruition," was spoken because there is no obstruction once an opening has been provided.

For instance, the Blessed One remained in seclusion regarding the matter of the third *pārājika* offense; however, since this sutta mentions one who "possesses bodily misconduct," the possession of the arising of fruition is not obtained here.
(The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
The explanation of the meanings not [otherwise] expounded in the commentary on the *Aṭṭhānapāḷi* is finished.
16. The Text on the Single Dhamma (*Ekadhammapāḷi*)
(16) 1. Commentary on the First Chapter of the Single-Dhamma Text (Ekadhammapāḷi-paṭhamavagga-vaṇṇanā) 296.
Regarding the commentary on the Single-Dhamma Text, the word *dhamma* here has the sense of "intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva*), as in such expressions as "wholesome states" (*kusalā dhammā*).
Thus he says: "of a single intrinsic nature. "Unilaterally" (*ekantena*) means "categorically" (*ekaṃsena*); the sense is "necessarily. "In the round" (*vaṭṭe*) refers to the round of saṃsāra.
“For the purpose of dispassion” means for the purpose of non-delight. “For the purpose of fading away” means for the purpose of non-attachment. “For fading away” means for dissolution;
therefore he said, “for the purpose of disappearance. “For the cessation of lust and so forth” means for the purpose of bringing about the cessation of lust and so forth by means of path-knowledge.
Since cessation by means of path-knowledge is the effecting of absolute non-arising, he said, “for the purpose of making [them] not arise.”
