Just as placing solid food in the mouth for the purpose of eating is only for the sake of swallowing it, so too the cessation of lust and the other defilements is solely for the sake of the cessation of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*); thus it is said: "or for the sake of the very cessation of the round.
Since, when the defilements are exhausted, the other two rounds are also necessarily exhausted, he therefore takes hold of the root itself.

“It approaches for the sake of the subsiding of the defilements,” he said. As for the "direct knowledge" (abhijānana) of conditioned phenomena, it occurs precisely through the application of the three characteristics therein; thus he said: “…for the sake of directly knowing impermanence and so forth.

The things to be fully awakened to (sambujjhitabba) are the Four Noble Truths, because there is no object of knowledge (ñeyya) apart from them. “For the sake of awakening to the four truths,” he said.
Having said this, in order to show by means of that knowledge through which this awakening (*bujjhana*) is accomplished, it was stated:
"Awakening is called... and so forth. "Of Nibbāna without conditions" means of the Deathless Element (*amatadhātu*).
"For the purpose of generating enthusiasm" means for the sake of producing delight in the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "Poison-thorn" is a conventional designation for sugar.
"‘In some place, the local dialect’—so say some. ‘Molasses’ (guḷa) is sugar-cane juice boiled to the point of equal consistency and mixed with powder and so forth, then formed into balls;

when not formed into balls, it is ‘treacle’ (phāṇita). Due to a particular degree of cooking, when it has broken into pieces, it is ‘crystal sugar’ (khaṇḍa); when it has reached a state free from impurities, it is ‘sugar’ (sakkarā).

It remembers, thus it is ‘mindfulness’ (sati). It remembers again and again, thus it is ‘recollection’ (anussati); alternatively, mindfulness that is appropriate [to the object] is also recollection. It is twofold."
"It occurs" is twofold by way of purpose: for the sake of gladdening the mind, which means for the sake of satisfying the mind in meditation by producing confidence toward an inspiring object;

and for the sake of insight, which means for the sake of the bliss of insight—for when the mind is concentrated through access concentration, it succeeds through the bliss of insight. "The arising of the mind" refers to the process of cultivation.
A state of consciousness has arisen. It is struck and buffeted because the object is repulsive. For that very reason, it becomes weary;
it neglects the meditation subject and loses its zest because the satisfaction derived from cultivation is not obtained. It becomes serene because the qualities of the Buddha are inspiring.
And thus, through the absence of the "thicket of the mind" such as doubt, it becomes free from hindrances. "Having tamed" means by the removal of the hindrances.
"Having made it free from agitation. Thus, showing a simile for the taming of the mind through the application of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he said, "How...
and so forth. "Who was this... who remembered? means: who was this that stood within me and remembered?

"Grasping [it]" is a demonstration of the absolute non-existence of a rememberer imagined by outsiders. Therefore he said: "There is no other whatsoever. "Having seen" refers to the method of searching.

"Having seen that it is precisely the mind of the aforementioned kind that recollects, [one realizes] 'all this'—that is, all this consisting of the differentiation of the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) and so forth.

Having briefly defined form and non-form as 'this is form' because its intrinsic nature is to be affected (*ruppana-sabhāvattā*), and 'the former is non-form' because it lacks that nature, one defines the five aggregates. This is the construction of the sentence.
“Sambhāvikā” means that which originates [the defilements]. “Of that” refers to the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*). “Cessation” (*nirodha*) means the sign of cessation.
“The section on absorption” (*appanāvāra*) is the concluding section of the teaching as it was begun. 297.

By the phrase “this same method,” it is indicated that the method of meaning (*atthanaya*) which was explained in the *Buddhānussati* by the passage beginning with “But this... and so forth, applies here as well.

The extension (*atidesa*) here—though stated as common to all nine recollections by way of their purpose—is set aside by this exception (*apavāda*), namely that in the case of the three subjects of insight such as mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), they function solely for the sake of insight;
thus, it should be understood that these [nine] share a single purpose.
Furthermore, there is the demonstration of the analysis of the compound term *dhammānussati* as "recollection of the Dhamma" (*dhamme anussati*).

He says, "This, moreover, is the word-meaning here," because [the phrase] "having taken the Dhamma as one's object" is a demonstration that the Dhamma is the objective domain for the recollection of the Dhamma.
This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. "Having taken virtue as one's object" means having taken one’s own virtue of purification as one’s object.
"Having taken generosity as one's object" means having taken one’s own quality of generosity as one’s object. "Deities..."

Regarding the word *ārabbha* (having taken as a basis): here, because of his resemblance to the qualities of the deities, he is designated by the same name as the deities—namely, in terms of his faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
For a designation for one thing is sometimes applied to something similar to it, as in the cases: "those medicines" or "this is Brahmadatta. Therefore, he said:
"having placed the deities in the position of witnesses," and so forth. In that context, "having placed the deities in the position of witnesses" means: "in whatever manner..."
Those deities who were endowed with faith passed away from here and were reborn there; such faith as theirs exists in me as well.
Those deities who were endowed with such virtue, such learning, such generosity, and such wisdom passed away from here and were reborn there; such wisdom as theirs exists in me as well.

"‘It exists’"—thus the deity is established in the position of a witness. The "sign of in-breathing and out-breathing" (assāsapassāsanimitta) refers to the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) obtained therein. "Attained" (gatā) means having approached and proceeded by way of making it an object.
"Cessation" (upasamo) is Nibbāna, because suffering ceases here. It is "ultimate cessation" because the three rounds of existence (vaṭṭattaya) cease absolutely herein.
Ultimate tranquility (*accantūpasamo*) is indeed Nibbāna. "Destruction" (*khayo*) means it destroys, consumes, or wears away; it is the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
That which brings about the very same [destruction] is "tranquility" (*upasamo*); it is the Noble Path itself. Thus, "the destruction and the tranquility" is *khayūpasamo*.

Now, since this state of tranquility is itself a phenomenon (*dhamma*), is the recollection of tranquility (*upasamānussati*) included within the recollection of phenomena (*dhammānussati*)? True, they are included as one, because of their commonality in being phenomena (*dhammabhāva*).

It has been stated separately, having extracted it from the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*), in order to demonstrate that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṅkhata-dhamma*) are superior because they possess the state of being most excellent and most sublime.
Indeed, with reference to this very distinction, the Blessed One, even after speaking of "recollection of the Dhamma" (*dhammānussati*),
spoke of "recollection of peace" (*upasamānussati*), because for one who recollects it, it appears as something particularly peaceful and sublime.

And having understood it thus, it should be seen that the inclusion of both "destruction" (khaya) and "subsiding" (upasaṃma) here is also capable of being justified. For just as, although the supramundane states are equal in their transcendental nature,
the state of Nibbāna is superior to the states of the Path and Fruition— according to such statements as, "Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are states, whether conditioned or unconditioned,
dispassion (virāga) is declared to be the foremost among them"— so too [is the inclusion of both terms justified].
The state of the path (magga-dhamma) is more wonderful than the state of the fruit (phala-dhamma) because of its abandonment of defilements;

therefore, it should be understood that the cessation through destruction (khayūpasama) is included along with the ultimate peace (accantūpasama). Why is it said that they exist only in the context of insight (vipassanā)?

Some say it is "because of such statements as 'for the sake of utter disenchantment' (*ekantanibbidāya*)," but that is not a valid reason, since such a teaching is also found in the recollections of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) and so forth.

Because they have come [to this state]. However, while meditation subjects such as the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati) serve both the purpose of developing insight (vipassanā) and the purpose of consolidating the sign (nimitta), these [meditations on the loathsome] do not do so;
rather, they serve solely the purpose of developing insight. Thus it was said.
The commentary to the First Chapter is concluded.
16. Ekadhammapāḷi (16) 2.
Commentary on the Second Chapter of the Ekadhammapāḷi 298.
That by which one sees wrongly, or that which sees wrongly itself, or the very act of wrong seeing—this is wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*).

Whatever constitutes a perverted view—therefore he said, "of the sixty-two kinds," and so forth. That which has wrong view is a "wrong-viewer" (*micchādiṭṭhika*); [the phrase] "of that wrong-viewer" refers to him. 299.
That by which one sees correctly, or which itself sees correctly, or which is merely the act of seeing correctly—that is right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).
"Fivefold" means fivefold by way of (1) the fact that one is the owner of one's kamma, (2) jhāna, (3) insight, (4) the path, and (5) the fruit.
Therein, knowledge included within the arising of a jhāna consciousness is right view of jhāna; insight-knowledge is right view of insight.
302. Inattention that proceeds by way of [viewing] the five aggregates as "permanent," etc., is unskillful attention.

303. The application of attention (*manasikāra*) proceeding by way of [the contemplation] beginning with “impermanent” (*anicca*) is [the preliminary stage]. “As far as the entry into the fixed course of rightness” (*niyāmokkama*) means as far as the entry into the fixed course of wrongness (*micchattaniyāmokkama*).
The method for entering the fixed course of wrongness, however, should be understood according to the manner explained in the commentary to the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* and its sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*).
304. This is said to be threefold and an obstacle to heaven (*saggāvaraṇa*) because it is extremely blameworthy due to having reached the state of a course of kamma (*kammapatha*).
Since there is nothing at all that can be said regarding its being an obstruction to the path when it is already an obstruction to heaven, it is stated: "and it is an obstruction to the path.
The ten-based false view consisting of the grasping of extremes, such as "the world is eternal," and so forth, is indeed an obstruction to the path because of its nature as a perverted vision;
however, the intention is that it is not an obstruction to heaven because it does not constitute a course of unwholesome action (akammapatha). This...
"But having rejected that formulation" means: "It is contradictory to say both that it is a wrong view and that it is not an obstruction to the Path," because of its being contrary to the Dhamma.
For if that were the case, one would have to admit the attainment of the Path even while the personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) has not yet been abandoned;
it is with this intention that he rejects the aforementioned formulation. "Not an obstruction to heaven" means not being a hindrance to rebirth in heaven.
Since those who speak [of such views] have even admitted that a view can lead to heaven, he, in rejecting that position, stated:
"A view is indeed incapable of leading one to heaven. Why? Because it is absolutely more blameworthy and more bitter in its consequence.
Therefore he said: "It causes one to sink exclusively into hell," and so forth.
305. "It destroys the round" means that right view of the path destroys both the round of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) and the round of kamma (*kammavaṭṭa*).

But what indeed destroys the round of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*)? It is said that right view of the fruit (*phalasammādiṭṭhi*) wards off existence—which has already been destroyed by its own cause—by way of providing an opportunity [for its cessation].
Thus, this is wholesome if it is capable of leading to Arahantship.
Thus, this non-attracting of rebirth-linking by insight is wholesome and blameless.
"It gives seven existences" means that the right view of insight, which serves as a condition for the path of stream-entry, gives seven existences to that person.
"In this way" is said with reference to all fivefold right view. Therefore he said: "Worldly and supramundane..."
"Right view has been explained. Regarding this meaning, however, it is said: "Monks, I do not see even a single thing...

and so forth; thus, it refers to the meaning comprised by the path leading to a destination. Because it is stated, "They are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world," it is said that these should be understood as merely mundane and productive of existence.

306. In the phrase *yathādiṭṭhi*, the word *yathā* is used in the sense of a desire for the exposition of meaning; therefore, it is a compound in which the meaning of the subsequent member is predominant.
Thus he says: “whatever view. “In accordance with each of those” means in conformity with each respective view.
“Entirely” means without remainder. Therefore he says: “complete. “Upheld” means equal and identical in the beginning, middle, and end.
"Having done" means taken up, grasped, and not relinquished. "That very thing" refers to what was stated by the passage beginning with "whatever bodily action," and so forth;
that is this bodily action. Regarding "bodily action established in a view":
as for the view that occurs in such ways as "there is no evil resulting from that [action]," for one who stands in that view—merely standing and not relinquishing it—[that is what is meant].

"Of one who possesses that view, bodily action": this refers to the bodily action co-arising with that view when such a person communicates their view to others by means of hand gestures and so forth;

it is the bodily action that arises simultaneously with that view. And no suspicion of verbal action should be raised here, because only [actions] such as the taking of life are intended. "Bodily action conforming to the view": as in the case of others...
It becomes manifest; thus, bodily action is performed having been made conformable to the view. Therefore he said:
"undertaken, grasped, adhered to. The passage beginning with "Therein," etc., is indeed easy to understand.

By the phrase "In this same way," [he refers to] verbal action consisting in speech established upon the aforementioned view, verbal action co-nascent with the view, and verbal action conformable to the view.
The phrase "it is threefold" and so forth is extended [to the other cases].

"Of one with wrong view" means of one who possesses wrong view that has reached the level of a course of action (*kammappatha*). Others say: "of one who is possessed of some kind of wrong view whatsoever.
"Co-nascent with the view" means the volition (*cetanā*) that arises simultaneously with the aforementioned view. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "Aspiration" (*patthanā*):

“‘I shall do this’—this is the aspiration of craving (*taṇhāpatthanā*). ‘By way of the aspirations of volition (*cetanā*)’ means by way of the mental concomitants of longing based on the aforementioned views (*diṭṭhigata*).

‘Fixing of the mind (*cittaṭṭhapanā*)’ means the directing of the mind toward an object. ‘Contact and so forth (*phassādayo*)’ refers to those phenomena such as contact that are distinct from volition, views, and craving.
Since the view is evil, therefore all those phenomena for that person lead to what is undesirable... [and so on].”
The construction is: "they lead to. "Of the former alone" means of the word *tittaka* (bitter) alone.
Both *tittaka* and *kaṭuka* (pungent) should be understood here as synonyms for the undesirable, as in such expressions as "later it will be pungent for you.

*Ambayo* means "this is a mango tree. "They honor that very same [tree]" means they honor that very same tree which previously received offerings such as being watered. *Nivesare* means they entered. *Asātasannivāsena* means by association with the unpalatable root of the nimba tree.
But having rejected that [view], it is stated... [as follows]: all wrong view, because it is exclusively blameworthy, leads to what is undesirable and to suffering;

this is the intended meaning of the statement. Regarding the phrase "having applied them in the immediately preceding sutta," they are to be understood as having been applied just as in the ninth sutta.
In the expression "the fixing of the mind itself is the aspiration," one should add the word "and the resolve" (*paṇidhi*).
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
16. Ekadhamma-pāḷi (16) 3.
Commentary on the Third Chapter of the Ekadhamma-pāḷi.

308. Regarding the first [type] of the third [person], "one with a view that is not according to reality" means one who has arisen views such as "permanent" regarding phenomena that are actually impermanent and so forth.
Therefore he said: "By that very wrong view, he is one of perverted vision.

Here, "saddhamma" refers to the true, praised, and beautiful Dhamma, which is also called the "human Dhamma" (*manussadhamma*). For it is from this [Dhamma] that one of wrong view would cause another to emerge.
Not from the standpoint of the noble Dhamma. Therefore he said: "From the standpoint of the ten courses of wholesome kamma. By the phrase "of such a kind," he includes Pāṭikaputta and others. 309.

"Omniscient Bodhisatta" means a Bodhisatta who possesses omniscience. By the word "etc.," those Bodhisattas for private enlightenment (paccekabodhisattas) who have fulfilled the perfections, as well as certain Bodhisattas for the disciple-vehicle (sāvakabodhisattas), are included.
310. "Supreme" means supreme by way of being highly blameworthy; the sense is that they have reached the highest degree. "Of these" refers to the deeds of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma).
“Delimitation” means the conclusion by way of result (*vipāka*). It is the root of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*);

therefore, the person possessing it is called a “stump of the round. Thus he said: “By that,” and so forth. If one does not relinquish that grasping, because it brings about the state of being [in saṃsāra] once again for him, it is said:
“There is no emergence from existence (*bhava*); however, this is not because there is an absolute absence of emergence. In whatever manner...

For it cannot be said that once this [unwholesome] view has arisen in dependence on its conditions, there will never again be a lifting of the head from it when dependent upon conditions opposed to it.
For this unwholesome state is weak and feeble, unlike the wholesome state which possesses great power.
Otherwise, just as with the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*), the certainty of wrongness (*micchattaniyāma*) would also be absolute.
It may be so, yet it is not an absolute certainty of wrongness (*micchattaniyāma*). For this very reason, it is said in the *Papañcasūdanī*:

"But is he fixed in this very same personal existence (*attabhāva*), or even in another? He is fixed in this very one; by way of habituation, he will find pleasure in that very view in another existence as well.
And for that same reason, it is also stated in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*:

Furthermore, when those who have adopted their doctrine sit at night or during the day in a standing or sitting posture and recite or investigate it—thinking, "No evil is done by the doer; there is no cause, there is no condition;
one who has died is annihilated"—then wrong mindfulness becomes established upon that object, the mind becomes one-pointed, and impulsion-moments (javana) proceed. In the first impulsion:
They are curable; likewise for the second and subsequent views. On the seventh, even for Buddhas, they are incurable and irreversible, like Ariṭṭha and Kaṇṭaka.
In that case, one might fall into one view, another into two, and another into all three; yet once one has fallen into even one, or two, or three, one becomes possessed of fixed wrong view.
One has reached the obstruction to the path to heaven as well as the obstruction to the path to liberation.
"He is incapable of going to heaven immediately after that existence, let alone to liberation;
this being is called a 'stump in the cycle of existence' (*vaṭṭakhāṇu*), a guardian of the earth, for generally there is no emergence from such a state of being.
"In the back of the world-system" (*piṭṭhicakkavāḷe*) means in a certain place beyond the world-system that is burning. Of those [beings] who are burning and not burning...
"In the interval between world-systems" refers to a certain space designated as the "inter-world hells" (*lokantarika-niraya*).
"It is indeed cooked" means that even while a world-system is burning or being consumed by fire, it is nevertheless cooked by the power of its own karma. 311.
Regarding the fourth [hell], it is said to have acquired this name based on the words "do not stumble" (*mā khalī*); for it is said that on a muddy [ground]...
As he was walking along carrying an oil jar on the ground, his master said, "Dear one, do not stumble!
He stumbled through negligence and fell; out of fear of his master, he began to run away.
The master ran after him and seized him by the hem of his garment. Abandoning the garment, he fled naked, unable even to cover himself with leaves or grass.
Not knowing [the truth], he entered a certain village just as one might with gold. When people saw him, they thought, "This ascetic is an Arahat, free from desire;
there is no one equal to him," and they approached him bringing cakes, alms-food, and other offerings.
Thinking, "Because I have no garment to wear, this [desire] has arisen in me," he did not put on a robe even after receiving one from then on; indeed, that very state was his renunciation.
He took [them]. In his presence, five hundred other people—one after another—went forth into homelessness.
Referring to him, it was said: "The founder of a sect who received that name by taking up the word 'Do not stumble'.
"At the place where they met" means at the point where the currents of two rivers converge. "Of the two waters..."
Of two currents of water. Because it must be thrown into the aforementioned place for the purpose of catching fish, it is "quick" (khippa);
that very thing is what is called "a net" (khippa) here. Therefore he said: "a net" (kumina). "With sugarcanes" means with water-sugarcane.
An empty man is so called due to the absence of noble qualities (ariya-dhamma). For he does not possess even mere meditative absorption (jhāna), so how could he have the noble path (ariya-magga)?
"Manussakhippaṃ maññeti" means that humans are like a fish-trap set out for the purpose of causing those who fall into it to meet with calamity.
Therefore he said, "Of the great multitude," and so forth. 312.
Regarding the fifth [section] and those following, the term "the teaching of outsiders" (bāhirakasāsana) is stated without distinction, because all of it leads to no transcendence (aniyyānika).
Because even one who professes to be a Teacher lacks omniscience. Therefore he said, "In that regard," and so forth. "The assembly" refers to the assembly of disciples.
"For the sake of becoming such" means for the purpose of being endowed with the state described by the Teacher. "A hundred legged" means many, numerous beings.
"Unwholesomeness reaches them all at once" means that even when they are all exhorted together, unwholesomeness reaches them [simultaneously].
Through unwholesome action, one attains unwholesomeness equally, even when inciting many people together, because of the powerful nature of such encouragement.
There is no need to speak separately regarding individual instigation.
For just as "good friendship" (kalyāṇamittatā) is to be described as equal in the practice of Dhamma, so too is "bad friendship" (akalyāṇamittatā) in the practice of non-Dhamma.
313. "Well-expounded" means expounded by way of being exclusively leading to liberation (*ekantaniyyānika*).

"And the Teacher is omniscient" is because one who is not omniscient would be incapable of explaining the state of leading to liberation. "And the Dhamma is well-expounded" because it has been proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

"And the community is practicing rightly" because they have been well-trained by the Teacher. The passage beginning with "and the instigator" should be understood as an illustration of right practice.
314. "The measure should be known" means that the measure should be understood thus: "This person subsists with this much;
it is appropriate to give this much to him. Regarding the excess... [as before] ...there is no attainment of Nibbāna because the Dhamma has been poorly proclaimed.
"Of him" refers to the recipient. The meaning is that in a poorly proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya, there is no such thing as the practice of fewness of desires.

315. The "power of the donor" (*dāyakassa vaso*) refers to the inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) characterized by the distinction between being noble or base. The "power of the gift" (*deyyadhammassa vaso*), however, refers simply to the smallness or greatness of the object to be given.
"One's own capacity" (*attano thāmo*) means the measure of what is sufficient for one's maintenance. The passage beginning with "If indeed...

(*yadi hi...*) is an expansion of the meaning stated briefly in the passage beginning with "How... (*kathaṃ...*). "Of one who has not arisen" (*anuppannassa*) means [the power] belonging to that person who has not yet arisen.
"He becomes one who has become an eye" means he is like an eye for the great multitude.
"He makes the teaching long-enduring" means he makes it endure for a long time by generating unarisen gains and by generating confidence in the great multitude.
"In the Kuṭumbariya Monastery" means in the monastery situated near the village of Kuṭumbariya. "For the purpose of eating" means in that very [place].
For the purpose of sitting down at home and eating. For the purpose of taking [the food] and going means for the purpose of going after having taken it from the house.
"Regular meals" (dhurabhattāni) means daily meals. "The junior attendant" (cūḷupaṭṭhāka) is a servant.
"Having investigated" means having investigated in such a way that it is not specifically prepared for him. "The great multitude thinks they should be few in desires" means the great multitude...
He considers himself to be one who has few desires by following the example of others. "Of the great multitude" means of the many people.
"Having spread out" means having made it extensive.
316. "The practice of the five fires" is the heating [of the body] by the heat of fire on four sides and by the heat of the sun above.
And that is during the summer season. Falling from a mountain peak with a precipitous cliff is falling from a precipice in the wilderness.
Turning toward the sun and revolving around it during the morning and other times is following the course of the sun.

"This one too" refers even to one who is lazy regarding the well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya. "Asceticism" means the practice of austerities. "Ill-conducted" means wrong conduct that is defiled. "Drags him to hell" means it drags him toward the suffering of hell.
318. "In the manner described" means in the manner already stated, such as the practice of the fivefold heat-exertion (*pañcātapa-tāpana*) and so forth.

319. "Thus" refers to the excellent practice (*suppaṭipatti*) called clarity of mind (*cittappasāda*) in the manner described. By this, he includes the happiness of performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). 320.
"In the Chapter of Nines" (*Navakanipāta*) is said with reference to the Chapter of Nines that will be explained in this very *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
"Nine persons" refers to the nine types of persons beginning with those who are reborn seven times at most and the family-to-family (kolaṃkola) practitioner.
"In all cases" means in all the remaining suttas spoken in this [Nikāya].
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
16. Ekadhammapāḷi (16) 4.
Commentary on the Fourth Chapter of the Ekadhammapāḷi 322.
In the first [sutta] of the fourth [chapter], "saññāṇabhūtā" means serving as a distinguishing mark (*upalakkhaṇa*). "[With] a trunk fifteen yojanas in circumference... and so forth.

The circumference of their trunks is fifteen *yojanas*. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and as," he includes the fact that trees such as the *kadamba* endure for an eon and are a hundred *yojanas* in height, just as [the *jambu* tree] does;
however, it does not mean that they serve as a signifier for Aparagoyāna and so forth, in the same way that the *jambu* tree serves as a signifier for Jambudīpa.
"Delightfulness" (*rāmaṇeyyaka*) means the state of being delightful. "In the remaining phrases" refers to the phrases beginning with "delightfulness of the forest."
"Ukkūla" means that which has a raised bank or a high state; "vikūla" means that from which the bank or the high state has departed.
Thus it is said: "the elevated place and the depressed place. "By the back of the *nandiyāvaṭṭa* fish alone" means by the back of the fish known as the *kujjaka*, *kakulisa*, and *makaca*.
In the second [section] and those following, the four states of deprivation (*apāya*) are intended, excluding humans; it is not the gods who are excluded, other than humans.
This is because a low birth is intended [as the subject]. Even by taking this or that [specific location], the Middle Country is obtained;
it is where there is access for monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as for others who are wise by nature, proponents of karma, and proponents of action.
That which is called a "suitable place" is thus referred to by the words, "the whole of it," and so forth.
324. *Eḷa* means fault. Therefore he said: “The meaning is ‘with a face free from faults. 326.

Having known the virtues of the Tathāgata, even seeing him with the eye is truly seeing; however, seeing him without knowing [his virtues] occurs even for animals. Thus he said: “Those who, having known the virtues of the Tathāgata,” and so forth. 327.
“Having made manifest, it was spoken” means having made manifest the Truths, it was spoken.
328. Regarding the statement, "The non-forgetting of the teachings heard is retention," it says: "They retain means they do not forget. 329.

"They examine what is the meaning and what is not the meaning" means they examine the meaning and the non-meaning [of a passage] by thinking, "This is the meaning of this text; this is not the meaning.
For the grasping of the meaning occurs through the avoidance of what is not the meaning, just as the practice of the Dhamma occurs through the avoidance of what is not the Dhamma.
330. *Anulomapaṭipadaṃ*: the practice that is in conformity with Nibbāna. 331. *Saṃvegajanakesu kāraṇesu*:

among the causes that produce a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), such as birth and so forth. Spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) is the knowledge of moral dread (*ottappa*) regarding those situations that inspire urgency.

332. *Upāyena*: by means of that method by which the cutting off of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) occurs; by that method. *Padhānavīriyaṃ karontī*: they exercise the energy known as the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*); they arouse it.

333. "Vavassagga" means that here formations (*saṅkhāra*) are let loose or released; thus it is said: "The unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) is called 'vavassagga' (relinquishment)," which is Nibbāna.
334. "Of the best foods" (*uttamannānaṃ*) means of the five kinds of excellent food. "Of the best flavors" (*uttamarasānaṃ*) means of the most excellent tastes.
"By the practice of gleaning" (*uñchācārena*): the practice of gleaning (*uñchācariyā*) is the act of gathering whatever has not been claimed by anyone, without asking for anything.
By the words "And here," etc., he shows that the "preeminence" of food and so forth means its being most agreeable and its being obtained at the desired moment, not merely the fact of obtaining it.
"They receive" means they give [it] because of its excellence. "A single bowl of rice" means a bowl full of rice.
"What indeed is this? refers to whether or not this is truly called "the peak of the peak of the flavors of food."
He asks: "By means of alms gathered in a bowl" means by means of mixed food. "Maintaining themselves" refers to the food for the purpose of maintaining life under the heading of "maintenance.
"Taking this as the 'foremost flavor'" shows that, relative to each respective [food], it should be understood as the supreme among the foremost flavors of food.

For the food of the Four Great Kings is superior to that of a Wheel-turning Monarch; in this manner, it should be carried on up to the gods who wield power over the creations of others (*paranimmitavasavatti*).
335. The "taste of the goal" (*attharasa*) refers to the four fruits of asceticism (*sāmaññaphala*), taking them as "the taste that is the fruit of the noble paths.
The "taste of the Dhamma" (*dhammarasa*) refers to the four paths, taking them as "the taste that is the cause of the fruits of asceticism.
The "taste of liberation" (*vimuttirasa*) refers to the deathless Nibbāna, taking it as "the stilling of all conditioned phenomena" (*sabbasaṅkhārasamatha*).
The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is finished.
The Table of Contents for Jambudīpa is finished.
17. Commentary on the Chapter on Qualities Inspiring Confidence.
366. "Addhamidaṃ" is stated in the Pāli with a short vowel due to euphonic combination (*sandhi*); the letter *m* is used for the purpose of joining words, as he says:
"addhā idaṃ. "Ekaṃso eso" means this reason for gains is one-sided.
"Pāpakaṃ nāma" means that even a small evil, once committed, he does not at all remove. "Tathassa" means for him who is thus practicing rightly.

By the inclusion of these ascetic practices (dhuta-dhammas)—namely, living in the forest (*āraññika*), and so forth, up to wearing only three robes (*tecīvarika*)—it should be understood that other practices of a similar nature are also included.
"The state of having attained stability" means the status of an elder (*thera*), which is the attainment of firmness within the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
"Perfection of deportment" refers to the perfection of that deportment described as: "I must adopt a different manner of conduct. "A son of good family" (*kulaputti*)...
“*Kolaputtiya*” means “the state of being a son of good family. “Possession of excellent form” refers to the excellence of one’s physical basis (*upadhi*).

“Sweetness of speech-activity” refers to the quality of sweetness and the melodiousness of the voice. Regarding the statement, “Thus his gain arises,” this is not intended to show a method for producing gain;
rather, it is intended to show the infallible cause of gain, namely that for one who practices correctly in this way, gain arises even against his own will.
It should be seen thus. As it is said:
“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I be a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,’ he should be one who fulfills his moral discipline.
The commentary to the Chapter on Qualities Inspiring Confidence is finished.
18. Commentary on the *Apara-accharā-saṅghāta-vagga* 382.
Regarding the phrase "This too is a sutta," the word "too" (*pi*) here includes the *Cūḷa-accharā-saṅghāta-sutta* mentioned above.
In the *Cūḷa-accharā-saṅghāta-sutta*, such a vast result was shown even for loving-kindness that had not yet reached absorption; how much more so, then, [for that which has]?
However, in order to show that this loving-kindness has reached absorption (*appanā*), he says: “For when it has reached absorption,” and so forth.
“There is no talk at all of result” means there is no discussion whatsoever regarding its result; or rather, this is the reading itself.
“By way of numerical sequence” means by way of the order of counting. “Arising first” means first; however, the statement “it enters [absorption] first” is not an absolute characteristic.

For one who has attained mastery and has won the eight attainments is able to enter them by proceeding from the beginning to the end, or by proceeding from the end back to the beginning, or even by skipping over intermediate stages.
However, it is called "first" in the sense of its prior arising. "In the Vibhaṅga" refers to the Jhāna Vibhaṅga. Regarding insight (*vipassanā*):
The task of contemplating the characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) being performed is accomplished by the Path because it destroys the delusion regarding those [characteristics].
Furthermore, the contemplation of the characteristics by means of insight is accomplished by the Path that has arisen; otherwise, there would be a reversal [of the process].
Therefore, the Path is the contemplation of the characteristics, not because it takes the characteristics of impermanence and so forth as its object, just as [the Path] is called "fruit" (*phala*).
It contemplates the unconditioned characteristic of Nibbāna by way of making it its object; the Path is likewise.
Thus, its state of contemplating characteristics should be understood. There is simply nothing to be said regarding its lack of jhāna-factors. The remainder is the distinction:
the meaning is that they indeed possess jhāna-factors.
386–387. *Hitapharaṇaṃ* means the pervading occurrence of jhāna in accordance with the welfare of beings.

It is called *cetovimutti* (liberation of mind) because by means of it one is liberated from what is opposed to the mind; it is loving-kindness (*mettā*) that has reached absorption (*appanā*). Therefore he said, "In this case," and so forth.

By the phrase "this same method," he extends [the rule] to compassion (*karuṇā*) and the others as well, indicating that they too reach absorption. They are called "rounds" (*vaṭṭa*) because they constitute the round of kamma. They are the "bases of the round."
"They are" means they serve as the cause for the cycle of kamma-result (vipākavaṭṭa).
"By way of internal preparation" means by way of performing preparatory work upon one's own hair and so forth. "Of eighteen kinds" means of eighteen varieties.
"In the body" refers to the material body (rūpakāya); for here, the material body consists of the limbs and members as well as the hair and so forth.
In the sense of a collection of phenomena (*dhamma*), "body" (*kāya*) is intended here in the same way as a "body of elephants" (*hatthikāya*) or a "body of chariots" (*rathakāya*).

Because the word *kāya* refers to a collection and because it takes on a collective form, the singular number is used in the phrase "in the body" (*kāye*) with respect to the aspect of foulness (*asubhākāra*).

Likewise, although consciousness (*citta*) is divided into many types according to the distinctions of its objects and so forth, it is taken as a single unit by virtue of the commonality of its nature as consciousness.
“Citte” is used in the singular. To show the meaning of “contemplating the body,” he says:
“contemplating that very same body with wisdom. By the restrictive phrase “that very same body,” he excludes contemplation of feelings and so forth.
It should be understood that by this, the purpose of taking up the word “body” once again is indicated. For even after saying “in the body,” [he says it] again...

“Contemplating the body” (*kāyānupassī*): the second mention of “body” is made for the purpose of showing its definition through non-confusion, its resolution as a compact mass, its analysis, and so forth.

By this, even though the occasion for contemplating feeling and the rest arises—since they too are based here and bound here—one is not a contemplator of feeling, mind, or mental objects; rather, one is specifically a contemplator of the body.
By the very demonstration of the mode of contemplation of the body within the objective basis of the bodily formations, its definition is shown as being unmixed [with other modes].
Likewise, one does not contemplate a single phenomenon in the body apart from the limbs and members, nor does one contemplate a woman or a man apart from the head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth.

Furthermore, even regarding that "body" which is a collection of primary elements and derived matter consisting of the head-hairs, body-hairs, and so on, one does not contemplate any single phenomenon anywhere apart from those primary elements and derived matter.

Then, like one observing the parts of a chariot, he contemplates the collection of limbs and members; like one observing the components of an elephant, he contemplates the collection of head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth;

and like one who separates the layers of a plantain trunk or unties an empty fist, he contemplates the collection of primary elements and derived matter—thus, in various ways, by way of the aggregate alone, [he contemplates] that which is termed "body."
By the seeing of the physical basis, the analysis of the "lump" (ghana) is demonstrated.
For herein, neither a body, nor a woman, nor a man, nor any other phenomenon whatsoever is seen apart from the aforementioned collection;
rather, beings merely within that collection of phenomena as previously described form various kinds of false attachments.
"In eighteen ways" means eighteenfold. "Of one who develops the foundations of mindfulness" means of one who is cultivating the development of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
It is called *ātāpa* because it scorches (*ātapeti*) defilements within the three realms of existence; this is a name for energy (*vīriya*).

For although the abandoning of defilements is indeed "scorching," that [abandoning] also exists in the case of right view and the other factors. However, just like the word *ātapa*, the word *ātāpa* refers specifically to energy.

It is conventional. Alternatively, because energy (*vīriya*)—which proceeds by way of the exertion of associated states for the sake of abandoning opposing factors—is preeminently self-heating (*ātāpana*), it is energy itself that is thus called [“heating”], and not other states.
Therefore, “heating” (*ātāpa*) is the name for energy; one who possesses this is “one who heats himself” (*ātāpī*). And this vowel *ī* signifies praise and excellence.
Or, by the inclusion of the term "ardent" (*ātāpī*), he shows possession of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*).
For this very reason, he said: "Ardent... [etc. ...possessed of energy through energy. "Clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*) means endowed with the knowledge designated as clear comprehension.
For this reason, he said: "Clearly understanding in eighteen ways... [etc. ...rightly comprehending. Furthermore, the etymological meaning here is: "Rightly" (*sammā*) means all-around (*samantato*).

The meaning is: being mindful and clearly comprehending, he understands thoroughly and correctly—by way of discerning it as unmixed and by not observing any other phenomena—through the full knowledge of all its modes, and by proceeding in a manner that brings about successive higher distinctions.
And since "body" (kāya) here is intended in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating, he said: "In that very thing called the body..."
"In the world": this refers to craving directed toward the five strands of sensual pleasure, namely form and so forth.

Since, in this context, covetousness is included by the mention of "lust for sensual pleasures" (kāmacchanda) and ill-will is included by the mention of "dejection" (domanassa), the abandonment of the hindrances is stated here by way of showing these two powerful factors comprised within the hindrances.

It should be understood that [this] occurs. Furthermore, it should be specifically understood here that through the removal of covetousness (*abhijjhā*), there is the removal of attachment rooted in bodily excellence;
through the removal of ill-will (*domanassa*), there is the removal of aversion rooted in bodily deficiency; through the removal of covetousness, there is the removal of delight in the body;

through the removal of ill-will, there is the removal of lack of delight in the cultivation of the body; and through the removal of covetousness, [there is the removal of] the perception of non-existent qualities such as beauty and pleasure in the body.
By means of the removal of dejection and the elimination from the body of the impure, painful, and unreal states that have been superimposed, abandonment is described.
By this, the power of yoga and the capability for yoga of the practitioner are illuminated. For this is the power of yoga:
namely, being free from attraction and aversion, enduring both the unpleasant and the pleasant, and being devoid of the superimposition of the unreal and the removal of the real.
And he is one who is free from attachment and aversion, capable of enduring both the unpleasant and the pleasant, excluding what is unreal and not omitting what is real;
thus he is competent for yoga. It is said that this is simply the contemplation of pure form because it is stated solely as the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyānupassanā*).

"In feelings distinguished by pleasure and so forth" means in feelings distinguished by pleasure, pain, neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and those associated with worldly objects (*sāmisa*) or dissociated from them (*nirāmisā*).
In this context, it is called *sukhā* (pleasure) because it brings happiness; the meaning is that it causes the associated mental states and the body to obtain satisfaction.

Alternatively, it is called *sukhā* because it thoroughly consumes (*suṭṭhu khādati*) or digs away (*khanati*) physical and mental affliction; or, it is called *sukhā* because it provides easy room (*okāsa*).
It is called *dukkhā* (pain) because it causes suffering; the meaning is that it oppresses and vexes the associated mental states and the body.
It is painful because it eats or digs poorly, both physically and mentally; or else, it is "painful" (*dukkhā*) because giving space for it is difficult.
By way of the negation of both pain and pleasure, "neither-pain-nor-pleasure" (*adukkhamasukhā*) refers to equanimity (*upekkhā*).

It is called "feeling" (*vedanā*) because one feels, that is, experiences the flavor of the object. "Feeling" (*vediyamāno*) means experiencing. "I feel a pleasant feeling" (*sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyāmīti*).
"He understands" means that when one experiences a pleasant feeling, whether physical or mental, one understands: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.

In this regard, it may be granted that even infants lying on their backs understand, while experiencing a pleasant feeling such as drinking milk, "We are experiencing a pleasant feeling"; however, it is not of such a nature [as the understanding intended here].
This was said with reference to a specific kind of understanding.

For such knowledge as that does not abandon the perception of a being, does not eliminate the notion of a self, and is neither a meditation subject nor the development of the foundations of mindfulness.
But the knowledge of this bhikkhu abandons the perception of a being, eliminates the notion of a self, and is both a meditation subject and the development of the foundations of mindfulness.
And it is so. For this was said with reference to the act of feeling for one who is thus clearly comprehending: "Who feels? Whose is the feeling? For what reason is there feeling?
In that context, as for "Who feels?": no being whatsoever, nor any person, feels. As for "Whose is the feeling?": it belongs to no one at all.
It is the feeling of a being or a person. For what reason is it called "feeling"?

Because its basis and object are the same as those of the being. Therefore, he understands thus: "Feeling itself experiences by taking as its object that very form and so forth which have become the basis for various states such as pleasure;
yet, based on the occurrence of that feeling, there is the mere conventional expression, 'I experience.'"

"...arises. Thus, one should understand that when he observes, "It is feeling alone that feels, having made form and so forth—which are the bases for pleasure and the rest—its object," he understands, "I feel a pleasant feeling.
Alternatively, "he understands, 'I feel a pleasant feeling'" means that at the moment of a pleasant feeling, [there is no] painful feeling...
When experiencing a pleasant feeling due to the absence [of others], one understands: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling indeed.

Because of the prior non-existence of that painful feeling which had occurred before, and because of the present existence of this pleasant feeling, and because of its subsequent non-existence after this, one thus understands:
"Feeling is indeed impermanent, unstable, and subject to change."
In this regard, he is fully aware. The same method applies to such passages as "He understands: 'I experience a painful feeling,'" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "sensual pleasure" (*sāmisaṃ sukhaṃ*) and so on: because they are to be touched by the defilements (*kilesa*), the five strands of sensual pleasure are called "sensual objects" (*āmisa*). Because they are accompanied by these sensual objects by way of being made into objects of perception, they are "sensual" (*sāmisa*);
therefore, what is called "sensual pleasure" is that which is dependent upon the sensual objects of the five strands of sense pleasure at the six doors.
The arisen pleasant feeling accompanied by attachment is called "worldly suffering.

That [feeling] should be understood as the feeling of displeasure based on the strands of sensual pleasure that arises for one who thinks at the six sense doors, "I shall not experience a desirable object," or "I am not experiencing it.
The so-called "unworldly happiness" is that which is based on renunciation.

This is pleasant feeling (*somanassavedanā*). It should be understood as the pleasant feeling that arises in one who, when a desirable object has come into range at any of the six doors, is able to exert himself by establishing insight (*vipassanā*) into the impermanent nature and so forth, and who thinks, "My insight has progressed.
This is the pleasant feeling born of such progress.
“Non-material suffering” refers to the feeling of mental grief based on the six bases of contact.

This arises when a desirable object enters the range of the six sense doors, and one, having directed a longing toward the noble fruit-dhammas known as the supreme liberation, is unable to exert oneself by establishing insight into impermanence and so forth for the sake of attaining them;
[thinking] “Even during this fortnight, even during this... [he feels grief].”
The feeling of mental distress that arises from grieving, thinking, "I have been striving for insight for this month and even this year, yet I have not been able to reach the plane of the Noble Ones.

The so-called "unpleasant-and-not-unpleasant" feeling associated with the material is the feeling of equanimity accompanied by attachment; and that [occurs] at the six doors when a desirable object [is present].

Just as flies settle upon a ball of molasses when it comes into their range, so too, the equanimous feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) based on the strands of sensual pleasure arises, having become attached and clinging right there by following after visible forms and the other sense objects.
The "spiritual" (nirāmisa) equanimous feeling called "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" is that which is based on the sixfold renunciation.
That, moreover, occurs when a desirable or other object enters the range of the six doors, and one does not feel lust for the desirable object.
The feeling of equanimity associated with insight-knowledge that arises in one who is not attached to the unattractive, who does not become deluded through lack of regard—
this is what was stated in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. "That very feeling should be understood" means that,
in the sense of breaking down and falling away, that feeling should be understood as the "world" (*loka*).
Thus it is explained in detail: "He understands a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust'; or a mind without lust...

[and so on] ...a mind with hatred, a mind without hatred, a mind with delusion, a mind without delusion, a contracted mind, a distracted mind, an exalted mind, an unexalted mind, a surpassable mind..."

"or a mind with lust, or a mind without lust, or a mind with hatred, or a mind without hatred, or a mind with delusion, or a mind without delusion, or a contracted mind, or a distracted mind, or an exalted mind, or an unexalted mind, or a surpassed mind, or an unsurpassed mind, or a concentrated mind, or an unconcentrated mind, or a liberated mind, or an unliberated mind"—thus, regarding these sixteen kinds of minds as set forth in detail in the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*:
therein, "with lust" refers to the eightfold [consciousness] accompanied by greed; "without lust" refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate [consciousness]. This...
However, because comprehension (*sammasana*) is not a combination of phenomena (*dhammasamodhāna*), therefore here even a single word does not pertain to the supramundane (*lokuttara*).
The remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses (*akusalacitta*) belong neither to the former category nor to the latter.

"With hatred" (*sadosa*) is twofold, being accompanied by grief (*domanassasahagata*). "Free from hatred" (*vītadosa*) refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate states. The remaining ten unwholesome consciousnesses...

They do not partake of either the first or the last category. Delusion (*moha*) is twofold: that accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchā-sahagata*) and that accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca-sahagata*).
However, because delusion arises in all unwholesome states, the remaining [unwholesome factors] are also included here.
Indeed, within this very dyad, the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are fully encompassed. "Free from delusion" (*vītamoha*) refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness.
"Contracted" means overcome by sloth and torpor; for this is called "contracted consciousness" because it proceeds by way of contraction toward the object.

"Distracted" means accompanied by restlessness; for this is called "scattered consciousness" because it proceeds with a state of diffusion through a particular degree of distraction toward the object.
"Exalted" refers to the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere.

"Non-exalted" (*amahagga*) means belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). "With something higher" (*sauttara*) means belonging to the sense-sphere. "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) means belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*).
Even there, that which has something higher is the fine-material sphere, while the unsurpassed is only the immaterial sphere.

"Concentrated" (*samāhita*) refers to that which possesses either absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*) or access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*). "Unconcentrated" (*asamāhita*) is devoid of both types of concentration. "Liberated" (*vimutta*) [means liberated] by way of liberation through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgavimutti*) and suppression-liberation (*vikkhambhanavimutti*).

"Released. "Unreleased" means devoid of both types of release. However, there is no occasion here for the discussion of release by cutting off (*samuccheda-vimutti*), subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*), or escape (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*);
this absence of occasion should be understood because the intended scope is the mode of comprehension (*sammasanacāra*).

The aggregates are the "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānakkhandhā*) because they are the heaps of phenomena that serve as the conditions for clinging; they are the "masses of phenomena" (*dhammarāsi*).

The meaning is as follows: Alternatively, the aggregates (khandhas) that are to be grasped by means of clinging (upādāna) through the functions of taking as an object and so forth are the "aggregates subject to clinging" (upādānakkhandhā).
"The six internal and external bases" refers to these: the six internal bases, namely eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
and the six external bases, namely visible form, sound, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena (dhamma). Herein...
However, supramundane states (lokuttara-dhammā) are not to be included here, because the scope intended is that of the practice of comprehension (sammasana-cāra).

"The seven factors of enlightenment" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment beginning with mindfulness (satisambojjhaṅga). They are called factors of enlightenment (sambojjhaṅga) because mindfulness and the others are either limbs of enlightenment (sambodhi) or limbs for the sake of enlightenment.
For it is the practitioner (yogāvacara), starting from the time he has initiated insight (vipassanā), who awakens (sambujjhati) by means of them.
Enlightenment (*sambodhi*) is that harmony of the seven factors beginning with mindfulness by which one awakens, rises from the sleep of the defilements, or penetrates the Truths;
that harmony of factors is enlightenment. The "factors of enlightenment" (*sambojjhaṅgā*) are the limbs of that enlightenment, or of that process of awakening.
"The Four Noble Truths" refers to the four noble truths thus stated: "Suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
Among these, the first two truths constitute the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) because they are the cause for its occurrence;

the latter two constitute the unrounding (*vivaṭṭa*) because they are the means for turning away from it and for its attainment. Of these, the monk's application of his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is directed toward the round.
It exists by way of its own form and because it is possible to comprehend it. In the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*), there is no misapprehension (*abhinivesa*) because it is not an object;
and when it is not an object, there is no purpose [for such misapprehension]. "Among those stated fivefold" means among those stated in the *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*.

"Merely the comprehension of the formless" means that, being unmixed with form, it is exclusively the comprehension of the formless. This is because the aggregates, bases, truths, and sections are all included within the five aggregates.

“Contemplation of the material and immaterial” has been stated. Because the preliminary stages of the foundations of mindfulness are also included, he said: “They are explained as being a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
(394) “Of those not yet produced” means of those that have not yet arisen. “Exert effort” (*payoga*): here *payoga* is intense application;
*parakkama* is simply effort. The meaning is: they exert themselves in what is termed effort. “The mind uplifts itself” means [to prevent it] from falling into the side of indolence.
He expels by means of the *apadāna* (the act of casting out). "Exertion-vigor" (*padhānavīriya*) is vigor that has attained the characteristic of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*).

"Worldly" refers to the discourse on worldly right exertions. "In all prior stages" means in the stage preceding all paths. "By way of the *Kassapa-saṃyutta*" refers to the sutta found in the *Kassapa-saṃyutta*:
"Evil, unwholesome states that have arisen in me, if not abandoned, lead to harm..."
Because it is stated [in the text], “they would conduce to,” it should be understood as mundane (*lokiya*).
By means of the restriction “tranquility and insight” (*samatha-vipassanā*), the Path is excluded; and showing the reason for that exclusion, he said, “But the Path...,” and so forth.
The phrase “having arisen once” is merely a statement of fact. Of what has ceased, again...
He said, "So indeed," and so forth, lest one should suspect that because [the wholesome states] do not arise, there is no benefit whatsoever.

Immediately following this, it is stated that the giving of conditions for these [wholesome states] occurs precisely through their manifestation in such a way that the fruit arises. "In the previous instance as well" refers to the passage:
"If unarisen wholesome states were to arise, they might lead to my harm. This was stated in the *Porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā* (the Ancient Commentary).
However, that statement as it was spoken is not tenable; for just as in the second case, there is no reason for the non-inclusion of the first path.
If the first path were not included, one would fall into the undesirable conclusion that a path which does not arise when the first is absent would lead to a lack of purpose;
yet this is not tenable, because when that [first path] arises, the primary goal is accomplished. This is by way of accomplishing the four functions.
By way of accomplishing the four functions, such as the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states.
"In the manner stated" means by the manner stated [in the text] beginning with, "either by way of non-occurrence or by way of not having experienced the object," and so forth.

"Existing" means possessing a present intrinsic nature (*dharamāna-sabhāva*). Because they are included within the three moments, those possessing arising and the other phases exist by virtue of their state of being present.
"Arisen" (*uppanna*) means arisen as currently occurring. For that which has fallen (*panna*), from the moment of its arising until its dissolution, is called "arisen" in the primary sense.
"Disappeared after having been experienced" (*anubhavitvā vigata*) and "disappeared after having existed" (*bhavitvā vigata*):

here, both the acts of experiencing and existing are expressed by the word "having existed" (*bhutvā*) through its commonality with the act of existing; for it is precisely this commonality [of existence] that is indicated by the prefix.

It is distinguished as follows: here, by way of experiencing the result (*vipāka*), the object-of-repetition (*tadārammaṇa*) is called "arisen after having been experienced and having passed away" (*bhutvāvigatuppanna*) because it has become [the state of having passed away] due to the non-disappearance of the unripened result in every respect.

And the kamma is likewise called "arisen after having been experienced and having passed away" (*bhutvāvigatuppanna*) by way of its mere state of having become [past] and having passed away, because the result has not yet ripened.

It is not like in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, where [it refers to] a javana that has passed away through being experienced by way of passion and so forth, or that which has passed away simply because it has arisen and ceased.

"Conditioned" means arisen after the primary elements have passed away. Therefore, here it refers only to resultant [consciousness] that has arisen by making space, and not to kamma as it is presented there [in the *Visuddhimagga*].
For in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, "arisen after the primary elements have passed away" and "arisen by making space" are shown differently.
Indeed, it is stated there:
“Wholesome and unwholesome [kamma] that has ceased after experiencing the flavor of its object is called ‘ceased having been experienced.
The remaining conditioned phenomena that have ceased after reaching the three kinds of clinging are called ‘ceased having become. These are termed ‘arisen having become.
Even though the kamma described by such phrases as ‘those karmas he previously performed’ is past, it is still [present].”
"Because it stands having set aside another result and made room for its own result;
and because even though that result has not yet arisen, it will inevitably arise when such room has been made—therefore it is called 'arisen by making room' (okāsakata-uppanna).

However, here [in the *Visuddhimagga*], "arisen after having ceased" (*bhutvāvigata-uppanna*) and "arisen by making room" (*okāsakata-uppanna*) are shown according to the method stated in the *Sammohavinodanī*. For it is said in the *Sammohavinodanī*:

“Furthermore, when the kamma has ceased after having experienced the flavor of its object, the resultant state that has arisen and ceased is called ‘ceased after having been experienced’ (*bhūtvāvigata*).

When the kamma itself has arisen and ceased, it is called ‘ceased after having been experienced. Both of these are reckoned as ‘arisen after having been experienced and ceased’ (*bhūtvāvigatuppanna*).
Wholesome or unwholesome kamma, having warded off the result of another kamma, [brings about] its own result...”
“He makes room. When the result arises once this room has been made, it is said to have arisen starting from the moment the room was made.
This is what is called “arisen by making room.
In this regard, the intention in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* is as follows: “Even though all mental arisings have the nature of being experienced...”

However, in a continuum that is subject to perversion (*vipallāsa*) during the experience of an object, there occurs— due to the mental formation (*cittābhisaṅkhāra*)— a mode of experiencing the object that is distinguished from the indeterminate (*abyākata*),
being preeminent over both the wholesome (*kusala*) and the unwholesome (*akusala*). Just as, by way of grasping through conceptualization,

the unwholesome and the wholesome experience the flavor of the object in its primary sense (*nippariyāyato*) through passion (*rāga*) and their opposites respectively, it is not so [in the case of the indeterminate].
It is not a result (*vipāka*), because it is projected by the force of karma;

nor is it a functional state (*kiriyā*), because those that are rootless (*ahetuka*) are extremely weak, and even those with roots (*sahetuka*)—such as the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) arising in one whose defilements are exhausted—are exceedingly tranquil in their occurrence. Therefore, the experience of the flavor of the object (*ārammaṇarasa*) through passion and so forth is preeminent.
This applies to both the unwholesome and the wholesome, which are alike in their commonality of having arisen and then ceased.
It is stated: "The conditioned [state] consisting of consciousness is 'passed away from the primary elements' (*bhūtāpagata*).

However, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is stated that the resultant [consciousness] is "passed away" (*bhūtapagata*) by way of having merely existed and not yet vanished, because its object has not entirely departed while the fruition is still unripened; whereas the kamma is "passed away from the primary elements" (*bhūtāpagata*) by way of having experienced the fruition.
For this very reason, in that context, the term "arisen in the space provided" refers only to the resultant, and not to the kamma as well.

Therefore, here too it should be understood that "what has arisen after having been" and "what has arisen by way of providing an occasion" are analyzed according to the same method stated in the *Sammohavinodanī*.
As for the statement "the five aggregates are called the 'ground' of insight," this is said because they serve as the basis for comprehension (*sammasana*). Regarding the phrase "among these":
Regarding the distinctions of past and so forth: "underlying defilements" (anusayita-kilesā) refers to those not yet abandoned, which are intended here as those to be abandoned by the Path.
Therefore he said: "They are either past... [etc. ...or they should not be so described. Let it be for now that they cannot be described as "past" or "present";
but why should they not be described as "future"? For are they not, insofar as they have not been abandoned, liable to arise once they encounter their causes?
Is it true that the defilements which have become firmly established are called "latent tendencies" (anusaya)? This is true;
however, because their future existence is not delimited in the same way as other future aggregates, it is said that they "cannot be called future.
For if their future existence were delimited, then they could be called "present" or "past" once the conditions for their arising have come together.
However, the designation "future" should be understood there by way of its potentiality to arise. This is called "arisen by having reached the plane":
this aforementioned class of defilements is called "arisen by having reached the plane" in the sense of being unabandoned;

for when the requisite conditions are met, they perform their function because they exist. "In those various planes" refers to the personal existences (attabhāva) comprised of human, divine, and so forth.
Regarding the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*): they are called "planes" (*bhūmi*) because it is within them that the defilements (*kilesa*) exist by way of taking them as objects.

"Not having reached eradication" (*asamugghātagata*) means not having reached eradication—that is, not having reached complete cutting off—because they have not been brought to a state of non-arising within this or that continuity (*santāna*).
"Arising obtained through the plane" (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*) refers here to that which has obtained a plane.

It is said that it is "obtained on a plane" (*bhūmiladdha*), like fire being kindled. Furthermore, regarding the term *okāsakatuppanna*, according to the method presented in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, the word *kata* (done/made) should be understood as having undergone a shift in grammatical position (*paranipāta*) in two senses:
"space was made by this wholesome or unwholesome karma," and "space was made for this result.
However, here, by the term *okāsakatuppanna*, [it refers] specifically to the result (*vipāka*).
Because it has been grasped, the analysis (*viggaha*) should be understood as: "An opportunity has been made for this result.
That which has reached manifestation due to being possessed of the three moments is "arisen through manifestation" (*samudācāruppanna*). Therefore he said: "Only that which is currently occurring.
That which proceeds having seized and firmly grasped its object is "arisen by seizing the object" (*ārammaṇādhiggahituppanna*). By way of suppression-elimination (*vikkhambhanappahāna*),...
"Not abandoned" means not suppressed. "Not eradicated" means not abandoned by way of complete cutting off (*samucchedappahāna*).

Because the object is grasped through the seizing of its signs (*nimittaggāha*), that object—by virtue of standing as a cause for the arising of defilements at every moment it is recollected—is said to be "grasped. Thus he says: "Because the object is grasped."

And here, the object apprehended by way of grasping the sign should be regarded as like a milk-yielding tree that has been brought [to the mind], while the object of the defilements contained within [the mind] due to their non-suppression should be regarded as like a milk-yielding tree that has not been brought [to the mind].
Those who grasp the sign, or those individuals whose defilements are not suppressed, are like the milk-yielding trees that have been brought and those that have not been brought.
"In the same manner as before" refers to when they have arisen without being suppressed.
In the same manner as previously stated. Regarding "it should be elaborated": one cannot say, "They will not arise in this particular place.

Why? Because they have not been eradicated. How so? Just as if one were to strike a milky tree with an axe, one could not say, "In this particular spot, no milk shall come forth"—so it is here. This is what is called "arisen without being eradicated" (*asamugghātituppanna*).
Having thus applied the names, it should be explained in detail.

"When these have arisen" means when the eight [defilements] as previously described have arisen. This is not to be abandoned by the Path because its object is not something to be abandoned by the Path.
That which is to be abandoned by the Path is so called because its object is something to be abandoned by the Path. "Lusting" means being possessed by lust. The same method applies to "hating."
"Deluded" (mūḷha) applies here as well. "Bound" (vinibaddha) means bound in a distorted way by the fetter of conceit (māna-saṃyojana).

"Misapprehended" (parāmaṭṭha) means that, through the misapprehension of views (diṭṭhi-parāmāsa), one has overstepped the true nature of phenomena (dhamma-sabhāva) and grasped them as something else. "Reached no conclusion" (aniṭṭhaṅgata) means not having reached a definitive conclusion;

the meaning is that one has fallen into doubt (saṃsayāpanna). "Firmly rooted" (thāmagata) means having attained strength by way of underlying tendencies (anusaya). "Yoked together" (yuganaddha) refers to the pair consisting of that which is to be abandoned and that which abandons.
They are like drums being beaten because they occur simultaneously. "Defiled" (*saṃkilesika*) means accompanied by defilements (*saṃkilesa-dhamma*).

"In the text" (*pāḷiyaṃ*) refers to the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* text. A young tree that has not yet borne fruit was cited in the text to show the absence of effort even regarding defilements belonging to the three times;
however, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated that there is no such thing as a "being who has been born" (*jāta-satta*) whose defilements have not yet arisen.
Having stated, "It should be illustrated by means of a tree that has already borne fruit," the passage beginning with "Just as" was spoken in order to explain that meaning.

Alternatively, the tree that has not yet borne fruit was cited in the Canon by way of simile in order to make manifest the fact that only those defilements abandoned by the Path cannot be described in the three ways—
past, future, and so on— and also for the purpose of showing that the past and other [times] have not been abandoned.
"It should be illustrated by means of a tree that has borne fruit," so it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). In this context,
just as fruits that were destined to arise on a tree do not arise once the tree has been cut down—

and thus cannot be described in terms of past, present, or future states, such as "they have existed," "they exist," or "they will exist"— so too should the defilements abandoned by the Path be regarded.
Because [those states] that ought to arise when the path has not yet arisen are entirely and completely absent once it has arisen.
And just as the cutting down of a tree is purposeful because, if it were not cut, fruits would continue to arise, so too should the purposefulness of the cultivation of the path be understood.
Nor does he "not abandon": this is said because he abandons those things that ought to arise. "Having arisen" refers to the characteristic [of arising].

The word *tvā*. For, just as the activity of abandoning the origin and realizing Nibbāna characterizes the activity of the path’s arising, so too does the activity of fully understanding the aggregates characterize it.
"He abandons those as well" means that he indeed abandons even those acquired aggregates (*upādinnakkhandhā*) which are to be produced by those defilements.
Because of the cessation of the volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) that has that as its cause. Therefore he said: "And this too has been stated," and so forth.

"By the cessation of volitional consciousness" means by bringing about the state of non-arising for karmic consciousness (*kammaviññāṇa*). "In this" refers to this knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimaggañāṇa*), which serves as the cause.
"These" refers to the formations (*saṅkhārā*) designated as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). From all existences...
“They say it emerges” means they say that the path of arahantship indeed emerges from all states of existence, because after its arising there is no further rebirth into existence and no defilement.
With the intention that the path lasts for only a single moment of consciousness, [the question is asked]: “How is there development for the non-arising... for stability?”
[The author] asks: "Does it happen? Because both functions are accomplished precisely through the occurrence of the path, he says:
"Precisely through the occurrence of the path. He explains this meaning with the passage beginning "For the path... It is called "unarisen";

therefore, its cultivation should be construed as "cultivation for the arising of those [factors] that have not yet arisen. It is appropriate to say so because it is simply the occurrence of the path.
Stability consists of exactly those supramundane states that have been produced. 398–401.
Having made the desire for action (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) the dominant factor, the concentration attained is called "concentration through desire. This is stated as:
"Concentration proceeding in dependence on desire is concentration through desire. These are the formations of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*), which accomplish the four functions.
This is a designation for the energy of right striving (*sammappadhāna*). Therefore he said: “Volitional formations that have become striving are ‘striving-formations’ (*padhāna-saṅkhārā*)”.
In this context, “become striving” means become energy. The term “striving” is included in order to exclude conditioned formations (*saṅkhata-saṅkhāra*) and so forth.

Alternatively, it is called a formation (*saṅkhāra*) because it forms (*saṅkharoti*) various distinctions; thus, it refers to all energy. In that regard, [it is distinguished] by way of accomplishing the four functions.
The inclusion of the word "exertion" (*padhāna*) is for the purpose of excluding the others; the meaning is that they are of the nature of exertion, that is, they are preeminent.

However, because the fourfold energy (*vīriya*) is intended here, the plural form is used. "By those states" means by desire-concentration (*chanda-samādhi*) and the formations of exertion (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*).
Regarding the term "basis of success" (*iddhipāda*): here, it is called "success" (*iddhi*) because it succeeds, that is, it is accomplished and brought to fruition.
*Attha*. Or else, it is called *iddhi* because by means of it beings succeed (*ijjhanti*), become successful, prosperous, and reach the highest excellence.

According to the first meaning, *iddhipāda* is simply *iddhi* that is a "foot" (*pāda*); the meaning is "a factor of success. According to the second meaning, *iddhipāda* is the "foot" (*pāda*) of success;
"foot" here means a foundation or a means of attainment. For it is by means of this [foundation] that one attains the success known as successive distinction.
