They go forth and they reach; therefore it is called a "foot" (*pāda*). Thus he said: "The foot of success (*iddhipāda*) means either the foot that is success, or the foot consisting of success.
Alternatively, by way of its accomplishment, in the sense of succeeding, beings succeed by means of this; thus it is "success" (*iddhi*).

The meaning is: by this method—that they are "grown" (*vuddhā*) or have "reached the peak" (*ukkaṃsagatā*)—the collection of the remaining [mental] states and mental factors is the basis for those things reckoned as "successes" (*iddhi*), which are associated with wholesome consciousness such as access concentration;
it is their foundation in the sense of being the support for the volitional formations of desire, concentration, and exertion.
For this very reason, in the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga*, it is said: "The 'basis of success' is the aggregate of feeling... [and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness of one who has become thus."

It has been said. And because that very supernormal power (iddhi), when spoken of in that way, has the three factors of desire-concentration and the volitional formations of striving as its basis and foundation for each successive higher stage compared to each successive lower one, it is therefore said:

"the foot that has become supernormal power" (iddhibhūtaṃ pādaṃ). Likewise, the factors mentioned below are both supernormal powers and bases of supernormal power; however, the remaining associated factors are...
The four aggregates are indeed the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).

The three factors—consisting of energy, concentration of mind, and concentration of investigation—as well as their respective formative activities (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*), are both psychic powers and bases of psychic power; however, the remaining four associated aggregates are bases of psychic power alone.
Furthermore, it should be understood that each preceding stage is called a "basis of psychic power," while each subsequent attainment is called "psychic power."
This meaning should be illustrated either by way of access concentration or by way of insight.

For the preliminary work for the first jhāna is called the "basis of psychic power," while the first jhāna itself is called "psychic power. [The same applies to] the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna... the base of infinite space...

the base of infinite consciousness... the base of nothingness... and the preliminary work for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called the "basis of psychic power," while that attainment itself is called "psychic power."

The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called "success" (iddhi). The insight into the stream-entry path is called the "basis of success," while the stream-entry path itself is called "success.
The insight into the once-return, non-return, and arahant paths is called the "basis of success," while the arahant path itself is called "success.
It is indeed appropriate to explain it also by way of attainment: for the first jhāna is called the "basis of success," and the second jhāna...
What is called "success" (iddhi). The second jhāna is called the basis of success (iddhipāda), and the third jhāna is called success...
[and so on] ...the path of non-returning is called the basis of success, and the path of arahantship is called success.
"In the rest" refers to those beginning with energy, concentration, and so forth; for there, having made energy, mind, or investigation the dominant factor (adhipati), [one attains success].

The meaning should be understood as follows: "concentration attained" refers to concentration through energy (*vīriya-samādhi*), concentration through mind (*citta-samādhi*), and concentration through inquiry (*vīmaṃsā-samādhi*).
Regarding "one among desire and the rest": the intention is that among the four factors beginning with desire, it is the first one mentioned—the primary factor—that is "desire.
For this very reason he says: "Then for him, this is the first basis of accomplishment (*iddhipāda*). The same applies to the others; by this, energy and mind...

This shows that the second basis for psychic power, beginning with energy (*vīriya-iddhipāda*), should be applied by way of those who reach *arahantship* after increasing insight (*vipassanā*) based on investigation (*vīmaṃsā*).
For by this sutta, the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) reaching its ultimate point for four types of bhikkhus is demonstrated.
For one bhikkhu relies upon desire (*chanda*), through the wholesome desire for the Dhamma and the wish to act, in the accomplishment of the goal.
When one thinks, "I shall produce supramundane states;
there is no burden for me in producing them," one produces supramundane states by making zeal the chief, zeal the yoke, and zeal the precursor.
One relies on energy, another on concentration, and another relies on wisdom; it is through wisdom that the accomplishment of the goal occurs.

When one thinks, "I shall produce the supramundane state; there is no burden for me in its production," one produces the supramundane state by making wisdom the eldest, the leader, the yoke-bearer, and the precursor. How so?
Just as when four sons of ministers are wandering about having sought positions of authority, one [of them] attends upon [the king].
He relies: one on bravery, one on birth, and one on counsel. How so?
For among them, the first, by being diligent in attendance and thereby achieving his purpose, relies on attendance, thinking, "If this position is available, I shall obtain it.
The second, though diligent in attendance, [thinks], "When a battle has presented itself, some are unable to stand firm..."
“He cannot [do it himself], but the king’s border will surely revolt;
when that has revolted, we shall perform service before the chariot, win over the king, and have him grant us this position”—thus he relies on his own courage.
The third [considers]: “Even if one possesses courage, some may be of low birth; having cleared up the matter of birth, I shall grant the position.”
"He will give me [a position]," he thus relies on his birth. The fourth [type of person] thinks, "Even one who possesses birth may be unconsultable;
when a task requiring counsel arises, they will cause this person to be brought to that office," and so he relies on his mantra.
All of them, by the power of their respective reliance, attained their respective positions.
In this regard, having become diligent in his attendance and having attained a higher station, he relies upon desire;
through the wholesome desire for the dhamma consisting of the wish-to-act, thinking, "If the accomplishment of the goal is possible, I shall produce the supramundane dhamma;
there is no doubt in me regarding its production," he makes desire the chief, desire the burden, and desire the precursor, thereby becoming a producer of the supramundane dhamma.
One should look to the Elder Raṭṭhapāla as an example. For that venerable one, thinking, "When there is such zeal, how could they not grant permission?
did not eat for seven days until he had obtained his parents' consent. Having gone forth and relying solely on his own zeal, he realized the supramundane Dhamma.
Just as he attained a high position by winning over the king through his courageous nature, so too should one proceed.

One should be seen as a producer of supramundane states by making energy the chief, energy the burden, and energy the forerunner, just like the Elder Soṇa. For that venerable one, having made energy his burden, produced supramundane states.
Just as one who has attained a high station through excellence of birth [makes that status primary], so too the mind is the chief, the mind is the burden, and the mind is the forerunner.
One should be seen as a producer of supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*), like the Elder Saṃbhūta.
For that venerable one, having made the mind the chief, the mind the burden, and the mind the forerunner, produced supramundane states.

Just as one who has relied upon a mantra attains a high station, so too [one produces supramundane states] by making investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) the chief, investigation the burden, and investigation the forerunner.
The Elder Mogharāja should be regarded as one who, having made the supramundane Dhamma his objective, brought it forth.
For that venerable one, making investigation his chief, making investigation his burden, and making investigation his precursor, brought forth the supramundane Dhamma.
Indeed, the Blessed One spoke to him on the discourse of emptiness, saying, "Behold the world as empty," and [did so] for the purpose of suppressing pride dependent upon wisdom.
Though questioned twice, he did not answer the question. In this context, it is said that the repeated arousal of desire is like "pleasing" (tosana);
thus, desire is described as being similar to a "presence" (upaṭṭhāna). Because of its state of firmness, energy (viriya) is similar to "bravery" (sūratta).
And because of the statement, "The king is the lord of the six doors," the primacy of consciousness (citta) is similar to a "noble birth" (visiṭṭhajāti).
402–406. "In its own duty of faith" means in the act of believing, which is its own function of faith (*saddhā-kicca*).

"It exercises lordship" means that it exercises lordship over the associated states by way of following them; therefore, because it is faith itself that is the faculty in the sense of predominance (*ādhipateyyattha*), it is called the "faith-faculty" (*saddhindriya*).
Likewise, regarding energy and the others in their respective functions, he says: "In the case of the energy-faculty and the rest..."

“The same method applies,” he said. “Purifying” means purifying by way of three causes characterized by: avoiding opposing sides, cultivating one’s own side, and gathering similar and proximate conditions.
“Avoiding persons lacking faith” means avoiding coarse individuals who are devoid of faith due to the absence of confidence and affection toward the Buddha and the other [Three Jewels].
"By avoiding them entirely. "Associating with persons endowed with faith" means associating with those resolved upon faith in the Buddha and so forth, such as the Elder Vakkali.

"Inspiring confidence" refers to discourses such as the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*, which bring about confidence. "Reflecting" means reflecting and contemplating each [point] individually according to both the text and the meaning.
"Is purified" means that, by way of conditions, it becomes pure through the removal of the stains of opposing factors.
The faculty of faith becomes purified through natural purity and through the production of the fruit of purification. This same method applies to the remaining [faculties] as well.

Regarding "the right efforts" (*sammappadhāna*), it refers to the discourses connected with the right efforts. This same method applies to the remaining [foundations of mindfulness, bases of psychic power, and faculties] as well.
Regarding "the jhānas and liberations," this refers both to the jhānas beginning with the first jhāna and to the liberations beginning with the first liberation. And here, although—
The jhānas themselves are the liberations; however, they are mentioned separately by way of their modes of occurrence.
"The range of profound knowledge" means the sphere of activity for profound knowledges. Therefore he said: "subtle and delicate," and so forth.
"The difference between the aggregates" refers to the diversity of the aggregates by way of their intrinsic nature, genus, plane, and so on. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
"Without prior adherence" means without prior adherence to the development [of concentration] performed previously. "In the case of those whose burden is faith, etc.
means in the case of those whose burden is faith (*saddhādhura*) and those whose burden is wisdom (*paññādhura*). "At the conclusion" means at the end of the development.

"Having turned away" means having turned away from conditioned phenomena as an object and having made Nibbāna the object. "He attains Arahatship" means he attains Arahatship through a succession of paths. "In the sense of being unshakable" means...
By way of being unshakable by opposing factors. By this very [quality], its stability among the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma) should also be understood as being revealed.
For without stability among the associated states, it is impossible to be unshakable by opposing factors.
Indeed, it is precisely through stability among the associated states that these [states]—whether unwholesome (akusala) or indeterminate (abyākata)—attain their state of strength.
"By lack of faith" means for the sake of lack of faith. This is an ablative expression used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. 418.
"Of the initial terms" means of the terms beginning with mindfulness (*sati*). "In the sense of remembering" means in the sense of recollecting what was done long ago and what was said long ago.

"Having the characteristic of being established" means having the nature of being established upon those objects by way of clearly discerning the modes of foulness (*asubha*) in the body and so forth.
*Upaṭṭhānaṃ* (establishment) means standing by having approached the object, or not relinquishing the object. It has the characteristic of non-forgetting; its nature is that of not being forgetful.
Like a gourd in water, it does not allow the mind to drift away from the object;

like a stone, it is the placing of the object so that it remains motionless, the act of remembering, making it not forgotten—this is *apilāpana*. *Sāpateyyaṃ* (property)... [is]... *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "Sāpateyyanti".)*

*Santakaṃ* means "one's own. *Apilāpanaṃ* means he makes it not forgotten; he causes it to be remembered. The meaning is that he makes the king recognize and recollect his sovereign prosperity morning and evening.
*Kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāge dhamme* means phenomena characterized by contrast, namely those reckoned as dark (*kaṇha*) and bright (*sukka*).
For the dark phenomenon has its counterpart in the bright, and the bright has its counterpart in the dark. The word *vitthāra* (elaboration) [is used here].
This is the meaning of the word *ādi* (etcetera). By that [word], it is meant: "These four things are the right efforts;

these four are the bases of psychic power; these five are the faculties; these five are the powers; these seven are the factors of enlightenment; this is the noble eightfold path; this is serenity; this is insight;
this is true knowledge; this is liberation; these are the supramundane states"—thus [it is said].
"O Great King, mindfulness has the characteristic of not forgetting"—this includes the remainder of the canonical text. "By the Elder" means by the Elder Nāgasena.
For he, having established the function (kicca) as the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of phenomena, defined them thus: "Mindfulness has the characteristic of not forgetting;
applied thought has the characteristic of striking," and so forth. For in this way, phenomena become easy to understand. Non-forgetfulness is the function that is the opposite of forgetfulness.

He did not say "the mere absence of confusion," but rather said, "its essence is non-confusion. That state by whose power associated mental states are directed toward the object is mindfulness (*sati*).

Therefore, it is said that it "manifests as the state of being directed toward the objective field" (*gocarābhimukhībhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā*), because it presents to them their state of being directed toward the object, or because it itself stands present by way of being directed toward the object.
It is a "factor of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) because it is rightly praised as a factor of enlightenment.

Or, it is a factor of enlightenment because it is a limb of enlightenment—that is, of the harmony of states that will be described as "enlightenment," or of the noble disciple who possesses enlightenment. With the words beginning "For that which... and so forth, he explains in brief that very meaning already stated.
The connection between the phrase "this harmony of states" and the phrase "is called enlightenment" is as follows: "by the harmony of states."

The connection is with the phrase "by means of a collection of phenomena" (*dhammasamūhena*) and "by means of which harmony of phenomena" (*yāya dhammasāmaggiyā*). Regarding "establishment" (*patiṭṭhāna*) and "accumulation" (*āyūhanā*), the commentary on the *Oghataraṇa Sutta* states:
"Establishment is by way of the defilements (*kilesa*); accumulation is by way of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*). Establishment is by way of craving (*taṇhā*) and views (*diṭṭhi*);
accumulation is by way of the remaining defilements and volitional formations. Establishment is by way of craving; accumulation is by way of views."
“Establishment by way of the eternalist view; accumulation by way of the annihilationist view. Establishment by way of sluggishness; accumulation by way of restlessness.
Establishment by way of devotion to sensual pleasure; accumulation by way of devotion to self-mortification.
Establishment by way of all unwholesome volitional formations; accumulation by way of all mundane wholesome volitional formations.”
These [factors] are to be understood by way of those not mentioned here among the seven modes thus stated. Regarding the phrase "as the opposites":

herein, the collection of factors (dhamma-sāmaggī) dominated by investigation of phenomena (dhamma-vicaya), energy (vīriya), and rapture (pīti) is the opposite of the adherence to indolence, the basis of stagnation, devotion to sensual pleasure, and the view of annihilationism;

while that dominated by tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā) is the opposite of agitation, the accumulation [of defilements], devotion to self-mortification, and the view of eternalism.
The harmony of the Dhamma is the antidote. Mindfulness, however, is required for both; for it is described as "beneficial in all respects.

By the phrase "it awakens from the sleep of the continuity of defilements," he shows that mindfulness and the other factors possess the nature of enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) even when accompanied by insight that has reached its culmination.
For insight leading to emergence proceeds precisely while suppressing the defilements.
With the words "Four indeed," etc., he shows the state of being enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*) belonging to those [states] accompanied by the path and its fruit.
Regarding the objection—"How is it to be known that penetration of the truths occurs when the seven enlightenment factors are developed?"—he says "As it has been said," and so forth.

By the phrase "like the jhāna-factors, the path-factors, and so on," he indicates that the terms *bodhi* (enlightenment) and *bojjhaṅga* (enlightenment factor) refer respectively to the whole and its parts.
[The text] shows [this]. "Like the parts of an army or the parts of a chariot"—by this, he shows that the designation of a person (*puggalapaññatti*) is a designation of what does not exist.

It is said, "they lead to enlightenment, thus they are factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*)," taking the word *aṅga* (factor) in the sense of a cause. "They awaken, thus they are enlightenments (*bodhiyo*);

the factors of those very enlightenments are the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgānī*)"—thus it is said: "They awaken, thus they are factors of enlightenment. [This refers to] insight (*vipassanā*) and so forth.

Because they awaken correctly (*sammā*)— that is, directly (*paṭimukhaṃ*) through direct perception (*paccakkhabhāvena*)— in accordance with the truths that are to be awakened to, such as the causes and so forth,
the terms "anubujjhanti" (they awaken after) and so on are stated by means of prefixes (*upasaggehi*) that illuminate these specific meanings.
For the word *bodhi* generally encompasses awakening endowed with all its particular qualities, while the prefix *sam-* denotes praise.
And because it is seen in a beautiful state, he says: "The enlightenment factor that is praised and beautiful is the *sambojjhaṅga*.

It investigates phenomena (*dhamma*), thus it is *dhammavicaya*. Therein, "phenomena" refers to the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths, since there is no phenomenon possessing an intrinsic nature apart from them.
For that very reason, its characteristic is investigation. Its function is to illuminate the object; it does so by way of non-confusion.
"Attends closely" means it has non-delusion as its manifestation.
"Vīriya" is the state or the activity of one who is *vīra* (heroic). "Because it must be set in motion" means because it must be put into operation.

"Having exertion as its characteristic" means it has the characteristic of uplifting the associated mental states, not allowing them to fall into the side of indolence. For that very reason, [it upholds] the associated mental states...
It has the function of supporting. It means not sinking, not subsiding.

"Satisfies" means it refreshes. Through its function of satisfying, there is a refreshing of the body by means of the sublime material qualities produced by that [joy], just as there is for the associated mental states.
This characteristic is stated by way of pervading joy; likewise is its function. It is the state of elation.
It presents elation; thus it is "having elation as its manifestation. This is said by way of uplifting joy (*ubbega-pīti*).
"By the allaying of bodily and mental distress" means by the calming and subsiding of bodily distress and mental distress.
Therefore he said: "It has tranquility as its characteristic," meaning it has the characteristic of subsiding bodily and mental distress.
This is the meaning. Here, "body" (*kāya*) refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*). "Affliction" (*daratha*) means agitation;
it is a designation for the defilements such as restlessness which are conditions for suffering and mental distress, or for the four aggregates when they proceed in that manner.
By the crushing of affliction, there is a state of coolness free from feverish burning and agitation; this is the state of coolness through non-agitation.
Right placement of the mind is concentration (*samādhi*). Non-distraction is the state of being undistracted in those associated [mental factors].
That phenomenon by which the associated factors become undistracted is non-distraction. It is the state of not dispersing itself.
Alternatively, it has the characteristic of non-distraction because it is the opposite of distraction. Like water for bath-powder, it [unifies] the associated phenomena.
It is characterized by non-distraction because its function is to collect [the mind]; thus it has non-distraction as its characteristic.
It manifests as the stability of the mind, like the steadiness of a lamp in a windless place; thus it has the stability of the mind as its manifestation.
It is so called because of its equanimous observation of associated states, like a charioteer observing horses that are proceeding evenly.
"Having the characteristic of reflective discernment" means having the characteristic of reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) consisting in investigation while remaining in a state of neutrality.
"Having the characteristic of equalizing" means having the characteristic of causing associated states to proceed equally, without partiality, in their respective functions.
Even though it proceeds with a neutral disposition, it causes the other associated states to proceed in their respective functions, just as...
Even while sitting in silence, the king administers justice in the court of law, remaining diligent in his respective duties.
Because it is a condition for conduct that is neither dejected nor arrogant, its function is to prevent deficiency and excess. Its function is to sever partiality;
that is, to act in such a way as not to proceed by way of favoritism, thinking, "Let this matter be minor," or "Let this matter be more important."
It has the function of cutting off partiality, as it were, by severing bias; thus it is "of the nature of cutting off partiality.
It presents itself with a state of neutrality toward the functions of the associated states in their respective roles; thus it is "manifested as a state of neutrality.
Since the very production of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) one after another constitutes their intensification and growth, he says: "it produces."
Mindfulness and clear comprehension are "mindfulness-and-clear-comprehension"; alternatively, clear comprehension based on mindfulness is "mindfulness-and-clear-comprehension.
Because it brings about the state of acting with mindfulness in all situations, it serves for the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*).

Just as the abandoning of contrary states and the cultivation of corresponding states lead to the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen, so too does the avoidance of persons devoid of mindfulness [lead to their arising].

By the phrase "mindfulness and clear comprehension," etc., he shows this meaning: that associating with persons who act with mindfulness and being intent upon that [practice] leads to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor.
Regarding the "seven instances": "In advancing and in retreating, he acts with clear comprehension;
in looking forward and in looking aside, he acts with clear comprehension; in bending and in stretching, he acts with clear comprehension..."
“He is one who acts with clear comprehension when wearing the outer robe, the inner robe, and the bowl; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting;
he acts with clear comprehension in performing the excretory functions; he acts with clear comprehension when going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
Thus it was said regarding these seven instances beginning with “walking” (abhikkanta), etc., by the Elder Tissadatta.
He who, at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), took a golden stylus and challenged the assembly, asking, "In which of the eighteen languages shall I preach the Dhamma?"—
this refers to the Elder Abhaya, meaning the Elder Dattābhaya. "Adherence" (abhinivesa) refers to adherence through insight (vipassanā).
“Being inquisitive” means the state of questioning after having investigated thoroughly.

For one who, having attended upon a teacher and investigated the five Nikāyas together with their commentaries, asks about whatever therein constitutes a point of difficulty—asking, for instance, regarding the meaning of the aggregates, bases, and so forth, “Venerable sir, how is this?
What is the meaning of this?”—the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*) arises.
It arises. Therefore he said: “The abundance of the aggregates, elements...

[and so forth]... and the frequent practice. Regarding the phrase “making the basis pure”: here, because it is the locus for the occurrence of consciousness and mental factors, the term “basis” (vatthu) is intended to mean the body as well as the robes and other requisites connected with it. These should be used in such a way that they bring happiness to the mind.
The instrument for these is the act of cleansing. Therefore he said: “Of the internal and external,” and so forth.
“With accumulated humors” means with humors increased by way of wind, bile, and so on. “Smeared with sweat and dirt” means smeared with both sweat and the bodily dirt known as *jallikā*.
By the word “and” (*ca*), he includes other things that cause affliction to the body, such as over-crowding and the like. “Or a lodging” (the word “or”): by this word...

The inclusion of bowls and so forth that have been stained by dirt should be understood [here]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by means of making repairs, etc.," the inclusion of boiling bowls and similar acts should be understood.
Regarding the phrase "when the object (*vatthu*) is not corrupt": this refers to when the physical basis (*vatthu*) is not corrupted, or when it is the objective domain (*visaya*).

How can those internal and external bases be the domain for one intent on meditation? It is stated [so] precisely by way of the successive arising of mental states (*cittuppāda*) occurring from time to time.
For those arising of consciousness lead to a state of impurity in one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*).

Regarding the phrase "in consciousness and mental factors" (*cittacetasikesu*), this refers to the consciousness and mental factors that serve as the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) and so forth. As for the word "also" (*api*) in the expression "knowledge also" (*ñāṇampi*), it has the sense of inclusion.
By this, it is meant: "It is not only the physical basis (*vatthu*) that is impure; rather, when that [basis] is impure, knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is also impure."
Just as the impurity of that which depends upon something follows from the impurity of its support, it shows that the impurity of the subject follows from the impurity of the object.
"Making them equal" means, in terms of function, making them neither deficient nor excessive. The faculty of faith becomes powerful regarding the object to be believed.

Due to the condition [of the object], because the function of resolve is more prominent, because wisdom is not yet clear, and because energy and the other faculties are lax, the faculty of faith becomes strong. Therefore he said: "The others are weak.
"From that" means: from the state of the faculty of faith being strong and the others being weak. [This leads to] falling on the side of indolence.

Exertion (*paggaha*) is the grasping and providing of support for the associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*) without giving them away. "The function of exertion" (*paggaha-kicca*) means exertion itself as the function.

This should be connected by supplying the words "it is not able to perform. Establishment (*upaṭṭhāna*) is the act of approaching and remaining with the object, or the non-relinquishing of it. It is the opposite of distraction, or that by which the associated states become undistracted.

That is non-distraction. Just as the eye cannot perform its function of seeing—perceiving the true nature of an object as it really is—it is unable to do so because it is overwhelmed by the powerful faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
For among co-nascent phenomena that arise together while exercising their respective lordship (*indaṭṭha*), the accomplishment of the purpose occurs only through their mutual partiality.
"Not otherwise. By the word "therefore" (tasmā), he refers back to the very meaning already stated as being the cause. "That" refers to the faculty of faith (saddhindriya).

"By means of reflecting on the intrinsic nature of phenomena" (dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena) means: when the faculty of faith has become strong through the exceptional occurrence of resolve (adhimuccana) regarding the excellence of the object to be believed—such as its loftiness—and [one reflects] upon the distinction between that condition (paccaya) and the arisen state conditioned by it (paccayuppanna), etc.

By means of investigating according to reality. For when things are thus grasped according to their true nature by way of the principle of suchness (*evaṃdhammatā*), there is no expansive resolve (*adhimokkha*), because the operation of wisdom (*paññā*) is predominant through the thorough understanding that "this is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of these phenomena.
Indeed, among the factors that bear the burden [of the path], just as when faith is strong, wisdom becomes weak; [so it is here].
Thus, when wisdom is strong, faith becomes weak. Therefore it is said: "It should be diminished by reflecting on the specific nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva).

Likewise, regarding "by non-attention": this means not engaging in the cultivation of meditation in the same manner in which the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) became strong for one who was previously devoted to that cultivation. Here, [the weakness] of the faculty of faith is twofold.
The state of being powerful arises either from the predominance of its own function due to specific conditions, or because the functions of energy (*vīriya*) and the other faculties are weak.
In this regard, the first alternative shows the method for weakening [the faculties], while in the second alternative, it shows how—

just as the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) becomes strong through attention (*manasikāra*) by virtue of the weakness of the functions of energy and the others— it likewise becomes strong through non-attention (*amanasikāra*) to energy and the others.
The faculty of faith should be diminished by one who brings it into a state of equal flavor with those [other faculties] through a mental attention that produces proficiency in their function.
By this same method, the procedure for diminishing the remaining faculties should also be understood.
Regarding the case of the Elder Vakkali: for that venerable one, having performed his duties through devotion to faith, was intent on beholding the form of the Teacher.
While he was dwelling thus, the Teacher instructed him in the manner beginning with, "Vakkali, what is the use of seeing this foul body?
He who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me," and directed him toward a meditation subject;
yet, failing to apply himself to it and being dismissed, he climbed to a precipice to cast himself down. Then the Teacher—
Having manifested himself by emitting a radiance while remaining seated, he said:
“The bhikkhu who abounds in gladness, who has faith in the Buddha’s teaching,
shall attain the peaceful state, the bliss that is the stilling of all conditioned formations.”
Having spoken this verse, he said, "Come, Vakkali. Bathed by that very nectar, Vakkali became joyful and elated and began to practice insight (vipassanā);
however, because of the excessive strength of his faith, he did not enter the path of insight.
Knowing this, the Blessed One purified a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) for him and gave it to him so that he might bring his faculties to equilibrium. Then, by the Teacher...
Abiding by the method of giving, he intensified his insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahatship through the sequence of the paths. Therefore it is said:

"The story of the Elder Vakkali is the illustration here. "Here" refers to the state where, due to the predominance of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), the remaining faculties fail to perform their respective functions.
"The distinction of other functions" refers to the specific roles such as establishing mindfulness (upaṭṭhāna) and so forth. "Serenity and the rest" refers to [the factors] beginning with passaddhi.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of the concentration and equanimity factors of enlightenment is intended. Regarding the phrase "should be diminished":

just as the strength of the faculty of faith is diminished by reflecting on the intrinsic nature of phenomena, so too the excess of the faculty of energy is diminished by the cultivation of tranquility and the other [factors], because that [tranquility] belongs to the side of concentration. For it is thus with the faculty of concentration.

Just as the cultivation of energy and the other [faculties] protects the preponderance of the energy faculty from falling into indolence, so too the cultivation of tranquility and the others protects the preponderance of the energy faculty from falling into agitation;
thus it exclusively causes [that preponderance] to diminish. Therefore it is said: "It is to be diminished by the cultivation of tranquility and the others.
The story of the Elder Soṇa refers to the story of the delicate Elder Soṇa; for that venerable one was in the presence of the Teacher...
Having taken up his meditation subject, while dwelling in the Sītavana forest, he resolved: "My body is delicate, and it is not possible to attain happiness merely through ease;
even by undergoing hardship, the duty of a recluse must be performed.

Thus, applying himself to striving and fixing himself solely upon standing and walking, he maintained firm energy even as blisters arose on the soles of his feet, remaining equanimous toward the pain.
While practicing, he was unable to produce any distinction because of his excessive energy.
The Teacher went there, instructed him with the "Lute Simile" discourse, and having purified the meditation subject by showing the method for balancing energy, He departed for Vulture Peak.
The Elder, too, applying the balance of energy according to the method given by the Teacher and developing it, further intensified his insight.
He was established in arahantship. Therefore it is said: “The story of the Elder Soṇa should be illustrated.
“In the remaining ones as well” means in the case of the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
“Balance” refers to the state of neither deficiency nor excess between faith and wisdom, and likewise between concentration and energy. Just as...
Indeed, it is especially desirable that faith (*saddhā*) and wisdom (*paññā*), which serve as distinct primary factors (*dhuriyadhamma*), do not overstep one another in their functions;

for through their balanced equilibrium, absorption (*appanā*) is achieved. Likewise, when concentration (*samādhi*) and energy (*vīriya*)—which respectively belong to the sides of laxity (*kosajja*) and restlessness (*uddhacca*)—possess an equal flavor (*samarasatā*) due to their mutual support, there is an absence of falling into the two extremes among the associated mental states (*sampayuttadhamma*).
Thus, absorption (*appanā*) indeed succeeds. The passage beginning with "one of strong faith" (*balavasaddho*) is an exposition by way of contrast (*byatirekamukhena*) of that very same meaning.

Its meaning is as follows: one who is endowed with strong faith but lacks clear knowledge (*avisadañāṇa*) is one whose confidence is superficial (*mudhappasanno*), not one whose confidence is rooted in penetration (*aveccappasanno*).
For such a person places confidence in what is not a true basis, just like the disciples of the heterodox teachers (*titthiya*). This refers to the "Kerāṭika faction."

He sides with deceit. Running ahead of wisdom that is devoid of faith, he imagines such things as, "Merit consisting in giving arises even by the mere arising of the thought, without the relinquishing of the object to be given," being deceived by fallacious reasons.
Being thus, his mind is parched and ravaged by dry logic, and he does not accept the words of the wise or their persuasion.
It does not progress. Therefore he said: "Like a disease arising from medicine, it becomes incurable.

And just as here the mutual balance of faith and wisdom brings about welfare, while their imbalance brings about harm, so too the mutual balance of concentration and energy brings about non-distraction, whereas the other [imbalance] brings about distraction; thus, [balance] overcomes indolence.
The intention is that, because of this, one does not reach absorption (*appanā*). The same principle applies here to the statement "it overcomes restlessness" (*uddhacca*).
"Both of those" refers to the pair of faith and wisdom, as well as the pair of concentration and energy. "Should be made equal" means it should be brought to a state of equilibrium (*samarasa*).
"For one whose work is concentration" means for one whose meditation subject is calm (*samatha*). "Thus" means this being so, when faith is slightly stronger.

The meaning is "being present. "Having faith" means not thinking, "How can the arising of jhāna come about merely by attending to 'earth, earth'?", but rather having faith and generating confidence, thinking, "Surely the method taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One will succeed.
"Resolving" means resolving by way of conviction as if entering into the object, and thus leaping forward into it.
One-pointedness must be powerful because meditation has concentration as its dominant factor.

"Of both" refers to concentration and wisdom. Since, for one whose task is concentration, an excellence of wisdom is required just as much as an excellence of concentration, he says, "also by way of evenness";
the meaning is "by way of equality. "Absorption" refers to mundane absorption; for it is said, "it certainly exists."
He speaks with apprehension. However, for them, supramundane absorption is intended precisely through the balancing of these factors. As it is said:
“He develops serenity and insight coupled together.
If, specifically, the equality of faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy, is intended, why then does he say “mindfulness”?
"But mindfulness must be strong in all cases. "In all cases" refers to the five faculties belonging to the side of lethargy and agitation.
Taking those belonging to the side of agitation, he says, "faith, energy, and wisdom.

It should also be understood that it could be stated otherwise; for it is likewise said [only] with concentration belonging to the side of sloth, and not with "tranquility, concentration, and equanimity."
*Sāti* means "mindfulness. One who is appointed to all royal duties is a "minister for all affairs" (*sabbakammika*).
"By that" means by that reason of being desired in all circumstances; this is what was said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

They are "all-purposeful" (*sabbatthika*) because they are required in all circumstances—namely, when the mind is either sluggish or agitated—or because they must be sought after by the entire group of factors conducive to enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) belonging to the side of both sluggishness and agitation.
In all places, that alone is "all-beneficial. "Mind" refers to wholesome consciousness (*kusalacitta*).
For that, mindfulness is the refuge and the ultimate resort for the attainment of what has not been attained and for the realization of what has not been realized. Therefore he said:

"manifested as protection," and so forth. "For those whose wisdom has not plunged into the divisions of the aggregates and so on" means even by way of great learning in the scriptures regarding the aggregates, bases, and so forth.
For those whose intelligence is unestablished, service to the learned brings about knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*).
Even one who possesses nascent insight (*taruṇa-vipassanā*) is certainly called "wise" because he is established in knowledge consisting of mental development (*bhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa*); thus it was said:
"Service to fifty... [persons] endowed with wisdom. By way of the profundity of the phenomena to be known, there is the grasping of the profundity of the knowledge that delimits them.
He said: “By means of profound wisdom proceeding with respect to the profound aggregates and so forth.

For that object of knowledge is called the "profound course of knowledge" because one must proceed toward it with such wisdom; or, the "profound course of knowledge" is the detailed engagement of that wisdom therein.
Its reflective contemplation is what is meant by the phrase: “the reflective contemplation of the distinctions of profound wisdom.”

Because they generally inflict the fivefold torture upon a being reborn in hell as the very first thing, and because this is stated at the beginning in such discourses as the *Devadūta Sutta*, he says: "starting from the fivefold torture.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the time of carrying carts, etc.," he refers to other times when [the being] is tormented by humans and animals.
He gathers [them]. "One interval between Buddhas" (ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ) is stated with reference to beings who arise among the same successive classes of *petas*;
or it is stated thus because some *petas* or some animals might have long lifespans.
For instance, even though the Naga king Kāḷa had lived through the presence of four Buddhas, he was still present at the time of Metteyya as well.
They say that he will obtain the presence of the Blessed One, which refers to his being said to have a lifespan of an eon (*kappāyuka*).
"Thus seeing the benefits" means that all mundane and supramundane attainment of distinction depends entirely upon energy;
such is the nature of one who sees the benefits in energy. "The path of travel" refers to the practice leading to Nibbāna together with its preliminary stages.
It is the sequence of the Noble Path together with insight, or the succession of the seven purifications.
For that is called the "path of travel" because it is the way to be traversed, the way to be entered, by a bhikkhu for the purpose of departing from the round (vaṭṭa).
"Abounding in bodily exertion" means being intent on strengthening the body in whatever way possible. "Almsfood" means the alms-food of the country.

"Piṇḍapātāpacāyana" (honoring the almsfood) means honoring the alms-food by making the gift-givers perceive that their service toward oneself has become highly fruitful through one's own proper practice.
"Taking it out" means taking it from the bowl-bag. "Hearing that sound" refers to hearing those words of the female lay follower at the door of the leaf-hut.
Remaining [in this state], having heard with the divine ear (*dibbasota*) through the attainment of the five higher knowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*):

"Human success, divine success, and the success of Nibbāna—these are the three successes. Will you be able to give? means that by means of meritorious deeds consisting of giving (*dānamaya*) and service (*veyyāvaccamaya*) performed by you, through attaining the status of an excellent field of merit, there will be successive successes among gods and humans.
"Will you be able to grant the attainment of Nibbāna?"—thus the Elder asks himself.
"Smiling" means smiling out of the joy that arose at the conclusion of his reflection, thinking, "I have indeed transcended the suffering of the round of existence without difficulty.
"A time free from danger" means a time without calamity; at such a time, the requisites for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus were easily obtained.
The intention is that there is no mental affliction caused by external conditions. "Even while they are looking on" uses the genitive case in a sense of disregard.
"A milk-cow" means a cow that gives milk. "Having done some work" means having performed some kind of labor for wages.
"The work of the sugarcane mill" refers to the task to be performed at the sugarcane mill shed. "That very path" refers to the path entered upon by the lay follower (upāsaka).
"Upakaṭṭhāya" means when it is near. "Vippaṭipannaṃ" means one who has practiced wrongly by transgressing the duties of birth, the duties of family, and so forth.

"Evaṃ" means just as a son who has practiced wrongly, by that very wrong practice, becomes an outsider from the family lineage and does not share in the inheritance from his father, so too the lazy person, by that very state of laziness, does not practice rightly.
He does not partake in the noble inheritance of wealth to be obtained from the presence of the Teacher. Only one who has aroused energy obtains it by practicing correctly.
The construction is: "the enlightenment factor of energy arises. This applies in all cases.

"Great" means great and vast in qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth, and not shared by others. Showing that this greatness of his qualities became manifest in the world through the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system (dasasahassilokadhātu), he said: "Of the Teacher," and so on.

Because the state of being a follower of the Sakyan (Sakyaputtiya) arises for one who has gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation by virtue of that very act of going forth, he spoke the words beginning with “unbroken” (*asambhinnāya*) in order to demonstrate the status of being a son of the Buddha.

Avoiding from afar those individuals who are like animals— those who are lazy, who do not know even the mere name of meditation, who are preoccupied with physical strength, who eat as much as they desire,
and who devote themselves to the pleasures of lying down and so forth— is what is meant by “avoiding the indolent person” (*kusītapuggalaparivajjanā*).
He said: “‘Like a python standing with its belly full,’ and so forth.

By means of the commencement of meditation through such passages as, “We shall purify the mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the day,” for those who have initiated energy and possess firm exertion, approaching them from time to time constitutes “service to persons who have initiated energy”; thus he said, “to those who have initiated energy,” and so forth.
In the *Visuddhimagga*, however, this pair—reflection on the greatness of one’s birth and reflection on the greatness of one’s fellow celibates—is not included;
rather, this pair—dispelling sloth and torpor and reflection on the right exertions—is included.
Among these, reflection on the right exertions is included precisely because of the vision of their benefits for the attainment of mundane and supramundane distinctions.
Because it is seen as being dependent upon energy (*vīriya*), the dispelling of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) is already included by the very fact of being intent upon that [energy].
For one who is devotedly engaged in the arousal of energy, the dispelling of sloth and torpor is indeed accomplished as a matter of course.

In this regard, [the overcoming of sloth and torpor] occurs by way of avoiding persons who are lazy in dispelling sloth and torpor, associating with persons who have initiated energy, being intent upon that [energy], shaking off opposing factors, and providing the necessary conditions.
The contemplation of the fear of the states of misery and so forth should be understood as producing the energy enlightenment factor by way of providing encouragement.
Because the access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) is reached through the recollection of the Buddha, it is said: "as far as access.
"Pervading the entire body" means pervading the whole body with sublime material qualities originated by rapture; [likewise] the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha...
Even for one who is recollecting [the Buddha], the enlightenment factor of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*) arises, pervading the entire body up to the stage of access concentration (*upacāra*).

In this same way, it should be applied to the remaining recollections (*anussati*) and to the reviewing of inspiring discourses (*pasādanīyasuttanta*), since that too belongs to the same category by virtue of being a basis for liberation (*vimuttāyatana*).
At such a time refers to the time mentioned as "in times of fear due to famine, etc. ... *samāpatti* ... not.

"They practice" is said by way of the recollection of peace (*upasamānussati*). For, even when there is a limited pacification of formations (*saṅkhāra*), because the attention of meditation proceeds in such a way as if it were an unlimited pacification, it becomes capable of suppressing the defilements;
bringing about access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*) and being endowed with such joy and gladness, it [serves] for the factor of enlightenment of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*).
"Dependent upon [this], it comes to be. In this context, the reading is "the defilements have been suppressed.

The word *iti* in the phrase "they do not manifest" has the sense of a reason. The construction is: "because they do not manifest, therefore, for one who reflects upon that non-manifestation of theirs...
For it is not logical that the arising of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) occurs for one reflecting upon the defilements; rather, it occurs in relation to inspiring objects.
Coarseness is the state of having a coarse heart due to the absence of clarity and affection. This is understood through the failure to show respect and reverence therein;
thus it is said: "in the manifestation of coarseness through lack of careful performance.
"The practice of refined food" means the practice of refined and suitable food. By the inclusion of "pleasure in climate and postures,"...
The adoption of postures conducive [to meditation] should be observed.

For when all three types of such conduct are practiced as being conducive, they bring about mental fitness by producing physical well-being, and thus become the cause for both kinds of tranquility (passaddhi).

"Pleasure and pain found among those beings who are without roots (ahetuka)" is one extreme; however, "the view that there is an unequal cause, such as a Supreme Lord (issara) and so forth," is another.
This is the second [extreme]. Not approaching either of these two extremes, thinking "one comes to be according to one's own karma," is the middle way of practice.
One whose application is neutral is "neutral in application"; the state of being such is "neutrality of application.
For this is the cause for natural non-excitement and for that tranquility of body; it brings about the two kinds of tranquility. By this very [means]...
It should be understood that avoiding persons with agitated bodies and associating with persons with tranquil bodies is praised as bringing about those [qualities].

It has been stated that making the physical basis pure and balancing the faculties bring about wisdom; yet they also bring about concentration. Because they bring about concentration, they likewise bring about wisdom; thus it was said: "Making the physical basis pure... should be understood.
This is because there is no interval between skill in the causes and skill in development, and because skill in protection is rooted in them.
“Skill in the sign” (nimittakusalatā) is said to mean skill in apprehending the kasiṇa-sign. And the phrase “of the kasiṇa-sign” should be regarded as merely illustrative;
for skill in apprehending any sign whatsoever that serves as the basis for the arising of jhāna—such as the sign of foulness (asubhanimitta), and so on—is indeed skill in the sign.
By the word “etcetera” in the phrase “through excessive laxity of energy, etc.,” the dullness of the application of wisdom is included.

And it includes the lack of application. Its "exertion" is the lifting up of that sluggish mind from its state of lethargy by arousing the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor and the others. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"But on whatever occasion, monks, the mind is sluggish, that is the time for the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor."
It is the time for the cultivation of the energy factor of enlightenment; it is the time for the cultivation of the rapture factor of enlightenment.
Why is that? Because, monks, a sunken mind is easily uplifted by these states.
Just as if, monks, a man were desirous of kindling a small fire, and he were to take dry...
“If one were to throw dry grass into it, throw dry cow dung into it, throw dry wood into it,
blow upon it with the breath of the mouth, and not scatter dust over it, would that man be able to kindle the small fire? “Yes, venerable sir.”

And here, it should be understood that the development and arousal of the factors of enlightenment beginning with the investigation-of-phenomena factor (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga) occurs according to their respective nutriment; this has already been explained immediately above.
By the phrase "through excessive energy and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the application of wisdom and the power of exertion, as well as the agitation caused by joy.
"Its suppression" refers to the suppression of that agitated mind by means of the arousal of the concentration-enlightenment-factor (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga) and the others.
The restraint of an agitated offense. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the mind is agitated, at that time it is the right time for the development of the tranquility enlightenment factor, the right time for the development of the concentration enlightenment factor, and the right time for the development of the equanimity enlightenment factor.”
For what reason? Because, monks, the agitated mind is well-pacified by these qualities.
Just as if, monks, a man wishing to extinguish a great mass of fire were to throw wet grass there, place wet cow dung there, and set wet wood there.
"Should he throw [fuel] into it, blow upon it with his breath, and scatter dust over it,
would that man be able to extinguish the great mass of fire?"— "Certainly not, venerable sir. In this case as well,
the development and arousal of the enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility occurs by way of their respective nutriment.

These are to be understood. Therein, the development of the tranquility enlightenment factor (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga*) has already been stated; that of the concentration enlightenment factor (*samādhi-sambojjhaṅga*) is being stated now;
and that of the remaining one will be explained immediately thereafter.
"Due to the dullness of the application of wisdom" means due to the smallness of the activity of wisdom. For just as giving (*dāna*) is dominated by non-greed (*alobha*), [so too is this case].

Virtue has non-hatred as its predominant factor; likewise, development has non-delusion as its predominant factor. In that regard, when wisdom is not strong, then the development does not bring about successive distinction.
Like food that is unpalatable to a person, it does not produce delight in the mind of the yogi; therefore, it becomes devoid of flavor. Likewise, through the practice of development... [properly]...
One does not find the bliss of tranquility through a practice that lacks the right path; for that reason as well, the mind becomes disinterested.
Therefore it was said: “Through dullness in the application of wisdom... [the mind] becomes disinterested.

To show the remedy for that—which consists in the arousal of a sense of urgency (*saṃvega*) and the arousal of confidence (*pasāda*)—he said: “The eight bases for the sense of urgency,” and so forth. Among these, birth, aging, sickness, and death...

Since beings exist in both happy destinies (*sugati*) and miserable destinies (*duggati*) according to their deserts, the suffering of the states of deprivation (*apāya*)—which is distinct from those [other forms of suffering] and caused by the fivefold bondages, hunger and thirst, mutual injury, and so forth—should be understood separately.
All of that [suffering] is taken as pertaining to the present existence of those various beings;
therefore, the sufferings rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) belonging to the past and future times are taken separately. As for those beings...

It should be understood that the eighth basis for spiritual urgency (*saṃvegavatthu*)—the suffering of the livelihood not shared with others, which consists in being dependent on food and dependent on the fruits of one’s exertion therein—is included here.
This is called "encouragement at the proper time" (*samaye sampahaṃsanatā*);
it refers to the method already stated for generating spiritual urgency at the time when the mind in meditation should be encouraged.

And "properly gladdening" means gladdening by way of producing confidence (*pasāda*), which is the act of satisfying through the production of confidence preceded by the arousal of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

"By resorting to right practice" means by resorting to the practice of cultivation that is truly right—that is, non-uneven—by way of the path of serenity (*samatha*) free from both laxity (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*).
In the phrases beginning with "not lax," it refers to the absence of excessive states belonging to the side of indolence (*kosajja*).

It is not sluggish; it is not agitated because the factors conducive to agitation are not excessive; and it is not dissatisfied because of the attainment of the bliss of tranquility through the perfection of the application of wisdom.
For that very reason, it proceeds evenly toward the object and has entered the path of serenity (*samatha*).

Alternatively, it proceeds evenly toward the object by virtue of being neither sluggish nor agitated, and it has entered the path of serenity by virtue of its lack of dissatisfaction. By means of this even proceeding...
Or rather, it should be understood as being neither sluggish nor restless, and not finding satisfaction in the course of practice for serenity (*samatha*).

In that regard, one does not exert effort in encouragement (*paggaha*) due to the absence of sluggishness, in restraint (*niggahe*) due to the absence of restlessness, or in gladdening (*sampahaṃsane*) due to the absence of dissatisfaction.
This is called "equanimity at the proper time" (*samaye ajjhupekkhanatā*); this refers to the cultivation of the mind at the time when it is to be looked upon with equanimity.
Equanimity is said to be the act of looking on with indifference after having overcome the opposing factor characterized by being occupied with the acts of encouraging, restraining, and gladdening.

Because it suppresses that opposing factor and because it serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā), even access concentration (upacāra-jjhāna) accomplishes the state of one who is concentrated by fulfilling the function of concentration;
thus, it is described there as being of equal weight [to the higher jhānas].
“Either access or absorption. This arises; that is, this concentration enlightenment factor (*samādhi-sambojjhaṅga*), when unarisen, arises.

Equanimity (*upekkhā*) as a state of neutrality is the cause of the equanimity enlightenment factor, because it is accomplished when that [neutrality] exists and not accomplished when it does not exist.
And that state of neutrality is twofold according to its object.

He said: "Equanimity toward beings and equanimity toward formations. Since conflict with both of these is already far removed by the cultivation of the tranquility enlightenment factor (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga*), the passage beginning with "equanimity toward beings" was stated in order to show the method for abandoning only that which is concordant [with it].
Therefore he said: "Avoidance of persons who are fond of beings and formations. For, specifically, regarding equanimity...
Lust is the opposite. Thus it is said: “Equanimity is the path of purification for one who has an abundance of lust.
“In two ways” means by these two reasons: reflection on the fact that one is the owner of one’s own kamma, and reflection on the emptiness of self.
The restriction “only in two” is for the purpose of showing the equality of the number; here only the number is the same, not the things numbered.
"In every respect the same": the state of being ownerless is the lack of self-ownership (*anattanīyatā*).

For if there were a self, then by virtue of its being something belonging to that self, the robe or anything else might be called "belonging to the self"; however, the intention is that no such thing exists at all.
"Not lasting" means not enduring for a journey; it does not remain for long, but is brief and impermanent—this is the meaning. "Temporary" is a synonym for that very same thing.
"Mamāyati" means he makes it "mine"; having grasped it with craving, he remains thinking, "It is mine. "Dhanāyanta" means making wealth their substance. 419.
"Characterized by right vision" means having the nature of seeing correctly and non-erroneously by way of impermanence and so forth.
"Characterized by right application" means having the nature of rightly directing the mind toward the object. Speech endowed with four factors [inspires] people...

It is called "embracing" (*saṅgaṇhāti*) because right speech, whose intrinsic nature is the abstention from its opposite, possesses the function of embracing both people and associated mental states by abandoning divisive wrong speech; thus it is said to have "the characteristic of embracing.
For, being the opposite of untruthfulness and so forth—which are harsh and non-embracing—it has the nature of embracing through its quality of being gentle.
Right speech has the characteristic of embracing (*pariggaha*), for it proceeds by embracing the people who receive well-spoken words as its conditions and the mental states associated with them.
Just as the activity of work (*kammanta*), consisting of the application of tasks such as robe-making,
gives rise to and accomplishes the robes, dyeing, and so forth that are to be done, so too does [right speech] produce each respective action.

Or, volition—known as the mental formation of action—gives rise to physical activity such as the movement of the hands. Thus, by abandoning wrong action which gives rise to blameworthy deeds that ought to be done, right action has the function of giving rise to blameless deeds that ought to be done in a blameless manner;
therefore it is said: "it has the characteristic of giving rise rightly. Alternatively, "giving rise" (*samuṭṭhāpana*) means the lifting up of associated states.
It is like the lifting of a burden through physical action.

"Having the characteristic of right purification" means that its characteristic is the thorough cleansing (*vodāpana*)—that is, the complete purifying—of the livelihood itself, or of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of a living person or of associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*).
Alternatively, it refers to the body, speech, and the continuum of the aggregates (*khandha-santāna*).

Right livelihood, through the abandoning of wrong livelihood which is a state of defilement, is said to have "the characteristic of purification. Regarding right effort, mindfulness, and concentration, what needs to be said has already been stated above.
Because wisdom is the forerunner of wholesome states, all unwholesome states are its opposites.
It is said: “Also together with other defilements that are its adversaries.

Alternatively, the defilements that are its adversaries—ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth—are those associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhekaṭṭhā*), because they are directly opposed to wisdom (*paññā*). It “sees” means it is as if seeing, due to the absence of obstruction.
Therefore he said: “Because of the non-obscuration of that... [etc. ...due to non-delusion. [This applies] to right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) and the others.

He says, “right intention and so forth... abandon,” because wrong intention and so forth are the direct opposites [of their counterparts]. By the phrase “just as before,” he brings forward this meaning:
that [they abandon] together with their own respective opposing defilements. “By way of distinction” means by way of the specific function attributed to right view.
“In this context” refers to these factors beginning with right intention.
“This is what is called right view” is said by combining both the mundane and the supramundane together, because they are not mixed [in this specific context].
Therefore he says, “In the prior stage,” and so forth. It has a single object because its object is Nibbāna.

It is so called “by way of function” because the task that was to be performed here by the knowledges of suffering and so forth in the prior stage has been accomplished here, or because the function of this very knowledge is the illumination of suffering and the other truths.

It receives four names because it accomplishes the four functions beginning with the full understanding of suffering (*dukkhapariññā*). It receives three names because it brings about the function of abandoning the intentions for sensual pleasure (*kāmasaṅkappa*) and so forth.
In the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*, it is stated: "The volition of abstinence (*viraticetanā*) and the states associated with it are the training precepts (*sikkhāpada*).
Therein, by way of the primary volitions of abstinence, he says: "They are both abstinences (*virati*) and volitions (*cetanā*), etc. "Right..."

Because the meaning [of the path] is possible through such statements as "he speaks with this," the three factors beginning with right speech are both abstinences (*virati*) and volitions (*cetanā*), etc.
At the time of refraining from false speech and so forth, they are abstinences; at the time of uttering well-spoken words and so forth, they should be understood as volitions and the like.

However, at the moment of the Path (*magga-khaṇa*), they are only abstinences, because they have attained the characteristic of the Path. For volition does not have the nature of deliverance (*niyyāna*). Now...
Just as a single knowledge possesses the nature of knowing suffering and so forth, and just as a single abstinence possesses the state of being an abstinence from false speech and so on,

so too, because a single volition— by its very nature of accomplishing the three functions of right speech and so forth— establishes the state of being right speech and the rest, it is said: "At the moment of the Path, there are only the abstinences."
"He acquires four names" means he acquires them by way of the four right endeavors (*sammappadhāna*) and the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

The connection is made by bringing in the phrase "at the moment of the path" (*maggakkhaṇe*). Even in the preliminary stage and even at the moment of the path, it is precisely right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*);
for although there are four jhānas by way of the applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth—namely, fixing, smoothing, gladdening, and intensifying—which are conducive to concentration.

Right concentration is analyzed [into four]; nevertheless, just like effort, it does not fulfill the fourfold function of effort—such as the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states—and just like mindfulness, it does not fulfill the fourfold function of mindfulness—characterized by the abandoning of perceptions of beauty and so forth regarding the body and other objects which are actually foul, painful, impermanent, and non-self.
Thus, a single concentration does not accomplish the functions of the four jhāna concentrations; therefore, even in the preliminary stage, there is the concentration of the first jhāna.
The meaning is that the first jhāna concentration [is present] even at the moment of the Path, and likewise the fourth jhāna concentration [is present] even in the prior stage;
indeed, the fourth jhāna concentration itself is present at the moment of the Path.
But is this the sequence of teaching for the factors of the Path merely because of their arrangement according to the order of speech, or rather—
In the investigation [of the phrase] "on account of some particularity," he says "of these" and so forth to show what that particularity is.
Therein, the great serviceability of right view consists in its being the fruit of cultivation, its attainment of an exceedingly sharp and clear state through a marvelous and extraordinary capacity,
its total destruction of opposing factors, and its awakening to the true nature of phenomena as they really are.
It should be understood. Therefore he said, "For this," and so forth.

"Of that" means of right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*). "A great help" means it is of great assistance in the penetration of the Dhamma. Now, in order to clarify that meaning by means of similes, he said, "Just as," and so forth.

Thought (*vitakka*) is the maker of the distinction in speech; it is also [the cause] of right speech (*sammā-vācā*), which has the mode of turning away from and engaging in faulty and faultless distinctions of speech.
"It is indeed a helper," he said: "This [right intention], ... pe ... is also a helper for right speech.
For right intention is a specific condition for both truthful speech and speech of abstinence, because it abandons wrong intention and the defilements associated with it.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "having arranged," "arranging rightly" refers to the purpose of one's work by means of entirely blameless verbal and bodily actions.
"It should be desired" should be understood as indicating both the planning by way of verbal expression and the actual application of the action of abstention.
For in this way, the great utility of right speech for right action is illuminated.
This is because the abstention from verbal misconduct, which governs vocal expression, is supportive of the abstention from bodily misconduct, which governs physical activity. Likewise...
For one who is not restrained from false speech, such as lying and the like, will certainly not refrain from wrong action either. As it is said:
"For one who has transgressed even a single factor... there is no evil that he would not do.

Therefore, one established in right speech, such as non-deception and so forth, necessarily fulfills right action as well; thus, abstention from verbal misconduct is an aid to abstention from bodily misconduct.

Since what is called purity of livelihood is preceded by the abandoning of immorality, it was stated—"but fourfold," and so on—in order to show that right livelihood was taught immediately after right speech and right action. "To this extent" means merely by means of pure virtue and livelihood.
"This energy" refers to the energy of the four right endeavors (*sammappadhāna*).
To show that even the arousal of energy brings about Nibbāna only when it is embraced by right mindfulness, and not otherwise, the words beginning with "thence" (tato) were spoken.
"Well-established" (sūpaṭṭhitā) means it should be made well-settled by abandoning outward distraction.
The factors conducive to concentration are the purification of the aforementioned objects and so forth; the non-conducive factors are those that are the opposites of these.
They should be understood. "Destinations" (*gatiyo*) means results or attainments. "Having thoroughly investigated" (*samanvesitvā*) means having sought correctly.
Just as talk concerning women is called "concerning women" (*adhitthī*), so too that which proceeds with reference to the self is "internal" (*ajjhattaṃ*).
It is with the underlying intention: "By proceeding in this way, we shall arrive at the grasping [of the notion] 'self'."
"Internal" means that which occurs with reference to or directed toward oneself, being included within the continuity of one's own existence. Regarding "internal form":

the meaning is the *kasiṇa*-form based on the physical matter of one's own head-hairs and so forth. In the phrase "perceiving internal form by way of preparation," it means perceiving internal form by way of performing the preliminary work (*parikamma*), not by way of absorption (*appanā*).
For absorption, which has the counterpart sign as its object, does not have the internal as its domain.
It is possible. However, that kasiṇa-sign obtained by means of internal preliminary work (*parikamma*) is indeed impure;
it is not pure like that obtained by means of external preliminary work. Therefore he said, "But that," and so forth.
"For whom such preliminary work has arisen internally" refers to that person for whom, in the manner described, [the sign] has arisen internally.

The preliminary work has been accomplished. As for the phrase "the sign externally": the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) is "external" because it does not belong to one's own continuity (*sasantati*).
"Limited" (*parittāni*) means they are just as much as were obtained, merely the size of a small stream; therefore he said, "unincreased.
"Only by way of the limited" means that even though there is attention (*ābhoga*) by way of color, this base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) is [achieved] only by way of the limited.
It is said that here, smallness (*parittatā*) is the cause for overcoming (*abhibhavana*). It is called "overcoming" (*abhibhu*) because it overcomes whether the beauty is present or not;
it refers either to the preliminary work (*parikamma*) or to knowledge (*ñāṇa*). That which has this as its sphere of overcoming is a "sphere of overcoming" (*abhibhāyatana*), namely, the jhāna.

Alternatively, it is a "sphere of overcoming" because it has as its sphere—that is, as its object—the thing to be overcome, which is designated as the objective field (*ārammaṇa*). Or else, it is so called because of the overcoming of the object.

That base and its sphere are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*) because they serve as the foundation for specific states of bliss for the meditator, and because they consist of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dhammāyatana*).
The cultivation of the bases of mastery occurs only for one of sharp wisdom, not for another;
thus he says, "a person whose excellence is knowledge. Having mastered them, he attains [them].
Here, both the mastery and the attainment [of the base] occur as the arising of absorption concentration immediately after the achievement of access concentration;

thus it is said: “Right with the arising of the sign, one reaches absorption here. And the phrase “right with the arising of the sign” is a characteristic statement for the absence of a preparatory period (*parivāsa*) for absorption.
Even for one who is called “one of quick direct knowledge,” the development of the bases of mastery belongs specifically to one of superior knowledge.
"In this" means in this sign (*nimitta*). "Brings it to absorption" means it leads it to the absorption of meditation (*bhāvanā-appanā*).

And here, some say: "When access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) has arisen, those two or three impulsion-moments (*javana-vāra*) that occur taking that as their object belong to the side of access concentration itself;
immediately after that, through the dwelling in the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-parivāsa*) and the cultivation of access, [absorption arises]."
And they say that absorption occurs without [the preliminary work], reaching absorption at the very moment the sign arises; but that is merely their own opinion.

For an absorption procedure is not intended by means of the duties of one on probation (*pārivāsika*), nor is retrospective reflection absolutely required in access concentration as it is in the sublime and measureless jhānas. Therefore, after the attainment of access concentration—
Reaching absorption at the conclusion of a few bhavaṅga moments, it is said that "one attains absorption right at the arising of the sign.
This statement, "right at the arising of the sign," is intentional (adhippāyika) and not of explicit meaning (nītattha);
the intention therein should be understood in the manner already stated. Within the attainment itself, there is no such mental application (ābhoga) at that time.

Because it is impossible [for that to occur]. It should be understood that for one who has emerged from attainment, the mental application (*ābhoga*) occurs by way of prior-stage cultivation, having grasped the mode of mastery (*abhibhavana-ākāra*) that occurred at the moment of the jhāna. However, in the *Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"By this, his prior application is explained. But since there is no such application within the attainment itself at that time, why is there still the perception of jhāna?
He said, "It is so stated because the perception of mastery exists even during the internal attainment.
"Increased in measure" means "of vast measure"; it does not mean they have been brought to an increase of one or two finger-breadths, for such an increase is impossible here.
Therefore he said, "Great. "The bowl increased with food."
The meaning is: food given after having increased it in the bowl while eating; or, half of the food that is to be eaten by a man at a single sitting.
