"Perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*) means perception of form; one who has that is "possessing the perception of form. One who does not possess the perception of form is "without the perception of form" (*arūpasaññī*).

He speaks of *jhāna* by way of its characteristic mark, which is perception. Here, non-arising of the perception of form itself is what is meant by "non-attainment. "Arising only externally" means arising only upon an external object.
arisen. And herein:
"Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally, limited, beautiful or ugly.
Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally, immeasurable, beautiful or ugly. Not perceiving forms internally..."
“He sees external forms, limited, beautiful or ugly. Not perceiving form internally, he sees external forms, immeasurable, beautiful or ugly.
Thus, here the four bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) are presented. In the Abhidhamma, however: “Not perceiving form internally, externally...”
“He sees forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly; he sees forms that are immeasurable, beautiful or ugly”—thus it is stated.
And the reason for this has already been explained in the *Abhidhamma-ṭṭhakathā*. For it is said in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:
“But why, then, is it not as in the Suttanta, where it says: ‘One percipient of internal forms sees external forms that are limited,’ and so forth?”
It has been said that, instead of saying it thus, here in all four bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) only the state of being "percipient of the formless internally" is mentioned.
This is because internal forms are not to be mastered. For whether there [in the first two] or here [in the latter two], it is only external forms that must be mastered;
therefore, those [external forms] must necessarily be stated.
Regarding that, it has been stated both there and here: “‘Perceiving forms internally’ and ‘not perceiving forms internally’—this, however, is merely a display of the Teacher’s teaching skill.
But this is the intended meaning here: one overcomes all limited forms, whether beautiful or ugly, both those accompanied by attention to color and those devoid of it.
For the teaching of the Suttanta is indeed an exposition given by way of a figurative method (pariyāya).

In the Abhidhamma, however, because it is a teaching in the direct sense (*nippariyāya*), they are stated separately as being devoid of the mental application of color (*vaṇṇābhoga*), and likewise when combined.

For there is a distinction in the manner of overcoming (*abhibhavana*) in both cases. Likewise, here, because it is a teaching in the indirect sense (*pariyāya*), there is also a way of speaking regarding the "overcoming" of the liberations (*vimokkha*);
thus, in the first and second bases of overcoming (*abhibhāyatana*), [the text says] "perceiving forms internally," and so forth.

The first liberation, the second liberation among the three and four bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*), and the third liberation among the bases of mastery are included by way of the attainment of mastery.

However, in the Abhidhamma, because it is a teaching according to the direct method (*nippariyāya-desanā*), the bases of mastery are explained separately from the liberations in order to teach them without confusion; thus, setting aside the liberations, the bases of mastery are discussed.
All the functions of liberation (vimokkha) pertaining to the jhānas have been explained in the teaching on liberation.

However, it is understood that a specific definition has been established for this because, although the two bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) beginning with "perceiving forms internally" are mentioned [in the Sutta], they are not included among the bases of mastery in the Abhidhamma;
whereas the expressions beginning with "possessing form, one sees forms" are common to all the functions of liberation. Thus, the distinction is made.

"Because internal forms are not to be overcome": this is the statement of the reason for the fact that nowhere in the Abhidhamma is it said, "he sees internal forms," but rather everywhere it is stated, "he sees external forms.
Therefore, whatever statement in the Suttas says, "he sees external forms" due to some other cause, that was spoken by virtue of this very reason.

However, as for the statement in the Abhidhamma that internal [form] is "without perception of form" (arūpasaññitā), which is caused by the elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsa*), it shows that no other reason need be sought for it.
Furthermore, the fact that internal forms are not overwhelmed is because they are not clearly manifest (*avibhūta*) in the way external forms are.
And this elegance of the teaching should be understood by way of the aforementioned definition (*vavatthāna*).
This is because one speaks by means of a mode of expression that exists [in reality] according to the disposition of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

Indeed, what is called the "elegance of teaching" (*desanāvilāsa*) is the manifestation of a mode of expression that exists and is appropriate to the disposition of those to be trained, and not just any [mode of expression whatsoever].

Therefore, the delimitation described in the passage beginning with "because here there is a teaching by way of a mode of expression" should be understood as being based upon this elegance of teaching.

If it is argued that the "bases of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*) such as blue and so forth need not be mentioned because they are already established by the phrase "beautiful and ugly colors," [the answer is:
No, because for those who have applied themselves to the practice regarding blue and so forth, it is precisely the state of being blue and so forth that is the cause of mastery.
For it is neither the limitedness nor the immeasurability of those pure or impure colors that is the cause of mastery; rather, it is indeed their very nature as blue and so forth. And among these...
In order to show which of these bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana) succeed for one of a particular temperament among the limited kasiṇa-forms, it is said:
"But among these... and so forth.
"By way of including all" means by way of the commonality of blue color, blue appearance, and blue luster. "By way of color" means...
By way of its natural color; by way of demonstration means by way of its being visible, that is, by way of its being graspable by the eye-consciousness process.
By way of radiance means by way of shining due to its luminosity. "Or from a color-element" refers to a color-element such as that of collyrium, silver, cloth, and so forth.
These are purely mundane because they consist of fine-material-sphere jhāna.

435. Regarding the term "possessing form" (*rūpī*): here, that form included within one's own continuity (*sasantatipariyāpanna*) by which this person is endowed is the distinguished form that serves as the cause for the meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
That very absorption, characterized by the form included within one's own continuity, is what is called "possessing form" by virtue of that distinguished form.
However, in this context, it is said—"internally, among the head-hairs, etc."—to establish the state of possessing form in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*).
“Rūpajjhānaṃ rūpaṃ” is stated by eliding the latter member of the compound, as in the case of expressions such as “rūpūpapatti.
“He is intent only on the beautiful” refers to this third liberation.

Having shown that here it is stated by way of jhāna on the kasiṇas of extremely pure blue and other colors, [the text] now demonstrates its occurrence in the Paṭisambhidāmagga by way of the jhānas of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra).
To show this, the passage beginning with “In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, however,” has been commenced.

However, since the divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) are already included here in the subsequent text, that method is set aside, and the liberation of the beautiful is authorized solely by way of the kasiṇas of pure blue and so forth. 443.
“Even on preparatory ground”: whether it be unprepared or prepared, even on preparatory ground consisting of a firm circle and so forth.

It should be understood that the name "earth kasiṇa" is applied to the learning-sign (uggahanimitta) and so forth by way of a metaphorical designation for the support, just as one says, "the beds are shouting.
"Virtues" (sīlāni) refers to the four virtues, beginning with the restraint of the Pātimokkha. "Having purified" means by not committing [an offense] and by restoring what has been committed.
And having purified it by not being oppressed by defilements. For there are three ways of purifying virtue:
non-transgression, restoration after transgression, and not being oppressed by defilements.

It is called a "hindrance" (*palibodha*)—the letter *r* having been changed to *l*—because it hinders, obstructs, and does not allow the cultivation of the meditation subject to proceed; the meaning is "obstacle. "Having cut off" means...

"Having restrained [the mind] by means of a grasp through meditative attainment (samāpatti), or by means of a support (saṅgāhaṇa)"; the meaning is "having made it free from obstacles. "Having approached a good friend (kalyāṇamitta)" refers to one who is:
"Dear, venerable, and worthy of esteem; one who speaks and is patient with what is said;
one who delivers profound discourse, yet does not urge one toward what is inappropriate."
Having approached a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta) who is endowed with such qualities as these, who is solely intent on one’s welfare, and who stands on the side of progress;
[one should avoid] an unsuitable dwelling—that is, one possessed of any one of the eighteen faults. For this has been said in the Commentaries:
“A large dwelling, a new dwelling, a dilapidated dwelling, and one by a road;”
A drinking vessel, a leaf, a flower, and fruit that has already ripened;
A city made of wood, a field with unsuitable soil,
and a port located on a frontier border where a friend cannot be found.
“Having understood these eighteen points, a wise person should avoid them from afar, just as one would a path full of dangers.
Regarding “suitable”: it is endowed with five factors, such as being neither too far from nor too close to the village used as a resort. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“And how, monks, is a lodging endowed with five factors?

Here, monks, a lodging is not too far and not too near, is well-suited for coming and going, has little crowding by day, and is quiet at night, with little noise, little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping creatures. And in that lodging...”
While he dwells there, robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick arise for him without difficulty.
Now, in that monastery, elder bhikkhus dwell who are learned, of inherited knowledge, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā.
Approaching them from time to time, he questions and interrogates them: "This..."

“Venerable sir, what is the meaning of this? Those venerable ones then reveal what was undisclosed to him, clarify what was not made clear, and dispel his doubt regarding various points that might give rise to uncertainty.
“In this way, monks, a lodging is endowed with five factors.”
And herein, "not too far, not too near, and well-situated for coming and going" constitutes one factor;
"little crowded by day, with little noise and little clamor at night" constitutes one; "free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping creatures" constitutes one;
"for one dwelling in that lodging... [as far as] requisites" constitutes one; and in that same [lodging]... [as far as].
"The elders [dwell] in the lodging... dispelling doubt"—thus the five factors are to be understood.

"Having cut off minor impediments" means: having cut off minor impediments by cutting one's long hair, nails, and body hair, and by cleaning the robes, dyeing the robes, boiling the alms-bowl, and tidying the bed, chair, and so forth.

"In regard to the bloated, etc."—here, by the word "etc.," the livid, the festering, the fissured, the gnawed, the scattered, the bloody, the worm-infested, and the skeletal [stages of decomposition] are included.

The inclusion [of this term] should be understood. In this context, it is "swollen" (*uddhumātaka*) because, like a bellows filled with air, it has become bloated by the gradual emergence of a state of putrefaction following the exhaustion of life;
or, it is "swollen" (*uddhumātaka*) because it is "swollen" (*uddhumāta*) in a contemptible sense due to its repulsiveness. This is a designation for such a corpse.
"Vinīla" means a disintegrated blue color; "vinīlaka" is simply that which is vinīla. Alternatively, because it is repulsive, it is "badly discolored," hence "vinīlaka.

This is a designation for a corpse whose flesh has swelled up and is red-colored in those places, white-colored in those places where pus has accumulated, and predominantly blue-colored in those places that are blue, like a body covered by a blue cloth.

In places that have broken open, the pus flows out and is putrid; "putrefied" (*vipubbaka*) means that which is putrid, or it is called "putrefied" because it is loathsome due to its state of being putrid.
This is a designation for such a corpse. "Torn apart" (*vicchidda*) refers to what has been split into two by cutting;
"torn apart" (*vicchiddaka*) means that which is torn apart, or [it is so called] because of its loathsomeness.
It is called *vicchiddaka* because it is cut apart (*vicchindati*) in a loathsome way; this is a designation for a corpse severed in the middle.
It is called *vikkhāyitaka* because it has been gnawed (*khāyita*) in various ways here and there by dogs, jackals, and the like;
or rather, it is called *vikkhāyitaka* because it is loathsome (*kucchita*) due to being gnawed (*vikkhāyita*), as it is repulsive. Of such a [corpse]...
This is a designation for the physical body (*chavasarīra*).
It is variously scattered and strewn; thus, being strewn, it is "the scattered" (*vikkhittaka*). Or, because it is loathsome, it is "the vilely scattered," hence "the scattered" (*vikkhittaka*).
[It is so called] because one hand is here, another foot there, and another head elsewhere—in this way, from that...
This is a designation for a scattered corpse. That which is both "struck" (hata) in the manner previously described and "scattered" (vikkhittaka) is called "struck-and-scattered" (hatavikkhittaka);
this is a designation for a scattered corpse whose limbs and members have been struck with a weapon in the shape of a crow's foot and then scattered according to the method already stated.
It is so called because it scatters (kirati), disperses, and trickles here and there as blood.
*Lohitaka* is a designation for a corpse smeared with trickling blood. *Puḷava* refers to maggots;
because it scatters maggots, it is called *puḷavaka*, which is a designation for a corpse filled with worms.
*Aṭṭhika* is simply bone, or it is called *aṭṭhika* because it is a repulsive or loathsome bone; this also applies to a skeleton.
This is a designation for even a single bone. Among these ten kinds of foulness, only the first jhāna arises, not the second and so on.
Therefore he said: "here, perception accompanied by the first jhāna.
For instance, on a river with turbulent waters and a swift current, a boat stands still only by the power of its rudder; it cannot be kept stationary without a rudder.
In the same way, because the object is weak, the mind remains one-pointed only through the power of applied thought (*vitakka*);
it cannot be established without applied thought. Therefore, only the first jhāna occurs here, not the second and so on.
And the weakness of the object here consists in its inability to establish the mind by means of its own repulsiveness.

In such expressions as “the tree is dead,” “the metal is dead,” and so forth, although the continuity of aggregates (khandhappabandha) upon which the designation “tree” and so on is based has not been severed, the conventional usage of the term “dead” based on the disappearance of greenness and other qualities is *saṃmutimaraṇa* (conventional death).

*Khaṇikamaraṇa* (momentary death) is the moment-by-moment dissolution of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*). *Samucchedamaraṇa* (death by total cutting off) refers to the complete cessation of the continuum of an Arahant.
Death is the state of annihilation; this is said by way of the development of insight (vipassanā).

However, in the development of the recollection of death (maraṇānussati), none of these three types is intended, because they do not serve as grounds for spiritual urgency (asaṃvega), they do not manifest clearly, and they are not common occurrences.
For in the recollection of death, what is intended as "death" is the cutting off of the continuity of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) as delimited by a single existence.

[It is so] because of its being a basis for spiritual urgency, because of its manifestation, and because of its abundance. Now, with reference to this very death, showing another alternative formulation, he said:
"Or [it has] the characteristics stated below," and so forth.
"In the division of what is eaten, drunk, etc. means in the division of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted; that is, in the classification of what is to be eaten, chewed, and tasted.

The meaning [of "edible"] is derived from the absence of any desire to express a distinction of time, as in the word "milk" (*duddha*). It is called "edible" (*kabaḷīkāra*) because it is made into mouthfuls;
it is called "nutriment" (*āhāra*) because it is taken in; thus, it is "edible nutriment" (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*) because it is both edible and nutriment.

This is stated by way of its physical basis (*vatthu*), for here it is specifically the nutriment together with its basis that is intended as the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*). As for that which has the characteristic of nutritive essence (*ojā*):

Food is called "food" because it brings in nutritive-essence octad materiality; however, that [type of food] is not intended here, because it is impossible for it to be apprehended in its repulsive aspect.
"The nine repulsives" refers to the nine repulsives by way of the repulsiveness of going, seeking, enjoyment, abode, cause, unripened fruit, and ripened fruit outflow.
As for the repulsiveness of smearing, since it is found among enjoyment and the others, it is not mentioned separately here.
It was not included; otherwise, one would have to say "the ten repulsives" along with it.

However, in the *Visuddhimagga*, although washing is found among the uses [of the body], it is specifically taken as a separate repulsive because it is particularly repulsive by way of its natural outcome (*nissanda*);
thus, the state of being repulsive is described in ten aspects.
"Perception that arises" means perception arising by way of grasping the aspect of repulsiveness.

This word "perception" (*saññā*) occurs in such contexts as "perception of forms," "perception of sounds," etc., where it refers to a phenomenon characterized by the act of perceiving; it occurs in such contexts as "perception of impermanence," "perception of suffering," etc., where it refers to insight (*vipassanā*);
and it occurs in such contexts as "the perception of a bloated corpse" or "the perception of a festering corpse," where these phenomena are synonymous.
In such passages as "Or is it not so?", it occurs in reference to serenity (*samatha*). Here, however, it should be understood in reference to the preparation for serenity.

The apprehension of the repulsive aspect in nutriment, or the access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) developed therefrom, is what is intended here by the term "perception of the repulsiveness of nutriment" (*āhāre paṭikūla-saññā*).
"Perception of disenchantment" (*ukkaṇṭhita-saññā*) means a perception that arises in the mode of becoming disenchanted. Regarding "perception of impermanence" (*anicca-saññā*): here, impermanence...
The five aggregates, by virtue of their state of arising, passing away, and change, or because they do not exist after having existed, are impermanent.

The perception that arises regarding those impermanent five aggregates as "impermanent," which grasps the characteristic of impermanence, is the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*). Therefore, he said: "of the five aggregates of clinging," and so forth.
Therein, "arising" (*udaya*) is the characteristic of manifestation, and "passing away" (*vaya*) is the characteristic of transformation.
Changeability is aging. By the apprehension of changeability in arising and passing away, he shows the characteristic of impermanence.
For it is because of the state of arising, passing away, and changeability that the pentad of aggregates is called "impermanent.

And that by whose intrinsic nature the pentad of aggregates is called "impermanent" is the characteristic of impermanence; for by means of that, it is characterized as "impermanent," and it is the characteristic of impermanence.

Because of a lack of attention to rise and fall, and because continuity is concealed, [the characteristic of impermanence] does not appear. However, once rise and fall have been discerned and continuity has been disrupted, the characteristic of impermanence appears according to its true nature.
For one who correctly observes rise and fall, there is no other state for phenomena occurring in a prior and subsequent sequence.
When the continuity [of the aggregates] has been dismantled through close observation, phenomena appear not in a state of connection, but rather in a state of disconnection like iron rods;
thus, the characteristic of impermanence becomes even more clearly manifest.
According to the statement, "That which is impermanent is suffering," that same pentad of aggregates is [seen as] suffering because it is constantly oppressed.
Suffering (dukkha) is the state of constant oppression; this is the characteristic of suffering. For this very reason it was said:

“In regard to the five aggregates which are impermanent… [he] develops perception. In this context, “oppression” means the state of being incessantly oppressed and afflicted by formations according to their determined arising and passing away.
And the characteristic of suffering consists in this constant oppression.
Because it is concealed by the postures (*iriyāpatha*), the characteristic of suffering does not appear when there is no attention (*amanasikāra*).

However, when one attends to the constant oppression [of the body] and the concealment of the suffering found within the postures is stripped away, the characteristic of suffering appears according to its true nature.
For indeed, because it is concealed by the postures, the characteristic of suffering [does not appear].
These postures appear; however, they become concealers of the constant affliction through non-attention.
For when pain arises in one posture, another posture acts as its concealer by dispelling that pain;
so it is with the others as well. But when the manner in which each of these postures is subject to its respective suffering is known as it truly is—
The state of those formations concealing suffering is said to be "uncovered" because it becomes evident that they are incessantly pierced by suffering.
Therefore, by reflecting on the constant oppression and uncovering the state of concealing suffering as it occurs in the postures,
the characteristic of suffering appears in its true nature.
“Because of the statement, ‘That which is suffering is non-self,’ that same pentad of aggregates is non-self due to the lack of mastery over it;
however, the mode of lacking mastery is the characteristic of non-self. Therefore he said, ‘In the sense of oppression,’ and so forth.
And the characteristic of non-self does not appear because it is concealed by a mass [of perception] due to the lack of attention to the resolution of the various elements. The various elements...

However, when one has analyzed [the aggregates] by separating them out, thinking, "The earth element is one thing, the water element is another," and so forth, and likewise, "Contact is one thing, feeling is another," and so forth—
thus performing a thorough analysis of the compact mass and breaking down both the compactness of the collection and the compactness of functions and objects—
the characteristic of non-self appears according to its true nature. For this [characteristic] exists among those things which mutually support one another...

When material and immaterial phenomena have arisen together, there is a "mass by aggregation" (*samūhaghanatā*) due to the unexamined tendencies of those who, through the adherence to a sense of unity, claim "this is mine.
Likewise, there is a "mass by function" (*kiccaghanatā*) when those various phenomena, despite having distinct functions and fixed natures, are grasped as one.
Similarly, although there is a distinction in the way objects are made the focus among phenomena that possess objects, they are [grasped] as one...
The density of the object being grasped, when it is seen after having been analyzed by knowledge into the four elements,
comes to dissolve like a lump of foam being rubbed with the hand; as these phenomena proceed according to their respective conditions,
they are seen to be merely phenomena, and the characteristic of non-self— defined as the state of lack of mastery— becomes more manifest.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Apara-accharāsaṅghāta is finished.
19. Commentary on the Chapter on Mindfulness Directed to the Body (Kāyagatāsati-vagga). 563.
“Pervaded by the mind” means suffused by consciousness. And the pervasion by consciousness occurs in two ways regarding the ocean.

He said: “Pervasion is twofold,” and so forth. “By the former meaning” refers to the meaning stated as “they partake of clear knowledge by way of association. “By the latter” refers to that stated as “they function within the portion of clear knowledge, within the category of clear knowledge.
Regarding the phrases “it leads to great spiritual urgency” and so on, there is this other method: because it makes known the intrinsic nature of the body as it truly is.
It leads to great urgency. "For the good" means for the sake of welfare pertaining to the present life and so forth. "For the security from bondage" means for the state of safety from the four bonds.
"For mindfulness and clear comprehension" means for non-separation from mindfulness in all circumstances and for the sevenfold clear comprehension.
"For the attainment of knowledge and vision" means for the realization of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). "For the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation" means...

[It is] for the purpose of making manifest the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*), the mind’s resolute intention (*cittassa adhimutti*), Nibbāna, and the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).

Regarding the sixteen terms beginning with "for the attainment of wisdom" (*paññāpaṭilābhāya*), among these, the four—namely, "for the attainment of wisdom," "for the increase of wisdom," "for the expansion of wisdom," and "for the abundance of wisdom"—are expressions of the state (*bhāva*) by way of wisdom;
the remaining twelve are [expressions] by way of the person (*puggala*).
These are terms expressing states. "Association with good persons" means attending upon good persons.
"Hearing the true Dhamma" means hearing the words of the true Dhamma that elucidate the practice of virtue and so forth in the presence of those good persons.
"Careful attention" means attending by way of skillful means through the investigation of the meaning of the teachings one has heard. "Practice in accordance with the Dhamma" means...
The practice of the path-dhamma consisting of virtue and so forth, which follows upon the supramundane dhamma.

"Of the six kinds of direct-knowledge" (*abhiññā*) means of the knowledge of supernormal powers, the divine ear, penetration of minds, recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

"Of the seventy-three kinds of knowledge" refers to those stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: "Wisdom regarding the application of the ear is knowledge consisting in what has been heard; having heard..."

[This refers to] the knowledges—both those shared with and those not shared with disciples—as defined in the discourse on knowledge beginning with, "Wisdom regarding restraint is knowledge consisting in virtue" (*sīlamaye ñāṇa*).
For among these seventy-three knowledges, sixty-seven knowledges, such as the knowledge consisting in what is heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*) and so forth, are shared with disciples. [The remaining six are:

"knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings," "knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies of beings," "knowledge of the Twin Miracle," and "knowledge of the attainment of Great Compassion."
“Knowledge, omniscient knowledge, unobstructed knowledge”—these six are the unique knowledges not shared with disciples.
Regarding the seventy-seven knowledges:
here—“The knowledge that ‘with birth as condition there is aging-and-death,’ and the knowledge that ‘in the absence of birth there is no aging-and-death. In the past also...”
The knowledge that "in the past, aging and death are conditioned by birth," and the knowledge that "in the absence of birth,
there is no aging and death"; the knowledge that "in the future, aging and death will be conditioned by birth," and the knowledge that "in the absence of birth, there will be no aging and death"—
even this knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, and subject to fading away.
Knowledge that [all things] are subject to cessation; knowledge that birth has existence as its condition …pe… knowledge that existence has clinging as its condition,
knowledge that clinging has craving as its condition, knowledge that craving has feeling as its condition, knowledge that feeling has contact as its condition,

knowledge that contact has the six sense bases as its condition, knowledge that the six sense bases have name-and-form as their condition, [knowledge that name-and-form has consciousness as its condition].

Knowledge that "this is name-and-form," knowledge that "consciousness has formations as its condition," knowledge that "formations have ignorance as their condition," knowledge that "when there is no ignorance,
there are no formations," knowledge that "in the past time too, formations had ignorance as their condition," knowledge that "when there was no ignorance,
there were no formations," and [knowledge that] "in the future time too, [formations will have ignorance as their condition]..."

"Knowledge that 'these are volitional formations,' knowledge that 'when ignorance is absent, volitional formations do not exist,' and also the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) that he possesses—
knowledge that even this is subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Thus, in the Nidāna Vagga,
the Blessed One spoke of seventy-seven knowledges by applying seven knowledges to each of the eleven factors of dependent origination, beginning with aging-and-death.

Therein, "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is knowledge of the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). For the mode of conditions is called the "stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhiti*) because it is the cause for the persistence of phenomena, which is to say their occurrence; knowledge therein is "knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
This is a designation for the sixfold knowledge described by such statements as "with birth as condition, aging-and-death [comes to be]. "Subject to destruction" (*khayadhamma*)...

"Subject to destruction" (*khayadhamma*) means having the nature of passing away. "Subject to vanishing" (*vayadhamma*) means having the nature of fading away. "Subject to dispassion" (*virāgadhamma*) means having the nature of becoming free from passion. "Subject to cessation" (*nirodhadhamma*) means having the nature of ceasing; this is the meaning.
Regarding the passage beginning with "gain" (*lābha*), "acquisition" (*paṭilābha*) is said by qualifying "gain" itself with a prefix. Furthermore, for the purpose of explaining its meaning:
“Attainment and achievement” is what is said. “Touching” means touching by way of realization. “Realization” means realization as acquisition.
“Full attainment” means bringing to completion. And regarding “the seven trainees”:
they are called trainees because they train in the three trainings; these are those designated as trainees, such as those standing on the path of stream-entry and so forth.

Of the seven. And of the "virtuous worldling" (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*): that is, of the worldling who is designated as "virtuous" (*kalyāṇa*) in the sense of being excellent because he is engaged in the practice leading to Nibbāna.
"Increasing the increase by one" means the growth of what has already increased.

This refers specifically to the growth of wisdom (*paññāvuddhi*) by way of the wisdom of the Arahant, out of all the eight kinds of wisdom mentioned above; likewise, for the expansion of wisdom (*paññāvepulla*).
The accomplishment of the function of any particular dharma that is especially appropriate should be understood as "great.

Demonstrating this accomplishment of its function, he said: "It grasps great meanings," and so forth. In this context, the greatness of meanings and the rest should be understood as their having a vast range;
and their vast range is according to the method set forth in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

It should be understood [in this way]. Furthermore, the greatness of the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) should be understood by way of its greatness as cause, its greatness as condition, its greatness as support, its greatness in classification, its greatness in function, its greatness in fruit, and its greatness in benefit.

In this context, the causes are non-greed and so forth. The conditions are moral shame (*hiri*), moral dread (*ottappa*), faith (*saddhā*), mindfulness (*sati*), energy (*viriya*), and so forth. The support is...

The fixedness [of destiny] regarding disciple-enlightenment (*sāvakabodhi*) and solitary-enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*), as well as the specific types of persons who possess them; their classification according to the divisions of conduct (*cāritta*), restraint (*vārita*), and so forth;

their function, which is the destruction of opposing factors by means of the "limbs" (*tadaṅga*) and other methods; their fruit, which is the attainment of heaven (*sagga*) and the attainment of Nibbāna;

and their benefits, such as being dear and agreeable—this is the summary here. For the detailed exposition, however, one should consult the *Visuddhimagga*, the *Ākaṅkheyya-sutta*, and other such texts.

And it should be understood according to the method already stated. By this same method, the greatness of the aggregate of concentration and the other aggregates should also be set forth after determining it appropriately for each.
Furthermore, the greatness of the "possible and impossible" (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*) and so forth should be understood by way of their vast range of objects.
In that regard, the vast range of objects of the possible and impossible is to be understood according to the method presented in such discourses as the *Bahudhātuka Sutta*.
The vast scope of the dwellings and attainments is to be understood by way of the method for determining the vast scope within the aggregate of concentration;
that of the Noble Truths by way of the method presented in the *Saccavibhaṅga* and its commentaries, as they encompass all vehicles;
that of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth by way of the method presented in the *Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga* and its commentaries and so forth; and that of the fruits of recluseship...
Because it brings about great benefit, great happiness, great welfare, and great security from bondage;

because it is peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, and to be realized by the wise; because the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) possess a great accumulation of requisites, a great objective range, a great function, great power, and a great fruition;
and because Nibbāna accomplishes great purposes such as the quelling of intoxication.
And its greatness should be understood. "Grasps" means it grasps by delimiting from its own nature and so forth;
the meaning is that it knows and penetrates.
Regarding "wide wisdom," the meaning here too should be understood according to the method already stated. However, this is the distinction: *puthu*...

“Knowledge proceeds with respect to the various aggregates” means that knowledge proceeds based on the differentiation of the five aggregates as follows: “This is called the aggregate of form... [and so on]... this is called the aggregate of consciousness. Even among those, the aggregate of form is of one kind...
[and so on]... the aggregate of form is of eleven kinds. The aggregate of feeling is of one kind... [and so on]... of many kinds.
The aggregate of feeling. The aggregate of perception by way of a single mode... [and so on] ...the aggregate of perception by way of many modes.
The aggregate of mental formations by way of a single mode... [and so on] ...the aggregate of mental formations by way of many modes.

The aggregate of consciousness by way of a single mode... [and so on] ...the aggregate of consciousness by way of many modes. Thus, for each aggregate, by way of its single mode and so forth, and also by way of the past and so forth.
Knowledge proceeds by depending on differentiation.
Regarding the phrase "in various elements": "This is called the eye-element... [and so on]... this is called the mind-consciousness-element.
Among these, sixteen elements belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), and two belong to the four planes. Thus, knowledge proceeds by depending on the differentiation among the elements.
It occurs. This is stated by way of the clung-to elements (*upādinnadhātu*).
For it is only with respect to the clung-to elements that the knowledge of Paccekabuddhas and the two Chief Disciples occurs regarding their differences;

and even that, moreover, only partially, not exhaustively. The differences among external, unclung-to elements (*anupādinnadhātu*) are outside their domain; this belongs to the Omniscient Buddhas alone.
However, it is said: "Because this element is predominant, the trunk of this tree is white; that is black; that is smooth;
that is rough; that has thick bark; that has thin bark. The leaf of this one is such-and-such in terms of color, shape, and so forth.
The flower of this one is blue, yellow, red, white, fragrant, foul-smelling, or of mixed fragrance."

Knowledge proceeds in dependence on the diversity of elements (dhātu), such as: fruit that is small, large, long, round, beautiful, ugly, smooth, rough, fragrant, foul-smelling, sweet, bitter, sour, pungent, or astringent;
or a thorn that is sharp, not sharp, straight, crooked, copper-colored, blue, red, or white. Thus knowledge arises by way of the variety of elements.

“Diverse in various bases” means that knowledge proceeds by way of the diversity of the bases (āyatana) as follows: “This is called the eye-base... pe... this is called the mental-object-base (dhammāyatana). Among these, ten bases belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), while two belong to all four planes.

“Diverse in various dependent originations” refers to the factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda-aṅga) which are manifoldly divided according to the distinction between internal and external, and according to the distinction of individual continua (santāna).
For each factor, beginning with ignorance (avijjā), is individually designated as “dependent origination. Therefore, he said:
In the *Saṅkhāra-piṭaka*, it is said: “Twelve conditions, twelve dependent originations.
“Various, diverse, empty, and unapprehendable” means: in various entities that are devoid of permanence, essence, and so forth; in entities that are empty by nature;
and for that very reason, in entities that cannot be apprehended as woman, man, self, belonging to a self, and so on. Here, the letter *ma* serves to join the words.

"Various in many meanings" refers to the various meanings such as the conditionally arisen (*paccayuppanna*) and so forth, which are the objects of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
"In phenomena" refers to the various phenomena such as the conditions (*paccaya*) and so forth, which are the objects of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).

"In expressions" refers to the various expressions consisting of definitive words used to determine those very same meanings and phenomena. "Various in many insights" refers to the objects of the analytical knowledge of meaning and the others.

Among the various kinds of knowledge that have received the name "insight" (*paṭibhāna*) because they arise as such-and-such an inspired flash or because they stand forth [clearly], there are these knowledges which illuminate this or that meaning.
In passages such as "in the various aggregates of virtue" (*puthu nānāsīlakkhandhesu*), the multiplicity and diversity of virtue have already been stated; as for the others...

However, because it is easily understood according to the method already stated, it is self-evident. As for the fact that Nibbāna is undivided and one alone, its plurality should be understood there by way of metaphorical designation;
thus he said: “Having transcended the various phenomena common to diverse people.
By this, its plurality is illustrated through such expressions as "the crushing of intoxication" and so forth.
"In vast matters" means in great matters; for the word *vipula* is a synonym for "great. Regarding "in profound [matters]":

just as the great ocean cannot be fathomed by crocodiles and the like, so too knowledge proceeds toward the aggregates (*khandha*) which cannot be reached by those who have not accumulated the equipment of knowledge (*ñāṇasambhāra*).
Thus, through the profundity of the object, the profundity of the knowledge is made manifest.
Because it is uncommon due to qualities such as its sharpness, pungency, and nature, it is not within reach of the wisdom of others; rather, it is "far, far away" (*suvidūravīdūra*).
By shortening the vowel *ā* in *asamantapaññā*, it becomes *asamantapaññā*. Some read it as “*asamatthapaññā*” (wisdom that is incapable); for them, the construction is:

because it is uncommon to others through the aforementioned qualities and so forth, there is no other [wisdom] capable of reaching it, thus it is “incapable wisdom” (*asamatthā paññā*). From the determination of the meaning (*atthavavatthānato*):
Because of the definitive determination of the various categories of meaning as they truly are, no one else is able to "attain" it—that is, no one else is able to reach the range of such knowledge;
therefore, this is "far-far-seeing" (*suvidūravidūra*), meaning wisdom that is not universal.
Now, in order to clarify "non-universal wisdom" (*asamantapaññā*) by way of different types of persons, the passage beginning with "of the virtuous worldling" (*puthujjanakalyāṇakassa*) is commenced.

“Skilled in the distinctions of wisdom, possessing penetrative knowledge, having attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), endowed with the four grounds of self-confidence, bearing the ten powers,
a bull among men, a lion among men, an elephant among men, a thoroughbred among men, a stallion among men, possessed of infinite knowledge, infinite majesty, and infinite fame;
wealthy, of great riches, powerful, a leader, a guide, one who leads others, one who makes things known, one who causes others to understand, one who looks upon all.”
He is one who inspires confidence. For that Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path;
he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path.
And his disciples now dwell following that path, having subsequently attained it.
“For indeed the Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he has become vision, become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma;
he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata.
There is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, unrealized, or untouched by wisdom to that Blessed One. Regarding the past and the future...”
Based on the present, all phenomena in every aspect come within the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Whatever is called "knowable" exists—all that must be known—whether it be for one’s own benefit, for the benefit of others, or for the benefit of both;
whether it be a benefit pertaining to the present life or a benefit pertaining to future lives; whether it be a shallow meaning or a profound meaning.

Whether it be a hidden meaning, a concealed meaning, a meaning that requires further interpretation, a definitive meaning, a blameless meaning, a meaning free from defilement, a purified meaning, or the ultimate meaning—all of that revolves within the Buddha’s knowledge.
“Every bodily action of the Buddha, the Blessed One, follows after his knowledge; every verbal action of the Buddha... [follows after his knowledge].”
The Blessed One’s mental activity follows after his knowledge; all mental action of the Buddha, the Blessed One, follows after his knowledge.

The Blessed Buddha’s knowledge is unimpeded regarding the past, the Blessed Buddha’s knowledge is unimpeded regarding the future, and the Blessed Buddha’s knowledge is unimpeded regarding the present; as far as there is anything to be known, so far extends his knowledge.
Knowledge. To the extent that there is knowledge, to that extent there is the knowable. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit.
Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, nor is there a path for the knowable beyond knowledge.
These two phenomena stand as mutual limits, just like two covers of a casket that fit together perfectly.
The lower lid of the casket does not overpass the upper lid, and the upper lid does not overpass the lower lid;
they stand with their limits meeting one another. Even so, the range of the Buddha, the Blessed One, and his knowledge stand with their limits meeting one another.
As far as the range extends, so far extends the knowledge; as far as the knowledge extends, so far extends the range.
The knowable is bounded by knowledge, and knowledge is bounded by the knowable.
Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, nor is there a path of the knowable beyond knowledge. These phenomena stand as mutual limits.
The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, proceeds regarding all phenomena.
“All phenomena are dependent upon the advertence, the desire, the attention, and the arising of consciousness of the Buddha, the Blessed One;
the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, operates regarding all beings.
The Buddha knows the disposition of all beings, he knows their underlying tendencies, he knows their conduct, and he knows their inclinations.”

He understands all beings— those with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust in their eyes, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those of good disposition and those of bad disposition, those easy to instruct and those difficult to instruct—
as well as those who are capable; the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans,
revolves within the range of a Buddha’s knowledge.
“Just as whatever fish and turtles there are, even including the *timitimiṅgala*, revolve within the great ocean,
even so does the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its gods and humans, revolve within the Buddha’s knowledge. Just as whatever winged creatures there are, even including the *garuḷa* Venateyya, [revolve] in the sky...”
Just as they move about within a small portion [of space], even so those who are equal to Sāriputta in wisdom move about within a mere fraction of the Buddha’s knowledge.
The Buddha’s knowledge stands having pervaded and surpassed the wisdom of gods and humans.
And as for those wise kṣatriyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise ascetics—those who are subtle and skilled in the doctrines of others—[they too are surpassed].

“Skilled in discerning wisdom, with fathomless knowledge... [omitting intermediate text] ...having formulated question after question,” he said, showing by way of an abbreviated formula (*peyyālamukhena*) the canonical passage (*pāḷi*) pointed out by such expressions as: “They move about, as it were, piercing through the positions of views (*diṭṭhigata*) with the range of their wisdom, like those who pierce a hair-tuft, having formulated question after question.”

In this context, "one whose knowledge has become differentiated" (*pabhinnañāṇo*) means one whose knowledge has reached differentiation regarding the meaning and so forth. They also read it as "one whose knowledge is of differentiation" (*pabhedañāṇo*), which has the same meaning.
"Those questions" (*te pañhe*) refers to those various questions intended by himself. "With the reasons demonstrated" (*niddiṭṭhakāraṇā*) means with the reasons having been answered.
"Those who have been cast near" (*upakkhittakā*) means that the disciples (*antevāsikā*) become those who have been cast near by the Blessed One’s analytical wisdom (*paññāveyyattiyena*).

It is called *bhūri* because it "becomes" (*bhavati*) or "overcomes" (*abhibhavati*). What does it overcome? Lust and the rest. Even though there is a prefix (*upasagga*), that same word expresses that meaning;
thus, even without the prefix, that meaning is to be understood, because verbal roots have multiple meanings.

Therefore, it is said: "it overcomes" (*abhibhuyyati*). This is stated according to the sequence of grammatical cases (*kāraka-vyattaya*); therefore, by itself, that specific path-wisdom overcomes lust.
One overcomes and masters the passion that deserves to be slain by oneself; the meaning is that one intoxicates [with wisdom].
"Overcomes" means that each respective wisdom of fruition (phala-paññā) crushes, overcomes, and tramples upon each corresponding passion; thus she is "one of vast wisdom" (bhūri-paññā).
Alternatively, the reading is "the conqueror" (abhibhavitā), though some also read "having conquered" (abhibhavitvā). The phrase "having conquered" shows the completion of the action. Wisdom.
This being established, the overcoming of lust is also established; the same method applies to the remaining [defilements] as well.
Among lust and the others, lust has the characteristic of coloring; hatred has the characteristic of hating; delusion has the characteristic of being deluded.

Anger has the characteristic of being angry; resentment has the characteristic of persistent ill-will. Anger occurs at an earlier time, while resentment occurs at a later time. [Malice] has the characteristic of smearing over the virtues of others.

Deceit (*makkha*) has the characteristic of grasping at a pair; flattery (*palāsa*) has the characteristic of [seeking favor]. Envy (*issā*) has the characteristic of disparaging the success of others; avarice (*macchariya*) has the characteristic of concealing one’s own success.
Guile (*māyā*) has the characteristic of hiding the evil committed by oneself; craftiness (*sāṭheyya*) has the characteristic of proclaiming qualities that one does not possess.
Obstinacy (*thambha*) has the characteristic of inflation of the mind; contentiousness (*sārambha*) has the characteristic of seeking superiority in action.
Conceit has the characteristic of loftiness; overweening conceit has the characteristic of excessive loftiness. Intoxication has the characteristic of a state of being intoxicated;

negligence has the characteristic of the mind’s relinquishment toward the five strands of sensual pleasure. It is called *bhūri* because it "becomes" (*bhavati*) and "overcomes" (*abhibhavati*) the enemy (*ari*);
here, by means of a dissimilar form (*asarūpato*), the letter *a* of the word *ari* is elided. Therefore he said: “Wisdom that crushes the enemy is ‘vast wisdom’ (*bhūripaññā*). Herein, it becomes...

“Bhūri” (vast) is said to refer to the earth as it is called “bhūmi” (the ground); thus, “vast wisdom” (*bhūripaññā*) is so called in the sense of being extensive and wide, and because it endures everything.
Therefore he said: “By that,” and so forth. In this context, “equal to the earth” means equal to the earth precisely in the sense of being extensive and wide.
“Extensive” means extensive regarding the objects to be known, not restricted to a single part.
“Vipulāya” means “exalted. “Samannāgato” refers to a person. The word “iti” has the sense of a reason;
thus, the meaning is that because the person is endowed with vast wisdom (bhūripaññā) by this reason, his wisdom is called “vast wisdom.

While it would have been more grammatically precise to say “the wisdom of one who possesses vast wisdom is ‘vast-wisdom-wisdom’,” the word *paññā* has been elided once, and it is therefore stated as “vast wisdom” (*bhūripaññā*).
The phrase "And also" (apica) is stated for the purpose of showing another method of explaining wisdom (*paññā*). "This is wisdom" (*paññāyamatam etan*) means this belongs to wisdom.

"Designation" (*adhivacana*) means a superior expression. "Vast" (*bhūrī*): it delights in objects such as the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth that have come to be (*bhūta*) by way of their true nature;

it is not non-existent like a false view, thus it is "vast. "Intelligence" (*medhā*): it crushes and destroys defilements (*kilesa*) like a thunderbolt (*asani*) strikes a mountain peak; thus it is "intelligence," being swift.

Or, *medhā* is so called in the sense of grasping and retaining. It is a "guide" (*pariṇāyikā*) because it guides that being in whom it arises toward the practice for one's own welfare and toward the penetration of the true characteristics of phenomena as they actually are; thus it is a guide.
These, and others as well, are synonyms for wisdom (*paññā*).
“Abundance of wisdom” (*paññābāhulla*) means one who has much wisdom (*paññābahula*); the state of being such is “abundance of wisdom.
And since that abundance of wisdom is simply its occurrence, in order to show this meaning by way of a person for whom wisdom is weighty, he said:

“Here, a certain person is one for whom wisdom is weighty,” and so forth. In that context, “a certain person here” refers to a noble person (*ariya*), specifically a virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*).

Or: one for whom wisdom (*paññā*) is heavy is "one who values wisdom" (*paññāgaruka*). One who has practiced or proceeded by means of wisdom is "one who practices wisdom" (*paññācarita*); or, one whose practice and activity are wisdom is "one who practices wisdom.

One for whom wisdom—consisting of the divisions such as conformable patience (*anulomikakhanti*) and so forth—is the underlying disposition (*āsaya*) is "one whose disposition is wisdom" (*paññāsayo*).
One who is intent upon wisdom and inclined toward it is "one intent on wisdom" (*paññādhimutta*). Wisdom is a banner (*dhaja*) in the sense of being raised high.

"Of this" refers to one for whom wisdom is the banner. "Wisdom as a crest" is a synonym for that same thing. One for whom wisdom is the sign and the governing principle is "one who has wisdom as his governing principle.
One for whom investigation—which is synonymous with wisdom—or the frequent discernment of the specific nature of phenomena, is predominant, is "one who abounds in investigation.
One for whom the frequent discernment of the specific nature of phenomena in its various modes is predominant is "one who abounds in thorough investigation."
One for whom the appearance of phenomena as they truly are (*okkhāyana*) occurs frequently is "one who frequently appears" (*okkhāyanabahula*).
Rightly observing each phenomenon with wisdom is "clear vision" (*sampekkhā*); the movement or proceeding of clear vision is "the course of clear vision" (*sampekkhāyana*);

one whose nature or characteristic (*dhamma-pakati*) is this course of clear vision is "one whose nature is the course of clear vision" (*sampekkhāyanadhamma*). Or alternatively, the course of clear vision as it truly is...

That which has the nature of seeing as its intrinsic characteristic is "that which has the nature of looking on" (*sampekkhāyanadhammo*). One whose habit is to dwell having made all categories of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) manifest and clearly discerned is "one who dwells in manifestation" (*vibhūtavihārī*).

In the phrases beginning with "one whose conduct is that" (*taccarito*), the word "that" (*taṃ*) refers back to wisdom (*paññā*); therefore, in those instances, it is expressed as "one whose conduct is wisdom" (*paññācarito*), and so forth.
The meaning should be understood as follows: "One for whom that wisdom is practiced, honored, and frequent" means one who is characterized by it, who honors it, and who is frequent in its practice.
"One who is inclined toward, bent toward, leaning toward, and intent upon that wisdom" means one who is directed toward it, inclined toward it, leaning toward it, and resolved upon it.
"That wisdom is the dominant factor; having come from that dominance, one is 'dominated by it' (tadādhipateyya). [This applies to] the terms "one who honors wisdom," and so forth.
In passages such as, “He knows one who indulges in sensual pleasures [only] that ‘this person values renunciation’,” these matters are stated from the perspective of previous births.

Phrases such as “because of his conduct” are stated with reference to this present birth. Now, in order to show the very same point by way of illustration, the words beginning with “just as” are spoken.
The words beginning with “in exactly this way” constitute the conclusion of what has been demonstrated.
“Swift wisdom” (*sīghapaññā*) is wisdom that functions swiftly within its own domain;
when undertaken, it accomplishes its own task of wisdom quickly, without being sluggish or dilatory. Therefore he said: “He fulfills the precepts very swiftly,” and so forth.
In this context, the phrase “very swiftly” (*sīghaṃ sīghaṃ*) is stated twice for the purpose of including the many virtues such as the precepts and others. Regarding “the precepts” (*sīlāni*):
The morality of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is prescribed by way of both positive conduct (*cāritta*) and prohibitive restraint (*vāritta*).
Alternatively, setting aside the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) because it is taken separately, there are the other three types of morality.

"Restraint of the sense faculties" means the warding off and closing of the six faculties—the eye and so forth—by means of the bolt of mindfulness, without allowing passion or aversion to enter. "Moderation in eating" means...
The state of knowing the proper measure in food by way of consuming it with reflection. Regarding "application to wakefulness" (*jāgariyānuyoga*):
one is awake and does not sleep during the three periods of the day and during the first and middle periods of the night;

one performs only the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). Thus, one is "awake" (*jāgara*). The state of being awake, or the activity of being awake, is "wakefulness" (*jāgariya*). Application to that wakefulness is "application to wakefulness."
That application to wakefulness. The aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) refers to the aggregate of virtue of those in training (sekha) or those beyond training (asekha).

The other aggregates should be understood in the same way. The aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha) consists of both the mundane wisdom of those in training and those beyond training, as well as the wisdom of the Path (magga-paññā).

The aggregate of liberation (vimuttikkhandha) is the liberation of the fruit (phala-vimutti). The aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha) is the knowledge of review (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa).
The description of quick wisdom (*lahupaññā*) is exactly like the description of swift wisdom (*sīghapaññā*), and likewise is the description of joyful wisdom (*hāsapaññā*).
However, the description of impulsive wisdom (*javanapaññā*) proceeds by way of the method of comprehension by groups (*kalāpasammasana*).

The description of sharp wisdom (*tikkhapaññā*) proceeds by way of the intensification of energy (*vīriya*), while the description of penetrative wisdom (*nibbedhikapaññā*) proceeds by way of the perception of non-delight in the entire world (*anabhiratasaññā*). In that context, "urgent action" (*turitakiriyā*)...
Swiftness (*sīghatā*). Unslowness is lightness (*lahutā*). Impulsiveness is quickness (*khippatā*). "Abounding in laughter" means abounding in joy (*pīti*).
The remaining terms are synonyms for that same state. Alternatively, "abounding in laughter" is the root term;
"abounding in rapture" is the explanatory term referring to the feeling of mental pleasure associated with that very joy. "Abounding in contentment" (*tuṭṭhi*)...
"By means of moderately strong rapture" refers to the state of being uplifted by moderately strong rapture. "Abounding in gladness" refers to the state of being gladdened by strong rapture.
"He fulfills the precepts" means that, being joyful, exceedingly joyful, elated, and full of affection, he accomplishes the precepts.
For wisdom accompanied by rapture and joy proceeds as if blooming and blossoming upon the object through its delight; it does not proceed in this way when accompanied by equanimity.
"It swiftly impels [the mind] toward impermanence" means that it proceeds with momentum, thinking "the pentad of aggregates is impermanent.

Because the previous volitional formations have become exceptionally powerful due to the removal of their opposites, it penetrates the characteristic of impermanence with speed—like a thunderbolt hurled by Indra—without missing its mark, without faltering, and without delay;
therefore, the meaning is that it is called "impelling wisdom" (*javana-paññā*).

The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Having thus shown impulsive wisdom by way of insight having the characteristics as its object, the passage beginning with “form” is stated in order to show it by way of powerful insight.
Therein, “in the sense of destruction” means that because it has the nature of destruction, it breaks up right where it arises. “In the sense of terror” means because of its terrifying nature.
"By way of being pithless" means by way of being devoid of a core consisting of a self, and by way of being devoid of a core such as permanence.

"Having weighed" means having weighed with the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*), which serves as a scale. "Having scrutinized" means having scrutinized with that very same [wisdom] which serves as a scrutiny.

"Having analyzed" means having made manifest by disclosing it according to reality. Alternatively, "having weighed" means having weighed by means of the comprehension of aggregates (*kalāpa-sammasana*).

"Having scrutinized" means having scrutinized by way of contemplating rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*). "Having made manifest" means having made it clear by way of contemplating dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*) and so forth.
"Having made it evident" means having made it pervasive by way of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and conformity (*anuloma*).

"In the cessation of form" means in Nibbāna, which is the cessation of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). "It runs swiftly" means it runs by way of being inclined, sloping, and leaning toward it.
It proceeds. Now, in order to show the wisdom of impulsion (*javana-paññā*) by way of insight that has reached its culmination, it is said again, beginning with "form.
Since the sharpness of knowledge is to be understood specifically through the thorough eradication of its opposites, it is stated:

"Wisdom that quickly cuts off defilements is 'sharp wisdom' (*tikkha-paññā*). Having said this, and wishing to demonstrate those defilements by way of their classification, [it says]: "When arisen..."

He said, “sensual thought,” and so forth. Although [such thoughts] have been abandoned by means of suppression through serenity (*samatha*) and by means of its constituent factor through insight (*vipassanā*), because they have not been uprooted by the Noble Path and have not transcended the nature of arising, they are called “arisen in an unuprooted state. That is what is intended here by the term “arisen.
“Does not tolerate” means he does not allow them to take root in his mental continuum. “Abandons” means by way of total eradication.
He abandons. "He dispels" means he casts away. "He makes it vanish" means he makes it reach its end. "He brings it to non-existence" means he causes it to go to non-existence;
the meaning is that by means of the sequence of insight (vipassanā), having reached the Noble Path, he brings it to non-existence through total eradication.
And herein, thought associated with sensual desire is "thought of sensual desire. [The thought] "May these beings die"—this is [thought of ill will].
Thought associated with the death of others is a thought of ill will (*byāpādavitakka*).

The thought associated with the harming of others, thinking, “May these beings be harmed,” is a thought of cruelty (*vihiṃsāvitakka*). “Evil” means base. “Unwholesome states” means states produced by lack of skill.
One of sharp wisdom is one who possesses swift direct knowledge, and his path does not waver; thus he said: “In one...”
“On the seat, there are the four noble paths,” and so forth.

The penetration of the truths is accomplished through seeing things as they truly are: “All conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) are impermanent, suffering, subject to change, conditioned, dependently arisen, and subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.”
To show penetrative wisdom by way of its cause, it is said: “He is full of urgency regarding all formations,” and so forth.

In this context, “full of urgency” means that he frequently experiences a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) toward all formations by way of the method beginning with “All formations are impermanent.
“Full of trepidation” means that his mind is repeatedly terrified toward all formations due to the fear induced by knowledge.

By this, he speaks of the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*). "Abounding in weariness" means abounding in weariness due to being directed toward the unconditioned (*visaṅkhāra*) beyond conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
By this, he speaks of the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*). With the phrase "abounding in dissatisfaction," etc., he describes its successive arising.
"Outward-facing" means having the face of knowledge directed toward Nibbāna, which lies outside all conditioned phenomena; likewise, it has the face of liberation as it thus proceeds.

Penetration (*nibbijjhana*), piercing through (*paṭivijjhana*), and breaking through (*nibbedha*)—that which possesses these is "penetrative" (*nibbedhikā*). Or, that by which one penetrates is "penetrative";
that very wisdom is "penetrative wisdom. "Never before pierced" means never before pierced by reaching the end within the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
"Never before shattered" is a synonym for the same, by way of bringing about its final end.
The meaning is "not previously crushed. "Lobhakkhandha" means a mass of greed, or a portion of greed.
The commentary on the Chapter on Mindfulness Directed to the Body is finished.
20. Commentary on the Chapter on the Deathless (Amatavagga).
600–611. *Amata* means that which is not subject to death or destruction; thus it is called *nibbāna*. Therefore, it is said: "They enjoy *nibbāna*, which is free from death.

Alternatively, because it is the cause for attaining the deathless *nibbāna*, and because it partakes in a happiness similar to the deathless and is free from affliction, mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) is called "the deathless" (*amata*). "They enjoy" means they utilize it by entering into the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
"Failed" (*viraddha*) means it has been missed due to non-attainment. Therefore he said: "What is failed is not attained.
"Commenced" (*āraddha*) means accomplished or brought to completion. And since that is called "complete," he said: "What is commenced is complete.
Regarding "they were negligent" (*pamādiṃsu*), he said: "they are being negligent" (*pamajjanti*), because this is stated in terms of temporal sequence.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Immortal (Amatavagga) is finished.
Thus ends the Elucidation of the Unexplained Points in the Commentary on the Single-Verse Section (Ekakanipāta) of the Manorathapūraṇī, the sub-commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
The first part is finished.
